A fun, but slightly glitchy/laggy shoot&loot. Fair, easy to get into, not badly pay to win, and easy to play with friends. Progression is gradual and never leaves you starved for things to do, and the class system is fun and easy to grasp. Imagine Runescape with guns. The translations are pretty bad, but the game is legible and the quests are self-explainatory enough that it doesn't take away from anything. Lots of variety and weapons, fun customization options. The quests do start to feel a lot of the same after a while, but the gameplay is fluid enough that it'll keep your attention longer than a lot of other free to plays.
Pros
+Easy to understand, easy to grasp, easy to follow
+Dungeons, missions and lengthy story
+Fun to explore, maps are varied
+Not pay to win
+Small download, easy to run on most computers
+Looting is fun and rewarding, you never feel like you can't get your hands on something you want
+Good customization and weapons list.
Cons
-Bad translation, feels like the dev threw it in google translate and called it done.
-Quests can get repititive.
-Sometimes glitchy, many enemies on screen at once generates copious lag in some places.
VERDICT: 8/10

Awful combat, mediocre graphics even for its time and incredibly limited exploration are not enough to drag this game down. So for anybody planning to play this make sure you can push through the middle section of the game because the later parts are worth it. It is also worth playing as an introduction to the Witcher series.

The graphics are dated, but the art style is gorgeous.

The combat is more rhythmic than skill-based - to attack something, you click it. If you're lucky, you can click it a second time, and if you're good, you get to click it a third time. Maybe even a fourth.
Despite its flaws, I love this game. Best dollar I've spent in a while.

This is my all time favorite rpg and one of my favorite games period.  It and Oblivian set the standard for what a good rpg should have.  It is open world with a rich story and has so many side quests you need a guide to even find them all.  You have the freedom to play your character however you want but there could consequences for the actions you take.  There are lots of factions to join all with their own story lines.  You want to be a battlemage or a spell thief? Well you can build and play your character however you want without a strict class system.  The graphics are a bit dated now but the game is still well worth playing!

Morrowind has long been one of the best of the best.  What makes it so are the setting and the freedom.  I got into the franchise with Skyrim, but Morrowind is truly its pinnacle.  Sad to say we are unlikely to see anything like it as long as the corporate higher-ups at Bethesda see the Skyrim model as a safer bet.  Sure, Skyrim is prettier, and many people prefer its combat, but it just can't do as much, not even with mods.
Really, I think what turns most people off the combat system isn't that it's based somewhat in RNG, it's that it's based somewhat in RNG but there's no animations showing what happened, leading to ridiculous situations where people go "I stabbed that rat in the face at point blank range and missed!" rather than "It dodged again?!  I guess rats are really fast..."  I think the latter is enough more immersive that many people would be able to ignore it...so long as they know WHY they're missing (usually low fatigue because they're running everywhere).  While there doesn't seem to be a mod to accomplish this now, when the open-source engine OpenMW hits version 1.0 and a full release, this kind of mod should be entirely possible, among a host of other options, such as natively working on Linux.  (As of this review, OpenMW is on version 0.40 -- perfectly playable, but somewhat buggy and doesn't work with all mods.)  There are, however, mods to make the combat like that in Skyrim and Oblivion -- I recommend the mod Oblivion-like Combat, which, as far as I know, is still only found on the official Bethesda forums.
Finding mods for Morrowind can take a bit more searching than it does for Skyrim.  Skyrim mods are mostly consolidated on the Nexus, with a few exceptions.  Morrowind mods on the Nexus are few and far between.  Most are found on Morrowind Modding History, Great House Fliggerty, or the personal websites of the authors.  MMH in particular is an archive for all the mods formerly hosted on sites like Planet Elder Scrolls and ElricM which have gone down over the years.  You can find some truly impressive and interesting stuff there and the quantity swamps the Nexus, with almost four times as many mods uploaded.  Between GFH, MMH, the Nexus and all the other small sites out there hosting a handful of mods, I'm pretty sure there are more Morrowind mods available for download than Skyrim, and they're capable of affecting a lot more.  Much of what's hardcoded in Skyrim's engine is able to be altered in Morrowind's, and because of the way the engine processes them as well as the scripting language used, scripts are both safer to use and more versatile.  Beyond that, for things that ARE hardcoded, we have external utilities like the Morrowind Code Patch to make the changes we need, in addition to the script extender and others.
The other enormous advantage Morrowind has over its sequels is its setting, which is strange, and alien, and very good at telling a story through the world itself.  Morrowind is also where most of the series' interesting lore comes from.  If you don't know how anyone can care about TES lore and haven't played Morrowind, that's probably why.  One of their major writers for the game has written stuff that makes it look like he can't possibly be sober, and yet it somehow works.  If you don't know what I'm talking about, look up Michael Kirkbride.  The man is some strange variety of storytelling genius, even if he doesn't appear to be at first glance.
Other majorly good things about Morrowind include its main quest, which is probably the highest-quality out of the series  (by a very long way if you're only comparing it to Skyrim, and a bit less if you also include Oblivion).  There's just something special about getting dropped on Vvardenfell with not a coin to your name and no idea what you're doing or why you're there, and working your way up to godlike power so you can face down a terrible threat to all of Tamriel...Or is he?  Delve into the lore and the backstories, and you find it's not all so cut-and-dry.  Are those who would see the armies arrayed in secret shrines and ancient ruins destroyed truly your friends, or did Dagoth Ur have the right of it the whole time?  You may need mods to actually side with the seemingly crazed living god, but even without them, you can see that he may not actually be the villain all the citizens of Morrowind are making him out to be.  That ambiguity makes for a fascinating main story, and unlike the later games, it's paced very well for an open-world game, because your foe is a schemer.  He's incredibly dangerous, but you never know how imminent that danger is.  There's no false sense of urgency; instead, there's a sense of inevitability about impending doom if you don't act.  You can leave the main quest completely alone in favor of side quests for hundeds of hours right in the middle and go back to it afterwards and it still feels like it makes sense in-game.
The guild quests have no overarching story, but their self-contained stories are generally interesting, and it's far less immersion-breaking to become the head of every major faction because A) you need the skills that faction cares about to ever be promoted anywhere near that high, and B) as the Nerevarine, you are a uniter of squabbling factions against the threat from Red Mountain, and so it makes some sense to have you leading numerous guilds that would otherwise oppose each other when you need to make arch enemies cooperate in the face of a common threat.
The side quests are also quite good, all of them hand-placed and written with care.  None of those stupid strings of radiant dungeon-delving quests we got in Skyrim.  Also, remember all those little pieces of DLC made for Oblivion and sold for a few bucks each?  Remember Horse Armor?  Well, Morrowind has a few of those as well, but they're completely FREE.  Nothing as stupid as horse armor, either.  Instead, you get small but good dungeon mods, short but decent quest mods, item mods with and without quests attached, and small immersion increases, and none of them cost you a penny.  They are also all excellent, and generally recommended, except where you can find versions you prefer made by the community around ideas they got from the official version.
Finally, I would be most remiss not to mention the magic system.  There are all sorts of crazy things you can do.  Enchanting is also much more versatile than in Oblivion, let alone Skyrim.  On-use magic items are something that Oblivion did away with completely, but in Morrowind, you could use a ring to summon creatures, or an amulet to shoot fireballs.  Enchanting weapons with constant effects is gone in the later games as well.  Beyond that, people of a particularly diabolical mindset have been known to enchant robes with constant effect damage health and place them on NPCs they want to see die, and on-use items allow you to get powerful effects that would be beyond overpowered if they were constant, either at the level you get them or at all.  Furthermore, no TES game since has had anywhere near the diversity of magic effects found in Morrowind.  Spells having a chance of failure if you try to cast ones that are too powerful is also something that makes sense to me as a lover of fantasy and an effective self-balancing mechanism.  Yeah, you could try to cast that enormous fireball, and if it hit, everything you're after would die...but it only has a 55% chance of succeeding, and would drain most of your magicka to boot.  Maybe try something safer?  This means there's no hard skill checks, no magic number at which you suddenly get access to spells you couldn't cast before.  If you have enough magicka and are willing to take the chance of failure given, you can try any spell you can think of.  You might have to increase your skill for it to be worth the risk in the heat of battle, but trying new things in the middle of combat has always been a dangerous move in any case.  But it could pay off...

A game similar to Gundam's old fashioned combat arcade and Strike Suit Zero's dogfighting, which came out as a pretty good dogfighting humanoid game.
Pros:
1. An interesting twist of using humanoid machines as the fighting machine instead of fighters
This gives out more possibilities in manueovers as you can go in different directions and avoid missiles/projectiles, which is usually impossible in other dogfight games that lacks backward motion.
2. Super fast paced combat game
Compared to other similar dogfighting games, this game has the fastest pace I've ever seen as the velocity of everything (including your own mech) is super high.
3. Homages to other mecha series
Some said this game is like Armored core (unfortunately I did not play that game so I can't be sure), and I'm certain that I've heard a Gundam reference about 3 times the speed somewhere, a nice little touch.
4. Low requirements
Despite the nature of the game even a weak laptop can run this game smoothly most of the time, given that there aren't many flying objects in the screen as this game doesn't eat a lot of ram.
5. Short and to point mission briefing and voice records
The mission briefing gives a pretty nicely made cutscene (in 3D) which states most things that you will need to know. The records can be heard or not to be heard, which does not affect gameplay but good for players who wanted to know the story more. This is a nice touch as it balances both gameplay and story in a nice blend.
Cons:
1. Speed might be a little bit too high
Sure this is the sell point of the game, but the game is sometimes too high that you can't actually see what is happening and you're just like fire fire fire fire all your missiles and boom. Especially painful if you are playing in a tight area as you are way too fast to be controlled comfortably.
2. Mech designs and movements are too crude
Although the railguns/missile pods do activate correctly which is pretty nice, the fact that the Mechs' movement is slightly too plain which harms the visual experience. Adding the fact that humanoid machines are counter-productive for aerial combat, the designers should try and make aerial machines more aerial-like (such as Strike Gundam which needs the Aile to fly in extended periods of time), instead of just some mechs that thrust around in the air. However I'm no pro so that's up to the designers.
3. Voice actors are not too good
Mirai's voice actor doesn't sound like her avatar shown in the pic. Apart from that, the voice actors are a bit too bland similar to Strike Suit Zero who suffered from similar issues (which is understandable because of the lack of voice actors). Apart from that, during the start of a mission or some important part of the story (such as the part where the pilot switches from the M1 to the M3) should also have some cinematics, which is lacking the the game.

Don't go in expecting any sort of depth on par with other mech combat games. There really isn't any strategy here, just lock on and shoot. There's only 3 situations where you have to move:
1) Forward. Because you're not close enough to lock on.
2) Left and right, rarely backwards. Because something outdamages you.
3) Somewhere, because tiny things behind god knows how many obstacles.
You can hit F to never take damage from missiles, too.
The projectiles are god awfully slow and there's no way for you or the enemy to hit anything other than locking on, unless you wanna struggle with melee. The problem with locking on is that any change in trajectory after the projectile is fired is a miss. This goes for both you and the enemy. However, the enemy will not actively dodge. You can A/D+Space for godmode.
So how does this differ from games like Armored Core?
Because in AC, you have significantly less room to outright spam your mobility. Boosting around a lot will leave you empty and vulnerable. In PN however, even if you run out of booster (somehow.), if you're far enough back, the enemy will still miss from normal movement.
AC had limited ammo, and in the later games, different damage types. This means you have to conserve, and make sure you're using the right weapons on the right enemies. Or pack a sword, which, felt much more clean to use, however, drains your energy upon use. PN you can just fire everything as they reload. Nothing is being wasted, you're just clearing faster. And none of the enemies seemed any different from each other. They were too small to notice any visual difference, and the only seemingly functional differences were the speed their healthbar depletes, and whether or not I need to press F. Thankfully, the speed of healthbar depletion means nothing, it'll be dead when it's dead, and the game constantly reminds me of when I need to press F.
Press F to pay respects.

The Fall is labeled a Side Scroller, Action and those are things I really enjoy. But before those labels it's first called an Adventure game and I really don't like most adventure games. This game follows the formula of most adventure games: search out obscure objects for your inventory then try them out on every point of interest in the game until you get frustrated and have to look up a guide.
I'm not a fan of the inventory that has to be utilized by trial and error method of gameplay. I'm also not a fan of using my controller, which you must do to even play this game. Then the controller has you holding down 2 and 3 buttons at a time just to try inventory on objects. If the inventory piece doesn't work you have to hold the buttons all down again, aim it just right, and try again. Also not all objects in the game are interactive. And some objects only appear after certain requirements are met. As well, the game does not tell you the objects have appeared or anything has changed. Plus, many times you will need to go from point A to B except you have to discover and finish point XYZDTG first. Those objectives are not on the way from A to B; so you have to guess at where and what you're supposed to be doing and never sure if you're right or wrong.
Basically if you love games that make you go over a level with a fine tooth comb, do 1 thing after trying 3 dozen combinations of things, and then having to go back over the same level with a fine tooth comb again to see if something changed... Well my friend, this is your game. Otherwise stay away.

Some kind of Steam bug caused my hours played to not log when I first played through this game. It's about 7-10 hours long, if I remember correctly.
Anyway, I think it's worth noting right up front that this is- essentially- a POINT AND CLICK ADVENTURE game (although you technically do not point and click the mouse, it definitely FEELS like that's the genre). From looking at it, I don't think that's apparent. I certainly didn't. I got it because I didn't know it was. I generally dislike those kinds of games. And yet I ended up rather enjoying this one.
Why? Because it doesn't rely on bad humor and pop culture references; it tries to take itself seriously and be original. Although there are humorous moments. They come from character interaction rather than forced silliness. Also, I'm a sucker for stories with zero interaction from human characters. The story is a bunch of AI's arguing with each other, all trapped in their different kinds of programming. It's great.
The gunplay is passable. I don't think it's meant to be a draw, though. It's just there to add gameplay variety and instill tension via the knowledge that you can be shot and killed.
There's also MOSTLY a lack of those infamous way-too-obtuse "puzzles" you find in point and click games. There is still one of those instances in this game (the "crying baby" puzzle), but I find a proper game makes you use your brain to solve its problems rather than just "click everything" or "drag everything onto everything."

- This review considers only the main game without any DLCs or Mods -
Very good game, if you are willing to invest time.
You start off as a simple vagabond after a short questionnaire for traditional character creation.
You get a first task you can use to make your startining money, serving also as a nice tutorial replacement.
After that, you are pretty much left on your own, so the learning curve is pretty steep at the beginning. Reading a Guide right after your first missions from the local merchant is a good idea.
Once you get into the swing of things, you will find tons of possibilities.
The two main roads are a) joining one of the various factions (all which own unit types and upgrades, however you are always free to recruit troops from anywhere, with their spefic skillsets) or b) stay independent getting your missions from commoners, or by serving as a Mercenary on a contract. Additionally, there is a alternative main quest, in which you support a rival candidate to the throne of one of the Kingdoms. However, that quest line usually leads to you joining the Leader you helped in his claim, since building your rep is one of more time-consuming aspects of the game.
All in all,  this game keeps you entertained as long as you can set yourself new goals. You'll have to define them for yourself... the game won't be feedining you quests and carefully guide you along the main storyline so you don't miss anything. You'll have to get creative and ambitious, but can squeeze months of fun out of the game if you do.
Controls are straightforward and intuitive. Good 50-50 in the accessibility vs detail department.
Graphics are obviously dated, but suffice for good gameplay along with the decent damage models. Battles are a good mix of battlefield strategy and straight bloodbathing, but won't allow you too much detail (as evidenced by lack of a battlefield map).
I see only three weaknesses:
1. Travelling is a pain in the neck, since there is no quick travel / time compression option and travels are generally a fairly dull affair here. Crossing the entire World Map with an average sized group will take you multiple minutes, so sometimes you will find yourself travelling around the map for 10-15 minutes, only to run some minor errands. Also movement of other units on the world map seem quite random at times and coordination issues make chases or finding people very annoying.
2. Menu-design definetely is a problem. Most commonly used options are easily accessible, but others (talking to town elder / guild master, buying cattle) require you to enter the town, ride in on your horse, find the person and talk to them personally, since that particular option is only available in the conversation, but not the city window like most other options.
3. Repetitiveness can be an issue sometimes, and the above mentioned issues make some minor sidequests too time-consuming for the reward.
Play this game if you enjoy a good balance between complexity, creativity and action, while not being afraid the occasional "grind".
Avoid this game if you prefer constant action and clear instructions on what you can / should do next (i.e. Mass Effect, GTA).

Ok, that review sucks, doesn't it? You still know nothing about what the game does and why I like it. However, the whole "Fable" part is quite important. You see, the game oozes the fairy tale atmosphere. It manages to be a fable in the form of a game. Everything, from character design to writing to you being the hero makes clear that this is an interactive fable.
Aren't you the hero in pretty much every RPG out there? Well, sure you are. But no game ravels in this the way Fable does. You are renown, the game revolves around that. Case in example: Trophies aren't (just) for you to look at. They're to run around with, showing off to everyone in vicinity. They're to brag about, to beat your personal highscore of how many people you've showed your trophy in the face of. I am a well-renown little devil.
Speaking of the devil, the game has an excellent cartoonish/fairy tale depiction of good vs. evil. Instead of helping a ghost of a dead sailor helping his wife, you can just as well kill her. That makes the ghost disappear, solving the overall quest (getting rid of the ghost), and you get bad karma points. Those aren't just points! My dude has bright red horns, blue veins over the white face, red glowing eyes and he oozes an eery red mist. The best cartoonish evil depicion since Overlord!
What else is there to say? Well, the game offers what you're used to from RPGs. You have stats, you have equipment including upgradable weapons, you can have a bard sing of your deeds, you have magic if you want to use it. The RPG aspects aren't ground-breaking, but solid. If you're into the whole fairy tale atmosphere and want to be the hero with a holy halo or devil's horns, Fable got your back.

Morrowind has long been one of the best of the best.  What makes it so are the setting and the freedom.  I got into the franchise with Skyrim, but Morrowind is truly its pinnacle.  Sad to say we are unlikely to see anything like it as long as the corporate higher-ups at Bethesda see the Skyrim model as a safer bet.  Sure, Skyrim is prettier, and many people prefer its combat, but it just can't do as much, not even with mods.
Really, I think what turns most people off the combat system isn't that it's based somewhat in RNG, it's that it's based somewhat in RNG but there's no animations showing what happened, leading to ridiculous situations where people go "I stabbed that rat in the face at point blank range and missed!" rather than "It dodged again?!  I guess rats are really fast..."  I think the latter is enough more immersive that many people would be able to ignore it...so long as they know WHY they're missing (usually low fatigue because they're running everywhere).  While there doesn't seem to be a mod to accomplish this now, when the open-source engine OpenMW hits version 1.0 and a full release, this kind of mod should be entirely possible, among a host of other options, such as natively working on Linux.  (As of this review, OpenMW is on version 0.40 -- perfectly playable, but somewhat buggy and doesn't work with all mods.)  There are, however, mods to make the combat like that in Skyrim and Oblivion -- I recommend the mod Oblivion-like Combat, which, as far as I know, is still only found on the official Bethesda forums.
Finding mods for Morrowind can take a bit more searching than it does for Skyrim.  Skyrim mods are mostly consolidated on the Nexus, with a few exceptions.  Morrowind mods on the Nexus are few and far between.  Most are found on Morrowind Modding History, Great House Fliggerty, or the personal websites of the authors.  MMH in particular is an archive for all the mods formerly hosted on sites like Planet Elder Scrolls and ElricM which have gone down over the years.  You can find some truly impressive and interesting stuff there and the quantity swamps the Nexus, with almost four times as many mods uploaded.  Between GFH, MMH, the Nexus and all the other small sites out there hosting a handful of mods, I'm pretty sure there are more Morrowind mods available for download than Skyrim, and they're capable of affecting a lot more.  Much of what's hardcoded in Skyrim's engine is able to be altered in Morrowind's, and because of the way the engine processes them as well as the scripting language used, scripts are both safer to use and more versatile.  Beyond that, for things that ARE hardcoded, we have external utilities like the Morrowind Code Patch to make the changes we need, in addition to the script extender and others.
The other enormous advantage Morrowind has over its sequels is its setting, which is strange, and alien, and very good at telling a story through the world itself.  Morrowind is also where most of the series' interesting lore comes from.  If you don't know how anyone can care about TES lore and haven't played Morrowind, that's probably why.  One of their major writers for the game has written stuff that makes it look like he can't possibly be sober, and yet it somehow works.  If you don't know what I'm talking about, look up Michael Kirkbride.  The man is some strange variety of storytelling genius, even if he doesn't appear to be at first glance.
Other majorly good things about Morrowind include its main quest, which is probably the highest-quality out of the series  (by a very long way if you're only comparing it to Skyrim, and a bit less if you also include Oblivion).  There's just something special about getting dropped on Vvardenfell with not a coin to your name and no idea what you're doing or why you're there, and working your way up to godlike power so you can face down a terrible threat to all of Tamriel...Or is he?  Delve into the lore and the backstories, and you find it's not all so cut-and-dry.  Are those who would see the armies arrayed in secret shrines and ancient ruins destroyed truly your friends, or did Dagoth Ur have the right of it the whole time?  You may need mods to actually side with the seemingly crazed living god, but even without them, you can see that he may not actually be the villain all the citizens of Morrowind are making him out to be.  That ambiguity makes for a fascinating main story, and unlike the later games, it's paced very well for an open-world game, because your foe is a schemer.  He's incredibly dangerous, but you never know how imminent that danger is.  There's no false sense of urgency; instead, there's a sense of inevitability about impending doom if you don't act.  You can leave the main quest completely alone in favor of side quests for hundeds of hours right in the middle and go back to it afterwards and it still feels like it makes sense in-game.
The guild quests have no overarching story, but their self-contained stories are generally interesting, and it's far less immersion-breaking to become the head of every major faction because A) you need the skills that faction cares about to ever be promoted anywhere near that high, and B) as the Nerevarine, you are a uniter of squabbling factions against the threat from Red Mountain, and so it makes some sense to have you leading numerous guilds that would otherwise oppose each other when you need to make arch enemies cooperate in the face of a common threat.
The side quests are also quite good, all of them hand-placed and written with care.  None of those stupid strings of radiant dungeon-delving quests we got in Skyrim.  Also, remember all those little pieces of DLC made for Oblivion and sold for a few bucks each?  Remember Horse Armor?  Well, Morrowind has a few of those as well, but they're completely FREE.  Nothing as stupid as horse armor, either.  Instead, you get small but good dungeon mods, short but decent quest mods, item mods with and without quests attached, and small immersion increases, and none of them cost you a penny.  They are also all excellent, and generally recommended, except where you can find versions you prefer made by the community around ideas they got from the official version.
Finally, I would be most remiss not to mention the magic system.  There are all sorts of crazy things you can do.  Enchanting is also much more versatile than in Oblivion, let alone Skyrim.  On-use magic items are something that Oblivion did away with completely, but in Morrowind, you could use a ring to summon creatures, or an amulet to shoot fireballs.  Enchanting weapons with constant effects is gone in the later games as well.  Beyond that, people of a particularly diabolical mindset have been known to enchant robes with constant effect damage health and place them on NPCs they want to see die, and on-use items allow you to get powerful effects that would be beyond overpowered if they were constant, either at the level you get them or at all.  Furthermore, no TES game since has had anywhere near the diversity of magic effects found in Morrowind.  Spells having a chance of failure if you try to cast ones that are too powerful is also something that makes sense to me as a lover of fantasy and an effective self-balancing mechanism.  Yeah, you could try to cast that enormous fireball, and if it hit, everything you're after would die...but it only has a 55% chance of succeeding, and would drain most of your magicka to boot.  Maybe try something safer?  This means there's no hard skill checks, no magic number at which you suddenly get access to spells you couldn't cast before.  If you have enough magicka and are willing to take the chance of failure given, you can try any spell you can think of.  You might have to increase your skill for it to be worth the risk in the heat of battle, but trying new things in the middle of combat has always been a dangerous move in any case.  But it could pay off...

The Fall is a new and interesting way of rethinking Isaac Asimov 3 laws of robotics. In this game you play as the robotic AI A.R.I.D. who's human pilot has been critically injured and needs to go to the medical bay immediately. Unfortunately you crashed into a mostly run down recycling plant for haywire AI's and you must pass multiple tests to make your way up to the medical bay. Along the way you encounter the hostile caretaker bot who seeks to destroy you because he says that you are malfunctioning. You also meet the helpful but law abiding AI Administrator who is friendly towards you and lets you go through the loopholes to get the caretaker away from killing you.
The Fall's story is very compelling and thought provoking by how it utilizes the personalities of AI's to personify the robots and gives them a soul. The story focuses on what happens to a rogue AI in three different ways: the self aware and self conscience Administrator who finds every loophole in his rules, the rogue caretaker who kills malfunctioning robots and humans alike, and the buggy ARID who erases her own logs to justify her actions. The end of the game leaves you on a cliff hanger and also serves to make you question what a robot can do without any directives.
The music and dark art style capture the essence of the story perfectly and build upon the overall direction of the game. While being dark and having a suspenseful score the game does not shout horror, rather the game uses the darkness to highlight ARID in the dystopian future that she belongs to.
Sadly, the gameplay and mechanics are flawed. The game seems to be better suited for a point and click adventure instead of a sidescroller shooter. The aiming is finicky and the combat seems forced. Trying to find something hidden is a pain and quickly interacting with it is nearly impossible. While the story has great pacing the gameplay itself is bumpy, going from a fast puzzle to a slow and methodical one makes the game seem rushed. While the puzzles were all great the execution was flawed and it ultimately brings this game down.
What The Fall lacks in gameplay and mechanics it makes up for it with its story and presentation. Overall this game gets a 69/100

The game is exactly what it says on the tin: A fable. </review>
Ok, that review sucks, doesn't it? You still know nothing about what the game does and why I like it. However, the whole "Fable" part is quite important. You see, the game oozes the fairy tale atmosphere. It manages to be a fable in the form of a game. Everything, from character design to writing to you being the hero makes clear that this is an interactive fable.
Aren't you the hero in pretty much every RPG out there? Well, sure you are. But no game ravels in this the way Fable does. You are renown, the game revolves around that. Case in example: Trophies aren't (just) for you to look at. They're to run around with, showing off to everyone in vicinity. They're to brag about, to beat your personal highscore of how many people you've showed your trophy in the face of. I am a well-renown little devil.
Speaking of the devil, the game has an excellent cartoonish/fairy tale depiction of good vs. evil. Instead of helping a ghost of a dead sailor helping his wife, you can just as well kill her. That makes the ghost disappear, solving the overall quest (getting rid of the ghost), and you get bad karma points. Those aren't just points! My dude has bright red horns, blue veins over the white face, red glowing eyes and he oozes an eery red mist. The best cartoonish evil depicion since Overlord!
What else is there to say? Well, the game offers what you're used to from RPGs. You have stats, you have equipment including upgradable weapons, you can have a bard sing of your deeds, you have magic if you want to use it. The RPG aspects aren't ground-breaking, but solid. If you're into the whole fairy tale atmosphere and want to be the hero with a holy halo or devil's horns, Fable got your back.

It’s hard for me to say this, but I can’t recommend The Impossible Game for PC.
Gameplay wise, it’s not that bad; after all, this was the style of game that inspired Geometry Dash. Also, don’t get me wrong, it can be addictive; when I got this game on my iPod touch back in 2011 I was playing the heck out of it.
However, there is very little replay value as there are only four levels, and although there is a level editor, there is no easy way to browse and play levels that other people have made.
The main reason I’m not recommending this game is because of how poorly optimised this game is for PC – the game constantly freezes on some frames and skips some frames, making it borderline unplayable for me to play it.
So in closing, if you’re looking for a game like this that has much more levels, a lot more elements to it, a fantastic soundtrack and spectacular visuals, get Geometry Dash instead (Not to mention – it is cheaper!)
But if you really want to get the Impossible Game, get it on Xbox or a mobile device as it is a fraction of the price and runs so much better.

A truely amazing experience.
'Superflight' is one of those titles that you stumble on which then go on to become a staple of you daily consumption.
early on, it's clear that each map is unique and every one promotes a sense of exploration (to the point it's really difficult to have a 'safe run' - you may start out with the calmest intentions, but those gaps are sooo very inviting)
The sense of risk/reward is foremost in your mind whilst playing and for the strong minded there is a game of two beautiful extremes (a score chasing daredevil session or a meditative, Zen like experience) both have their place, but I find I am best served when I utilise a composite of the two styles.
The seed system deserves mention: Within the 'Maps' option, you can type a word/sentence to generate a unique map which also allows you to share them with other people. Any currently loaded map can be saved too, allowing convenient access to the many fantastic maps you will discover while in flight.
On paper, it all sounds very simple and unimpressive, but it really is more than the sum of it's parts.
I strongly recommend 'Superflight' without reservation, it's a really well put together package, with a simply beautiful asthetic, glorious sound design, tight controls and unlimited enviroments to discover, explore (and share)

After finishing up to act three, I feel comfortable giving my opinion on this crazy game
Pros:
-Flying is so much fun fun. This game has a crazy sense of speed but not in a way that makes me feel like I can't control it
-So is shooting. Its pretty heavily reliant on lock on, but against faster enemies just keeping them in range of that and on your screen can be enough of a challenge
-Good cockpit interface. Despite all the missiles and enemy and allied mechs and whatever eyes that can be flying across the screen, the game does a good job of laying out what's what without making it impossible to fly into buildings
-You haven't lived until you've fired about 50 missiles at once and watched the glory of all those blue and red lines turning your foes into fireworks
-Soundtrack. While it doesn't vary too much, what they do have is absolutely excellent and I love it
-Cool mech design. Prequisite to even bother playing a mecha game
Cons:
-Some game mechanics aren't very clearly explained.
-The graphics are only ok, but apparently more than a few people have had problems with it. I don't mind so much, especially since this is a smaller studio making, but its definitely not AAA beauty on your screen
-Story. Its like there's the skeleton of a good story being but together, but its all very haphazard right now. Especially at the start where it basically feels like there's not actually a story
-The voice acting is incredibly hit or miss. There are a few good eggs (lookin at you Mirai and Russian commander/lt.) but almost all the non-main characters read their lines stilted, definitely not a pro job. Weird pauses between line readings don't help, and if you complete objectives too fast the lines can overlap
But overall the positives far outweigh the negatives for me! There's really nothing else out there right now that has the same high speed mech combat, and there's a wonderful kind of joy that can only be had by filling the air with a trillion missiles while doing your best not to be filled with holes by a sky-full of enemy mechs. And despite putting it under con I still like some of the characters and story, so I'll be glad to see how it ends. Good fun, 7/10 even in its early access state.

It's available all the time, you just have to unlock it first by playing a mini-game. Machinarium is rather short, it takes about seven hours to finish it without using hints or about three hours if you play for the second time and know exactly what to do. Is it worth it? Absolutely. I would say that for this price you won't get a more charming game than Machinarium. I have good memories with this game. Reminds me a little of Stanisław Lem's book, "The Cyberiad". Rotieer is a tilt maze, but with horizontal movement. I don't think that's been done before, which is why it was on my wishlist.
While I only played the game for 4 minutes, the experience was unbearable and had enough bugs to make this game "definitely not worth your money".
1. Player movement is extremely slow. We're definitely talking "turtle speed" here, in comparison to how fast the player drops due to gravity.
2. Stars and other items (even the exit!) can only be collected when standing on solid ground, making some stars uncollectable (and I'd hazard a guess at "some levels unbeatable") as well.
3. A lives mechanic in a puzzle game?! No thank you.
Three counter-puzzle-experience drawbacks in the first 4 minutes; is it any wonder why I would consider this an insult to the whole puzzle genre? Definitely don't buy this. Hell, at this point, I'd have to ask the developer to pay me money to keep me playing (under the guise of "bug-testing").
A lesson to you, developers: Make sure your game's actually designed right. Don't just release your game and forget about it; listen to the feedback of the community (or hire some playtesters to make sure the game is alright!). I could certainly wait, at least, if the developer showed any signs of listening to feedback, but given that this game's been out for a whole year and it's still this buggy, I don't think the developer even remembers that he made this.
I'd refund this, but like
, I had bought the game long before I had started playing it, during one of Steam's many sales. Still, even
is worse than this, because this game actually starts off with puzzles. Just not very good ones.
All in all, a piece of garbage that deserves NO money.
EDIT: It looks like Steam actually requires you to play the game for 5 minutes before you can review it. Amazing. I literally have to slog through more of this game just to tell people that it's junk. My previous comment about the developer having to pay me to play it no longer stands for the next minute I need to play the game.

Awesome sandbox game that sometimes feels a bit repetative. I feel I must repeat Sandbox, after a brief (15 min) tutorial, the game dumps you right into the meat and potatoes with no real guidance. You can literally do whatever you want (mostly, dialogue choices are a bit limited with diplomacy, unless you mod) and it is a bit overwhelming at first.
Do you want to start your own empire, you can do that, good luck! Want to join a current faction, sure thing! Want to depose a current king with a pretender? it can be done! Just a few of the many options in the "native" way to play. There is an active modding community that increases difficulty, adds new factions, makes it like Lord of the Rings, and much much more.
There is not much to say, there isn't much story, or character. You literally role play as a warlord that is trying to take over the world one way or the other. Gameplay is pretty good, enemy AI is hit and miss. Sometimes they make astoundingly terrible choices, and other times they hit you right where it hurts. Essentially there are 2 game modes: the map AI, and battle AI (total warish). Except on the battle, you actually play as your character and get to smack enemies around or snipe them from afar, as well as direct them in combat. Limited stategic options in battles as there is a lack of direction and formation options for your troops. Usually it is either charge, or wait to be charged (for open battles). Siege battles are a bear to get through, and are what you spend the majority of your time doing in the late game (who only builds one ladder or tower to take a whole castle?).
Despite the issues, it is a very fun game to play, and I highly expect my first play through to conquer the map to have taken me somehwere around 100 hours. Which is about 2-3 years in game time. Something keeps me coming back, and I think it is the challenge of unruly lords, managing your empire, and kicking butt on the map when outnumbered 5:1 (which getes harder the higher the unit cap).

Stylish and sharply written, The Fall reminds me of the great short stories you could find in a sci-fi anthology.
Y'know. Back when those still were a thing.
Most of what makes the fall special is in the writing, but the puzzles are fine, and the developers find clever ways to use them to advance story and character instead of just roadblocks to keep to from progressing too quickly. Adventure game veterans will find them on the easy side, and you're always able to brute force a solution since the interactions are pretty limited and the locations contained, but that's preferrable to the horrifying obtuseness the genre at its worst indulges in.
The action sequences that occasionally break up the puzzles on the other hand, while usually a welcome change of pace and easy, can only be described as clunky.
Most people will play through it in three or four hours, but it feels like the correct length for the scope of the story. Part 2 being in the pipeline, but the ending is satisfying enough to make Part 1 feel like a complete expericene, while still being open for continuation.
Two thumbs way up.

A interesting and intruiging storyline propells this game to its maximum potential. If you're looking for lots of action, combat and gameplay, The Fall is not for you.
The Fall is a 2D side-scrolling puzzle game that relies more on its story, rather than its mechanics, to keep you playing. You are the A.R.I.D onboard a Mark 7 combat exoskeleton, whose pilot may or may not be injured. Activated moments before you crash-landed on a planet to save whoever's inside, your job now is to verify your occupant still lives.
That's not even remotely a quarter of the entire plot, which will keep you guessing for the next few hours as you find out why the combat exoskeleton crashed onto this planet to begin with.
The gameplay itself is pretty straightforward. The A.R.I.D uses the flashlight on her sidearm to highlight points of interest in the background or around her. She can then interact with the objects in question if possible. Each of these 'nodes' have well written descriptions, some of which will prod at your thinking and judgement.
A.R.I.D won't see much combat in the game, but you mostly have 2 options: Stealth takedowns, or pop out of cover and shoot while they reload. The security bots you see in the game can take more punishment than you or your occupant can, so most of the time you'll be using your active camo or taking cover to avoid shots. However the combat mechanic itself is simple: A.R.I.D can switch her sidearm's flashlight into a laser pointer to shoot with pinpoint accuracy. There's not much to it other than that, as like I said before, The Fall focuses more on its storyline and puzzles than anything else.
The puzzles in game will keep you entertained, and you will stumble upon many 'aha!' moments during the course of the game. Sometimes the puzzles don't seem obvious, but it just takes a little ingenuity, and personally I don't find it that difficult.
While The Fall has a incredibly interesting storyline, only 1/3 of it is actually in the game. As the first of 3 games, The Fall at its current state has a story and game long enough to occupy at most, 2-3 hours of your time. If you're fast enough you could probably buy it, finish it, and then refund it for absolutely nothing. I didn't, mainly because I took my time. The Fall won't entertain you for long, but it's good enough that you won't want your money back.
Overall, if you want a game with a awesome story, this is for you. And the next 1-2 sequels.

Really brought back the memories. As soon as i got use to the old school controls again the game was fantastic. I had forgotten how cool survival horrors use to be. They did a great job bringing it up to today's standards felt like a brand new game. Hoping they will remaster resident evil 2.

- Graphics :
A 13 years old game with a nice upscale to 1080p & constant 60FPS. No drops. Ever. So yeah, it has aged, you can't deny that, but it's still very pleasant to the eye.
- Sound & Musics :
Voice acting is bad, let's not even try to hide that fact. Seems to be a trademark of the RE franchise though. Musics are nice, the same as the 2002 Gamecube classic. I had a few mini crashes in the sound department (the music suddenly stopped and got back on track 2 sec later), but nothing to lose sleep over.
- Gameplay :
The exact same thing as the original Gamecube classic : weird camera angle, weird control, inventory being restricted. Not a fan of it to be honest but I can get around it. If you're new to this style it might take some time for you to get along with it but you'll see, it's quite nice when you get the hang of it. As for the old fans, well... isn't this the game you prefer from the franchise ?
- Storytelling :
HAHAAAHHAHAHAHAHAHAHAHAHAH.
HAAAAAHAHAHAHAHHAHAHAHAHHAH.
...
Oh, wait, you're seriously asking ?!
HAAAAHAHAHAHAHAHAHHAHAHAHA !!! HAAAHAHAHAHHA
...
But seriously, no. The story's not very clever, it never got very clever in the RE franchise.
- Length :
Takes about 10H to beat one of the two "stories", both are quite similar (Chris really is the Hard mode of the game so if you want an easier time, you should try Jill first). Then if you want to end with both characters on max difficulty well... that will just make things longer for you. So your call, really.
CONCLUSION :

A fun game, if it doesn't quite reach it's potential.
Will Wright's Spore started out as a grand experiment in evolution, equal parts game and educational tool. When it saw release, fans of Maxis were dissapointed to find many of the touted features had been stripped out (including an entire stage) and everything given a cartooney makeover, seemingly in an attempt to replicate "The Sims" success with the casual market. It seemingly worked as Spore was a very popular game.
Despite this, what we have is still an intiresting game. There are five mini-game like stages where the early goals are to survive and evolve while eventually growing your culture.
CELL STAGE
You start out as a microbe and must feed either by hunting other microbes or grazing algae. intermittently throughout, you can find a partner and evolve your species. This is done through the "creature creator" where you can attach various body parts such as claws, defensive spikes or pretty much anything you want. More and more parts are unlocked as you collect "evolution points" throughout the stages. The creature creator is the easily the best part of this game and the amount of customisation is staggering. There is also some strategy as various body parts have different atributes attached to them and can effect the type of build you are going for.
CREATURE STAGE
Once your creature is large enough, it grows a pair of legs and climbs out onto land. Gameplay is much the same, keeping your species alive and evolving but now you can interact with other creatures as you try to grow your brain size. The "creature creator" options expand enormously. In my opinion this is the best stage of the game.
TRIBAL STAGE
Having achieved sentience, your species forms a primitive tribe and must either go to war or ally with other tribes. As you are now a society, your biology is locked and can no longer evolve. Instead of evolving your creatures, you can now deck them out with basic tribal outfits and jewlery.
CIVILIZATION STAGE
Now that your society is more advanced, you have a home city where you can design the various buildings and veicles. Your goal now is to subjugate the various races on your planet by either warring with them or converting them to your religion. This is in my opinion the least intiresting stage, thankfully it is also the shortest.
SPACE STAGE
Having conquered your planet, your eyes now turn towards the heavens. You design & build a ship and explore a vast galaxy. You make trade deals and alliances with other races and try not to go to war with the games villains, the Grox. You can visit hundreds of worlds, establish colonies, terraform planets, even abdust creatures from one planet and seed them on another. It really is quite complex but can be overly repetative. There are various optional objectives, reaching the highest rank, conquering every other race, reaching the centre of the galaxy, but there is no real end-state so you can continue indefinately.
There is no way all the creatures and plants can fit onto the disc so the other really notable feature is that when connected to Maxis' servers the creatures designed by other players can populate the various worlds.
If you haven't noticed, the gameplay in each stage seems to follow a pattern, either befriend or kill all your competition. There really isn't much variation between these stages. There was also a stage cut from the game during development process. Set between cell & creature, the fish stage would act as a bridge from sea to land.
While Spore is not the game it could have been, it's still worth the €15 asking price for the creature creator and space stages alone.

Unforgettable adventure game. Machinarium is a flash-based, point and click game with great hand-made graphics and a stunning soundtrack composed by Tomáš Dvořák. There are many interesting, untypical puzzles to solve, some are quite hard, but you can always use "The Tome of Tips", as I like to call it, if you're stuck. It's available all the time, you just have to unlock it first by playing a mini-game. Machinarium is rather short, it takes about seven hours to finish it without using hints or about three hours if you play for the second time and know exactly what to do. Is it worth it? Absolutely. I would say that for this price you won't get a more charming game than Machinarium. I have good memories with this game. Reminds me a little of Stanisław Lem's book, "The Cyberiad". If you are still uncertain then try out the demo on the official website. No need to download any files!

I've decided to play a game with logic puzzles and brain teasers so I came across Machinarium. I was encouraged by generally favourable reviews and its distinctive hand-drawn style. What's more, I heard that game characters never speak, they use animated comic bubbles instead.
Presentation:
The game world meets you with beautifully drawn and animated environments and soundtrack of great quality. However, despite of having a "fullscreen" option, the game doesn't utilize the whole screen area so the screen appears letterboxed.
Puzzles:
The adventure is full of good puzzles which will make you spend a while -- you have to figure out the puzzle goals and rules yourself. The part I didn't like is point-and-click pixel hunting because the game never tells you what you're looking for. However,  the game has a hint system that can give you a general direction in a comic bubble.
Conclusion: recommended for persistent puzzle lovers. Don't be shy to use hints when stuck.

PROS:
WoW-style servers where everyone shares one world with different maps for each area.
Diablo-style graphics, loot, and camera angles.
Similar playstyle as the arcade zombies from call of duty.
The loot system is GREAT. 5 stars on this front. It's if Diablo 2 met Diablo 3 and they had a baby: if you are in a party (which goes up to 3 players unless your in a special mission), then there is a shared loot system. If you are not in a party, other players in your server can see your drops - but they cant pick them up. Nothing is bound on pickup other than items from quests ONLY. Most rare/super rare/legendary/set items are bind on equip, which means... you guessed it...
There is an Auction House. Lovin' it. If you get tired of grinding, you can always try to take control of the AH. Theres is a decent yet small enough community where the prices fluctuate a lot but things still sell easy enough so long as you are smart about it. Many times if you need that 1 last set piece, it wont be there.., BUT.... theres the same chance it will be there. It's a 50/50 chance really. Yet something of some sort of help will always be available until you reach high end levels, so long as you've got the CRI (which is the free ingame currency). If you like playing the AH like me, you can easily become rich fast here. I'm not - I liquidate everything cuz I'm too impatient - but someday perhaps ^_^.
Rushing characters is not possible. At all. Two thumbs up. You MUST play through the game. ... I like it.
Types of customizable gears include armors/legs/boots/helmets/gloves/plate which is like a shield/neck/rings/weapons/etc. Types of weapons are pistols/shotguns/machine guns/flamethrowers/rocket launchers/snipers/chainsaws/rifles. Any of these can be crafted, but it's not viable until later on in the game.) Additionally, you can get gear called avatar from certain quests or from the coin shop (real money shop) that will alter your ingame appearance and may have some large boosts for dmg, def, move speed, etc. This is a separate tab and is worn "over" your regular gear. Enjoy! =)
You build and level up a character of one of 4 classes. Not difficult to grasp. Each class has its skill tree specific to it,
You can dodge (ninja-roll) which is surprisingly effective.
CONS:
Not much information for this game is available on the web.
The game is a little choppy/buggy - not too bad for me yet, but it's happened to others from what I've heard.
Graphics could be better - but this could also be seen as a PRO because you don't need a super video card or processor to run it.
Monotonous grinding aspect to the questline.
Bad translations - which can be funny at times, but can also be confusing at times. "If you don't give me delicious, I'll be at play." ...... what?
Game gets progressively more difficult, inspiring it's users to pay money for temporary buffs from the coin shop - however this isnt entirely necessary. Could be seen as a PRO because it inspires you to try harder aswell and get more skillful.

Some quick suggestions for the developers: (Just to improve upon the framework that you already have)
-Mithral's CO has some lines that are either mispronounced (Ships Bow is pronounced "bo") or that have grammatical issues. You may want to have someone go through the lines when you get out of heavy development and clean it up.
-The reflection in the Prison level is insane. If you could turn that down a bit it would make that tough level just a little less tough or at least make it easier to see. (The second part of this mission is a defense mission that is super tough because of your underpowered machine and the size of the map)
-When people are talking it would be nice if the subtitles told us who they were. There is such a multitude of characters it's pretty hard to keep up especially early on.
-I'd like to see some story between the missions. The first couple missions felt scattered and a bit like proof of concept. A little story there could have helped me more easily figure out what was going on. That said the missions following the UAC (aka Russans) were well done in a way that it felt like there was an over arching story. It might be worth giving every faction their own distinct act or campaign to facilitate this.
-The machine gun has too short a magazine size it doesn’t feel as useful as some of the other weapons. In the missions where you are forced to use it exclusively with the missiles it feels really limiting.
-I wish the missiles where more visible. At least let you know if you are doing the correct thing. (Also mechanically I really like the way they did missiles in Robotech Battlecry, it would be cool if missiles were implemented as more of a muti-target weapon.)
-I do like the specialized weapons though Anti-Ship Laser and Funnels (YAY! Gundam) are really cool.
-Sometimes the characters talk over each other in battle. It makes it hard to understand what is going on. Although it does add a bit of a chaotic note to the battle.
-UAC missions are really fun. Letting you choose the pilot makes it feel like the player has greater control on how the game is played and also lets them play the way they want to.
-I would like to see some more content focusing on Mirai as her Suit is one of the best. Yuliana has another great suit that I enjoy playing with.
Also love the Gundam and other mecha references. Red suit that is 3 times faster and Funnels! Good job fitting those in!
Think the Devs are doing a great job and hope they can keep it up!

I've played 6 hours of this game and I gotta say, I'm really liking it. The action gets fast paced and exciting, and the story is filled with anime mech goodness. It's kind of like Ace Combat, but with robots.
The game has you piloting a "Battle Frame" flying in a 3-Demensional plane using weapons that range from the standard machine guns to awesome ones like smart missiles that auto-track targets, and "Funnels" which are little drones that you can either have attack a target or defend you against missiles. When you're wathicng those funnels rip your targets to shreds while your pounding them with other weapons, it makes you feel like badass. That with the character dialog really makes you feel like an ace pilot. Did I mention that some Battle Frames have laser blades? Yes. You even have a laser blade!
That being said, there are some problems with the game. The gameplay can get so frantic at times that you're not quite sure what's going or what's actually hitting you. The bullet time mechanic does help alleviate the problem, but I still found my self just spamming all my weapons until the green blip I'm shooting at is gone, hoping that it was the thing acutallty landing hits on me. Some of the missions also get a little frustrating to complete, but I think that's only if you're playing on anyhting other than Casual, where your health replenishes.
The story itself is pretty standard fare. It's not bad by any means, it certainly gets the job done, and the optional audio logs before the start of some missions are a good listen. It definately amps up mid way through the game, especially during the final mission in Act II.
All in all, it's been pretty fun so far and I can't wait to see the next updates. I'd say it's at a stage where it's worth buying. If you like mech combat that gets fast paced, you're not gonna regret trying this.

PROS:
Let me just begin by saying that all in all I highly recommend this game. I for one have just recently discovered the marvelous world of indie side-scrollers so I haven't played many of them yet. Nevertheless, so far The Fall has been the best by far.
The atmosphere of it slightly resembles The Swapper, giving the game a sort of a cosmic, mysterious touch which I really fancy. The mostly dark surroundings logically match the location your character is playing in, although for some reviewers the entire game has seemed too dark. It's a matter of taste I guess but it certainly didn't bother me. Adding more lighting would have probably ruined the general idea of the set the character's in.
The visuals per se are nice and no detail really scratches the eye. There is no overly artistic aura eminating from the game; there are no magical landscapes and pink fairies, that is. The AI is depicted in a realistic key with a touch of humour and the graphics really support the cause.
In terms of dialogues they are really well written and spoken, making them a joy to listen. The main character does a good job of expressing her opinion on the location and her surroundings,  quite often I found myself asking the same questions she did. Hence I believe the dialogue really helps to connect with the main character.
In terms of gameplay The Fall is just fine. Having to examine your surroundigs with a flashlight in order to progress and find items really syncs with the beforementioned dark theme, making the solutions quite often hidden from the eye at first.
Oh and the story... wow. The ending.. wow. I might get amazed too easily, but.. yeah, wow. I also liked the fact that playing the game for the second time (to get the achievements for example) really brings out the small details you'd miss when playing it initially.
CONS:
For me there are no real cons to this game. I did get stuck for a couple of times so I used the help of YouTube but the game isn't really to blame. Throughout the game countless hints present themselves, leading a way to a successful (and a surprising) finish, you only have to pay attention.
At times it felt like I had to backtrack my steps a little too often but I guess the game and the suspense would have ended too fast without it so I found myself embracing the backtrack quite a bit.

Now in most games, this might be considered a bad thing, but in Superflight its the opposite. Without the progression system that most games with similar mechanics have, you have nothing to lose from taking crazy risks. You wont lose your plane you grinded 3 hours for, if you die you just try it again. And thats what makes it so fun, its all about doing quick tricks and challenging yourself to do something so crazy that it just might work. Exactly what I've been looking for.

I had originally played the Lost Chapters back in the day, and in general love the Fable franchise. An faithful high-definition remaster to the original Fable released in September 14, 2004.
Remembering that time where I first played it, it was quite immersive and eye-catching during its heydays at old Xbox console introduction, and at this point of time in future I feel like the Anniversary has delivered the very same gameplay but looks far more different on characters and the story being more vibrant if little buggy depending on the circumstances in the actual gameplay.
What I found it to be perfect for me is because it has tons of replayability especially with heroic mode which I've finished everything else on the game thus so far, there's no point going back to the one of the greatest RPG games made exclusively for Xbox and after that is the Lost Chapters on PC/Xbox.
Basically the game might be a little harsh on first timers or people who have gotten back to it, but brings a fairly moderate learning curve, the keyboard may take time getting used to but I understand it's considerably far more easier to deal with an controller. You're always welcome to do so.
Pros:
+ Open world environment with beautiful graphics enhanced with Unreal Engine.
+ Variety of weapons for you to choose from crossbows to greatmaces.
+ Tough bosses regardless of the difficulty, that makes it even more fun.
+ Late game is far too easy since overpowering and upgrading everything is bound to be
game breaking.
+ Immersive and non-linear sometimes.
+ Enough for any RPG lover to enjoy this one, it has everything you need out of an game.
Cons:
- Horrible framerate at specific equipment such as AMD, I'm not sure about that.
- Making gold of going slow is quite tedious, you wouldn't get high-end weapons unless you were to keep at this for over few days.
- Marriage isn't a fully involved feature until Fable II or III which is a limited aspect to what it can deal in Fable Anniversary.
- Heroic Mode is quite difficult, even more so than the normal mode. You'll get hit extremely hard in earlier part of the story instead.
- Some textures look out of the place, plus some NPCs can get stuck in certain areas.
Trust me! You'll like this classic and remastered RPG once you look past its flaws. It's almost perfect enough for myself.

Multiplayer is a little more eh--while it's well balanced and the game modes offer interesting tactical challenges, it can also feel clunky at times. The community can also be a pain--not as bad as some other games, but noticibly annoying at times.

Project Nimbus is a great game that really gives out my inner love for mecha. This game will always leave you breathless because of the awesome fast action gameplay and the great visuals. The game is still on early access by the time I made this review, but it already has good premise for a bigger and wider group of players.
The gameplay is fast. You need to think thoroughly on how to defeat your opponents. Sometimes the game would even send 10-15 enemies at once! You will need to be fast. Keep shooting while moving. The game has a good number of mechas that you can use in the game's storyline and survival mode. The controls are like water; easy and precise.
Surely most of you also bought this game because of the cool design of the mechas. The designs of each mecha is just gorgeous. Props to the art and design team for making these cool and unique mechas!
The story is a little bit neglected in my opinion. I sometimes ask myself: "Why am I shooting these guys down again?". The game focuses more on the gameplay side than the story. I know there is a story, but I wish there was more background and life on the different characters found in the storyline.
The scenery is gorgeous. The explosions and the laser beams just whizzing around is amazing! I can really feel the guns blazing as I rain hell upon my enemies. The graphics of the game is not top notch but it does give out a cool scenery that leaves me breathless.
The soundtrack is just amazing! It fits in so well with the gameplay as you try and kill your enemies. Really brings out that inner adrenaline punch! I am hoping for more tracks in the future.
All in all, it's an amazing indie game. I rate it 8/10! For those who love watching mecha animes, this game is truly for you. Buy it now and support the team that created this beauty!

It's really tough, because there is so much about this game to like.  It can be fun to channel your inner mecha, and I haven't found a good fix for that in a while.  However, this is not that game.  Yet. The biggest issues come from the story, which is complete nonsense, and the game gives you very little reason to care about the characters you play as, which jump around from faction to faction with as little transition as possible.  It seems like there is something there that could be interesting, but at the moment it's just a handful of anime action tropes loosely tied together with some (poorly translated and acted) opening briefing. As for the game-play, many of the Armored Core games were criticized for their cumbersome controls and uneven difficulties.  This game suffers from both these and worse.  It's not as though the controls are bad necessarily, it's more that you find yourself very unsure of whether going left or right, or up or down really makes much of difference is the grand scheme of "I should probably keep moving so I don't get hit". This game feels really really Alpha-y, and that's disconcerting for a game that has been in development for 3+ years.  I'm going to go get my money back, and hopefully Project Nimbus proves me wrong and I come back and repurchase it in a couple years for it's compelling and tactical game-play and gripping and cohesive plot...  But I'll believe it when I see it. Sorry.

Attention Metroid/Castlevania enthusiasts: this game may interest you.
The following includes many references to Metroid elements. If you are confused, please search online for more information regarding the Metroid games.
When a human is incapacitated for any reason in an A.R.I.D. Mark VII Battlesuit, the onboard A.I. takes control of motor functions and seeks medical attention for its wounded pilot. In
, the A.I. onboard a battlesuit, nicknamed Arid, has just crash-landed on a planet. Her pilot is seriously injured and unconscious, so the A.I. takes full control of the suit she resides in and starts to explore…
Sound familiar? For Metroid gamers, this is a twist on the classic “start on an alien planet with no upgrades as Samus.” The backstory behind the lack of equipment in this game is that you have it equipped but are simply not authorized to use it (like in Metroid: Other M). Unlike the lame excuse presented in Other M, though, The Fall’s explanation actually makes sense; an A.I. is prevented from using certain functions without a human’s permission except in dire circumstances. More on that last part later.
The atmosphere in
is incredible - dark, mysterious and foreboding. Similar to Metroid Prime, there are points located above objects of interest scattered throughout the 2D world. You start with a weapon that has two modes: laser sight (for firing; disabled initially) and a flashlight for finding info points. Another note: each point of info has a few interaction options, such as picking up a tire iron or activating an elevator. The items are kept until needed at another info point. You acquire access to more suit functions  and circumvent the need for human approval in certain situations where the pilot’s life is in imminent danger.
I didn’t think too much of this game from the store page, but I absolutely love the Metroid games and so I thought I’d give it a go. For
, this game is very satisfying: the puzzles and endless backtracking really makes you think to progress. The fascinating dialogue (sometimes monologue) explores the nature of artificial intelligence and its bounds in way that only an android could. The game itself is
, however.
for my initial playthrough with no guides, one hour for my second playthrough.
Some of the mechanics could use a little work. The switching between combat and discovery (flashlight) mode is uncomfortable at times, and finding just the right angle to activate an elevator while standing directly adjacent to it is maddening. You cannot change direction in mid-air. Aiming with the laser sight can be a bit strange at times, trying to compensate for distance to target.
, I still give a enthusiastic recommendation to this game.
Not Recommended
Recommended With Caution
Recommended
Recommended as Essential
P.S. The Fall 2 is announced and in development.
P.P.S. I have never played any of the Castlevania games. I am guessing that Castlevania players will like this, but am not sure. I do know almost for certain, however, that Metroid enthusiasts will enjoy this.

The original fable was released in 2004, and it was one of my favourite games when I was a kid. I can't tell you how many hours I've put into that game.
And after all those years, my disc for The Lost Chapters got too damaged to be used, so I was left without that game. And to be honest, once you get used to the graphics of 2017/2016, it gets very painful to look at the potatofaces the older games have (Oblivion has the same problem, fable is just a mild case)
So when Anniversary went on sale, I bought it. 15 euro for the full package (dlc's included)
And honestly, it was just the same.
Sure, things looked better, and hearing the old voices and music made me feel nostalgic. But at the core, it's still the same game. With the same mechanics and boundries as in 2004. The biggest issue I have here is the area system. The world is cut into smaller areas, which in 2004 was fine and understandable, but nowadays we don't have to do that anymore, and it really takes away from the atmosphere of the game.
The gameplay is still the same as well. Probably the most basic you can get, attack, block, magic, or ranged. Again, understandable in 2004, but I hoped more from Anniversary.
Let's talk DLC's. because boy, they aren't worth it.
All the DLC's consist of is outfits. Which really seems like they wanted to put in the game to obtain for microtransactions, but because of the backlash microtransactions got/still get they released it as a dlc. Honestly, buying these isn't worth it at all. There's about 2 good looking outfits.
So, should you get Anniversary?
If you really enjoyed fable like I did, then probably yes. But wait for a sale. Not worth it at full price.
If you think fable is alright, and are hoping this game will change your mind. Then don't buy it. Because it won't.
(all in all you're probably better off buying The lost Chapters, which is also available on steam.)

Mount and Blade: Warband is a game based in the war-torn kingdom of Calradia, where several resulting factions fight for dominance. Start a Campaign, create and customize your character (both appearance and statistics), and travel to Calradia to begin your adventure!
As an adventurer new to the land, you are practically a nobody. Go throughout the land, explore it, embark on quest, and more. Enlist as a mercenary, expand and improve your skills, troops, and reknown to gain an upper hand. Watch as you slowly rise up the social ladder, and how your actions impact your popularity with kings, nobles, and the people. Want to break the rules? Claim your right to the throne and create your own kingdom! Buy and sell a variety of weapons(such as bows, swords, spears), armour, food, and miscellaneous. The Campaign alone can easily offer one-thousand hours, depending on how you go about it.
Don't like the solo experience? Jump into Multiplayer and test your mettle against players around the globe. Compete in several modes, join and participate in clans, and even roleplay. Play on massive servers and engage in gigantic conflicts.
The game in itself has an amazingly simple-to-learn but hard-to-master combat system, and offers many playstyles to fit your taste. The graphics are effective but nothing too flashy, and occasional bugs may be found.
The only real downside is the Campaign at times can be quite hard, but otherwise the game is quite amazing! I would also recommend the Napoleonic Wars DLC and trying mods found on the Steam Workshop.

This is a game with a lot of potential and I've had a bit of fun playing it.  It's not without a few problems; poor localization, occasional bugs, and limited ability to configure the ui.  Still, these can be forgiven and don't detract too much from the game itself.
This is a game ruined by it's business model.  Not only is it pay to win at it's very worst (selling costumes with large stat increases) but even lauds this as dlc.  They imply that a pay to win costume and some xp increases is the same as the Dragonborn dlc in Skyrim or Old World Blues in New Vegas.  You're paying more for this pay to win "dlc" then many games in their entirety.
At best this serves as a display that these kinds of games are still in demand.  Perhaps some other publisher can pick this up and salvage the situation, but for now this is a game to be wary of.  You may have some fun here, it's worth checking out at least, but I could not in good conscience recommend paying any money for it.

Pro's -
- Decent 2.5D Graphics and model designs
- Interesting concept of character classes and builds
- Upgrading Weapons (Enchanting weapons to higher Stat grades) making them stronger
Con's -
- Cash Shop - Cosmetic and Pay to Win real money cash store - This would normally be an instant game killer for me, but its so small and not as intrusive as most games cash shops are. The suggest using it but you can get by without ever needing it.
- controls are clunky in the style of Twin Stick only working with mouse and keyboard. Would work better with Controlelr support.
- Animations**
- Movement Animations are very clunky and dated, especially with vehilce mounts and mission oriented vehicles.
- Skill & combat animations are not as precise as they could be. Not saying im looking for the accuracy of a AAA game, you will notice if you play that using certain weapons or skills that they tend to miss while landing dead on pretty frequently.
For what the game is worth I grant it a PLAYABLE  6/10
From there take it as you wish.
