TL;DR Stop reading reviews (they're clearly all good) and buy the damn game already.
I can't really say anything about this game that hasn't been said already, but what the hell, I'll give it a go.
+ Hundreds of hours of gameplay (my Steam hours don't factor in the hours and weeks I poured into it on Xbox back in the day) in a vast open world that puts Oblivion and Skyrim to shame
+ Old-school RPG elements that toss you into the deep end and make you work for success (choose your skills wisely, and don't expect any quest markers or easy fast traveling), but not to the point where it's unforgiving
+ An engaging, intriguing, and well-paced story that you will probably never finish due to being distracted by all of the other content, be it exploration, artifacts, side quests, or crime sprees (you can steal what you want and kill anyone you want without console commands, and it makes you feel like their deaths matter)
+ If the base game isn't big enough for you, the DLC should prove more than sufficient, with new worlds and new opportunities to do things like become a werewolf, seek out a lost airship (!), or face off against the biggest ♥♥♥♥ing cumwad♥♥♥♥♥♥sniffing backtalking piece of♥♥♥♥♥♥evil dickbreath ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ peasant you will find in gaming history (thanks for all the laughs, Gaenor)
+ The setting and the monsters within it are both unique and stand apart from other Elder Scrolls games without making you feel removed from Bethesda's style of fantasy
+ Character customization and advancement offer a lot of options, whether through attributes/skills/birthsign combinations or the variety of weapons, armor, spells, etc. available to you
+Ultimately, and most importantly, this is an RPG that offers you immense freedom to roam where you want, be whoever you like, take what looks good, and take on anyone who makes you mad -- there are consequences to all of these choices, of course, but that's what makes them so fulfilling
+Music, as always, is top-notch
If you want the shiniest new graphics or the smoothest combat interface, look somewhere else.  But if you don't mind a little bit of clunkiness and some early-2000s graphics (which were damn good for their time) and if any of the above endorsements appeal to you, or if you're looking for a game that will consume your life and maybe even make you fall in love, then buy this game now.  Play it now.  Don't be afraid to ♥♥♥♥ up at the start.  Just have fun with it and make it your own, because that sort of ownership of the experience is more possible in this game than any of its predecessors. Fable Anniversary Review.
Fable Anniversary is a xbox game ported to steam with a complete graphics and texture overhaul and more options. Fable Anniversary was one of the best selling RPG on the original xbox.
Fable is a classic game and was made by lionhead studios and former bullfrog developers made in the UK. It is a beautiful port of the xbox game. If you already played fable, before then played fable the lost chapters and maybe even got fable the lost chapters on PC why should you get Fable Anniversary? I would say the best reason is that this is the best port of fable with the lost chapters content, running on the unreal engine 3 it looks beautiful, it also has some poor mod support, fable one is the best fable game, faster load times, it has a heroic difficulty mode and it has achievement's.

But why might you not want it? It is very expensive the price has dropped somewhat and on a sale its not a bad deal, the mod support is so awful that only a few mods have any noticeable use the only one I can mention is the one that removes scars, fable does not have a feature that the old PC port has where you could make your own tattoos with a program. Fable is a short and easy game even with heroic difficulty and you could get it cheaper for the original xbox missing a few improvements.
The game is very very very very easy. You should play it on heroic difficulty without using many items for it to be a challenge, fable does have a interesting gameplay mechanic called boasting where you agree to a challenge like no healing no using weapons etc but unless you are using your fists it is really easy. I was playing fable on heroic and I still was able to get hundreds of potions and I still have nothing to do with them. Sure you don't get revives and mana potions are harder to find but it is not very hard to get hundreds of items and break the economy.
Fable it is quite fun to play the game unlocking everything getting all the silver keys demon doors etc breaking the economy all the weapons, doing all the quests. The game has very very fun mechanics that are fun to exploit and master. I have put hundreds of hours on and off steam playing Fable on xbox, xbox 360, PC, and steam. I have beaten the game 6 times and the game does not have much replay value it is just really fun to make a new game and play it over.
We can't forget how fable was very hyped up by peter molyneux where he promised thing's like you could plant a acorn and age though the game and watch it grow into a tree and plenty of his promises were not kept but a few false promises about minor details and features in the game do not change how good the game is and I do not feel it was that bad of false advertising.
To Conclude, Fable Anniversary is a great game that is very fun, its is quite a simple game to get the hang of it looks beautiful and has many interesting features but it is so easy that you need to make your own challenges to make the game hard. I have beaten this game many times even on heroic even doing the boasting challenges and I have not died once.
Do I recommend you get this game? Yes, it is a very good game and I think it is worth 40$-20$ and getting fable anniversary for under 20$ is a great price. You can easily get fable on the original xbox, xbox 360 or xbox one for a cheap price and you can even get fable anniversary on PC for a cheap price but fable anniversary on PC is the best port of the game and one I recommend to anyone who wants a fun game that has 3-5 hours just finishing the game and 25+ if you complete every side quest and collectible.

The first thing is, there's no customization in this game. You get the default Mech for the mission. There's no customizing your mech for specific missions and customizing your mech to your playstyle here.

Top-notch point-and-click adventure with beautifully drawn 2D environments. You begin as a robot in a scrap heap putting yourself back together. Your mission is to rescue your girlfriend and the story is charming, with minimal text and characters' memories and thoughts played out through animated comic bubbles. Combined with a perfect atmosphere, you'll easily be immersed in the mechanical world.
As far as how it plays, you do actually walk around and, when you find useful objects in the environment and click on them, you will either use them or eat them, which places them into your inventory to be used later. You can also stretch yourself vertically and will need to utilize that ability to solve certain puzzles. While there is some hidden object, the game is light on it; it's more a puzzle adventure and figuring out what you need to do on a few screens at a time to progress. A good variety of puzzle types and minigames. Sketch hints available if you're stumped. Highly recommended.

Destroying cubes in an aseptic minimalist visual style is both appreciable and satisfying, even though some of them take too many hits to pop. I was initially quite drawn to Grey Cubes and really enjoyed the first half hour or so. Yet my interest waned when its redundant level layouts, questionably sturdy physics and overly mellow pace became underwhelming.
Later levels feel more like automated pachinko machines, somewhat clinical and prone to boredom, with several cumulative minutes spent passively waiting without interaction as the ball gets lost in a maze you can barely influence.
The game offers well over 2 hours' worth of content, of which approximately a third feels fresh enough. Fewer levels with a focus on the better ones would have made it more stimulating. Its flaws confine an inexperienced grade to the game but the good bits are really worth checking out for a brief time. Additional challenges would add replay value beyond chasing high scores.
Given the game's very low price this is nevertheless a good value for fans of the genre.

You can rush through the main story line without interacting with the world at all. Or, you can become the head of every guild or group walking the blight ridden waste lands of Vvardenfel without ever really starting the main story. And, you can explore...
The lands may seem empty at first glance but around every corner, in every cave or shack there are things to discover, gather or learn. The game allows you, as a player, to have as much influence as the developers themselves. With enough passion and dedication you can craft powerful items imbued with potentially every spell in game. You can craft counter spells to make use of otherwise useless items because of their negative effects.
You can play the way you like. Sneaky assassin, bulky fighter or swift marksman everything is possible. There are only a few occasions mainly plot relevant that really enforce a certain solution to a problem.
Getting rid of an opponent? Why not bribe them to leave for the main lands instead of killing them. Or turn on the quest giver and get the reward from said opponent.
Be as honest or cruel as you please.

If you played any brickbreaker/ paddle and ball style game, tnen you know what to do here - Guide your paddle to hit the ball into all the bricks and prevent it from going into the pit. You have most of your typical power ups and power downs: Bigger or smaller paddles, bigger or smaller balls (giggity), a more powerful ball, a wiggiling, innacurate ball, a pit shield, 1-Ups, mystery power up. These pick ups are fairly large (likely due to it's mobile design origins) which also makes for a semi-challenging mechanics: sometimes your ball may reflect near a power up or power down, and sometimes you have to risk taking the power down to save the ball.
I'm not really the biggest fan of physics - I prefer snappy, prediticable mechanics in my games, and physics are highly unpredictable unless you're some high level mathemetician. It's the biggest reason why I don't like LittleBigPlanet even though I like platformers.  However it works well in Grey Cubes, adding an interesting twist to a stale genre - the angle of a brick will determine how a ball reflects, and bricks can end up in the corners of the map or even near or past your paddle (in which they disappear). This does also mean some of the later levels can be rather annoying to deal with, especially when the game employes mechanics that moves blocks around, create walls and platforms to make it temporarily impossible to hit blocks. makes blocks temporarily invincible or employ portals that move the ball to another portion of the level. Specifically, level 41 is a major pain and should be replaced. Thankfully, these mechanics generally add interesting and fun challenge to the game, and eventually, your paddle will unlock a magnet power up that you can use to attract the ball to straggling bricks - the developers were aware how physics could affect the game in a bad way and made a fair way to deal with it.
The Steam version could use a level editor, maybe custom music, and maybe custom color palletes since the game is monocrhomatic. Though, that would likely raise the price, and at $1, you're getting definite good value with the 60 levels here that generally take 2-5 minutes. A definite purchase for those that enjoyed Wizorb, Shatter and similar games.

Grey Cubes- A minimalist block breaker game. I'm going to try to skip most of the typical complaints about this genre, with exception made for things that need to be reiterated.
Pros:
+Graphics are sharp and smooth looking.
+Achievement tally updates appear like clockwork at the end of each level, instead of being distractions during the gameplay.
+Soundtrack is very clean, industrial and fitting for the modern setting.
+Mouse controls are responsive.
+Negligible hand-holding. You won't be forced to watch a tutorial. New powerups, downgrades and chance items are frequent and available/avoidable at the player's discretion. (There is a powerup to hasten the gameplay process at the end of each stage. You are also allowed to resume a previous session and "trade" points for continues.)
Cons:
-Controller support for analogue movement seems very lacking in fluidity compared to mouse. This seems like the most obvious critique, but as someone who used to play Araknoid & Breakout on 80's consoles and DOS/Mac, I feel strongly about this point.
-Some level designs look and feel uninspired. These bland stages are usually cluttered bookends for the quicker paced, more fun levels. I often used these "slow" levels as an excuse to quit the game and do something else with my time.
Grey Cubes looks and plays like a decent budget title. Aesthetically, it attempts to skirt the unavoidable comparisons to classic games with its simplicity; yet, it lacks anything noteworthy to separate itself from all the other shareware and freeware clones that have flooded the market in years prior. Lackluster gamepad movement in a modern-looking retro game is unfortunate, but the Steam Controller trackpad could solve that issue.
6/10 Recommended for block-breaking nuts with a trackball/Steam controller.

A welcome development from Capcom, this game contains the core elements of survival-horror genre within Resident Evil (RE) franchise. The setting is frightening, monsters are plentiful (some even break through the windows and doors to attack), camera angles are fixed, and ammo is limited; therefore players are likely to experience fear and nostalgia while exploring areas and proceed with caution. In addition, macabre puzzles and deadly traps make sure that players cannot take this game lightly as it progresses but are forced to explore most areas for clues and solutions.
Progress can be saved with use of ink ribbons and typewriters, but ink ribbons are found in limited quantity and typewriters are located in select-few areas, therefore the act of saving progress in this game may give the vibe of a tactical challenge.
Even though this game is a remake of the original version that was released in 1996, it is significantly improved with new content, expanded setting, more frightening atmosphere, and more menacing monsters. This game also features two types of control schemes; original and alternate. Players can try both control schemes to determine which works best for them. Personally, I recommend original control scheme for Old School fans of the franchise. In short, this game is a refreshing update to the original version and is just as exciting for the first-timers who have played the original version but not the 2002 remake version.
In the nutshell, this game is a masterpiece of survival-horror genre and highly recommended for fans of RE franchise and also for fans of survival-horror genre content in general.

The final age is just a few minor tweaks away from being perhaps the greatest game ever made, but as it stands, it's a no from me. Do not get. The first four ages are derivative and the final one has confusing missions.

Spore is one of my favourite games of all time. It allows absolute freedom and has countless of available choices you can make when evoloving your species and expanding their dominion throughout the stages.
There are 5 stages you can play: Cell stage, Creature stage, Tribal stage, Civalisation stage and Galactic stage. Whenever starting a new game on a different planet, you can choose at which stage you'd like to start, which furtherns the freedom you have and allows you to play what stage you want, as long as it's unlocked off course ;)
During the Cell stage, you control and evolve your cell. It's simular to an aquarium simulator game, but here your choices affect your future game. Choose which type of cell you are, Carnivore or Herbivore. Then, eat plants or meat depending on your creature's diet, compete with other cell species and unlock traits by killing cells that have them, or finding them in cracked meteor that fell into the ocean. In the end, you can end up being a Herbivore, Carnivore or an Omnivore.
Remember, your choices affect your future, and the traits your species have will determine how well you will survive int he upcoming stages.
During Creature stage, you control your creature on the land. Scavange for food, whether it's by hunting down other species for meat, or looking for vegitation on plants. As you progress, you'll have to develop your creature's brain, and by this you'll need to either hunt different species into extinction, or befriend them with your social skills. As your brain power grows, find friends that will be willing to join your pack. Roam around the world, looking for skeleton parts that'll unlock new creature parts you'll be able to put on your creature. Each part will determine how well your species do in combat, when socialising with other speices, your species looks and their traits.
Watch out, their may be some outer planetery vistis trying abduct some specimen.
This is the last stage where you'll be evolving your species traits, so remember, your actions affect your future.
Here, you can end up with being a carnivore, omnivore or a herbivore for the rest of the game.
The third stage is Tribal stage. Here, it's time to develop your tribe. Your species hav become sentient beings, and now must work together to gather food and expand their village. Build new buildings that will give access to weapons and tools for your tribe. Compete with other tribes that'll rise, whether fighting them into extinction, or befriending them by socialising. Defend your village from wild animals that'll try to steal your food, or attacking enemy tribe members. Dress your species with cloths that'll affect them how well they do in combat, and when socialising. Remeber, your choices affect your future. At the end of the stage, your actions will have determined how your species behave with other species. Whether they're religious, militarised or businessmen.
The fourth stage is Civalisation stage. Here you'll have to try and conquer the world. Design your cities with house, factories, theatres and other decorative items. Design how your houses, factore, town hall and theatre look with loads of options. Paint them, shape them and go wild with your imagination. When conquering the world, you have to first dominate your continet. Design your own vechile which acts like a tank. There are loads of options, from Industrial typical looking tanks, to futuristic flying tanks. Balance out the three tank categories, speed, attack damage and health. To fund this war, you'll need to the 'Spice resource'. This resource is generated from capturing spice mines and through factories in cities. Once you dominate your continet, take it to the sea and air with your own ships and planes. You design how you like with loads of options, just like when designing your tanks and buildings. Conquer the world through military power, or religious take overs, or perhaps buying your way into dominance. You start with a city that is relevant to your specie type. But when capturing cities, you can keep them as they are or converting them into your specie categorie: Military, Religious, Business. Remember, your choices of conquering cities will affect the galactic stage.
The last stage is the galactic stage, and the biggest stage of all. Desgin your space ship and explore the galaxy, and trust me, the galaxy is big. Colonise planets actross hundreds of hundreds of solar systems that lay across the whole of milky way. Terraform planets to suit life, discover new races across the galaxy. Locate other galactic empires, trade with them, ally or go to war. Each planet that has is controlled by a galactic power will offer missions that you can choose to complete. Explore planets for rare relics and fossils that each galactic power will be interested in purchasing. Upgrade your space ship with tools and equipment you may happen to stumble upon your journey or through purchase.
Expand your species galactic infulence and empire, make your empire's economy and yourself rich through the 'Spice' resource that'll be produced on planets that are controlled by galactic empires, or by trade and exploration.
Remember, your choices will affect your relationship with other galactic empires and yours.
I recommend this game highly. It's really fun and offers more than 40 hours of great fun.

I went into this game after having read some reviews on how it mixed up the match 3 formula into something new and interesting. I expected this to be a good match 3 game with a flimsy 'dating sim' slapped onto it. What I got was a really interesting game full of really versatile strategy, and a pretty direct dating sim mechanic with characters that were actually pretty diverse, consistent, and had more personality that a lot of mainstream game characters.
The idea is simple; meet girls, give them gifts
, ask them on a date. You have a finite amount of moves to fill a bar which serves as a score. An example would be that you begin a date with a score of zero and the goal is to hit a score of 100 before you run out of moves. Each girl has traits they like and traits they like less, so while a girl that likes
but dislikes
will still get points with either,
will net you more points than
for a match made on this date. Various other modifiers allow you to boost the score for each match and these can be activated during the date with
or before the dates by boosting your player stats with experience earned in the form of
You get experience for conversing with the girls, asking about them or answering questions in a way they agree with, or by giving them gifts they enjoy with
earned by winning dates. What they like and dislike in all of these categories are always available at a glance via a pretty simple user interface that resembles a smart phone (PDA), so there's really not too much guessing, just planning and strategy.
Some matches will also net you more moves to help extend the date and give you a bigger chance to win, and some
add points or modify bonuses that matches may provide
. There are also matches that can hurt a date, causing your points to decrease. Planning moves out in order to avoid combos that might actually do more harm than good is one of many key parts of winning.
The ability to mix up different reusable
really added a layer of strategy and planning I had not anticipated, and I found myself really planning my games out according to the girl I was dating. There are some strategies that seem to win very easily, and some that can make the game a lot more of a challenge.
There is some sexy content, more of which can be restored easily via a patch. It's pretty graphic, but no explicit sex is depicted even if it is strongly implied. Even without the patch this is definitely not a game for the kiddos.

As of this review I've clocked in over 60 hours, I guess time really does fly when I'm having fun. If you can get past the sexual aspects of the game you may find a pretty deep and satisfying match 3 puzzler.

Claustrophobic brick-breaker where the bricks aren't bolted to the floor.
Grey Cubes does some stuff I hadn't seen before, and I appreciate that. I've seen some 3D offerings that turned out to be really terrible, and this one is more than playable.
I will compare pretty much any modern brick-breaker to Breakquest (and, to an extent, Shatter). Breakquest was the first brick-breaker I played that offered a curved paddle, moving blocks, and a recharging secondary power for redirecting the ball (either for strategic use or just to get the ball unstuck). Many of the powerups and downgrades are similar as well, though to be fair there are only so many unique modifiers you can throw into a Breakout clone.
Here are some of the things I didn't particularly like:
I would like to see this concept expanded to make better use of the 3D. Instead of top-down, offer a tilted view with ramped tiers like a pinball machine. The level where you knock out supports (and then bricks slide down the resulting ramp) is a great starting point. Make board effects open up access and feel like an accomplishment, instead of hitting a barrier to make it slide out of your way for just a few seconds before returning.
The palette, lighting, and sound design are pretty bleak and somewhat ominous. While less visually dense than Breakquest or Shatter, this game is still fairly chaotic in certain levels. Many of the levels feel quite claustrophobic, since the camera needs to be close enough to the "floor" for there to be any meaningful 3D perspective.
Play this one if you collect paddle games.

A new take on the Arkanoid genre, but to me the original Arkanoid is still much better. The 3D and moving stuff and portals seems interesting at first, but it just doesn't work. It makes the game feel too random. Most of the time I felt like my only goal was making sure the ball didn't go below the paddle. It's often useless to try to be precise because of all the movie platforms and also the fact all the blocks that you need to break also move, so you can never try to go for a precise angle like you did in Arkanoid. It's trying to be precise and send the ball where you want it to go that made Arkanoid so much fun, but now all of that is lost in a big random mess.
I still played through all of it hoping it would get better at some point, but the more you progress the more it becomes a big mess and, as I said, all you do is try not to lose the ball, which in itself is difficult sometimes when a bunch of portals start moving around the screen sending the ball to other random portals. The last level took me 15 minutes because the final block got stuck behind one of those portals.
Anyway, adding the 3d and movement was a good idea to try in a game, but to me it doesn't add anything good to the genre, and actually removes what made Arkanoid such a good game.

Breakout clones have, for the most part, been not great, and Grey Cubes is perhaps the not greatest.
Like most games of this sort, it employs countless gimmicks to "update" the Breakout formula. This is fine on its own, but Grey Cubes is designed in such a way that all of the gimmicks strive to prevent you from doing the one thing you played this game to do: break bricks.
Every few levels a new mechanic is introduced and they're all frustrating because they all slow the progress you make to a crawl. You know how, in Breakout, you got to the end of every level and had to go through that part where you were just trying to get the last few bricks? Remember how that was kind of boring because you weren't making any progress? This whole game is like that, pretty much from start to finish.
I had to laugh at how fitting it was that midway through the game they introduce a mechanic where, if you hit a certain wall, it turns every block onscreen into metal, making it literally impossible to break any for a small time. Like they just gave up on making the mechanics seem challenging and just straight up made one that made it so you couldn't play the game for a small period of time.
That combined with the occasional glitches and semi-frequent crashes make this not worth much time, unless you were curious to find out what it feels like to be both bored and frustrated at the same time.

I picked up this game expecting it to be primarily action and story-oriented, as the commercials suggested a tense and fast-paced atmosphere. What I got, however, was a challenging puzzle game with controls that didn't seem to properly fit the combat segments, however short they were.
First, the story. One of the primary reasons I picked this up was because people were praising the story and atmosphere. Truthfully, the plot itself isn't stellar, but the characters are very likeable, and the ongoing theme of obedience vs purpose is engaging. However, the ending kind of ruined the overall experience, with sequel bait that left me deflated rather than satisfied.
The controls felt very clunky the entire time I played. I think it's fair to say that this is more a point-and-click adventure rather than a side-scroller or platformer, so moving around didn't feel quite as fluid as in other games, and this was made especially clear during the cover shooting segments.
I've played through it's entirety, but I have to say this game is not for me. It's not bad, it just wasn't what they advertised it to be. It's for the kind of person who prefers games that require heavy exploration and intuitive problem-solving. If that's not what you're looking for, then don't bother.

A true master piece of gaming history.
You can rush through the main story line without interacting with the world at all. Or, you can become the head of every guild or group walking the blight ridden waste lands of Vvardenfel without ever really starting the main story. And, you can explore...
The lands may seem empty at first glance but around every corner, in every cave or shack there are things to discover, gather or learn. The game allows you, as a player, to have as much influence as the developers themselves. With enough passion and dedication you can craft powerful items imbued with potentially every spell in game. You can craft counter spells to make use of otherwise useless items because of their negative effects.
You can play the way you like. Sneaky assassin, bulky fighter or swift marksman everything is possible. There are only a few occasions mainly plot relevant that really enforce a certain solution to a problem.
Getting rid of an opponent? Why not bribe them to leave for the main lands instead of killing them. Or turn on the quest giver and get the reward from said opponent.
Be as honest or cruel as you please.

I will admit, when I first got this game a few years ago, I was expecting a tad bit more out of it than I saw. Then again, Spore, in and of itself was an INCREDIBLY ambitious game in its early stages. It's not the perfect, all-encompassing game some, like me, might have hoped it to be, but it is incredibly fun and incredibly challanging on the higher difficulties, ESPECIALLY in space, which is pretty much nigh impossible to completely "finish", lest you have no life whatsoever. It's nice and kid-friendly with the cartoonish creature designs, and the quick gameplay up to the space stage is a boon for casual gamers. But for those seeking to conquer the galaxy, and get a real sense of action and adventure, the space stage has enough alien genocides, nuclear explosions, and planet busting for even the most hardcore 4X strategy gamer. It's an enjoyable game with a nice mix of everything and quite a few challenges mixed in. If nothing else, play it for the space stage; probably the best, least mundane part of the game.
The DLCs add some nice features as well; the new adventure feature in Galactic Adventures adds an interesting new level of complexity and depth to the already complex space stage, and makes nice use of the creature properties you all thought were going to be useless after the creature stage.
Side note, managed to make a decent-looking human with the in-game parts - a painful ordeal, to be sure.

Blood Bowl is one of those games that is hard to determine if you should recommend it or not. Humour is good, gameplay isn't bad either, yet sometimes the game gets just too infuriating for some reason. So I'm going to list the pros and cons of this game, and you can make your mind yourself.
Pros:
Good dose of dark humour from the two commentators.
Great variety of teams/races to play with.
Different play modes, and you can even edit the rules.
Blood, violence, and random, untinkable, kills (an elf single-handedly killing a minotaur? Who knew?)
Lots of skills, equipment, etc.
Cons:
Steep learning curve. Curve is so steep, it could be called a wall. Yes, the tutorial explains most of the gameplay, but there is too much "For this, reffer to the manual". Said manual is about 80 pages...
Evasion system is maybe too easy. With 4 Agility (base Agi for Agi-based players), there is just about nothing that can stop you
Battle system can also be somewhat flawed, as if you are against a strenght-based team, they will only put all their players around the one carying the ball, and due to the odds, you are very unlikely to stop even one of them.
Long story short, if you play this game, expect to lose, expect to get frustrated, expect that what you though to be a good strategy was a bad one. If you are unsure, buy this game while on sale, as it often seems to be.

EDIT: Apparently the low framerate was from me not switching cards manually, however the crashing remains a problem and I'm not able to get it to work on my other card so I can't really test this game at normal settings.  I'll try to figure out a way to do this to make the review more accurate.
It's a tough recomendation in the state it is in.  While technically playable, my computer well exceeds the recomended specs but regularly drops below 15 fps even on the lowest settings and menus don't exceed 30 fps ever.  That's not to mention the constant crashing, In the few hours I played this, it crashed five times in game and several more in menus.  I tried playing with the settings to remedy this, but it really didn't fix the issue.  Controls were slippery as well, with inputs feeling off and unresponsive at times.
Beyond the technical issues presentation is presently a mixed bag.  The graphics and story aren't presented well and feel very rough and unfinished, which they are.  I don't see the story ever becoming fantastic, but if they improve the cutscenes and presentation, they could have a fairly interesting, if cliche, mech storyline in the vein of Gundam (with some suprising parallels to Zeorymer).  Some of the Graphics are great, others are not, it comes with early access, but the game certainly looks passable and will probably continue to.  Music is fitting and feels very much like a mech show with lots of trumpets and strings.  The voice acting and sound effects could both use some work as the voice acting lacks emotion at times and the sound effects feel a little dull and lifeless given the scope of the battles.
Where the game really seems to shine is the gameplay though. It is super solid, playing like a mix of Armored Core and Zone of the Enders (more the later than the former.).  While a little -okay, a lot- unbalanced presently (the drones are kind of a win button) there is really the foundations of something really great here.
For the future, I would like to see the story expanded so we have a clear view of our protagonist (or is it protagonists, it doesn't really make that clear) and what is actually going on beyond that or just make it clear who we are playing as.  I would also like to see some cutscenes put in, even if they are only a mech hitting another mech.  I would also like to see the balace issues fixed, with weapons other than the drones being useful and the sword feeling like it actually does damage.  It would also be cool to vary up the gameplay beyond "shoot every thing on the screen by locking on and sending out drones" especially in what I assume are the boss fights as they really don't feel any different from every other part of the game.  Oh yeah, and the technical issues improved.
So for now, I would give a recomendation to those who enjoyed Armored Core (specifically 4 and For Answer) and ZoE as well as those who really like Gundam or similar shows.  If nothing seems to improve in a couple of months, I would probably hesitate even further to recomend this, it really needs work in the technical department.

I had played and finished Resident Evil so many times in my youth, on the PlayStation 1... oooh, so long ago! And then many years after, RE got remastered on the Gamecube. A good friend of mine got the GC exactly for RE Remaster so I could give it another shot and there it was... finished RE yet another time!
Now, almost a decade after the GC RE Remaster, we PC gamers, finally were able to get our hands into that fantastic piece of work! I have played this PC version for a few hours mainly to see the differences and they are notable quite frankly on the visual side. Graphics, textures, lighting and shadows were all contributed to the max of this Remaster.
The gameplay got fine-tuned to modern mechanic scheme. However, I couldn't play the game well with the keyboard and mouse. This is where you feel right at home with a gamepad, since this game is designed towards that after all!
Story is pretty much the same as GC RE Remaster so those of you who have played it, you won't be too surprised!
So without any more sidetracking, here's the rundown of pros and cons.
+Amazing visual upgrade.
+The true survival horror experience for the game that started it all!
+Modern controls for a revamped classic (gamepad speaking!).
+Return of the fixed cameras! Might put off newcomers who could become disoriented but this is how RE started it all so it is fine by me.
+Pure management of your inventory, of your saves, you health and when you should or shouldn't kill an enemy.
-Some awkward and blurry textures at times.
-Zombie clipping.
-Keyboard of mouse controls aren't that good. Use gamepad!
Good and fun revisit of the fantastic gloomy mansion! Might take a while to get accustomed to the controls mechanic vs the fixed cameras though! Just remember to use a gamepad!
I recommend this game as much to hardcore RE fans as the same to newcomers. This is the game that spawned the outstanding franchise so give it a shot!
However, if RE never was your bag long ago, it's doubtful it'll be with this one... best case, get on a deal!

A fun twist on the classic 'brick breaker' game,
Graphics are nice, although the aesthetic here certainly holds true to the game's title of being 'Grey'. The color palette is pretty much variants of grey, but oddly enough, it works. The lack of color makes you focus more on playing the game, and it gives off a sterile, futuristic look.
The fun twist in this game is that the bricks are dynamic in nature - as they get hit, they tumble around in all sorts of directions, and end up keeping you on your toes. The randomness of this can either help or hurt you, so no game is ever truly the same.
There's the typical 'good' and 'bad' powerups that occasionally spawn in as well. There's a total of 60 levels to keep you occupied here - some of them are made very well; others are just absolutely frustrating (who thought portals were a good idea?!).
I got all achievements in this game in about 5 hours. It's a fun little time waster for a buck. Don't expect anything too great, but have fun with it and enjoy its dynamic physics!

I really wanted to like this updated version of Brick Breaker, but very little effort was put into making this game appealing to gamers. There are a few novel ideas injected into the game, but they usually only appear in one or two levels out of the 60 that are playable. The experience itself is marred by poor game execution and frustration due to a lack of depth perception caused by the 3D environment displayed ONLY top down. Some levels contained pillars that came down from the ceiling and would drop cubes on the playing field, but they were large, obstructed your view, and never went away even after all blocks had been dropped! You can even see the ceiling pillars that obstruct your view in the game's screenshots (Screenshot #5). Additionally, I found that most of the power-ups ended up having negative effects on play. The question mark powerup was more-often-than-not a bad powerup such as shrink ball, shrink paddle, or wavy ball. The wavy ball powerup was seemingly programmed with the purpose of navigating to its death and around the paddle.
Also, the 3D buttons you had to hit to drop blocks, or the bumpers that would accelerate the ball speed, had a slight edge due to the fact they were 3D and this would almost always cause the ball to accelerate straight down to its death. It was extremely frustrating when i expected the ball to ricochet at an appropriate angle and it would instead be shot to death.
The major issue I had was the levels with a divide between two sections of the map in which the player's paddle would jump to the other side of the map if the ball entered a wormhole to transport it to the other side. The player would only have control of a paddle on one side of the map at any time, and the ball wormhole jumping between sides of the map would cause the player to lose control of the paddle. Sometimes the ball would repeatedly jump back and forth between sides of the map and then go directly out of bounds (to death) before the player could even see the other side of the playing field where the ball actualy was. Even if you were fast enough to move the paddle to intercept once or twice, the paddle would reset to a different position with each wormhole jump. One second you'd think you're about to save it, it would jump back and forth within a millisecond, and the ball would fly to death because your paddle reset to a different location.
Overall, I wouldn't recommend playing this game unless you wanted to complete it for the easy 100% achievements.

The Fall.
Where should I start?
The Fall is a sidescrolling puzzle game with a little bit of combat mixed in, so the gameplay is pretty straightforward. Most of the puzzles are complex enough to be interesting and frustrating (in a good way), but not impossible.
Combat is straightforward enough and not overly complex, just simple enough to be decent.
I was a bit offput by the controlls at first, but got used to them pretty fast.
Now, the best part: The story.
The story is singlehandedly the best part about this game, with great dialogue, interesting characters and an intriguing plot. There were times where I literally screamed WHAT THE F#%K! or HOLY S#@T!, something which few games manage to do these days. There are some legitamitely amazing (and horrible) (mostly horrible) moments in this that kept me on the edge of my seat throughout the game. The ONLY thing that kept the game from being almost perfect, was the fact that it ended on a mind♥♥♥♥ing cliffhanger, so I sadly cannot give it a full rating.
Still, on sale or not this game is entirely worth your time.
(9/10)

I grew up on Fable, and this is now the 4th time I've purchased the original. First when Fable came out, my older brother bought it for me for Christmas. Later that year, Fable: The Lost Chapters came out, so I re-purchased it there. I bought it on Xbox 360 when Fable: Anniversary first came out, and... was severely disappointed. The game crashed every 30 minutes, the graphical update really wasn't THAT great, the framerate was REALLY bad, leading to unresponsive menus and controls, and it honestly should have just held off for the proper 10 year anniversary and been ported to Xbox One.
Now, here we are, #4. I'm 3 hours in, the game crashed once in the first hour. Not off to a great start. I look it up online, and the solution is to have Steam verify the game's files. I go and do that, I've had no issues since. There's an odd little camera glitch where it kind of bobs and bounces when you're moving (when running with Vsync on), but it's better than screen tearing, so that's fine with me.
Honestly, for the actual review, the game is great. It's lovely playing the game at 60 Hz, the controls are incredibly responsive, the menus are great. I installed it onto my SSD, and those 30 second load screens of the original Xbox and 360 versions are a thing of the past. I load from anywhere in the game in under 3 seconds, and it's phenomenal.
So, is the game worth it? At $9, it's a steal. Are there bugs? Absolutely. Will the game crash again? Probably, but it's still happened MUCH less than on the 360 version, so it's a lot more stable on PC. Would I spend full price on it? Probably not, I would have gotten a refund after that first crash.

is a game that delivers exactly what it is meant to.  It is a casual experience that is truly casual; unlike the myriad of indie games that appear “casual” only to reveal themselves to be frustrating due to poor design/mechanics.  If you are looking for something relaxing to play after a long day, you’ll find that here.  The only down side being that it isn’t a very long game; there are only 60 total levels. But it is very reasonably priced and there is good replay value.
I grew up playing block-breaker games in the early 90s at the local pub. While my parents had their after-dinner drinks, I would pump quarters into the little touch-screen machine at the corner of the bar. So when I saw
for less loose change than I had in my pocket, I had to pick it up. And I’m glad I did.
is a very simple and enjoyable modern imagining of the block-breaker genre. It offers a nice blend of nostalgic charm and simple, relaxing gameplay. It is an excellent game to zone out to when you just need to unwind for a bit. But the best feature of
is how it remains pleasantly minimalist and simple while offering a nice array of unique and individualized takes on the long established genre.
It is also worth noting that the soundtrack is highly enjoyable and works perfectly to encapsulate the feel of the game.  This soundscape helps create a very relaxing and “Zen” atmosphere that is easy to zone out to. If music is an important part of your relaxing game choices, you should be pleased with what you find here.
Lastly, just be sure to note that
is a very short and minimal game. It won’t appeal to everyone; especially “hardcore” gamers.  But if you like having a go-to-list of simple, relaxing games for those days you’re too tired to play something mentally taxing, then you should consider this strongly as a candidate.

Grey Cubes is a Breakout/Arkanoid style game which ventures into using the third dimension. For the better or worse.
The level design is nothing short of impressive and most of the sixty levels feel unique. The main twist Grey Cubes brings to the table is the use of height. Sometimes it's as simple as hitting risen floor tiles or retractable walls to reach the blocks, it goes as crazy as rising the floor under your ball as it runs over it, changing the level dynamically, and even having two height levels to play at. But it doesn't stop there. Other often used features are portals for your ball to warp through, either on one field or to a completely independent area of the board, and levels where you control a top and bottom paddle. Some maps have angled walls to mess with you and even more have bouncing walls. Others have no blocks in them at the start and they will get thrown in over time or by hitting a switch. Or they are just invisible at first. One level is even a wind tunnel and after some time the whole board is blown to the other side. Or how about a level with a giant switch in the back which temporarily turns the blocks unbreakable?
In terms of pick-ups the game is much tamer. You have your standard size changing of ball and paddle (both only in one step up bigger/smaller), split balls (which sadly only affects the original ball), instant block destroy, security line, catching paddle ... pretty much everything you expect and know from other games. In each level you are also given a magnet power which activates after a certain threshold is destroyed and then recharges after use. During it's activation it will attract your ball towards the blocks. Excellent to use against some level elements and to deal with those pesky last few blocks you never seem to hit.
Sadly with all the effort put into layout it feels that player experience has gotten the short end. Sometimes the level elements and pick-ups are obstructing the view and height differences are not as recognisable as they could be.While the graphics are pretty stylized and minimal, it still happens that you lose track of the ball if everything around turns brighter. And don't get me started on a ball zipping through the portals like crazy only to besuddenly ejected right into the out. It's also missing no "dead zone" between paddle and blocks, so they can be bounced right next to the paddle or even go off the map. I also experienced some stutter though the frame rate stayed constant, the paddle suddenly going all the way to left and the ball going over the paddle thanks to coming from a higher level. None of this frequents much but it's annoying when it happens.
Those flaws hardly make it a bad game, but still one that could have been so much better.
Completion should take between 3-4 hours, depending on skill and luck. After that you can either improve your personal highscore for each level or grind out some of the achievements. The end screen promised new levels soon, though after a more than year of its Steam release it's anyone's guess if/when Deion Mobile delivers on this promise.
Anyhow, it's a well spent one dollar.

Probably my favourite game in the list of hyper-difficult platformers on Steam,
uses a simplistic art style with equally simple mechanics which work well together to create an enjoyable, addictive and challenging game, it also holds the "excellent soundtrack" trophy like many others of the same genre. The PC version also comes with a level editor which is a really nice addition and gives the game some more playability.
The objective is simple, jump, clear and doge oncoming obstacles and reach the end of the levels without dying. Sounds easy enough, but the short time window which you have to make your decision on whether or when to jump or not makes things incredibly difficult, though sometimes equally frustating.

".

This is the only thing about this game that I dislike, like which has been stated in many other reveiws. So with the occasional bugs aside, this is definitely a game to add to your collection if you are a fan of difficult platformers, it is definitely up there with Geometry, Super Meat Boy, Electronic Super Joy, Bit Trip Runer etc, it also has one of the best soundtracks around, so if this goes on sale, don't miss it.

What is Resident Evil HD Remaster?
An updated version of the 2002 Gamecube release, which was in turn a remake of the 1996 original.
Is it any good?
Its fantastic. The first game in the Resident Evil franchise has always been my favourite, and this has to be considered the best version. I never played the 2002 update, where many of the puzzles and area layouts were changed, new monsters and story details were added, so much of this felt like a fresh new experience for me.
What pleased me?
•	Classic survival horror gameplay. A smaller number of dangerous enemies compared to later games which have huge numbers of weak enemies. I actually got killed by the first zombie because I was overconfident! Limited ammo, health and save game items, so you need to be careful not to waste any.
•	Some puzzles don't have to be solved to complete the game, but they determine which of the multiple endings you get, which rewards exploration.
•	Playing as either Jill or Chris provides a significantly different experience, because they have access to different weapons, inventory size, damage resistance and story elements.
•	You can choose between the original "tank" controls or a more modern control scheme.
•	Updated graphics. The mansion and surrounding areas never looked so good.
•	Mostly stable. I had a couple of crashes after I quit the game (had to kill it on task manager) but no problems during actual gameplay.
What disappointed me?
•	There is a widely known bug which causes the mouse pointer to stay visible during gameplay, which will destroy immersion if you play with mouse and keyboard. You basically have no choice but to play with a gamepad (and then push the mouse off screen). Not a problem for me because I own a gamepad, but in 2015 there is no excuse for this bug to exist.
•	Fixed camera angles are a bit annoying. There were several occasions where Jill/Chris are looking at an enemy that is standing right in front of them but I can't see it because I'm looking at my character, which made me waste some ammo. Yes its part of the original experience, but I wonder if anything could have been tweaked to make this less of an issue.
Overall recommendation
Fans of the franchise should find alot to enjoy in this remake, especially if like me, you only played the original. And if you've never played any Resident Evil game, this is the best place to start.
I also just want to say that I've never had the opportunity to play either RE2 or RE3, so if Capcom would release a similar updated version of those games on Steam, I would buy them immediately.

Bad Engrish aside, this game is really fun.
It's like Diablo with magic/guns/scfi,
great loot drops all the time and from random monsters.
There's different types of guns and different branches (classes) use different special guns,
with a couple regular types (rifle, pistol) every class can use.
There's a support (healer/paladin) that uses shotguns,
panzer (warrior/tank) that uses chainsaw (no ammo req.) and flamethrower,
predator (mage) that uses minigun and rocket launcher,
and sniper (archer) that uses sniper rifle.
Each branch also has different skills/abilities with the usual skill tree and active/passive abilities unlocked by skill points.
There's a durability system, but it's pretty minor cost to repair, and it takes a while to lose it.
The tutorial weapon reward is a durability weapon that doesn't use ammo but durability (since it's like a temp weapon), but any other gun/armor, you can just repair and keep using.
There is a ammo system, but guns have a high max ammo amount,
and you can keep three guns types (with all different ammo types) equipped on your character to easily switch from (with hotkeys), and any other guns in your inventory to equip when you want.
Ammo can last a while if you use different guns, and the return to town skill has a 1 min cooldown, so it's not a big deal.
Armor you find actually changes the character's look, with different colors, too.
(Which is really nice, don't know how many games I liked that you couldn't effect the character's look with the armor you found/equipped).
Shooting/blowing up enemies or killing them with skills, is really satisfying.
So to sum it up, it's a fun hack&slash with some rpg.

Stay with me on this one. This is a tale of victory, of betrayal, of revenge, and of consequence.
I was but a simple lord with a simple goal. To make the Kingdom of the Nords the most powerful kingdom Caldaria had ever seen. I fought alongside my king and fellow lords as equals on the battlefields, and many a heroic battle was fought and won. I asked for very little, but my own slew of personal conquests saw fit to reward me with personal lands. I accepted these fiefs with grace, and invested all of my time, money, and effort into making sure my villages prospered and were safe from enemy attacks.
And that's when it all went bad.
It was a day, much like any other day. I was scouting around my castle for enemy lords who would dare assault me. That's when my weekly budget came in. I gave it a quick glance, and almost tossed it aside when I noticed some error; a village was missing. For a moment, I was confused. Had my messenger tower failed, and my village been raided without my knowledge? No, that cannot be, the village would still be listed. Bewildered, I investigated the cause of this discrepancy on the world map, and noticed that the castle to which my village belonged to was no longer allied to the Nords, but the Rhodoks. How could this be? We were not at war with them at the time, so how did this happen? As I investigated further, I found the cause of my problems.
Jarl Gearth. Or, as he is now known, 'Count' Gearth.
This weaselly dastard has always rubbed me the wrong way, and now all my suspicions had paid off in a most unfortunate manner. He had defected from the Kingdom of the Nords and allied himself with the Rhodoks. With him, he took all the castles he had owned, and with the castles went their adjoining villages. As such, Tadsamesh now belonged to the Rhodoks, and along with it, all my effort. It seemed to me, as a lord who was bound by honor, that there was only one course of action.
Long story short, I murdered Gearth's army and he's currently sitting in my dungeon. 10/10, gonna go take his castle now too, screw whatever peace treaty we had.

Project Nimbus, the 3D mecha-action game, is one of the more ambitious early-access titles that I've had the pleasure of playing. Alongside the sweet graphics, this game offers an intriguing plot (all two acts of it), and the missions showcase a great balance between "destroy this" and "protect that". The voice-acting and subtitles are a little suspect, but the space-opera vibe is appreciated.
Most importantly, the game is a lot of fun. The controls are fluid, and allow the player to easily soar in-between scores of enemy mechs. I love the amount of freedom available to the player. Enemy targets can be approached from any direction, and the chaos can take place anywhere, even at insanely high altitudes. The ability to boost from the ocean to the end of Earth's atmosphere in less than two seconds is just awesome. I also appreciate the little things, like how Survival Mode's scoring changes, depending on which mech is used. The slow-motion button is also really cool. Sometimes I use it just to admire some kills. Altogether, Project Nimbus is fast, frenetic, and very entertaining, and it'll undoubtedly impress gamers when it's finally completed.
But I believe that the game can be even better.
First off, I'm not too concerned about the amount of content in this game. The final version is going to include 27 missions, a "sand-box" mode, and Survival. While you can't expect a
amount of hours from Project Nimbus, you're certain to get your money's worth. However, If I could make a suggestion right now, it would be for additional maps in Survival mode. These maps could offer different sets of enemies, and perhaps even unique lay-outs. Perhaps the developer is already kicking around this idea, and they're just setting it aside until the campaign is finished. In any case, I expect this game to deliver in terms of content.
Secondly, it's worth pointing out that there are some technical issues present in the game. I had to restart a mission early on, because an enemy had somehow become trapped inside a building. The option to toggle v-sync is currently unavailable, which results in some bad screen-tearing. A number of the effects - such as bullets and booster-trails - look unfinished. The frame-rate can also take some knocks in a few missions. The camera can also be problematic depending on the current situation, but I'd hard-pressed to come up with a 3D game that hasn't suffered from camera troubles. These issues can be resolved, so I'm not too worried. Even now, the quality of the game still shines through these problematic aspects.
Now this is where it gets complicated. I have a few suggestions of my own that I'm going to share. While I believe that implementing them could make Project Nimbus an even better game, the possibility exists that it could have the opposite effect. Honestly, I probably shouldn't say anything, because I adhere to one of the strictest rules of game-design:
This is a rule that can go hand-in-hand with the saying: "It's not for everyone". If a game tries to do everything for any and all gamers, the final result is liable to be very bland and unremarkable. For the most part, the development team should stick to their vision, and try not to accommodate the whims of the gaming populace. All that said, here are my suggestions for improving Project Nimbus.
- The sword needs tweaking. Usually melee weapons in mecha games are immensely satisfying. Here, it just doesn't quite hit the mark. Most of the time it feels like swings don't actually connect, and my mech will just move past the target, and they may or may not be destroyed. It's hard to appreciate a good melee kill. To counter this, I'm thinking that the mech should swing the sword downwards, or perhaps at an upward angle. Better yet, there could be two melee attacks, with the trade-off being that the more powerful one can stop the mech just in front of their target, which could leave them open to attack. One thing I've noticed is that the sword seems to work better when not locked on to a target.
- Larger explosions. While I'm no rocket surgeon, I know when the "Heck Yeah!" sensors in my brain are being tripped. Destroying an enemy and being treated to a worthy explosion never really gets old. Granted, if the explosions are too large they can become disorienting, so it's best to shoot for a subtle but still noticeable effect. Also, while it can be difficult to notice (due to distance and scale), I'd like to see enemies shatter to pieces when they explode(especially when hit by a powerful gun). On occasion, I'll see a transporter or other ship break apart, but the effect looks rather cheap. Maybe the inside of the mechs (at least the parts that are exposed to the player) should have a basic "circuitry" texture. Players notice it enough to say "Wow! That's cool!" but not to the point where they'll think "Wait. Does that make sense?"
- Better damage indicators. Whenever your mech takes damage in this game, the screen turns red. I think it would be less distracting (and possibly more immersive) if damage caused the UI to scramble for a second, or even just blink red. The damage to the UI should match the severity of the weapon. A few bullets from a machine-gun should feel very different compared to getting hit with a missile spread or a blast from an ion cannon. The UI effects shouldn't be permanent though; just a visual effect to get the point across.
- Changes to the weapon system. Currently, the Mirai and its variants are a little overpowered. This is mostly due to the presence of smart missiles and funnels (AI drones). I propose that there should be a customizable load-out before each mission. This would give players the opportunity to select different guns. Furthermore, these load-outs would limit which weapons could be taken along. There's really no reason to have both missiles and funnels, as they offer the player the option to stay far away from most engagements and let the automatic weaponry do all the work. I suggest that players should be forced to make a choice, but also have a selection of weapons that allow them greater flexibility to develop their play-style.
Again, these are all just suggestions. Even if the developer of this game were to ignore them all*, I would still consider Project Nimbus a game worth looking into. Its development still has a long way to go, so I'll be sure to keep you all updated as it progresses.
*Although I really think they should look into the whole "screen turning red" business.

I went in expecting an Armored Core-like experience. I did get that, to an extent, but the game has a few too many technical issues. It lags even on the lowest graphic setting, the camera is really jittery and I can't see anything properly half the time, and the game has crashed a few times within the short period that I played it. I couldn't even access certain settings (like low graphical setting) without the game freaking out and showing me a bunch of puked up graphics on my screen. It was uncanny. Other issues include clipping, weapons being kind of buggy (the psycho drones in particular are awkward in terms of how you activate them, and half the time i'm not even sure if they activate or survive), and the worst would be severe frame rate drops if you're too close to an explosion.
I know it's still in early access, but I waited for almost 2 years for this to become stable. It's kinda like Starbound, where I doubt it'll be stable any time soon. Maybe it's just my personal experience,  but I wouldn't recommend it. It hurts me inside, because I'd love to see more giant robot games on steam, and I can't completely condemn Project Nimbus. It has some unique ideas and I see a concept of gameplay that could really shine through, but at the time, it's just not worth 15 dollars. I'll definitely consider looking at this game again once they finish the single player, which going by this rate should be around 2018 (if the dev releases 7 missons per year without delays). But I'm not getting my hopes up.

A long time ago, in computer terms, there was a game called Breakout. You moved a paddle across the bottom of the screen, bouncing a ball to destroy bricks in a wall at the top. It was a simple game, so simple that magazines would actually print listings of code in their pages that you could type in to get your own version at home. (Imagine that today!)
Later games, like Arkanoid, added new features that made it more interesting. Now comes Grey Cubes, which drags the whole thing into the 21st century. It includes many familiar power-ups and power-downs, like a longer bat or a multi-ball, and some new ones, but the big addition is 3D physics. Now when the ball hits a block it isn't immediately destroyed, but it moves, scattering blocks across the screen. Every level is a bit different, whether the blocks drop from the sky, or maybe there are walls that you have to hit to make them move out of the way. There is even a level where you can make gravity switch from one end to the other, making the blocks and the ball slide from one side of the screen to the other.
Graphics-wise, it is done in a muted grey-blue style, which fits the minimalist style of the game. The blocks are larger and fewer. There are plenty of power-ups, and there is even a 'magnet' which is very useful for getting hard to reach blocks. The game is certainly much more enjoyable and easy to play than the versions of old.
Too easy? There are sixty levels, but it doesn't start posing a challenge until the second half of the levels. It would be poor value for money if it weren't so cheap. But it
very cheap, and it's enjoyable, so I recommend it.
(Note, there are supposedly more levels coming.)

This is a slow-paced and oddly irritating brick-breaker. It requires a bit more in the way of patience than skill.
The main gimmick seems to be that the blocks can be knocked around when hit. Unfortunately, Shatter already did this, and did it quite a bit better.
Most levels have a sprinkle of puzzle elements: moving and flipping walls, portals, switches which must be hit to allow access to the remaining blocks. Some of them are interesting and creative, others are downright badly designed. For instance, some levels have portals which randomly change position, meaning that a portal could move onto the ball at any time and send it into the pit. Some levels have switches which temporarily turn all of the blocks unbreakable, which is just as annoying as it sounds. You have a magnet powerup which starts charging once over half of the blocks in a level are gone, which can help you eliminate the remaining blocks by drawing the ball towards them. However, the level design will often render it useless; since it will go directly at the nearest brick, it will often get stuck on a wall and just run out. Sometimes it even orbits the bricks without hitting them.
The minimalistic style kind of works… kind of. It seemed stylish at first, but I grew tired of it before the game’s end, as I couldn’t shake the feeling that it was just low-effort.
The campaign is 60 levels long, and the last 10 are profoundly infuriating, involving double pits, shifting portals, and moving pipes which obscure large portions of the play field at once.
There are more than a few glitches. On the final level, I encountered a glitch that caused the last brick to remain permanently unbreakable, undoing 20 minutes of progress. It’s also possible to soft-lock the game by activating the magnet powerup on level 1 before the tutorial message tells you to.
There are no leaderboards, so points really don’t matter. You’re supposed to lose 20,000 points whenever you run out of lives, but you can refill your lives anytime you want by quitting and restarting a level, so points matter even less.
The ending screen promises “More levels coming soon,” but fat chance on that.
I give the game a 5 / 10. For $0.99, it could have been a cheap and easy 100%... except that the last three achievements are quite grindy, especially the one which requires spending 4 hours playing (in-level time, I might add… and it’s only counted on levels that you win!) when the main campaign only takes about 1-2 hours. Overall, it’s an okay game; kind of creative but also kind of boring. You’re not missing much if you don’t play it.

Nice turn-based "american football" game with warhammer universe characters and tabletop rules.
Tabletop rules will take some time to learn so here is short guide of basics:
There will be events like picking up the ball from ground, blocking opponent character or moving out of opponents attack zone (all characters has attack zone around them).
These events use one of the characters ability to see result of this event, you even succeed or fail in that event.
Every time you fail, you lose your turn.
Example: Picking up the ball uses characters agility, the lower of your characters agility the more like you will fail picking up that ball, the higher your characters ability the more likely you succeed.
Block uses characters strength, the higher your characters strength the more likely you succesfully block opponent character.
There is also other factor when blocking, it helps if your other characters are near this target you try to block.
Not fully familiar with this rule yet, but it certainly adds your chances up if there is one enemy and he is surrounded by 3 of your characters.
Also all characters have attack zone around them.
You can enter this attack zone without getting blocked by enemy but when you try move out of this attack zone opponent will try automatically block you, then you need to dodge this block and this dodge uses your characters agility, so higher agility means you most likely dodge this block and wont lose your turn.
So that is the basics, there are much more rules and events and you will find yourself from many situations asking yourself questions but also you will find answers for your questions the more you play and meet those situations/conditions again again and again.
So characters have abilities like i mentioned earlier.
These are:
how many squares he can move
strength
agility
armor value (if this is low your characters will injury more easier and thats always bad)
Also these characters level up and gain skills.
Few example of skills
Block skill = Your character wont get knocked down when using "Both down" option in blocking situations.
(Normally you would lose your turn if your character gets knocked down, but this can prevent it but your enemy is still knocked down, unless he also has this special block skill)
Dodge = if you moving out of enemys attack zone and enemy succesfully blocks you, you will try dodge again
+ many many more skills
Anyways, i rlly recommend this game.

Released at a fair price and gorgeously-redone with better graphics, RESIDENT EVIL is pretty much where it all started; the first in a long long series that gave players the true definition of survival horror.
tl;dr at the bottom
Originally a GameCube remake of the PlayStation 1 game, Resident Evil: Director's Cut, this redux is perfect for newcomers to the series, gamers who started with later RE instalments and want to delve into its roots, or simply for horror game enthusiasts. Contrary to modern RE titles, RESIDENT EVIL favours subtlety and exploration, while also throwing abominations at almost every turn. You'll sometimes find yourself down to your last few bullets and need to make a quick decision to fight or flee.
Players have a choice of sticking with the original tank movement controls or opting for the RE6 style, where the character runs in a direction without having to turn. Thankfully this can be switched at any time, as there were moments I got stuck in rooms since the game uses fixed camera angles. In my opinion though, the controls and gameplay mechanics have held up extraordinarily well, so I just stick to the original control scheme.
The voice acting is a tad mediocre, as it was in the original, and the sound design is intact. This is exactly how I remembered RESIDENT EVIL, and feel that the root of the series has received a respectful and well-deserved HD treatment.
As I'm typing this, I'm sort of finding myself lost in nostalgia and don't feel like I'm really giving an objective review for those who may be new to RESIDENT EVIL, so I will quickly summarize down below.
SUMMARY
+The original game is perfectly preserved, but with a graphical upgrade
+Players have the option to use original tank controls or RE6 style movement and can be switched at any time
+Atmosphere is absorbing and monsters are terrifying in tight cramped corridors
+Gives a true survival horror experience, where ammo is scarce and random occurances can be fatal
+There are small added bonuses, like RE5 costumes for Jill & Chris, and an easier difficulty setting
+Perfect game for horror game fans and/or newcomers to the Resident Evil series
-Voice acting, like in the original, is subpar
-Some people will be turned off by the difficulty; even on lower difficulties, the game can be quite challenging
-With fixed camera angles, some areas of the mansion are difficult to navigate

To be honest and fair, this is more of a point and click game. I know this has been a huge seller to Gamers, but, Just not my thing. I'm more of a First Person/Third Person kind of Gamer. If this seems negative, it's not meant to sound like it, just wasn't what I was expecting. Thanks for reading.

I hadn't the opportunity to play the Gamecube version but was a massive fan of the original. I would say that yes this is a great remake to get feeling of nostalgia as well as something new. I don't think you should bother if you had already played it on Gamecube.
What's new is a whole lot of extra rooms in the mansion, its like everywhere they hit an external wall they made it a big bigger with an extra door leading to another hallway or an outside terrace etc. This stuff was all very nice. The puzzles in the mansion are different enough from the original that I was quite satisfied. Ultimately the new areas provide a new experience getting through the mansion. Also noteworthy is that the courtyard is hugely expanded. The Guardhouse and Lab have roughly the same amount of stuff to do as the original. All in all I found just enough extra puzzle work to tickle my brain and I thought I was stuck a couple of times, tempted to check the internet... but glad I didn't.
The mechanic of burning zombies was really awesome, though playing the game as Chris that fuel flask taking an extra slot, and only able to burn 2 zombies before needing to refuel, was slightly annoying. But only I think because in the past I would have had that extra slot for health or items. Honestly its a good extra challenge, and I came to the conclusion that I would burn some of the zombies in well frequented areas and the others, well just hope for the best. And I found out the hard way what happens if you use all your ammo killing every zombie in the mansion without bothering to burn any. Good gosh I had to restart the game I got myself in such a health/ammo pickle.
Actually the first run through the mansion is the main challenge of the game, and beyond that it is frankly really easy for the most part. I played as Chris on the hardest skill level btw. The Sharks and Plant42 were the only enemies I found threatening once I got out the mansion for the first time (wow the sharks, such an impressive scene compared to the original equivalent). I'm sorry to say, the snake boss was really easy on both occasions. I used to get swallowed by that thing in the original but now he seems just easy to dodge. The spiders and hunters seem to have trouble hitting you too. I never died to them once, whereas in the original I couldn't count the number of times a hunter had swiped my head off my shoulders. You get all these blue herbs and I'm not even sure why, you might get poisoned twice by spiders and that will be it for the whole game. And the end game tyrants are slow and easy to dodge. I don't like spoiling it but I think people ought to know, the second half of the game you could pretty much play without using an ink ribbon. I had about 50 shotgun shells left too. I collected every first aid can in the game but didn't use one of them. I used most of my herbs but probably 10 mixes left over.
But that first run through the mnsion, holy hell I thought that this was setting the stage for a really really tough adventure. I died so many times to the zombies and the super zombies that I nearly gave up. I ended up killing all the 'slow' zombies with the knife just so I wouldn't run out of ammo. Might not have been neccessary, you could dodge most of them, but this was just my playstyle I guess. By the time I was finished with the Guardhouse though, just felt like going along for a cinematic ride after that. Some mental challenges remained but no creature challenges. I actually felt guilty dispatching or ignoring the hunters so easily.
There is a lot said by others about the mixed bag that is the 'hd' backdrops. Personally I found that this did not bother me, The lower quality backdrops were in there, but if I hadn't read about it I might not have noticed. The character models look good and in general the game feels nicely polished in terms of storylines, cut scenes and just enough differentiation from the original to keep it interesting.
...Having grown up with the very first original - this is an A+ remake in my opinion. Loved it.
I've played almost all RE games but this one is just the best. It's a reliving of the old times with excellent HD graphics. Totally worth the time and money!!!

The gameplay is surprisingly deep for a match 3, and you'll find you may actually need to plan your moves ahead of time in later stages, at least occasionally.
There's some explicit artwork to be unlocked, and generally speaking, the artwork is fairly nicely done. Your mileage will vary, depending on how much you do or don't enjoy the art style.
The only thing I don't really like is the voice acting, which in many cases is average or below. By the same token, there's not very many match 3 games with voice acting and overarching plots (if any at all). Again, your mileage will vary, depending on your preferences.
The game runs smoothly, though some people have complained about difficulty/glitches in the girls' final stages.
This is definitely one of those games you can play in short bursts or extended sessions, depending on your available time. I find that to be refreshing, because there's so many games that require a much higher commitment of your time.
You can play for twenty minutes and feel like you've made progress, as opposed to some games where you're looking at a minimum of an hour or two before you feel like you've done enough.
Overall, I'd call the game a solid 8/10, though it's definitely banking on the sex gimmick to hold your attention and extend your playtime.
