That being said, the world is incredibly rich and absolutely massive. The music is still my favorite of the series, as is the terrain. From volcanic wastelands to snowy islands laden with werewolves, Morrowind has it all.
If you find yourself bored with the 100s of hours of content, there are thousands of mods for Morrowind, many of which are worth downloading. Are the graphics too rough for you? There's a mod for that. Want a better inventory management system? There's a mod for that too.
Whether you're a fan of Skyrim or fans of RPGs in general, you owe it to yourself to play this classic.

There are certain themes that, year after year, decade after decade, developers return to time and again.
In 1976, Atari released the block-busting Breakout, where players were charged with breaking down walls with nothing more than a ball and a paddle at the bottom of the screen to pat it with. It's a set up that has been tapped up as many times as Tetris or, if you're looking for a more recent example, even Flappy Bird.
Yet, as is sadly not often the case with many clones, everyone who takes on Breakout tends to bring something new to the table. A technical advantage afforded to them by the era the game is released in.
In the case of Grey Cubes – which has to have one of the most uninspiring names on the App Store – its unique selling point is a refined take on physics. Whereas most Breakout style games take a 2D-based top-to-bottom view, Grey Cubes plays as if viewed from above, with the cubes that adorn its name being knocked over like boxes in a storeroom.
It's a take on physics that allows Grey Cubes to be somewhat fluid, almost playful with the way its levels are set out. The game's intentionally stripped back, Portal-like styling facilitates block-based levels that move, interact and generally play havoc with proceedings. It's here that developer BulkyPix has attempted to bring a 30 year old classic slap bang into 2014.
The basic concept behind the game, however, is largely unchanged. Your one point of contact is the paddle at the bottom of each stage, which you move by simply sliding your finger accordingly. A swipe up flings the first ball into play, and then it's simply a case of clearing the board of all blocks while keeping the ball in the arena for as long as you can.
There are two main elements that help keep things interesting during Grey Cubes' 60 stages. Firstly, the addition of power-ups – and 'power downs', if you like – into play. These fall from smashed up blocks supposedly randomly, offering up everything from multiple balls to a safety net below your paddle should you catch them. Said power downs, of course, are somewhat less inviting, making your paddle smaller and, essentially, making it harder to keep control of the action.
The other element is the levels themselves which, as you progress, start to make their presence known, pushing more blocks into play, acting as barriers and generally making a nuisance of themselves. It's here, however, where BulkyPix has brought its creativity into play; while other Breakout clones spend their time simply mixing the patterns of the blocks up, Grey Cubes is far more focused on making the environment they sit in is pulling the strings.
And it's this that pulls you through. The beauty of any Breakout style game is that it can be pulled out and played in short bursts, and the variety of levels on offer in Grey Cubes – each one touching base with its predecessor, but still moving play forwards – ensures that it can serve as your go to game for your five minute on-the-way-to-work fix.
But, at the same time, while Grey Cubes makes every effort to merge a familiar concept with fresh forms of gameplay, it can't quite escape the fact that, when all is said and done, it's still Breakout. That's not to say developer BulkyPix should be criticised for not reinventing the wheel: ultimately, if you pull a game like Grey Cubes too far away from its origins it loses all structure and, in practice, what the studio has delivered here is a modern take on an undoubted classic.
Nevertheless, Grey Cubes is ultimately a game that'll serve as a better companion for those new to the block breaking genre rather than any Breakout stalwarts. It's delivery is impressive and its variety is to be admired, but – by choice or by accident – its structure will likely rekindle any retro players' affection for the original rather than spark an entirely new romance. For newcomers, however, Grey Cubes could well become a mobile classic in its own right.
Verdict
An inventive spin on Breakout and its clones that brings physics into play to a greater degree than ever, Grey Cubes is the perfect first stop for those new to the block-breaking genre and will revive old passions for the game that inspired it for longterm players. Just don't expect it to reinvent the wheel.

This fresh take on Breakout gives players new ways to strategize and offers an interesting twist at a gaming classic.  Just long enough to wear out its welcome, this game offers a good distraction to more casual gamers or those looking for something new yet familiar.

REmake (
esident
vil re
/remaster) is every bit the original with modernized graphics and controls. Resident Evil is a definitive classic zombie horror game revered since the mid-90s. Whether you are new to the franchise, seen the movies, or played the later titles, I don't think you'll have a better experience exploring the RE universe than playing REmake. I grew up playing the original but never completed till now and I wasn't disappointed. Maybe a little lol. You'll be reminded just how spoiled games of the past generation have made you.
To explain, the mansion estate is one confusing as hell place to navigate around as you investigate the mansion with many questions and little answers. This combined with the overall claustrophobic hallways, camera angles, zombies and you're set for an immersive scare. The developers know exactly when and how to enforce this without turning this into a shooter. You'll question who the hell ever made a mansion layout such as this and why doors are locked with different keys and why you have to micro manage your small inventory and WTF CRIMSON HEAD ZOMBIES?!?!
With the remaster, you'll enjoy the option for modernized controls and graphics. <- This: FFF tank controls, if you want to know what it feels like to be completely out of control, try these. Not being in control of the camera is enough for most, but this is next level. The modern controls feel great on both KB+Mouse and controller. The game ran exceptionally smooth and bug free experience from beginning to end. The updated graphics definitely helped expand upon the immersion.
Resident Evil is a good challenging game; fair without unnecessary hand-outs nor pity. Fight or run, it's up to you. Lost? Study the map, explore, remember what keys you need to open what doors, take notes. Be prepared to investigate and solve more puzzles than massacring zombies. Resident Evil is tedious, yes, but so is staying alive. Buy this and have fun! :InkRibbon:

This is quite easily the most frustrating, really-want-to-like-but-also-want-my-computer-in-one-piece game I have ever encountered.
I've played the game before, some two or three years ago. I was frustrated then by the absurd strings of dice rolls churned out by the game's Random Number Generator and was able to rather easily convince myself to put it down. After watching a few other people play it, however, I was just about ready to delve back into it, so I got it on sale on Steam and commenced with the delving over a weekend.
In the immortal words of Ron Burgundy, "I immediately regret this decision."
As someone who mostly plays single player games, the best element of Blood Bowl - its multiplayer experience, which is incidentally probably the best way to learn the game - is lost on me, and even when the tutorial does its best to explain things, there are still elements of the game that require studying the massive rule book to grasp, reminding me why I never got into Games Workshop titles in the first place. The game lacks accessibility for new players in its admittedly varied single player modes, often putting them in situations where they must lose *a lot* to master the game while the AI waffles between bafflingly stupid and gleefully exploiting the RNG. It's true that a number of studies have been undertaken to see if the dice lean a certain way and have come back negative for bias, but that doesn't ease the frustration of playing the game and experiencing the bizarre runs of ones and sixes and unsatisfactory results (nor does the small handful of very loud, very condescending voices in the established community who try to shout down frustrated players).
In short, there's too much luck involved for it to be an enjoyable strategy experience in a game with a steep learning curve that essentially requires having friends with the game to get the most enjoyment out of it. The only thing separating it from the actual tabletop version is the reasonable price, which works against it; if I wanted to learn how to play a tabletop game, I would take the extra time and effort to learn the board game rather than playing the video game version of it.
Unless you're a tabletop Blood Bowl player looking for the digital experience or have someone else (preferably a small group of friends) who is also looking to buy the game, stay away from this one.

I have over 500 games in my Steam account, and the vast majority of them are still unplayed. So now I'm dedicating an hour to each of these games and writing a series of One Hour Reviews. An hour isn't very long to judge a game on, so think of this as more of a first impression, and take this review in the spirit in which it's given. Be sure to read other reviews from players who have spent more time in the game.
One Hour Reviews #26 - Blood Bowl: Legendary Edition
I had heard of Blood Bowl, and knew it was based on a tabletop game, but otherwise I did not know anything about it.  So going in, I had no idea what to expect.
Since I hadn't played before, I started with the tutorial, hoping it would help me understand how to play the game.  After waiting awhile for it to load (longer than I would have expected), it opens with a pair of commentators to explain the rules of the game, with some groan-worthy humor thrown in.
The tutorial starts out simple enough by explaining the basic camera controls, and how to change cameras.  Then it covers "tackle zones" and placing your teams starting positions for the kick off.  It also explains the concept of re-rolls, which allow you to re-roll a die result, with each team only getting a limited number of these.
But things quickly get complicated once the actual gameplay starts.  The game is filled with all of these different skills that players can have.  Each skill acts as a conditional modifier, depending on the situation.  For example, when picking up the ball, the game will "roll a die" and if the roll is too low, then you'll fail to pick up the ball.  But, if your player has the "Sure Hands" skill, then the player gets a second roll when the first one fails.
It seems that pretty much every action in the game has one of these skills associated with it.  If I try to pass the ball, there's a 'Pass' skill that lets you re-roll a failed roll.  The game also starts talking about stats like Agility, and some kind of "Agility Table" that is used for skill checks, but apparently you have to read the rules to see that.
Next the tutorial moves onto blocking and pushing past defenders.  Now even more skill checks are coming into play.  Here the roll is based on the Strength stat, and not only are there skills for influencing the block result, but also whether or not players get injured or not.
As the tutorial continues into movement, dodging and blitzing, and even more die rolls and skills, I can feel my eyes starting to glaze over.   By the time the tutorial gets to the first turnover, I am pretty much lost.  I'm just kind of reading and nodding along at this point.
Just to give an idea of how quickly the tutorial starts piling on skills, here's one of the things it tries to explain to me:  "Since Krug Painspear has the tackle skill, Jean-Paul mussen is knocked down with a 'Defender Stumbles', even though he has the Dodge skill, which would normally allow him to regard that as a simple push-back."
The commentators swear that although it sounds complicated, it's all really easy after a few games.  I'm not so sure.  I'm reminded of this episode of Star Trek where Kirk has been captured by these gangsters, and he introduces them to a card game called Fizzbin.  Only the game doesn't exist, and Kirk is making up the rules as he goes, and the gangsters are completely confused as Kirk tries to explain the game.  That's exactly how I felt after finishing the tutorial.
So clearly there is a learning curve here.  So it comes down to whether or not it's worth spending the time to learn the game.  If you are a fan of the board game, then it seems pretty obvious you'll enjoy this as well.    If you like tabletop war games in general, and aren't intimidated by rules, then it's also likely you'll enjoy this.  But if you are more of a casual player, then this game will likely go right over your head as it did mine.

Heroes & Generals is a semi-realistic FPS with RPG elements. The maps are decently large, though they do lack a bit of detail. There are currently 3 factions with all different equipment and models.
Pros include:
1.Fun to play with epic moments (at times)
2.Rewards skill and thought. Actually tatics can win the day if your team actually tries to listen (weapon modifications and perks aside).
3.A interesting "War" system/map. Good for people who arent interested in the shooty bits of the game.
4. A decent selection of weapons, though some of them are more useless than others (You cant use the bipod on MG's, though their recoil is similar to how MG's actually handle, thus making them inferior in many situations where they shouldnt be.)
5. Has the party wagon.
6. Is currently still alive (receiving periodic updates)
_______________________________________________________________________
Cons include:
1.A horse-load of grinding if you are below rank 10 (rewards are complete crap for lower ranks). Weapon mods below this rank will make you go bankrupt.
2.A decent bit of pay-to-win with all the premium stuff (a rank 2 can get a tiger if he shills enough money).
3.Sniperrrrr!!
4. A lack of content normally associated with WW2 (No artillery, boats/ships, other nations and their equipment ((where the bloody hell is the bloody brits?!), etc).
5.Always online. If the servers go down or you dont have internet, you cant play the game. If the servers ever get shutdown, you've lost all that hard work on your character. This brings me to my next point.
6. No community servers or mods.
Overall, I think it is a decent F2P game thats worth a try at the very least. If you dont like it after you play it a bit, I can see why. There are similar games out there that do many things this game tries to do much better.

Warning, spoilers (although there is very little to spoil considering the lack of game AND the non-verbal story telling.)
I'll preface this by stating this, I tried to enjoy this game but ultimately it just wasn't worth for what it was.
For starters, the game is incredibly short and there's no room for alternate solutions. They've managed to overcomplicate the process of redoing missions. It offers no replay value unlike other programming puzzle games a-la Spacechem, Human Resource Machine, Factorio.
Unforunately, the issues don't stop there.
The other main glaring flaw of the game is how incomplete it is. You unlock gadgets to help you solve puzzles in a very linear fashion but they are incredibly underused. The tools merely offer themselves to overcomplicate a process such as the jumper pad who's sole purpose when introduced is so you can jump to platforms of a level. You pretty much never use items in conjunction with each other except on the final mission where you get some extra item to solve a single puzzle.
On the topic of incompleteness, the game lacks polish. It's an extremely buggy game in terms of collison and physics, not in the actual tools. I managed to clip outside the map twice on the second mission, the satsuma house forcing me to restart. On the rail cart level with the 3 carriages you enter via the moving platform with levers, don't noclip while on it or else you'll accelerate backwards and get it stuck while you remain at the starting point, unable to retrieve it. You can also bypass the third puzzle on that level by jumping through a metal grille.
On the final mission (which is the only mission remotely challenging and not for logical reasons but due to awkward puzzles and bugs) I managed to die from lack of oxygen while inside the vents twice. It almost happened a third time before the game realised I was indeed inside the vent and not outside so I stopped dying.
Outwith bugginess and incomplete mechanics, there is a segment in the game where you get attacked. You in turn reveal that your arm is indeed a gatling gun and a whole HUD comes up with a reticule for aiming. Funnily enough, the cutscene pauses, a loading screen appears and before you know it all the attacking robots are destroyed and your gun is gone. It was certainly the blue balling experience.
Well, moving onto gameplay it's incredibly awkward. It starts out pretty simple, you do the introductory level then you get your main tool for hacking, the computer. You do 3 missions on the same level, get paid and get some new♥♥♥♥♥♥ You sometimes get a cutscene to try and build the world around and such. This is okay pacing but it felt a bit underwhelming. This continues until the aforementioned robot attack where the pacing go completely off. You get this completely abstract 2 man mission level that plays completely different. You don't even hack with your main computer, you just do mainly clicking on things while changing character. You then get these intermediate levels of being in the "world hub" for lack of better words doing♥♥♥♥♥♥to progress the story.
The final mission goes back to the usual thing but it's so awkward because the difficulty comes with trying to figure out where you're meant to go.
Forunately the game isn't all that bad, the setting itself has promise and so does the premise. The story telling is done completely non verbally and it does an okay job at it.
Unforunately, I only really found myself playing this to see how more strange it could get in terms of playability. I was no longer playing the game for the game's sake but just to see how it all ended up.
Needless to say, it left me disatifised overall.
I even shed a tear in the end.

This game is my 2016 indie gem so far. Ever wondered how cool it would be to be a field hacker like the computer nerd sidekick on every action movie ever? It feels better.
What you may like:
-Using the hacking mechanic to bypass obstacles is extremely satisfying (if you are into that). You get in, find an obstacle, plan how to use your tools and commands and when you set everything in motion and pull it off you just feel badass.
-The hacking is very accessible, no previous programming knowledge required
-The variety is amazing, you'll start by simply using your field computer and as the game progresses, you'll get more tools that you'll have to know how to use so you can do things that you simply can't do by yourself.
-The game has a really nice level of detail that is essential for the game to tell it's story.
-The workshop support can give you a couple more hours out of this.
What you may or may not like:
-The game was relatively easy and short (about 4.5 hours) if you don't want to pay 20€ for that, then it is perfectly understandable that you should wait for a sale.
-The story is mostly told through the enviroment and the moments in-between missions. No voice acting, no written logs with lore, just visual storytelling (which I believe this game nails)
What you most certainly won't like:
-There is a number of bugs I came across while playing, picking up a turret in a mission made the game crash, the deck(the field computer you use for the hacking) had its screen stuck and another time, it inputed automatically the previous commands when selecting them, but nothing a level restart or small workaround wouldn't solve.

I can praise this game all I want, but ultimately your enjoyment of QC will depend on how much you like coding. At times the game's systems require tedious fiddling but overall I would recommend it in a heartbeat.

I'm a big fan of indie games, because they can still manage to do what the big companies fail to do now : create and tell a great story.

Excellent story, wonderful atmosphere, compelling protagonist -- all in all this was an exceptional experience.  I would eagerly and happily award the game a 9.0 out of 10.0.
It took a bit to get the hang of combat controls and there were a few bugs that required reloads, but once I got the hang of the combat it was a lot of fun taking advantage of A.R.I.D.'s impressive combat abilities.
The game has much of the puzzle-stylings of the old "Gabriel Knight," "King's Quest" or "Mission Critical" games (if you've played any of those), but I never missed any of the objects that you can interract with (which is usually a big problem in these types of games) and the puzzles were fairly straightforward and logical.  I didn't ever get impossibly stuck on a puzzle or need to solicit a walkthrough for help.  Also, many of the solutions to the puzzles are wonderfully amusing, twisted or horrific.
The voice acting was excellent and immersive as was the world-building.  I would describe the game most succinctly as an interactive movie (Sci-Fi, Action, Thriller).  I completed the game in 5 hours and am planning on a second playthrough so the game is not long.  It is an extremely rich experience however and I would consider this to be one of the best "Sci-Fi films" I've ever "seen" (let alone played).
I'm usually very reluctant to purchase games that aren't very long, but in this case I do not at all regret making an exception to that rule.  Nab this game when it's on sale (I got it for $3.99), turn all of the lights out, and have a great night!  You won't regret it!

A good title that explores ideas of humanity and freedom of thought, it develops insights on Asimov's rules of artificial intelligence.  The story was solid, and the environment engaging.  I would be sure to point out that the title could easily be considered "light horror", equally intellectually and atmosphericly:  although it probably won't have you jumping out of your seat, it will probably make you ask uncomfortable questions about the theme.  Personally, I enjoyed it from start to finish, but was somewhat disappointed by the sequel necessitating conclusion.
Regarding gameplay, "The Fall" did an excellent job presenting ques for objects in the environment that could be interacted with in a streamlined manner, adding to the setting in an unobstructive manner.  Unfortunately, the title suffers from the chronic issue of the genre, that being activity blocks where players may be uncertain what to do next, and may waste several minutes meandering around. I would strongly recommend bypassing such blocks by having one of the many guides (availible on steam and the web) onhand during gameplay.  There were several points where the next action in the sequence wasn't apperent, althought a glance or two at a guide usually had me on my merry way.  Frankly, I beleive such blocks may actually add to the story and ideas about A.R.I.D., the protagonist, and the nature of her artificail intellect.  Although there was combat, it was neither the focus nor a reason to shy from the title.
In summary the environment, plot, and gameplay of this title fit together well to convey a powerful narrative.  I recommend "The Fall" because of its well written story and insight on the developing existence of artificial intellects.

As I've been growing older I am finding fewer and fewer games compelling enough to play through completely.
This is largely due to the majority of this media being uninspired copies, ripoffs of an original work which did a much better job than it's imitators.
This game "The Fall" does not reside in the same criteria.
The Fall is an excellent game and an excellent story, voice actors, and dialog that doesn't warrant skipping.
I bought this game on the steam summer sale for $3.99 and after completing it, I wish I paid more.
10 out of 10

The developers of this game should have just made a webseries.  The story is intriguing if not actually compelling, the graphics and animation are excellent if not bleeding edge, and the voice acting is some of the best I've heard.
Unfortunately, as a game, The Fall lands short of the mark.  It is guilty of most of the usual adventure game failings.  The solutions to its puzzles usually make logical sense within the universe, but they oscillate between requiring no thought ("I have only one item in my inventory, so it must be the solution,") to requiring impossible intuition ("How could I possibly have known using this item on that piece of scenery would have that effect?") and are very rarely satisfying.  There are no "a ha!" moments in this game.
The Fall is also terrible at making the path forward clear to the player -- the dark graphics and 2.5D side-scrolling style conspire to make passable obstacles look like walls and walls look like passable obstacles, and the game really embraces backtracking as a mechanic.  Perhaps most damningly, the game forgets it's not an action game, which is something I cannot and do not forgive in any video game.  If you are going to subject me to reflex-based combat you had better give me a system that supports it, and The Fall does not.  It may resemble Shadow Complex visually, but it has none of that game's graceful fluidity.
Finally, the game is buggy and incomplete, ending on a cliffhanger after a final boss fight against an enemy simultaneously attacking you on the ground and stuck wriggling in the rafters, but these are the least of The Fall's worries.  Right now the game is on sale for $4 -- it's probably worth that much if you really love adventure games or science fiction mysteries.  But if you don't already own Gemini Rue, get that instead.
Oh, and don't buy the soundtrack.  I can't believe it's 17 tracks.  I felt like the same four bars were blaring in my ears for the whole game (there are no audio controls).

Ahhh Capcom. You lovers of corrupt scandals of never ending stupidity, I mean...DLC locked content on Disc? Haha, oooooh Capcom you stupid, stupid company and - *Sniff*, oh- ooooooh I smell more♥♥♥♥♥♥coming my way now, Capcom you did it again didn't you? Bad boy! Shame on you!
Now I'm not crazy, but I see a lot of reviews on this site from alllllll sorts of people. Praising the game to hell. 'IT'S AMAZING', to quote, 'THE BEST RESIDENT EVIL GAME EVAAAARRR!!X!', to quote another. But when you guys are reading through these reviews (if you do, I'm not sure), and you see all those lovely blue thumbs up, does it ever occur that maybe its too good to be true? Well as I found out, that old phrase is still around for a reason.
Before I go into the meat of things I will start off by saying this. THIS IS BASED OFF THE LAPTOP!! I know that high end desktop users haven't had any problems and I know that. You guys found the game great, and that's good. Cudos to you, have a muffin on me. But I want to bring attention to a more important issue...or issues.
1* The game does not work for laptops, period. Even if your laptop is the bees knees of the bees knees, chances are high that you will run into a very common problem, extreamly low game speeds and lagging issues. This was an issue from day 1, and still is to most people (you have my sympathies). Now despite messing around with system settings and laptop settings for hours and hours on end, they made no difference at all. Now oddly enough when I tested on the desktop it improved but only by so much.
Now you may be saying to me, - "OI SO WAT, U USED PC SO Y U BASHNG BOUT TEH GAME? RESI EVIL IS PERFECT,UR A NOB"
That's because not eveyone has a desktop PC, but a lot of people do have high end laptops that avery capable of playing these games. So my issue is, why does Capcom feel the need to port a game soley for desktop gamers?? Why no love for laptops?? I think partly the reason could be due to budget constraints, or just simply a lack of competence from Capcom's support....which very neatly leads me on to point number 2.
2* WHERE'S THE DAMN CUSTOMER SUPPORT?! Well quite simply there isn't any. Months down the line and not one word from Capcom about patches, or bug fixes. After months of torture and wasted money however, we were finally given the light. The word from Capcom, the almighty sign of change!!! An image of the mansion.
You mean, the first thing we hear from Capcom after months of silence about the port, about all the bugs, the lag, the frustration....and all we get is a shi**y picture???
You know, there is a joke somewhere about guy who buys a Capcom game, and suddenly the joke isn't funny anymore.
And that's the experience that I'm left with in the end, that this was a joke. Don't get me wrong, the game is great, fantastic and is one of the best resident evil games out there, if not THE best.
But seriously, the amount of trouble I went to get this game working, and the lack of support there is for the wider gamer community out there, just leaves me with a sour taste. It shouldn't be this convoluted just to play a game in my little spare time. And that's why I don't recommend this game, not because its a bad game, but because it is from a very bad developer. Buyer beware in deed.

This is a great game. I would need to double check, but at 185 hours, I am pretty sure this is the game that I have logged the most actual gametime hours on.
I am a fan of GW's products in general, but I had never played nor really been interested in Blood Bowl. I picked this game up during a Steam sale and fell in love.
Some of the other comments are true about the very steep learning curve. That may put some people off. What are all of these different skills? What does Armor Rating do? Why can't I ever score a touchdown? While it is fun, it can be a bit frustrating to play right out of the box. I had probably logged a good twenty hours before I started to figure things out.
Once you get it figured out, though, the sky is the limit. This is a brilliantly tactical game, elegant yet complex in design. I would actually go as far as to call it possibly the tightest rule set GW has ever produced. If you know anything about GW, then you know that they aren't exactly famous for good rule sets. But Blood Bowl's system can stand tall with the best of them. It really is that good.
Having said that, as usual with GW games, luck can play more of a factor than people would like. But there are so many ways to mitigate the potentially disastrous effect of poor dice in this game through sound tactics that it's not much a problem once you get the game figured out. The only time it can really sting is when your star player with a billion experience points winds up dead. But that's part of the game, and you knew that going in! Real soldiers get their noses bloodied and keep fighting anyway.
If you're able to get in with a good league, that's probably the best way to play this game. The online multiplayer community seems fairly active, but the multiplayer client is pretty wonky and getting games in can be a of a pain. That is definitely one of the flaws of this product.
In any case, if you're a fan of Blood Bowl or a fan of this kind of game in general, this game belongs in your collection. Don't hesitate to pick it up. Or, you can pick up the Chaos Edition, which has three additional playable teams (none of which I was interested in, so I got this one for slightly cheaper)

I have been playing this game long before they decided to put it on steam. When the starting point was inside of a tent rather than a medium action heli strike. And currently I hold 3 characters 2
<Correction it has been a while since I have played the game and did not realize they raised the cap again. So I have 2 characters sitting at 50. Current end game status is now at 60.
As many have said this game follows in the veins of Diablo (if Diablo had guns). But also I would like to include Shadowgrounds, Alien Breed, Space Siege, Torchlight...I think you are getting the idea...
One of, in the small handful of,
MMOARPG games out. If you have played Dekaron, Dragon's Nest or Defiance, then you are already familiar with how a true MMOARPG should feel. Fast fluid action & reaction, giving you the feeling you are almost chaining skills & attacks. Much like a platformer fighting game it makes you feel you should be watching for a combo meter when attacking.
1. Cash shop items. Only thing that may be desirable...costumes or a vehicle. Honestly neither are desirable. It's a gun game...you will get shot riding on your vehicle anyway as it is not fast enough to outrun bullets and you cannot shoot from your vehicle. Other vehicles are already available in game through a vendor & better PERMANENT costumes can be unlocked with "miles" just for playing the game. Even exp bonus/premium status is abolutely unnecessary even for those of us who work that cannot play everyday.
2. No actual gear can be bought in the cash shop. No crafting boost items can be found in the shop.
4. If you run out of ammo...then you really did not look at the game. Or you are a horrible shot. Every character can hold 3 (+1 Single use/mission specific) weapon slots max from the very moment it was created, even in the lacking intro tutorial you have this ability.  Each weapon type has it's own ammo pool. Shotguns only use shotgun ammo, rifles only use rifle ammo, etc...etc...starting pools are: Single Use Weapon 192 Max/ Pistols 772/ Rifles 970/ Heavy Machine Gun 100/ Shotgun 20/ Sniper 10/ Flamethrower Fuel 100/ Rocket Launcher 8. This is before bonuses on equipment and class specialization.
3. Rocket launchers are not supposed to be accurate like guns, they are splash damage weapons.
4. Again best things in life, or in this case, game...are free. And that is how they have built this game. The best weapons, armor, & recipes only drop. You will not find any of these in the cash shop. And this is a loot friendly game. Enemies are walking piñatas and drop loot like candy.
Compared to many other MMO's the interface is ridiculously simple.
Quests will carry you all the way out to current endgame status.
Loot, loot, loot...
All gear uses an RNG method for assigning bonuses to the gear when dropped, much like Borderlands & Defiance. So it gives you true tailorization of your character to fit your playing style.
If you want to play with a controller, well the option is not there unless you have programming software...but if you do you can play this game like a twin stick shooter.
Very laid back, sit in your chair and enjoy killing stuff type of game.
Lower tier equipment can be just as good and in some cases better than top tier equipment. This way you do not have to spend a good chunk of your life grinding for top tier items just to keep up with other players.
Account wide storage. There are 2 storage types, personal & account. Both storage types can be decently upgraded with game earned currency. Much like any other F2P game that uses storage to increase it massively will require real cash but, with the RNG bonus stat system and drop rates I doubt you will be storing much. I feel the account wide storage would see more use than personal. But that is just a personal opinion. More so, it's something you would have to see and experience yourself.
True character buidling, each class specialization can be built in different ways to fit how you play vs the old "one build rules all" most games with classes and character building accidentally fall into.
This is definitely not a "dedicate some time to" type of game. The grinding in quests can get repetitive. It's more heavily gun based than balanced between guns & skills. So if you are good with games of this type you can easily solo areas that were meant to be partied in. This is more of "have fun demolishing enemies with firepower when you want to with friends" type of game.
Yes, control can feel slightly sluiggish on any PC.
The game, though playable, has not even reached a 1.0 status yet, so the graphics engine could use some major tweaking. In short, I have seen full 3D games with much more immersive graphics run much faster than this more simpled 2.5d title, which is pretty sad.
There is my personal concern that, one particular class build is semi-godly overpowered to the point that it makes the strongest enemies look like paper, regardless of weapon level. Fortunately as long as I have been playing this game I have not seen anyone use this build so that information I will keep that to myself(No, I have no affiliation with this game, it was just the first character I built that I unwittingly found this unbalance on). The game is easy enough for anyone to play with just guns alone, so do not ask about it. I will put you on permanent ignore.
Currently, very short game for an MMO, I think I reached endgame on 2 characters in a week. But that week was also spent dedicated to this game. And it's why I do not suggest dedicating daily time to it. It is too quick to reach the current endgame status. But please bear in mind this game has not been out very long, even prior to it's steam release.
Classes vs Backgrounds - At the beginning you will see each character background has a bonus & once you reach the level to choose a specialization, it will not matter. If you are good at these types of games all the classes will feel the same unfortunately. Since I had mentioned earlier about being more gun based than skill + gun balanced, you will most likely forget you have skills and just gun everything down.

Set in a world where even the world doesn't like itself, humans live in floating cities due to the large amount of flooding and oceanic spreading that has covered much of Mother Earth.
Except that's ♥♥♥♥ing boring so let's bring out some goddamn mechs.
Pilots utilize large robots called Battleframes to fly around the barren oceans of Earth and usually battle for various tactical reasons that I'm sure make more sense in the actual world. Project Nimbus delivers as a mech shooter, with a wide variety of mechs and missile spamming to make any player seem like they're the protagonist of the next edgy gundam series.
Currently there's a campaign and survival mode. Campaign takes you through the eyes of various people, from an american mercenary piloting a japanese prototype (complete with waifu material voice acting by Amber Lee Connors) to a Russian ace pilot and his quirky female friend. Both have some interesting elements, such as ships or ace customs coming out, both good and bad.
Survival mode gives you a neverending supply of enemies to shoot down. Pick any mech you'd like and fly through an open area, where it's just you, your missiles, and those AI enemies. Survive as long as you can, basic stuff.
Combat is fairly satisfying. The wide variety of weapons, from automatic shotguns to funnels, can be utilized depending on which mech you have and everything sounds and looks great. Feedback on hits are obvious, with enemy parts wiggling, burning, and falling apart, and the entire game feels like it was designed by people who know what they're doing. Combat itself comes down to dodging and outdamaging your opponent. You attack via lock-on system, which essentially aims for you, making it forgettable and, admitedly, boring. But dodging is fairly fun, with boosting and quick sidedashes giving you a feeling of badassery.
The game's graphics aren't exactly beautiful, but the bloom spam and fairly nice looking models do hide the game's "2005 PS2 graphics". Performance is about what you'd expect. With an old graphics card like mine (Nividia 260x) I still got a full 60 FPS on all but the missile-spammiest missions, which are very rare.
Who the ♥♥♥♥ cares it's a mech game that isn't complete♥♥♥♥♥♥ it might as well be a godsend for us mech fans.
But really, it ain't too bad. It's Early-Access game, but it's an Early-Access game with some spirit. The developers are tough and responsive, and know what they're doing. I'd trust them with at least 30 dollars. Buy it, it'll be worth it if you're into the Mech genre.

Another short and sweet extravaganza of smoke and mirrors by the notorious Brendon Chung. Notorious because this is another game that you shouldn't buy for the quantity/price ratio. (The Interactive Art Book is overpriced for the extra $9, but as a horribly rabid fanboy I consider it a tip for the funding of future projects in the Citizen Abel universe.)
At release the game is $20 for 6-10 hours of content which most people should find outrageous, but I find that the experience never outstays its welcome.
The hacking feature is a total lie, as it boils down to a fancy lever pulling mechanic. But the implementation of the decking interface is just so finely tuned to fit with the environments that I found the glorified command line typing to be extremely immersive.
Art _quality in this game is amateurish but the art _direction is insanely brilliant. It's a joy to see how the sum of clunky blocks and hand-drawn doodles are combined into a scene that engages the imagination.
A bunch of interesting gameplay ideas are introduced with clever focus, but I was disappointed that those same ideas were never combined together into a cohesive climax.
Extras like the timed leaderboards and sticky notes left by friends are clever, but with the bugs plaguing global sync, it is hard to take such features seriously.
If you want to feel like a hacker in some 90s techno-exploitation flick, Quadrilateral Cowboy absolutely nails the execution. It won't teach you any programming and it will likely be disappointing in some burning way, but the experience will certainly leave an impression.

Quadrilateral Cowboy - The Setsuna Missions - With MaximumPower
Quadrilateral Cowboy is a single-player adventure in a cyberpunk world. Set in a strange demention of the 1980s, Quadrilateral Cowboy has you joining a gang of thieves who use there compurer hacking skills. Your main tool is a “hacking deck” that can manipulate the electronics around you, leveraging a basic, easy to learn programming language. As the game progresses, you get access to other tools, including programmable robots and guns.
THis is a puzzle game where you use your computer, the deck looks like an MS DOS prompt 256k computer, a visual that will make the most sense to people who grew up with computers in the 80s and 90s. By typing in string of "code' protocol to access remote computers, you can mess with the doors and objects to progress toward your goal. Though the game adds new and potentially interesting layers of complexity as the story moves forward.
Quadrilateral Cowboy offers the player a truly unique experience. I enjoyed playing this game! Two tuumbs up!

I stumbled upon this game much later than I should have, since I had fantasized about all that the game has to offer many times before discovering it.
The single player campaign is fun, even though the AI lacks in some aspects. (I think I put about 60 hours in single player)
I would have appreciated a way to jumpstart the single player experience, so that you can get right into the action you prefer, for example. I'm talking about becoming a lord within a faction sooner, for example, or allowing you to start with one castle as your own faction. After a few games, it becomes tedious to go through all the motions again and again as you try to build a viable kingdom.
Having said that, the game does many things really well, most notably the core gameplay of combat. Archery feels proper, and the various melee weapons and shields allow for a personal experience. Commanding troops can be challenging, but is usually fun and satisfying.
The rest of the hours I played a few hours in multiplayer, with a heavy focus on Siege mode. I think this is where the game shines. I love how single player doesn't prepare you agains multiplayer at all. In that sense, M&B: Warband is a psychological game at heart: will your enemy try to evade my arrows, or will he sprint straight towards a ladder? Will he try to feign his strikes, or will he swing through? After a certain amount of hours, you will get to know your enemies and turn their own tactics against them.
The multiplayer is prone to a few easy exploits, that arise through gaps in the game engine or mechanics. It's not perfect in that sense. But if you want to have a go at intense, seemingly realistic medieval battles, Mount&Blade: Warband is the game for you. Don't be daunted by the steep learning curve and persevere; this game might have delivered me the most fun I've ever had playing games.
Edit: I tried Viking Conquest, but I think I spent too much time in Multiplayer to fairly appreciate the pace of the SP anymore.

The Fall is a haunting story of a combat suit's A.I. trying to save her human occupant after crashing in a dark, mysterious, and uncomfortable place.
Deeply atmospheric, the game starts off kind of awkward as you are forced to fumble about attempting to find a way forward, figuring out what you can do, however in retrospect this is the perfect intro for what unfolds.
ARID's journey involves tackling puzzles differently than how they first appear, which fits nicely into the narrative in a way you'll only truly appreciate once the credits roll.
There are a couple of moments where this unintuitiveness begins to grate on you a bit (one specific puzzle involves testing your reflexes in order to see if you can hack something in time, with no indication that you were supposed to hack it, but other than that it's mostly about trying to figure out how to outsmart the challenges rather than out performing them)
Combat in the game is a bit clunky, as is the movement, but not in a way that's frustrating, and once again feeds back into the story.
Voice acting on the other hand is smooth as can be for a game where AIs are the primary speakers. Dialogue that should sound dull beyond belief is narrated in such a way that you can't help but be drawn in.
The Fall is currently planned as the first of a trilogy, but it is self contained and ends on a note that, while still open to continuation, is a great conclusion on its own.
Honestly this is a game I've been thinking about ever since I've played it, which is a great sign for it. One of the best Survival Horror games of all time and one of the best Remakes of all time finally gets the PC release it deserves.
You play as either Chris Redfield or Jill Valentine, members of the STARS team sent in to the Arklay Mountains to discover the mysterious murders of several people in that area.
The game features a mix of close quarters combat with limited supplies and inventory space, exploring large environments such as a Mansion, Guardhouse and Laboratory and some puzzle solving such as picture and block puzzles and both Chris and Jill have their share of differences both in gameplay and in plot.
Jill is by far the easier of the two with 2 extra inventory spaces and being able to also carry a Grenade Launcher, both also have their own side characters that will help them throughout the campaign and they also both carry their own defensive weapons for when enemies get too close to you.
The enemies range from Zombies, Mutant Dogs and Hunters to the awesome exclusive Crimson Heads which rise when you don't burn a downed zombie with kerosene that is also in short supply.
On higher difficulties it is best to avoid most confrontations as you can get killed in only a few hits and it is best to only kill enemies in areas that you will frequently revisit or are too narrow to evade.
The Remaster as a whole does a good job of updating the graphics of a 13 year old game to look really amazing on todays systems although some textures haven't been updated and as such tend to look pretty nasty and pixelated.
The audio is also great with some really atmospheric music and background sound along with the moans and other sounds of the monsters, the guns also sound particularly powerful.
The Remaster also comes with a few exclusive features such as the ability to turn off tank controls although i completed the game just fine with tank controls on a mouse and keyboard.
Theres also a fair amount of replay value as completing it with both Chris and Jill can take up to 10 hours and there are a couple of additional modes as well which will make the game more difficult.
Overall this is a great port of one of the best Sruvival Horror games of all time and in my opinion the best Resident Evil of all time.

TL;DR
--------
A fun, casual game for those looking to just relax and mess around. Can provide hours of gameplay since it's a dungeon crawler with varying classes that may use certain weapons. The translation is laughably bad, and the story isn't that really interesting. There's nothing special with the Cash Shop nor is there anything worth buying really, since inventory and bank space can be bought with in-game currency. Fun to play alone, or with friends.
Pros:
--------
- Fun and casual game for those not looking to play something hardcore and just want to kill time / relax on.
- Simple and easy controls / combat / UI
- Casual drop tables, meaning that rare items and up will drop often if you spend some time playing the game, rewarding players for just playing and killing mobs.
- Free mount at lvl 16
- Free gifts just for staying logged in
- Doesn't require a strong computer, so lower-end computer uses can enjoy the game as well
- Instanced missions that can be done with other players and will always give rare rewards at the end depending on how many points the entire team scored.
- Plethora of weapons to use, including chainsaws, rocket launchers and heavy machine guns
- Character customization and wearable armors to make your character look unique to others.
- Can buy more inventory and bank space with in-game currency (CRI).
- Game is not Pay 2 Win
- You can recall back to town, and teleport back to your previous location via the helicopter
Cons:
--------
- Cash shop at the moment doesn't really have anything appealing to buy (Mostly just mounts, costumes, and %magic find potions).
- Hilariously awful translations
- I have no idea what's happening in the story nor do I care
- Game is probably TOO easy for those looking for a challenging dungeon crawler
- Have to buy ammo (but it's cheap and can be found off mobs)

I really enjoyed this game.
The story is interesting, the gameplay is fun and the puzzles are unlike any puzzle in any other game I’ve played (this is because of the gameplay.) The shooting and puzzle-solving however are not what makes this game, as good as they are. The motivation for someone to buy this and play it would be story.
I actually got this in a bundle but I had heard of how good its story was long before. A robot trying to protect her pilot is in a strange place and she must go to extreme measures to save his life. Its an interesting premise that leaves you curious and as more of the story unravels, some questions are answered but more take their place. The whole thing is surrounded in mystery yet it never loses you and you always know just enough to understand your current situation but no more than that.
The atmosphere is truly engrossing with the art and sound all being spot on. You’re left curious, yet always apprehensive as the constant uneasiness and possible threat of danger leaves you effectively creeped out. It’s just fantastically well done.
However, many will warn you of two things. Firstly, this game ends on a cliffhanger and so is not a complete story. Secondly, this game is short. The cliffhanger was fantastic and not a bad way to end the game at all. Seriously, if the next game is as good as the first then the answers should be well worth the wait, so the cliffhanger is okay by me.
What I wasn’t so alright with was the length. Like everyone else I was warned of how short it was by reviews and it didn’t turn me off in the slightest. I’ve mentioned before that game length often does not bother me as many stories (though not all!) are best told in only a few hours. That being said, I was expecting somewhere around six hours for this game and instead I got half that. It wasn’t that the game felt incomplete due to the length. As I said, it ended very well, but I finished it today. I started it up expecting another, for want of a better word, level or area, but instead I walked a bit, talked a bit and it ended. It just felt like I had played a level of an adventure game instead of an adventure game.
This all being said my feelings towards the game are almost completely positive. Apart from the length there is very little to criticise and as a result I would definitely recommend to those looking for a unique new story. Looking forward to number 2 and the answers, and possible questions, it will bring with it too.

The game has run pretty stable for me, and I've encountered very few bugs (though there are some graphical glitches I've seen).  There seem to be features that are incompletely implemented, but nothing that has hurt my enjoyment of the game.

This game is one of my favourite games of all time. The mysterious and macabre Spencer Mansion is an intricate puzzle waiting to be solved. The early Resident Evil games weren't about the combat instead they were the grandchildren of more cerebral games like Sweet Home on the NES. If you want to experience true stressful survival horror I'd recommend playing on hard, especially as Jill. While many complain about the restrictive camera angles and 'tank' controls very few realise that these very mechanics were deliberate to create tension and a feeling of claustrophobia.
Strangely the dialogue in the game really isn't enthralling, Shinji Mikami wanted the game to have the impression of a B movie and that, combined with translation to English has left the voice acting rather cheesy. The games narrative truly shines with the backstory revealed through diary entries and files that leave the player to construct a horrifying tale.
I cannot recommend this game more to someone who likes their horror with a bit more mystery rather than gunning down hordes of monsters.

A bizarre art style, anachronistic retro-future setting, and seemingly disjointed set of spatial-logical puzzle mechanics belie the clarity of vision in Quadrilateral Cowboy’s design: the central theme of meticulous preparation followed by rapid execution. Everything from the VR heist simulation premise, through to the rudimentary act of typing up instruction sequences on the deck’s command prompt interface, will contribute to the feeling of technical wizardry when the plan comes together.

Blendo took a giant step in the right direction with this game. With some of Blendos previous games they could be considered "non-games" to some due to perceived lack of gameplay and more of a walking simulator with light platforming feel. But with Quadrilateral Cowboy there is much more of an emphasis on gameplay using items and hacking to complete puzzles.
The puzzles are mostly basic and pretty easy until the final few which blend together
of the tools you have learned through the game. My biggest complaint with the game is that there wasn't a single puzzle that used everything you have learned and you entire arsenal in one giant climactic puzzle, instead you are left wondering what could have been which may be intentional seeing as the story is deliberately left that way too.
Old fans of Blendo will not be surprised by the subdued storytelling, but for some it might be a turnoff. A lot is left to the player to piece together through intuition and studying the environment, which in my opinion is needed me in storytelling in gaming.
Another complaint is the length but that is mostly because I wanted more of the game as I loved it so much. Workshop support should help that out with (as of publication of this review) free maps being uploaded by the developers and fan maps hopefully becoming a thing in the future.
If you like puzzle games you owe it to yourself to play this.

Metal Reaper Online is an action-oriented MMORPG/Shooter set in a post apocalyptic future. You're a member of some rebel group of survivors or something... that's about all I could make out from the terrible Engrish during the "cutscenes." (Which are mostly just panning pieces of art.)
The game itself feels like someone decided to make a Diablo style game with a different setting, and guns. The gameplay feels pretty solid, it is enjoyable running around mowing down big groups of guys and collecting oodles of loot.
The downside here is that there's not really much more to the game than that. Everything you do feels about the same as everything else. Quests come in 3 flavors: Kill X number of this, go interact with x number of that, or collect x number of whatevers. Just about every quest in the game is some form of that. On top of that, there's an ammo system, which feels totally unecessary, and will require you to go back to town every so often to refill.
Graphically the game isn't bad. It's not amazing, but the graphics do the job well enough. Things look like you would expect them too, and it ties together well, though the enemies could use a little more variety.
Loot is plentiful, and fun to collect, true to the ARPG style, however the loot list seems quite shallow. I found myself collecting about 4 or 5 of the same item from a set over the course of an hour. The difference in weaponry is also negligible, outside of the damage output. Basically, just grab the rarest weapon you can find for your class because it will do the most damage. It's a bit like celebrating getting a new Porsche by taking it for a spin, only to discover that everyone else bought themselves a Porsche as well. There's almost no point to any of the weapons except the two highest rarities, because nobody will want them.
Sound is about average I would say, with the exception of the music. The music is great!..... the first time or two you hear it. From what I can tell though, there are only 3 songs in the entire game. One for the menu, one for town, and one for NOT in town. Which just repeats.... and repeats. As much as you might enjoy it at first, you'll turn it off soon.
Otherwise the game has a few more things that kind of bothered me.. one is the spawn rate. Dear LORD the spawn rate. You could literally stand in one place at points and complete missions because of the sheer number of mobs that spawn in so quickly. Things will respawn in seconds!
Another MAJOR problem with the game is the Engrish. It's HORRIBLE. I've played games in languages I don't even speak that were more intelligible than this. What's the plot? The storyline? I don't know, because I couldn't make sense of the stuff on the screen. Google translate could probably do a better job here if not at least as good.
Lastly, the game is EASY. I mean, ludicrously easy. I was able to run through group mission areas that I was underleveled for, solo, without so much as losing a single HP. It's almost to the point where it's a casual game, because let's face it, about the only way you're going to die is if you go AFK in the middle of a pack of mobs.
TLDR
All in all, the game is fun for a bit, it's not something I would stick around long term and play, but if you want something that's close to a casual action RPG, that you can play without too much time commitment,  give it a shot! If nothing else the head-scratchingly-bad Engrish is worth a laugh or two.

When you start this game, for the first 10 seconds it looks like another Limbo. It is not another Limbo.
The game gets into the story pretty quickly, as you play. You won't be playing for hours before the game opens up. You don't even start with a weapon, you just have a torch and a goal - to save the human inside the suit. You play the AI, the suit itself. Your torch is what allows you to interact with the environment, and that's how you progress through the game. If it sounds dull, believe me, it's not.
You start unlocking new abilities but not in the traditional way. As a computer, your only way of unlocking those skills is if you're given the order - which is impossible - or if the person inside the suit is in active danger of dying if you don't do so.
This is all just gameplay talk so far. The real gem of this game is the story. I won't go into that because it's a mountain of spoilers, but if you consider what an AI - you - might have to accomplish to progress through an unknown area and what you'll do to keep your human master safe, you might be able to imagine how innovative this story can get.
I bought this on sale, but it's worth full price.

Never wrote a review on any of my 151 steam games, but I HAVE to warn others not to waste 32 euros based on completely biased reviews here. Every other review focuses on how Fable is their childhood and its an amazing game. Some think the remaster is good, some think its bad. But I just want to write a review about it being A GAME. A game release for 32 euros.
TL:DR: If you are buying this only out of nostalgia, you belong to the only group of people that might enjoy this game. The remaster is still weak though. The Witcher III costs less than this... thing... There is no comparison, seriously. Also any other major RPG now and 10 years back has more value than this. There is very little content and the novelty morality and romance systems are a joke.
Positives:
Relatively speaking, compared to other RPGs on the market priced similarly - None. There are no actual positives. It has okey stylized graphics and the begining seems to be a start of something great... Its not though.
Crushed expectations:
SIZE: I thought the game is big, or at least comparable to other RPGs... Its not, even Morrowind has far bigger and FAR more interesting world and that was 12 years before this thing was released and 2 years before the original Fable was released. Every segment is tiny, and separated from others by a loading screen. Whats worse - the whole world is incredibly tiny as well. I thought the map will get bigger over time. NOPE. In first few hours, you have traveled through the whole map. To just walk the distance will take you like 10 minutes, INCLUDING the 20 loading screens. TINY!
COMBAT: Attempted action combat, extremely simplistic. The only interesting thing is that there are quite a few spells, but most of them are not worth it. There are very few weapons in the game and they behave samey, only have different speeds and dmg. They also have mostly the same model recolored for different quality.
STORY: I have to say, I couldnt force myself to finish the game. But the story didnt keep me interested too much. It might get better towards the end, but I wouldnt hold my breath. The main meat of the game is in the quests, that are... just there. On the map. You pick them, you go there... and then some story happens. The gameplay and story seemed to be completely separated. But the quests have an even bigger flaw:
GOOD/EVIL SYSTEM: The game was hyped for the moral decisions you can do. Well, no. Its quests again. You LITERALLY get a pair of quests on the map - One for good points, one for evil points. Example: "KILL THE FARMERS" or "PROTECT THE FARMERS"... Thats it. That is the morality system. The only other BIG INOVATION is that you can wear light colored stuff to be "more good" or dark to be "more evil". Also eating some stuff will give you good/evil points... like eating Tofu = good. Okey game, go home, you are drunk... Compare this to any serious title with actual moral decisions and you have to conclude this was made for small kids... But its not, sometimes it gets strangely dark, and you can gave PG sex... Which bring me to my next point:
ROMANCE: This is the worst letdown for me. When I realized this game is small, has boring combat, uniteresting story and the morality system shouldnt even be called a system, I recalled that there was romance and even SEX in the game... The sad truth is, its even more simplistic than the "morality system". All you have to do (and CAN do, unfortunately) to get to the pinacle of romance = mariage, sex - is to get gold to buy steel armor (a few hours) and buy some chocolates and a ring. Than you go to town and spam romance emote on a woman. She likes you after you emote her 5 times in that armor. You then give her the chocolate. She falls in love with you instantly. You give her the ring. BAM you are now married. Now go to your house (yes you can buy propery, it has no function tho, it just EXISTS there) and you emote her some more. BAM sex scene (= 5 times the same voice track. Literally the same OH sound or whatever it was 5 times, like a broken recorder. All while looking at black screen for 30 seconds. Exciting). Thats it. There is NOTHING more to it. If you wanted, you can do all this like 2 hours in the game, just buy more chocolates/flowers, you wont need the steel armor set.
I believe there might be a brothel somewhere later in the game,  but that most likely results in the same black screen with maybe some EVIL points added for good measure.
OVERALL: The game cant compete with any good or mediocre RPG nowadays and it probably coulnt compete with good RPGs even 10 years ago when the original version was released. The lack of content is stuning. The recolored weapons just reminded me of Vanilla WoW, and even that MMO game used it only for crafted low-lvl gear. The morality and romance systems are a joke and seem almost insulting. Could be interesting for very young audience 10 years ago, but not now. The fact that you can get Witcher III or Skyrim for less... is incredible.
Dont buy this as a game, only as a nostalgia token.

Great game. Port is meh, I didn't have any problems though.
The inventory was never good, even in the original. So take criticism of that with a grain of salt. Game length for first time might be around 9-15 hours or more. Right now I can finish an entire playthrough in about 4-5 hours pretty relaxed.
Realistically, you should be able to get at least 3 playthroughs of this game before you feeeeel like you've done everything.
If you are like me though, you keep coming back to the game at least once a year to run a character or 2 again. There is just something about this game that no other rpg really has. And you can come back to it, knowing you've done everything, just to do it again from a slightly different angle or paying attention to a specific part of the game. It also helps that the game isn't very time consuming especially when you know what you are doing, but the quality of the time spent is pretty nice. There isn't really any portion of the game that is frustrating or confusing, and you have a TON of freedom, even when the world is basically a really really big hallway.
I think its the progression system, the world is kind of interesting, or the combat being really fun (if a bit easy at times), who knows.
If you buy this game, my advice would be to have your first character on the normal difficulty, then just use the hard difficulty instead.
Reasoning for this is that the pacing of the difficulty is a lot "better" in the normal difficulty, but for the hard one they just ramped it up to 80-90% at the start and got rid of phials.
Oh, and last tip, don't look up exploits, there are quite a few in this game and once you know them it might be difficult to limit yourself, and a ton of the fun in this game is progressing your gear as well as your character.
TL;DR This game has a lot of really well done features that even games like skyrim could take a step back and learn from what this game did with the world and progression. Please excuse me if any part of this review is cold; I'm being honest in terms of the pitfalls of the game, hoping they'll be fixed at which point I'll revisit this review and change the rating.
If neutral was an option, I'd select that instead of no because the game is enjoyable when not dealing with the issues below.
Grey Cubes is poorly designed, full of bugs and annoyances, and I can't recommend it at the current stage of development.
If you have a joystick installed / plugged-in you can't play the game. It uses the throttle control to move the paddle left and right ( with 50% being don't move, 0 == left and 100 == right ). You can't disable joystick to use the mouse for the game if it is plugged in. If you unplug it while the game is open, the paddle hugs the side of the screen.
You can't change the volume for the music or sound effects, only mute them which is terrible.
The menu is non-existant; only icons.. no text. The only options are back, mute sound / music, from the main menu ( plus one other which doesn't do much ).
You can only access certain elements of the menu while in a level instead of from the main menu.
The paddle teleports at random intervals ( not the levels that teleport you from one box to another, this is a bug ) which causes you to lose a ball.
There is no depth-perception for levels with multiple levels / z... The ball stays the same size ( actually a very small change in size ), no shadow..
The ball frequently becomes hidden from view either by the power-up / down icons, the blocks floating above the level, etc... Poor design choice to hide the ball; this doesn't increase difficulty, it eliminates the player being able to play.
Powerup "Magnet / Attract" goes after blocks that aren't accessible ( other side of a wall [ in the teleport levels where you don't have access to these blocks at all ] or above / below the ball ). It should only go after cubes that are available ie same level and not blocked by a wall whereby you can only get to via teleport.
"More levels comming soon" output in the game.
Wormholes are annoying because blocks aren't affected by them, meaning a block can end up on a stationary wormhole and you can't hit it by entering the wormhole, only by leaving instead of allowing physics until the ball reaches the center ( it'd be better to have it act like a gravity source and if the ball reaches the center then it teleports instead of teleporting on the "event horizon [ which would be the related area for an ultra-dense-micro-planet otherwise referred to as a black-hole where the teleport activates ]"
It is possible for the ball to become stuck ( in the sense that it will hit one surface, return to another, and repeat ) which is why the developer probably added the magnetize "skill / option" instead of preventing it from happening.
This could be a good game if there weren't as many bugs as there currently are in the game, if we could control the volume and define what controller / controls we want to use, if our ball( s ) aren't blocked by powerup/down icons or blocks floating above the level ( which pop-out more blocks ), if after the blocks floating above the level are removed after they have finished producing all their blocks, if the menu actually served as a menu instead of a guessing game, if the menu contained all options from the main menu without needing to enter the game / level to adjust other options, if, if, if, if.......
There are too many annoyances to even consider this game a "good buy". With all that said, it could be enjoyable with the above fixed... 99 cents is too much to pay for a mobile game on PC, just like $60 is too much to pay for a several years old game ( such as GTA 5 ) which was ported to PC after being out on consoles for years despite being popularized by PC Gamers.

Beatiful artistic design (hand painted screens), cute characters (robot society), interesting dialogue design approach, interesting/challenging puzzles and a great soundtrack make Machinarium a good game to recommend. (Of course, provided that you enjoy these kinds of things and don't mind some tough puzzles. There's a cool puzzle helping system in place.)

I love the art in this game. I enjoyed walking through the many screens and seeing all sorts of neat things, especially the robots. The animation is both charming and hilarious. The sound direction is pretty great too, especially the music played after solving a particular series of puzzles.
Gameplay-wise, Machinarium is a point-and-click adventure. Most of the puzzles were easy enough to solve without help, though a few left me holding my head for a while. There was only one instance where I could not find the item I needed to progress. Figuring out what to do next was usually no problem due to a helpful "idea bubble" button, and there's also an INCREDIBLY WELL-ILLUSTRATED built-in walkthrough just in case.
The plot is minimal, in a good way. The lack of verbal dialogue added to the game's charm. I finished the game in just under 4 hours.
Overall, I recommend this game to anyone who wants to play an elegantly simple, stylistically astounding adventure game.

For some reason I feel at home with this entry. The Spencer Mansion is the blueprint for the series and quite frankly the most staple setting in the Resident Evil franchise at it's entirety. This is the original Resident Evil restored in HD and oh so beautiful it is. The 2d pre-rendered backdrops still hold up well as they did back in 2002 and ooze with atmosphere. The lighting effects and camera angles make you feel like you're in a classic horror film. Ironically, perhaps something along the lines of George A. Romero's Night of The Living Dead. The atmosphere helps create a unsettling mood that is missing in recent entries of the franchise. Also, there is a new option to use analog controls which was not present in the 2002 Gamecube version or 1996 PlayStation version. I find myself using this new control method mostly for the fresh experience, but to be honest you may find that the old "tank" controls suit this game much better. The only thing the analog controls seem to be good for is dodging enemies. Other than that, they can get a little wonky when camera angles change. However, it's not a huge flaw, but it's a present one. Capcom hasn't optimized the game very well and many have experienced framerate drops. Luckily, the game runs smooth on my PC at high resolution and settings. Make sure you meet the required specs listed on the store page. I still think the required specs are a bit high for a game that's over a decade old. With that said, I totally think this game is worth the purchase. This is truly how I remember playing survival horror and I guess I'm one of those nit picky Resident Evil fans that prefers nostalgia over the newer action oriented direction the series has taken. In my opinion, I really wish Capcom would go back to this sort of formula. This is how I remember Resident Evil...this is what gott// me...itchy....tasty. Seriously though, kudos to Capcom for releasing this. Screw Resident Evil 7...I'm already ready for the Resident Evil 2 HD remaster!

Capcom made an experiment, they wanted to see if people would like their games to go back the old formula. Guess what? We do!
Resident Evil HD remastered (REHD) Is a third person survival horror game based on the Game Cube version remaster of the 1996 PSone classic, So yes the remake of a remake.
I didn't have the opportunity to play the Game Cube version so I was very excited to get my hands on it and I must say I wasn't dissapointed. The game has really impressive visuals, the work with the lighting here is very impressive. The fixed camera  can be a deal breaker for many, but in my opinion it just helps to build the most important aspects of these games, the atmosphere, and that is where the game shines, giving you a feeling of being constantly watched and that you are never truly alone, even when you dispatched all the monsters. the limited health items, ammo and saves combined with the lack of continues keeps you tense at all times, knowing that if you die you have to restart from your previous save and you can't be constantly saving.
The story and voice acting may not be the best out there but you don't really buy a RE game for those things anyway.
I think this game is a really good value for the money as it will easily squeese at least 10 hours out of your time, all that for just $20. get it, enjoy it and join me as I wait for Capcom to remaster RE2 (my personal favorite)

I had been curious about this game for quite some time and had heard it was really good from multiple friends. So when I saw it on sale on Steam again, I asked my friends if it was still worth getting. It was a resounding yes from everyone who had played it.
So I bought this game and hoped it was as good as I had heard. I squashed all expectations instantly. Sure, it hasn't aged well in the graphics department. However, in every other department, Mount & Blade: Warband has it where it counts; gameplay.
I haven't played such a fun game with such solid single-player in a long time. Sure, I have plenty of online games to play with friends like Counter Strike: Global Offensive or Rocket League but I had been looking for a sandbox game that really got me immersed. This definitely has everything I want in a game.
There is a lot of freedom of what I want to do to shape every play through in being different. Even having only really played 3 characters that are all only at the start with 180 in game days each, I can definitely see I'll be playing this for a long time. Having to consider tactics and strategies with the units and positioning is definitely fun.
The sieges are fun but not exactly where it needs to be without mods. The ladders make it far too difficult to go in due to a single chokepoint. Multiple entries with multiple siege weapons would have been a wonderful feature that was probably overlooked. This would have made it far more balanced for those who are attempting to siege as it is far too difficult to siege without enough ranged units killing enemy ranged units and melee from afar before going through the chokepoint.
The mods are also fantastic. Although it is limited for being old, modders have found good workaround by combining some of the best mods and then adding new content on top of that.
The soundtrack definitely gives a great vibe. It makes things feel very epic and more grandiose with epic battles that go on.
I definitely think this was a great game to get into now of all times as I was able to see that Mount & Blade: Bannerlords is coming out. I am rather upset that I had missed out on such a gem until this point but at least better late than never.
It's time to be a butterlord and feast.
