For a long time, I decided against acquiring a remastered version of Fable. Having previously bought
a year after its' release, I saw no real advantage in buying what was essentially the same product a second time. But the call of nostalgia eventually got the better of me. That being said, objectivity obliges, I'll try not to drift too much down memory lane.
Fable is the incarnation of Molyneux's vision in so many ways, it would be tedious to enumerate those aspects. It suffices to say that the game follows a pattern which was already present in Black & White: that of the choice between good and evil. But instead of playing as a god, you are a simple child who will grow to become a hero after a fateful, traumatising event. What kind of hero you will become - a good magician, sneaky fighter, etc.- is entirely of your choosing.
Even down to its' very name, the world of Albion is a fantasy-folkloric rendition of medieval Britain. And it particularly excels in that area. The variety of English (mostly Northern and West Country) accents, Monty Python
dialogue, landscapes, myths (e.g. Huw's longsword, King Arthur anyone?), creatures, map (which oddly ressembles Wales and the Irish Sea) are always there to remind you of the inherent Britishness of the game. From the bandit-ridden forestlands to the Ale-brewing taverns, it succeeds in creating an aesthetically pleasing rpg and is more-than-atmospheric-enough to bring about a credible world of its' own. To put it differently, Albion sure looks like a beautiful place to live in.
Also worth noting is the musical score, the opening theme was composed by the ever so talented Danny Elfman (you might also remember him as the leading member of Oingo Boingo, the author of the Simpsons theme, Tim Burton movie soundtracks along with countless other film scores). Russell Shaw took great care of the rest, and much to his merit, one cannot understate the monumental influence of music in this game. It is literally the heart and soul of Fable.
This game easily ranks up amongst the best titles to have graced the Xbox console. So what of this new version?
Given that it is mainly a faithful reproduction of what was made a decade ago. There is very little in there to criticise.
One of the main criticism I can bring up against Fable is that it is two-sided. Playing neutral won't really satisfy you. This game badly wants you to vouch for one side over the other. Either become a total♥♥♥♥♥♥or an angelic figure. On the other hand, playing evil is great fun (even hilarious at times). This system offers double-replayability down to the smallest side quest.
What of the DLCs? Unless you seriously intend on looking like a total reincarnation of Jack of Blades at the end of the game, most of them aren't really worth buying. Of all the weapons featured in the game, only one will give you a true upper hand over your enemies (
), the DLC ones are no game-changers.
As for the graphics, it's a bit of a mixed bag in my opinion. Sure, the landscape looks splendid. But the characters look too plastic, especially when it comes to their face, it's almost like something straight out of
. The original Xbox version had a charm of its own which this Anniversary edition can't surpass.
All in all, these are minor flaws in contrast to the game as a whole. As someone who bears the unpopular opinion that Fable 2 was a downgrade and Fable 3 a slight improvement, I wish Lionhead studios had carried on the Fable franchise in the direction of the original game. Here's to hoping for a Fable IV reboot set in a prequel Old Kingdom world, much like I long for an Age of Empires IV (another franchise which Microsoft mindlessly destroyed).

The Impossible Game is anything but 'Impossible', and in some of the worst ways. The first of which is that this game isn't actually hard, challenging or difficult. It's artificially Difficult. The levels and mechanics are designed to give you a very small window to correctly execute what's required, often not enough for you to be able to react fast enough on the first try. There is not much actual skill required to beat this game, nor is it challenging, it's just a test of muscle memory. The only real way to play is to keep trying and dying in a level until you can remember what exactly to do. Couple that with the fact that dying sends you completely back to the start of a decently sized static level, you'll only find yourself getting frustrated at the game while slowly trying to get back to where you were to have another shot. If you're getting upset over the game instead of your own lack of skill, there's clearly something wrong.
Secondly, the port to PC is pretty bad. I've checked around the Steam Discussions and found mixed results, but there are clearly people experiencing troubles with the game, and there's no fix in sight. I personally experience some of the worst stuttering and motion blur I've ever seen in a game before, I literally have to play the game on the smallest resolution to make it even bearable to play for smaller play sessions, and that's completely dodging how hard it is to actually play the game while trying to focus on such a blurry mess. It's certainly not a problem with my monitor though, as when recording the game, the footage catches both the blur and the stuttering, which you can see in the video posted in the next point.
Finally, but most importantly, the game isn't even consistent! By far the worst part about the game is how random the hitboxes for the spikes are. I literally have recorded footage of the cube going half way into a spike and surviving while other times getting kill by the mere edge of the spike. I find it pretty hard to recommend any game with such ridiculously inconsistent hitboxes, especially when spikes are practically half of what this entire game is. Seriously though, I actually have a recording of this:
In all honesty, it's certainly a nice idea, and I was really hoping it'd be better, but It just didn't come together properly. Short of that though, the controls are tight, and it's undeniably fun to glide through a level nailing everything nicely, but with the game being built around artificial difficulty in such a way that encourages frustration, it's certainly isn't the most fun game you could buy. The best part of this game is easily the music, but that's all downloadable for free on the Newgrounds Audio Portal.
If all that doesn't sound too bad, you probably will enjoy the game for what it is, but I'd highly recommend you take your $5 and buy Super Hexagon instead.

Many people would certainly agree that Fable, The Lost Chapter should have been the only game of the franchise. yes, forget about Fable 2 or 3 which should have never see the light of the day  and say in their shady cave.
But what is Fable ?
Fable is a RPG, i which you control a "Hero", a young man going on an epic journey within the world of "Albion". Quests, mysteries and epic battles against various foes will be the main actions you will undertake during your adventure ! But beware ! every single action you will take will have an influence... Upon you... Live as a hero, inspire glory, pride and peace... Or end up as the worst evil being in Albion inspiring fear, bringing destruction and much more...
Yes, this is what made Fable one of the most unique games when it came out, at least 10 years ago from now: Each action you will take, will change your personality, your physic and how or what people will think about you. Becoming a bright angel or the darkest horned evil being... You decide !
We will only regret the few hours required to complete the game which I personally think should have been improved within this remastered version instead of adding (extremely) optional DLCs adding new gear. Note also that the inventory system is just... Well, let's say it is not really optimized...
Anyway, I would only suggest you to buy this game which is for sure one of the modern "classic" in terms of RPG. And if you like achievements, this rmastered version will offer you some, perfectly achievable at 100% without too much challenge !

This review was somewhat difficult to write - Neon Struct's a game that, when I saw the premise, I really wanted to like.  The original Deus Ex and Thief games are high on my list of all-time favorites, and this is a game that tries to pay homage to both.  Unfortunately, it falls well short of such lofty heights.
The Good:
1. A number of levels have several paths through them.
2. The neon art aesthetic is different, and sometimes works in some levels.  I like the synthetic neon trees.
3. Light propagates between rooms if doors are opened.
4. The shifting architecture in the VR level was clever, I would have liked to see more tricks like that.
5. It has community mapping support, so fans can make and share their own levels.  Nice!
The Bad:
1. The AI is incredibly crude, getting stuck on street lamps in wide open areas, soemtimes bumping in to you without detecting you, and virtually blind and deaf.  "Search" mode on hearing a noise or glimpsing something is laughable -- the AI will typically walk in a 5 foot circle, never branching out.  This is the worst stealth AI I have seen in 30 years of gaming.
2. Difficult to impossible to tell what the actual light level of a given spot is by looking at the world around you often -- one square will be 100% visibility, while the square next to it will be 0% visibility.  Only way to tell is to look at the light meter.  This problem is exacerbated by the odd choice to apply a shaded vignetting to the screen when you're crouched, that artificially darkens the edges of the screen.
3. Sound propagation and environmental audio are exceedingly primitive -- footsteps can be heard halfway across a map with almost no roll-off with distance.  Sometimes they don't even correctly play from the correct right/left channel, reversing at times.
4. Very little enemy variety, and what there is is mostly cosmetic, beyond humans can be knocked out, robots can't.  No real differences in behavior, detection ranges/styles, etc.
5. Tools are mostly pointless, as the AI is blind and brainless.  I beat the game without using any tools beyond throwing a few coins to try to distract enemies (they really don't respond much to them).
6. Minigames for hacking/lockpicking are, once again, an awful idea -- if I need to take an action frequently, do not make me play the same tedious minigame.  The real source of tension is the risk of getting caught while I spend the time taking the action, a minigame is not needed and is something I'm just going to grow to hate doing, and savescum if I fail.  Keep it simple, Looking Glass and Ion Storm got it right.
Bottom Line -- Neon Struct would be a laudable find if it were the project of an amateur developer posting their personal projects to itch.io or the like, and would warrant feedback to the creator to continue growing their skills and encouragement to keep working and keep posting.  But unfortunately, it's a $20 game being sold on Steam as a professional product, and in that circumstance, it's not something I can really recommend buying, not when there are much better stealth games out there.  Pass on this one and go buy Thief 2 and Deus Ex (the original, not the remake), and slap some high-res texture mods on to pretty them up a bit.
Worth $18 just for the mall level.  Everything else is good too.

An aircombat game with mechs, very few mech games around these days.   What you see in the screen shots is what you get.  You take control of a mech and shoot down the enemies.
Standard WASD controls for movement and mouse controls for angular poitioning of view seem to work well, space for boost so you can move faster. Movement is good enough as long as obstacles are not in the way(ie buildings or indoors), fortunitly there are very few indoor sections becasue movement controlls are not pollished enough for that as of the time of this writting, and it doesn't seem like the designers intend this to be like Armored Core, but rather closer to Zone of the Enders so as long as they keep the cramped areas to a minimum things will be fine.
Combat is very simple. You look onto an enemy, empty everything you have into him until he dies, rinse and repeat, dodge via boost and drop flares to shake off missles launched by other enemies. Switch from one weapon to another when it needs to reload.The weapons are adequate for most enemies, machine guns for close range, missle for fire and forget, and rail gun for longer range sniping will be your bread and butter.  Most mission have a mech with funnels and a secondary missle, although they don't feel like they do anything(Maybe they do but if the player can't feel it this is a problem).  A few things make the weapons feel lacking. The sound design is one main issue here, the weapons are supposed to be large and attached to a massive mech. The sounds created when they fire should feel very very heavy.  I don't get that vibe from them.  Another problem which has been partialy addressed by a flashing "hit" button is that due to the high speed of everything involved and the sheer distance enemies are from you it is very difficult to tell if an enemy is hit by your attacks, which again could be fixed by proper sound design. I should both hear and feel the metal twisting and breaking when my railgun shot impacts an enemy, and the destruction of an enemy even more so.  I almost forgot there is an energy sword, but it is almost impossible to hit enemies with it. Everytime I take a swing I end up missing the enemy entirely( it is possible I am hitting the enemy and not realizing it, see my previous comments about sound design)
The enemies themselves are another story.  Low level enemies can be brought down by the methods in the previous paragraph, and can feel somewhat satisfying to take down, again see the previous paragraph on the importance of sound design in a game.  The problem comes when very powerful and mobile enemies swarm you which feel like a chore to take down.  They can pretty much dodge almost everyhting you throw at them and it feels like they moving so fast and playing by a different set of rules than me. My machine gun feels useless, railgun ocasionaly connects, spamming missles seem to be the only good option but I feel like the game is taking away my options when I fight these enemies instead of allowing me to get creative with the tools given to me as the player. I can't help but wonder if a few tweaks to the AI, or improved aiming for your mech would solve this problem for the faster enemies so they don't feel invincible.  Becasue of this I can't recomend playing this on anything but the lowest difficulty setting. Enemy airships can be interesting and a nice boss fight, but they need to have a different move set and AI than mechs, right now I can see enemy frigates moving in ways that feel unnatural for a ship(ie moving verticaly upward or tilting themselve ar odd anlge that would be very uncomfortable for the crew of said ship), but would be quite natural for a mech.  End of act boss design seems promising, the large white mech you see in the trailer called the Patriot shows some potential and is very fun and satisfying to take down.  He starts out easy, as his health is depleated he starts throwing out more damaging attacks requiring you to keep up or die, and other than commiting the cardinal sins of infinity respawing enemies, and a time limit I give that fight an A+.
Level design is a bit of a double edged sword. Some levels have no structure to give you a sense of distance, and even the ones with a large structure(space elevator, floating city, etc) to give you some sense of bearings feel like there is a lot of unused empty space. Too much cluter would slow me down.  The ultimate result is an inability to judge relative speed and distance to enemies/objects. Due to the large distance, and high speed you can't see the enemies which is a real shame since the designers went to a bit of trouble detailing the mechs and designing them. They should let us see them on screen with detail more than 10% of the time. They try to rectify this by a subwindow that opens showing a zoomed in semi tranparent view of the locked on enemy, but the animations and movement of the zoomed in enemy seem choppy, like it is running at 15 fps or soemthing.  I suspect this has to do with optimaztion and level of detail so the game doens't spend resources rendering something that wont be visible to the player.  The developers may have painted themselves into a corner and this might be the only good option left at this point for us to see and appreciate the enemy mechs during play, but more work needed here. The other alterantive would require redesigning gameplay and levels from the square one and slow things down which seems unfeasable at this point.  Most levels are simply a variation on kill everything in sight which doesn't seem too bad since this looks like it will be a short and fast game once done which isn't necesarly a bad thing( see most games made by Platinum games).
The plot of the game is another issue. I can't help but feel the developers were very passionate about it and trying to make their own Gundam-esq story, but unfortunitly they can't seem to tell it within the framework of the game they have setup. Since this game is fast paced they need to carefuly edit the dialog and make sure everything said over the radio during a mission either fleshes out that charcter more and/or adds the world/lore building, no room for waste here.    No character physicaly appears during game so we can't tell who anyone is. If they can find space in the screen during the game perhaps a small window could show up with the character portrait when they talk on the radio.  Funny story, I didn't relieze until the Act 1 boss (Patriot) that my mech had a pilot and a copilot since that is the only point the 2 characters seemed to have a conversation. The plot involves a dystopian future where a massive war scoarched the earths surface to most humans took the sky, but terrorist organization operating on the remains of the surface threaten to upend a fragile peace bewteen the 3 superpower nations( US, Russia, and China? It's not entirely clear). Good news is you don't need a deep plot for a game like this to be good, it just needs to give me an excuse to blow mechs up.
I have probably ranted enough at this point, but the ultimate question of whether I enjoyed the game( well ~40% of the game is out now. This is early access after all).  The answer to this is YES, mostly. My rants earlier account for relativly small part of my gametime.  I may have seemed critical of a lot of the game, but I did not write the previous paragraphs out of spite, but becasue I believe the game has the potential to be better.  There really arn't many giant robot games out there, in contrast to FPS which are a dime a dozen. The developers clearly like mechs/giant robots, though I suspect this is there first time making a video game and I think there is only 10 people or so on the development team so I can let some stuff slide. So in conclusion, Project Nimbus is a roughcut gem, and if you like Mechs you owe it to yourself to give it a shot since there are not many of this kind of gem around.

So I've only so far played this game for forty minutes, so these are just my first impressions here keep in mind, but so far I really, really, really like this game, except for some glaring flaws. Now, I know this is still in Early Access, and probably/maybe/hopefully/I pray these flaws will be fixed soon enough as the game develops, but until they're eliminated entirely, they're still something to keep in mind and be wary of.
THE GOOD:
Project Nimbus is something I've wanted for a very, very long time: an Armored Core for the PC. Now, it's not a real Armored Core, obviously, but this game plays like one of my favorite missions in Armored Core: For Answer that it's really hard to care. Another thing about this game that I really like is that, unlike with so many games that involve a lot of arial combat, in this your movement is almost perfectly unrestricted. Inertia does make a mess of things at times, and with how fast your mech moves it becomes rather unwise to stay close to buildings, but on the whole these are small issues once you get into things. Another thing I really liked was the bullet time button. I don't actually know what the game calls it (again, 40 minutes), but with a button you can temporarily slow down time to take note of your surroundings, change weapons quickly and smoothly, set off emergency escapes, or make effective use of the missiles despite the .00353 femtanosecond window for lock-on. The last thing I liked, one that I always rank least important but still quite deserving of mention here, is that this game is simply gorgeous! Yes, the modling on the mech isn't always perfect (like the tacked-on look of the wings), but the textures and visuals on the game field and such are beautiful, and it makes the absolute chaos that is a close range firefight come alive in a way I haven't seen in ages, if ever.
THE BAD:
As mentioned, this game is still in Early Access, so hopefully these things will be remedied soon enough, but there are quite a few issues with it that cause quite a bit of strain. First, foremost, and King of the Mountain on things that cause problems is that the game has enough optimization issues to fill a novelette. At least, I'm assuming that they're optimization issues, because otherwise this thing just naturally chugs twice the data of an unmodded Skyrim and runs worse than Skyrim with a full 346 mods on it. I'm packing a mid-range Alienware from 2014, and while this thing -can- run it at graphics settings above Medium it becomes unplayable due to framerate issues. Even at Medium it seems to have constant issues with the framerate and the drop in quality is quite steep as you move down the ladder, to the point that I just get distracted by all the beauty I'm -not- seeing. Another thing that irks me about this game is that ever-dificult problem child of 3D games, the camera. For most things the camera is actually quite good, able to allow you to manuver in 3D with very few issues at all, but the moment you wind up in an enclosed space then you have some rather major problems, problems only made worse if, for some reason, you happen to be using the blade (like in the first part of the second mission, by requirement). Another flaw, one that I find in an anoyingly large amount of games, is that the controller support isn't getting as much attention as it needs. That's not to say that the controller support itself has too many issues, the only big one I noticed being that switching weapons was a task and a half, but the game makes the not-terrible decision to introduce a significant portion of new controls mid-battle, and none of them are shown as controller buttons, making me figure out exactly what button is supposed to correspond to the blade (R3, by the way) and what button is this new weapon mapped to. Lastly, the menu has this annoying thing where, with a controller at least, your cursor just drifts about slowly rather than actually moving between options. It's not as big a complaint as the others, but I still feel it needs mention. These are the biggest flaws I can think of for now, but I know there's more.
VERDICT:
I like this game. It's slick, fun, and (when I decide looks beat gameplay) very, very pretty.The developers have obviously put a lot of work into this, and it shows quite well. There are flaws and bugs, yes, but time (and money) will (hopefully) smoothe things out, and even with the issues present it's still a very nice game. One worth far more of your money than, say, Lichdom Battlemage (not bitter).

As a game that tries to faithfully re-create the mechanics of the table-top game of Blood Bowl, this game does a good job. It is not, however, a football game with a fantasy setting; and it is this point that frustrated me the most. As someone who had not played the table-top game before, much less possessed any skill at it, I found making effective use of the mechanics in this game hard and the results were disappointing due to the very steep learning curve; successes were rare and offset by the frustrating ease with which failure occurred for even the simplest of tasks, and with little in-game guidance it was very difficult to even grasp at what I was doing wrong. What I have since learned is that this is not really a game about strategy with random elements, but rather ongoing mitigation of the high randomness that occurs turn-to-turn; and that just rubs me the wrong way.
If you enjoy the table-top Blood Bowl game and/or you are very familiar with its rules, you'll probably enjoy this game. If not, this is likely to leave you just as frustrated as it left me; save your money for something else.

The Blue Flamingo is a SHMUP created by small independant(?) studio Might and Delight, of Shelter fame. Staying true to the unique art style of their other games, The Blue FLamingo has a very unique earthy aesthetic. It is advertised that most of the assets in the game are all hand-crafted models, and this shows itself in the game. The aeroplane models are unique and alive, it is easy to see the time and effort required to put together a game like this. The background map, also having been hand-crafted is a pleasure to look at. That being said, where this falls flat is the overall colour pallete of the game which could be summarised as "50 shades of brown", it is certainly not displeasing for the most part, though it does make distinguishing thing's a little difficult. When the game goes into a night-time cycle it becomes especially hard to distinguish models, I am not entirely sure if this is by design or not.
As for the mechanics, the game has pretty standard but also customizable controls; WASD for movement, and left/right mouse buttons for the weapons. The game plays fine though there is a little lag when controlling the plane where it will take a fraction of a second to come to a stop(i believe this is by design) which i personally find offputting. The plane itself seems to have a hit-box slightly larger then the model itself, again nothing major, but it does lead to some frustrating moments.
The Blue Flamingo is advertised as a bite-sized SHMUP, and I can see why some people may enjoy the aesthetic and simple gameplay, but for the rest of us there does not seem to be much reason to return as there is no challenge, no difficulty settings, and only one game-mode.

I just finished level 20 out of 60. This is a neat modern take on brick breaker type games that feels more realistic phyiscs wise, and the gameplay feels smoother. The levels are three dimensional and the blocks(or cubes in this case) can be stacked, move when hit, and are not always just a simple pattern where you see exactly what there is from the very beginning. The items are fairly standard though there are some that might be csondered unique. Some of the items, for example, are: smaller or bigger paddle, smaller or bigger ball, wall behind your paddle, multiple balls, and a magnet that attracts the ball to cubes. I'm sure there are even more great features that I haven't ecountered yet since I still have 2/3 of the game left.
The music in this game is very relaxing and matches the looks. On that note, the graphics are very visually pleasing. I highly recommend this game, especially considering it doesn't even cost a dollar.

Sometimes you just want to sit in from of a pc while sitting in front of your PC. If you're an idiot like me, I'd bargain this is the game for you. Blendo is back with their masterful pacing and obtuse storytelling, and even now comes with a video game packed inside.
Inventive and creative, Quadrilateral Cowboy is a very good game. No single mechanic is ever exhausted and QC captures a feeling in a way most games can't. You'll walk away from Quadrilateral Cowboy feeling like a true hacker, even if all security systems in this universe are extremely rudimentary.
A few twists and turns here and there keep things fresh and make QC a must-play for fans of indie games.
Not without its flaws though, there are definitely plenty of engine issues with Quadrilateral Cowboy. I found myself clipping through environments, stuck in walls, and dealing with sloppy transitions regularly. An overall clunky interface can also be a bear on the experience.
Luckily its flaws don't hold it back too much and there's plenty here to like.

I really want to like this game. The theme and the asthetic is great (I'm a big fan of oldschool/retro cyberpunk and sci-fi) and there is a lot of detail to be found. The mechanics seem very interesting (I'm also a fan of games that use a command line interface as one of the primary input methods) and are quite diverse. You have a little hacking device you can plug into datajacks, a cyberdeck (or should I call it a suitecase deck?) which allows you to hack doors and stuff, a little robot you can give commands to and a bunch of other stuff.
The main problem I have with the game is: It is not a puzzle game. If I look at those mechanics I think "puzzle game!" immediately. But it's not. The challenge of the game is not coming from "solving" any logical puzzles. Those are all trivial and very straight forward. Instead you are supposed to complete the different levels as quickly as possible to compete on a leaderboard.
So is it a good time attack/speedrun game? I don't think so. Because while the mechanics are interesting and diverse, controling them feels very cluncy (it almost feels like that is on purpose) and are not very fun to use after you get past the "oh! shiny command line interface!" hype.
I think this game would have benefitted greatly by being a puzzle game with interesting puzzle design. I'm very sad it is not.

In this game you'll basically jump on trucks, sometimes avoiding trucks flying at you or climbing truck demons - it's one of those indie games, full of chaos and distilled fun and frustration.
To help you jump on trucks you obviously need powerups, like slowing down time, creating trucks, propelling yourself through the air or yelling "SUPER" and "TRUCK'.
The game doesn't have too much content, but steam workshop along with leaderboards can help enjoy the game more while you try to beat your times or challenges you set for yourself.
The game developed well, probably at least partially due to how open development was - with a free and easily publicly accessible open alpha demo along with free copies distributed to speedrunners, the devs got a lot of feedback and were very active. While the game does have some physics bugs and other problems, most of the unintended physics oddities were ironed out early in the development cycle, which, once again, helped the game mature quickly.
This is not a game for everybody and I cannot say that anybody should buy this, at least not at full price, but damn me if I didn't enjoy every single level of it. If you like games where you'll have to repeat the same level over and over until you get a specific jump just right, this might be the perfect game for you. Otherwise, you can try to find the open alpha and play it to get a taste of what it plays like.

At first glance, ClusterTruck is a dumb game. You start a level on a truck, you jump on the series of trucks in front of you until you eventually get to the goal banner. It's the kind of thing you'd expect to be basic youtuber or streamer shlock, and really, it fulfills that duty well. However, when you really get down to it, it's a god damn great game.
As a level based first person platformer, the main meat of the game is found in its level design, which is on the whole fantastic. I made the decision to play the game through without the use of the multiple purchasable powerups available and feel the game was better for it. You'd think the level design would be disrupted by dumb truck physics but aside from one level, they're not. Every world has a different setting (forest, steampunk, laser) and every level in every world has its own creative gimmick they employ, adding a ton of variety to general truck jumping.
My only gripes are a lack of player shadow (makes long drops harder to judge where you're landing) and a lack of customizable controller options (aiming your camera is important, so having the option to map jump to a shoulder button would be nice). Beyond that it's great and with workshop support and seasonal level packs I look forward to more trucks in my life.

*Disclaimer; I had this game donated to me for my channel by WEB, one of my fans. In fact, I made the 100% hardest difficulty guide for this game, so my opinion is actually much more valuable than your average reviewer*
Neon Struct is a knockoff of Thief, which is in itself a really good thing. The original two Thief games were and still are some of the greatest stealth games ever made. Sadly, it didn't get too many of the the most important things right from those games, and it ends up really suffering for it.
The biggest problem is how awful the overall ambience is, due to the simple sound system, small maps and lack of detail on any of the levels.
Imagine Deus Ex footsteps in small, under detailed levels with music or dialogue. Neon Struct, because of the overall lack of actual sound engineering and detail, ends up feeling like one of the biggest worlds of cardboard I've ever seen.
You will get really, really tired of empty, hollow levels with what feels like robots patrolling everything. You will feel like you are sneaking in a vacuum.
Finally, the game has no lethal measures. This doesn't sound too bad until you realize KO-ing people puts them out permanently.
You might as well be killing people when you knock them out in terms of gameplay.
It makes all the opposite mistakes that the new Thief game does. It has complex enough mechanics that let the player decide how to approach things, and a solid story, but none of the adorning touches that make you actually care, the whole game feeling hollow as a direct result.
There is far better, it ends up overly expensive for what it is, and there isn't anything to set it apart from what you would compare it to.
If you want a better game, Dark Mod will be (or is) free on Steam, and Thief Gold, Thief 2 and Splinter Cell Chaos Theory go on sale routinely.
The only people I would recommend this game to are people who have played practically every other light-index based stealth game and are willing to toss money away on what amounts to a lesser quality level pack for Thief 3.
This game simply isn't worth the time due to the competition it had coming out, and the overall short length and lack of real difficulty or unique aspect to the game.

I have been a long-time fan of the Warhammer series and tabletop games, so Blood Bowl was an amazing addition to my library. The game also reminded me a lot of Deathrow, which I played to death on the original Xbox.
If you like the Warhammer series, dice-rolling mechanics (as seen in Star Wars: Knights of the Old Republic and Dragon Age series), turn-based (or real-time) strategy, football, and bloody, brutal mayhem, then you will enjoy this game.
The aesthetics are pretty good - there is a fair amount of detail put into the character models. There is not much customization for the different characters - you can change their colors and equip higher level equipement once they meet the reuirements (this takes a long time). The music and sound effects are great and add to the violent and competitive atmosphere.
The controls are not too complicated as you will mostly be using the mouse, however, the learning curve is moderate to difficult - especially if you are unfamiliar with dice-rolling being a core element of the game (it only uses 6-sided [d6] die vs. the 20-sided one used in other tabletop games like Dungeons & Dragons, so it isn't too complicated) and turn-based strategy games. There is a lot to take in, and playing through the tutorial is strongly advised, even if you are a veteran. Guides, walkthroughs, and wikis will help you out a lot if you get overwhelemed or lost, and I have used some beginner guides myself to determine which team to start off with. Try not to be too deterred by constant loses - your team will improve with experience and you will learn better strategies as you continue playing.
You can play a single football match, a campaign mode, or "story" mode, where you act as a coach for your team. Be advised, even on the easiest difficulty, the game has an absolutely brutal start. If you are used to playing sports games, you will understand that, as a new team, losing is completely normal (and expected). You can also choose to play in real-time vs. turn-based, and I would suggest turn-based to begin with. There is also an option for a quicker, playstyle or the original rules used in the actual tabletop Blood Bowl that the game is based off of.
Before you begin, you must select your team - each having distinct playstyles and different strengths/weaknesses. Many guides will recommend you play as the undead, as they are the most well-balanced team (especially in the beginning). Speedster teams like the Elves (and their variants) excel at dodging and run + gun strategies, however, you can easily be knocked out by stronger opponents. That being said, teams like the Ogres or Goblins risk being left in the dust of speedy opponents. Once you select your team, you will have a set amount of money to purchase players (having substitutions is very helpful and highly recommended), as well as other aids like coaches and cheerleaders (these provide a boost during turnovers).
In the pre-match screen, you are able to use pocket money to purchase buffs for yourself, or debuffs for your opponent. Examples include: a wizard who can "try" (again, success all depends on your dice roll) to damage the enemy team, potions to illegally enchance your players, or bribes to swing the referees' favor in your direction. You can also pay to have random tests on enemy players (they will be unable to play the match if they are caught using illegal enchancements), or purchase rioting fans that will attack any fans for the opposing team.
During gameplay, you are able to move everyone on your team depending on their Movement Points. A critical mechanic to be aware of is how turnovers work: turns will automatically end if you fumble, fail to pick up the ball, or have one of your players knocked down (all of these conditions also apply during the AI's turn). This allows for very deep strategy, as it is sometimes more pertinent to have your defending player knock both him//herself and your opponent down to force a turnover (say, if your opponent is close to scoring a touchdown). Whenever you roll, you will be able to select 1 dice from your resulting roll, so attacking with players who have more die (3 instead of just 1) is highly advised. You can buy team rerolls that are extremely helpful (ex: if you are on offense and roll two "attacker downs," meaning you will have your player fall down and cause an immediate turnover, you can try to roll for better results). Most players will waste a turn to stand up (unless you have a "jump back" skill that allows you to move after standing up).
The strategy in the game is excellent, as can gain flanking bonuses, blitz once during your turn (otherwise, you can only attack if there is an enemy next to your player), and select different skills when your players level up. An example of a useful skill is "block," which allows a player to ignore a "both downed" dice result (only your opponent will be downed). If both the attack and defender have "block," then no one is downed and the turn continues. Positioning is integral to success in this game, as units cannot simply move away from other players' "tackle zones" - a dodge roll has to be issued to determine if the unit can successfully move away from a nearby player. Dodge rolls must be calculated for each unit that has a tackle zone aroun the moving character (so "caging," or trapping key players - like the ball carrier - is a viable strategy)
Games last for 16 turns for each side (32 in total), and there is a timer during each turn so you cannot just idle around.
I really enjoyed this game, but I must warn people that you may find the game too slow or too boring if you are not used to games that incorporate dice-rolling into everything. You could still try real-time mode instead, but be aware that you do not completely control the outcome of your actions - chance plays a heavy role in Blood Bowl.
If you like tabletop (especially dice) games, football, Warhammer, and strategy, and challenging AIs, then1 you should definitely give this game a try.

The Fall reminds me quite a lot of the old Tex Murphy games, of which I played little. It's mostly a point-and-click adventure of finding the right items to use, as well as thinking of inventive ways of using the environment around you; interspersed with 1D combat (in the sense that verticality is not used) that doesn't really do a lot for the gameplay except break up the action.
The exploration and puzzle-solving breaks down a bit at times (which can translate to: I used a guide) due to the need to, say, closely analyze and then shoot a tiny bit of the dark unseemly corner of a room to find a key item to progress; or, the presence of a Network interaction that is almost never used, and is then critical when it finally is used.
BUT, there's some redeeming qualities. When the adventure/item-using stuff works, it works well. Some of the "merit badge" sequence of the game involves some really funny solutions to problems; and for the most part, the game's problem solutions make sense.
And as others have mentioned, the dialogue and writing in the game is really well-done. Dialogue at first appears a bit of a side-play to the main exploration tasks since primary characters are just robots. Then there's some people where you get interesting back-and-forths. You meet a mainframe who, as he's evolved, started talking completely like a human. Over time even Arid comes to change a bit; there's a chilling point late in the game where an early line, her opening greeting, ("I am the A.R.I.D. on-board a Mark-7 Combat Suit. My intentions are peaceful.") is re-delivered with very different voice acting.
The ending was definitely both very satisfying, and made me want to play the sequel if/when it comes out.

So, a part of me wants to recommend
because it actually does contain an interesting premise and a smart marriage of gameplay mechanics to story while having a strong sense of presentation.
But then I recall that this game is essentially incomplete, and mis-titled. It should be called, "
"
See,
is - despite the Metroidvania appearance - a point and click adventure game more than anything else. Which means that the action game elements are heavily de-emphasized and underdeveloped, while the greater burden of the game's enjoyment ends up in the story and tone department.
Which is fine, because the story does actually go to some interesting places and the tone is fitting and smart. So the game actually is enjoyable, until it just stops all of a sudden out of nowhere, right when it shouldn't. Basically, this is a prologue to a much more complete story than anything else.
The devs seem to think that they're creating a smaller version of Mass Effect. That they're telling a full complete story in
#1 here, that will be continued in a sequel which may or may not link directly with your save file, but will tell another full and complete story as part of a larger arc of a trilogy, that when examined together will be an even grander narrative.
Except, and here's the important part - the story told here
. It ends very suddenly with a reveal after what could essentially be considered the game's inciting incident and initial complication. On a story diagram chart, this doesn't even get to a middle body, let alone a climax, denoument or coda. Without any of those elements, the story cannot be considered self contained in the slightest, and worse, this means the game's creators obviously don't understand how story structure works in the larger context on which they're trying to tell one.
It comes down to this: if this game had marketed itself as an episodic adventure with another part along the way - this would be fine. In an episodic game series like Telltale likes to do,
would be a fine first episode, and the fact that it leaves off with a feeling of incompleteness would be acceptable due to the expectation that more is on the way. But since this is sold as a complete game, with any sequels also being sold as complete games, it must be judged as a complete game.
And
absolutely does not live up to that standard.
So, buyer beware.
may be worth it as an introduction to a more complete episodic series down the road if its sequels proves to be excellent and present a sense of completeness, but as a standalone title be prepared to get blue balled pretty hard here.

I thought a long time about whether to recommend this game or not. I finally decided to give this game a "no". Here's my explanation why:
I bought this game, knowing it was a short, but nonetheless story-rich experience. While the visuals might give the impression, this is sort of a "Swapper"-clone, its pace is much slower and more emphasis is placed on actual reading and getting to know your surroundings. All in all, it can be described as a 2D point n click adventure with combat elements.
While I really enjoyed the story and the atmosphere of the game, I was horribly overstrained by the gameplay. I know, I do not play many adventure games and never really have, so it should come as no surprise to me that I had some trouble, navigating through the game. However, soon the intense atmosphere was destroyed by the fact, that I was walking through the same corridor the sixth time or so with my flashlight on permanently, just to figure out, where in the surroundings it was, what I had overlooked. This is also a problem, since crucial objects blend perfectly into the background and you have to scan everywhere.
In the end, I had to look up a few solutions in a guide, since I wanted to finish the game, but gave up on finding a solution myself. Maybe I lack the patience and/or logic for such games, so if you are used to such a gameplay, you might love The Fall. If you are, however, like me, you will probably not enjoy it much and soon end up on a try-everything-in-your-inventory-on-everything-on-the-map-just-to-see-if-it-works-state.

There was also some care clearly put into making the world very interactive, though this typically amounts to just picking the item up and moving it around. The sticky-note system lets you leave tips & messages for your friends to see whenever they play through a level, akin to the Talos Principle's graffiti except you can actually type whatever you like on the note.  The notes are also small enough in size that someone worried about potential spoilers can avoid zooming in to look at them.
The gameplay itself has all the right tools for a stand-out puzzle game, though most of the levels are largely "I know I'm supposed to use this device, lets watch for where I use it".  By the time you're given all the tools at once and aren't being especially corraled, the game is over.  I ended up with 6.2 hours, and I spent some extra time on certain levels playing around with how smoothly & automated I could make things...building long batch files while in the "Casing" mode so I could sail through the non-casing mode with good timing and a few blink commands rather than frequently accessing the deck.  If you have several friends who play it, you may get some extra playtime by trying to beat your friend's fastest times on the various heists...at the time I played it, none of my friends had given it a go.
I highly recommend playing it if the concept sounds up your alley, but I'd wait for it to go on sale, or wait for the Workshop to add new levels or the like (I'm posting this review just a few days since release, so take that into consideration relative to whenever you're reading this review. The best way to describe NEON STRUCT is if Deus Ex, Minecraft and a Lava Lamp had a threesome. Thats a sobering mental image but the best i can do for you since im only about 30% through the game. Lemme' elaborate.
NEON STRUCT is a neon soaked minimalist stealth game set in a cyberpunk world rich with the classic government espionage and cloak and dagger themes all too familiar from games like Deus Ex or the movie Bladerunner. You navigate Jillian Cleary through a series of enviroments usually tasked with breaking into a complex and stealing valuablee information, the thing NEON STRUCT gets right is in its simple rules and gameplay whilst slowly turning up the difficulty and throwing you deeper in the conspiracy you're involved in.
If you've played the Thief series - Jillian uses almost identical tactics to the Thief protagonist Garret, in that you'll be sticking to the shadows, knocking out guards, picking pockets and infiltrating the level to complete your objective. Simple stuff but NEON STRUCT  is an homage to these old stealth bangers and does it well, now. Onto Music and Story
Firstly the music is superb, almost if Flock of Seagulls writ the OST for Deus Ex. Most simple levels are heightened by the amazing soundtrack that perfectly fits the game world. The hubs usually have a radio playing one of the more electronic disco songs that really set the tone of the world
Then theres the story, which at the moment seems pretty throw-away. The classic covert operation trying to impeach on peoples rights (last time i'll mention Deus Ex, but think Deus Ex) is whats in store in NEON STRUCT and while it fits for what the game is going for - it really feels like im going through the motions and no fork in the story has caught me by suprise.
But it feels like that's not what NEON STRUCT is concentrating on. Really, this is a well rounded minimalist stealth game that'll keep you entertained and is well worth the money, i'm having fun, and you should too. Christmas sale is around the corner, give up some sheckles for once.

I should have written this review ages ago but better late than never! Neon Struct has been the game that really got me into the stealth game genre. It’s one of my favourite games of 2015 and still to date my favourite from Minor Key Games’ library.
So, why do I love this game so much? Well, the gameplay reminds me a lot of the early Thief games (Thief 1 & 2) without the bow or weapons. It has grenades that stun enemies, area blackouts (I found this the most useful in my ghost runs), and later a grenade that teleports you where the grenade was thrown, and potions that can quiet your footsteps, cloak you, make you run faster, give healing and instantly hack cameras & computers without having to play the hacking mini game (where you are playing pong). With these items the game encourages you play it with a stealthy, pacifist approach or running around knocking everyone out. However, if you want to have the best grade of every level, you have to never get caught and collect all the geocaches that are spread throughout the levels (geocache tokens can help distract an enemy away from their patrol route). Money and items can also be collected. The levels in this game are well made and varied.
The smooth, minimalist and neon look to the graphics is very striking, and the featureless faces of the NPCs is unnerving and reminiscent of the themes of the story. The soundtrack of Neon Struct that plays in between missions is wonderful and in my opinion well worth the money. Neon Struct’s story is a little similar to parts of Deus Ex’s plot, but comes into its own by going in a different direction.
The only flaws of Neon Struct are there is no music playing throughout the mission levels of game making them too quiet (which was fixed in Slayer Shock), there could have been a little more detail in the level without messing up the look of the game, and it took me only seven hours to beat my first game and left me wanting more!!!

Fable was one of my favourite RPG games on PC when it was first released in 2004. The story is gripping, the graphics is certianly much more polished and the sound effect is for sure much better compared to 2004 version.
Fable has aged well, partly because some of its best ideas have since become action-RPG staples - things like real-time combat, good-evil alignment and a world that reacts to your actions. Fable didn’t invent any of these things, but it does them well and uniquely enough that it’s still fun to play today.
Fable has aged well, partly because some of its best ideas have since become action-RPG staples - things like real-time combat, good-evil alignment and a world that reacts to your actions. Fable didn’t invent any of these things, but it does them well and uniquely enough that it’s still fun to play today. It’s easy to feel at home in this fantastical version of England’s green and pleasant land, where the countryside goes on forever and nobody is from inside the M25, and you’re greeted by cheers and applauding admirers whenever you step into the village pub for a pint. The place feels alive.
Fable is a simple and recognisable heroic tale at heart - you go from young boy to storied warrior, leaving your mark on the land of Albion, and eventually avenging your family - but the setting and sense of humour make it much more endearing than the usual po-faced videogame fantasy.
The strange thing about Fable is that for all the choice it offers, there’s very little consequence. You can get married, but after that you can run off for literally years and leave your wife or husband alone and they don’t seem to mind. You can murder shopkeepers, but everyone soon forgets about it. Its morality is very simplistic and unsubtle by modern standards. This makes it feel rather shallow, but it also enables you to be playful with its morality, if the mood takes you.
Fable Anniversary hasn't added much to the original just save achievements and a harder 'Heroic Mode'. Updated graphics, improved controls, and a new save system.
If you enjoyed Fable, you will sure like this version

The Impossible Game...
I played this game on the iPhone and PS3, and I seriously enjoyed it back then, even supporting its Steam Greenlight. TIG still fails to disappoint me. While it may differ for you, it's CPU/GPU-friendly, and maintains a minimum of 15fps.
The game still retains its really fun challenge, and is great to kill time. Another perk of it is that you can show your friends and see how hard they rage when they get to Chaoz Fantasy or die on the Triple Spikes.
The Level Editor adds a new level of replayability to the game, and I'm still looking forward to see what the community has to offer with a new Impossible Level.
There are just a few problems I find with this version. The first - this is the version with a wider field of view (think iPad), giving you more time to react (and let's face it - Heaven becomes a tad easier). The Player Cube has a lower gravity effect, meaning those two Triple Spike groups (on the Yellow section on Chaoz Fantasy and the second Blue section on Heaven) become almost impossible (you had about three frames to jump and be safe on any other version - here you only have one).
Overall, TIG in general is a great game; the one thing is that it's more expensive on Steam - it's your decision if the Level Editor is worth it.
EDIT: Yeah, don't judge me, but I don't really like Geometry Dash, so I won't compare it to The Impossible Game. This one is worth more even though it has fewer levels, trust me.

The game starts you out slow - one room, one puzzle, and gradually works you up to several rooms with several simultaneous puzzles.
The overall atmosphere is very good... a little robot exploring a run-down robot city. And the sound is fantastic, with a variety of full-length songs and themes for each area you explore.

As someone who used to play Warhammer tabletop, yet only knew about Blood Bowl by name, I picked this up in a steam sale out of curiosity. I recommend to pick it up in a sale if it's the thing that tickles your fancy.
I'd describe it as a turn based strategy game that relies heavily on positioning and risk management mashed together with an (american)football manager.
While I first needed to get the hang of the way the mechanics work (how often I cursed at my players not being able to pick up or throw the ball forward), through trial and error I managed to grasp the game mechanics to the point where I'm now winning games vs the AI (btw, the tutorial - it does nothing. Try hotseat for your first games). This is the sour apple you'll have to bite through. So on to the game's selling points:
+In campaign mode - build your team from scratch and level up your players to grant them skills or (for Chaos/Nurgle/Skaven - mutations) to flesh out your playstyle.
+Lots of teams
+Great commentary (really, the comments add a lot to the game)
+There are inducements and things you can pay for like cheerleaders/coaches, bloodweiser babes, halfling cooks, bribes, potions and even the help of a wizard hidden in the audience.
-Progression feels a bit slow; you'll need to be succesful at a couple of matches to earn your first skill for one player and a match can take an hour.
-Some of the inducements seem a bit underwhelming and their use is not apparent unless you do a little bit research (example: having cheering fans without a wizard supposedly does nothing)
-Randomness of the dice - If all the rolls go right for the opponent you can still end up staring powerlessly as your opponent slips through your tight defense.
-This game requires a certain taste. Some may find this dull or too frustrating.
-Some might consider the graphics to be too poor at this day/age (in which case, I'd suggest looking out for BB2), though I wasn't bothered (except by the audience ;))

I attempted to try this game for ten minutes to determine whether I would continue to play it or delete it, and I ended up playing the whole thing through today.
I can best describe it as Limbo meets Dead Space and I highly recommend it to anyone who enjoys intelligent side scrollers with puzzles.
It's currently available for Steam for ten dollars and while the game itself is fairly short, it's an impressive storyline about an AI powering a suit that contains its injured human. I don't want to give anything else away about the storyline so I'll just list the pros and cons:
+ Excellent story about the restraints placed on AI that translates to a wider lesson about societal rules and constraints
+ 2D but a rich, atmospheric environment
+ A soundtrack that compliments the dark and artificial environment
+ Very little actual combat, which is great because the story is at the forefront here
+ Good dialog, solid voice acting
+ Puzzles strike the right balance between simplistic and ragequitting difficulty.
- Some of the puzzles don't really logically follow from step to step, so there will be a few moments of "Wait, what?"
- Controls are simple but not as fluid or accurate as they could be. This is a minor concern since combat is a minor part of the game at best, and it's easy to get used to the mechanics
- Too short. I finished the whole thing in just over four hours. However, at $10, that's decent value (and part 2 is in the works)

I've played through all of this game's 60.  It's very chill.  A very gentle difficulty curve.  I like it's trance-synth soundtrack.  It's you're basic Breakout clone with a twist.  The ball uses the standard 2D physics the game has always had, but the bricks use 3D physics.  Larger bricks are heavier, smaller bricks are lighter.  The bricks can also be stacked vertically.  The game has falling Arkanoid-style power-ups and power-downs that you can catch.  The game also has a magnet feature that makes the ball draw towards the bricks for a few seconds.  Trigger this while you have the electrical power-up for effective brick-busting!
PROS:
+ Chill, enjoyable casual arcade gameplay
+ Clean, visually-pleasing graphics aesthetic with ray-traced shadows
+ Score multiplier rewards those who can clear levels with speed
+ Arkanoid-style Upgrades / Downgrades to catch or avoid
+ Excellent value!
CONS:
- No Arkanoid laser gun upgrade.  Darnit.
- Mouse control doesn't work correctly when my flight stick is plugged in.
- Shows you multiple achievement progress reports after every level.  Minor annoyance.
- Only one graphics option
- Ambient occlusion combined with the existing ray traced graphics would have looked really sweet.
- No multiplayer
Anyone who has enjoyed simpler arcade games of the past should get this because the price is ONE DOLLAR!  This is a no-brainer!  Fun, relaxing little game with an excellent value.  Support this developer!

First Impressions Video:
Quadrilateral Cowboys is a crazy ride. It's not without its flaws, but it's a great time.
Basically, QC (because that name is WAY too long) is about being freelance "hackers" who steal stuff. Most of the game is an interplay between the real world around you and console commands that you type into your deck (in game computer).
The game is set in a strange cyber punk 80's setting. A probably dystopian society and more weirdness around every corner makes the world enjoyable to be in.
Now, the gameplay. This sits in a weird space for me. I really like it. The concepts behind it are great and the execution is enjoyable, but the levels never allow the depth that one would expect from a puzzle game. Every level brings in a new ability and each of those levels is focused on that thing. In other words, every level asks you "do you know how to use this ability?" but no level ever delves into the interplay between the abilities. I was always expecting to find a big level with complex puzzles necessitating the use of all of the skills I'd learned so far, but that level never came. Plus, the puzzles aren't that difficult. Most of the time I could easily see what needed to done, and succeeding was just a matter of things out.
But it's not al bad, because I've enjoyed the experience. The game was definitely fun, just not as fun as it could have been.
In the end, QC is unique and definitely worth the time, but it never manages to mature into a serious puzzle game. Is it worth picking up? At $20, I would say that if you really want to check it out, you can pick it up. If you're only interested in it, wait until it's on sale for around $10, because it's definitely worth that price.

I'm a big fan of Thirty Flights of Loving and Gravity Bone so i've been excited for this for while but I have to say I'm left a touch disappointed with it. The hacking mechanics work well and it has a quirky comic book vibe that's coupled with a lot of weird and wonderful set-design. The story is lovely too: a minimal tale about three wistful, nerdy friends just hanging out and hacking some. Unfortunately, it never builds into anything specific and ends up feeling a lot like a prologue for another game; one I’d definitely play if it ever came out. I do like the idea of constructing a game out of vignettes though, so I definitely await whatever project Brendon Chung comes up with next. If you like the idea of hacking and are big into, I don't know, something like Wes Anderson movies then I reckon you'll really dig it this, flaws and all.
Great game though short. Hopefully the workshop can add some more playtime. Got a short playtime since i initially pirated it.

While I don't want to diminish Brendon Chung's own artistic style, I find that the simplest way to describe Quadrilateral Cowboy is to say that it is cyberpunk with a heavy Wes Anderson flavor. Modernist visuals are skillfully blended with the attitudes of cyberpunk to make a universe that is truly fun to play in and examine.
You play as one of the members of a three-woman tech contractor firm which specializes in performing high-tech theft. You use a variety of black-market cyber tools to solve puzzles in order to steal whatever you've been paid to. During the breaks between jobs you have the opportunity to learn more about the personalities and histories of the other characters, adding an emotional dimension to the game without using dialogue.
Chung has also made an introductory guide for making mod levels for QC to accompany the game and it seems he is planning to update it further to answer questions people are having, which I really appreciate.
My main complaint is that it feels far too short. I really kept wanting to be able to see more of QC's world after it ended. But overall I truly enjoyed playing it. The high point of the game, for me, was being tasked with making digital copies of the brains of coma patients in a clinic floating in space.

I enjoyed this game immensely, even though I didn't expect to. I mean, it's indie with a minimalist (read: entirely devoid of detailed textures, faces, etc.) art style. And how many of those games have we seen come onto the market, only to end up being overhyped, overpriced, half♥♥♥♥♥♥♥turds?
Yeah, an awful lot, I know, but this game ain't one of 'em. Now, I'm not gonna spend too long fellating this game and telling you all the things I love about it- the atmosphere, the soundtrack, the story, the setting, how everything going on in the game has real-world sociopolitical questions to pose to the player as they experience the game- quite frankly, I absolutely positively adore this game, but there are some things that aren't so good that I suspect you'd like to know, like the AI- most of the time the AI is fine. You use darkness in this game to get around stealthily and avoid enemies, and they're believable enough when they grope around in the dark for a switch, but sometimes, they come after you like that one ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ you used to play tag with, you know the one, who would always peek and then pretend to not know where you were for five of the most aggravating seconds of your childhood? (I was that ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, but that's beside the point.) Well, the AI can seem like that sometimes, but you almost always have a gadget you can use to get away with, a coin to distract them with, so really, it's not a super big deal.
On top of that, it's a rather short game- don't get me wrong, this thing is an experience, but it's like a good book or TV series- you maybe don't like it in the beginning and don't care, but then it hooks you and you binge watch it, and then you're happy... And then it's over. You play the DLC, get a few questions answered, and then it's over again, and all you're left with is the memories. Fitting, given the cyberpunk setting and all, and I'm all for that mono no aware stuff, but yeah.
Also worth noting- there is no direct, offensive combat in this game. you have grenades that make darkness, stuff that can incapacitate or K.O. an enemy, but if you were hoping for some shway Receiver-like stealth gunplay, that's not a thing in this game. I don't feel like that's a problem, just thought you'd like to know.
I feel this game deserves your time and money, for the story, for the gameplay, for the atmosphere, for the questions it asks the player about the world around them, and for the questions it asks the player about themselves. And for the rockin' soundtrack and the sick aesthetic. But hey, don't take my word for it- there's a free demo for this game out, try it for yourself. I sincerely hope you enjoy it like I have.

This game has a lot wrong with it, but there are so few games like the orginal Thief and Thief 2 that I'd still recommend it.
Pros:

- Lots of interesting areas to explore.
- Enemies telegraph well, it was always obvious what had caused them to become alert/see me.
- Not all enemies can be neutralised and those that could had to be dealt with steathily - which forced me to play in a way that makes this sort of game more fun!
Neutral:
- I think the quality of the dialogue would have grated on me if it was a voice over, it was quite cheesey in places
Cons:
- I can hear the foot steps of the guy in the basement when I'm on the 3rd floor!
- Sound didn't seem very "directional" at all, often I couldn't tell where a sound was coming from.
- Large parts of the ending could have been left out and made for more satisfying experience.
- Mistakes are too cheap, enemies seem to "forget" too easily.
All in all, it's not a bad game. I think it just needs some more polish.

I initially wandered off from this game and got busy with other stuff, but after revisiting and beating the game, I realized it was the stealth game I'd been missing/needing for a while.  It's pretty easy if you don't want a good grade, but meeting the bonus objectives of no takedowns, no sightings, no alarms, etc really increases the challenge and satisfaction.  Story also is pretty cool, and I liked the Strangers' vague 4th wall breaking comments.  Also has a neat visual appeal, very minimalist like its gameplay, and it shows just how much game you can squeeze from a solid formula (instead of junking it up with all kinds of gimmicks).
I really liked the general lack of bottlenecking.  There's multiple ways to approach a level, and that's a nice breath of fresh air from a lot of stealth titles.  Geocache hunting was a nice touch, encouraging me to explore the level more thoroughly.
Also, I made it my personal mission to murder every security camera I saw... I'm not sure why I had it out for them in particular, but it felt right to methodically terminate them one by one and leave no witnesses.  ^_^
8/10, great way to build upon Eldritch's original engine and stealth system.  I recommend this to people who want a break from normal stealth games.

Chronicles of Teddy is not a good game.
It has beautiful graphics with wonderful backgrounds and top notch character designs and animation.
The music is also very good.
COT is a side scrolling action/exploration game in the spirit of Dragon's Curse and Monster world 4, even stealing the upwards and downwards slash from the latter. Some compare it to Zelda 2 although I have no idea why.
Unfortunately COT fails as a game in every single possible way other than the pretty looks and sounds.
The play control is so bad I can't understand how it got a release at all and after years of complaining about the control the devs just don't seem to care to fix it.
Imaging controlling a character who's hit box is twice the size of her actual sprite while trying to hit enemies who's hit box is the size of a single pixel. This unfortunate bit of lazy programing is combined with a weapon so useless and without range that you will wonder if your controller is broken. I assure you it will be if you subject yourself to this undercooked mess for very long.
A wicked set of sub weapons would have gone a long way to make this better but you are given none. Not one.
Instead of becoming empowered by power ups like a double jump and wall slide you are basically cursed one these are obtained. The wall slide alone will cost you your sanity as you will screw up jump after jump as your character sticks to walls when you don't want her to and randomly chooses to execute wall jumps at a slow or fast speed. It's like rolling the dice every time you jump.  Their is no continuity. No matter how much you play you will never feel good at COT because the physics for jumping and platforming are never on the money.
Sometimes you will land a downward stab perfectly, then, same jump, same enemy, and you take a hit. It makes no sense. After 35 years of playing difficult platformers I can honestly say that COT is the cheapest and most under-designed of any ever made.
The last form of the last boss has one opportunity to hit him. You have to wait for it. He did this move on an average of once every 5 minutes. Making the fight last almost 30 minutes. An appropriate end to a horrible gaming experience.
I couldn't recommended Chronicles of Teddy even if it was free.

Is the game pretty?
Yes.
That's it.
That's the good parts.
Anything regarding combat in the game is horribly designed. Your tiny range forces you to overwhelmingly rely on the downstab and upstab attacks because they last for more than a tenth of a second, unlike anything else you can do. Having such a tiny range could be less of an issue if it wasn't so easy to get inside an enemy's hitbox and then you take contact damage, forcing you to re-engage.
Most enemies that have some capability for defense you need to wait for a time where they're vulnerable - which may take a while - and on some of them this vulnerability isn't just so that you can damage them, it's so you can damage them without getting damaged, because sometimes you'll kill an enemy and in the process go through it and hit a trail of fire it left before it died. Some enemies are simply placed in such a way that if you get unlucky there's nothing you can do - such as a spike thrower enemy that will shoot roughly a dozen spikes at you in a hallway and you can only block low spikes and the hallway is not tall enough for you to avoid the other spikes so you either just get hit or try to hide somewhere and wait for it to end and hope you can get to the enemy before it begins.
I feel like the idea that's tried to be passed with the horrendous combat is that the player character is no fighter - which I'm fine with, it makes sense - and this is reinforced by the fact that other than bosses, very few enemies actually have to be defeated and doing so will barely reward you, if at all. This doesn't explain problems such as getting stuck inside big enemies and other clunkiness issues.
The music password system may be good in concept, but running around dungeons to get passwords to open doors gets boring, fast; if you have a walkthrough, you can just skip them, at least.
You eventually get a wall jump powerup - it behaves oddly with the previous double jump powerup in that you can't double jump after you touch a wall and sometimes you'll jump directly at a wall to try and slide on it and you'll instead do a double jump. Also, you can't attack immediately after a double jump, which takes some time getting used to, as there's a lot of sections where it feels like you have to attack at the apex of a double jump only to be reminded that, no, you can't.
I'm pretty sure the game didn't have a map when I first started playing, but I gave up for several months before coming back and now it has a map, so at least it's a bit easier to not get lost.
Also, during the final boss? You can't deal damage to it without taking damage afterwards. It's not a bug.

Ah, what fun it is to play the good ol' Blood Bowl! I used to play the tabletop version and fell in love. On the battlefield that is Spore reviews, I have to join the 'Good game' side.
Spore is split up into five different parts, and that's the main idea of the game. You start as a small cell, and have to work your way up to the point where you're an intergalactic space lord. The five parts of the game are:
Cell stage, where you, as a cell, must live out your carnivore/herbivore days to eat as much as you can to the point where you grow legs
Creature stage, where you and your newly found legs must waddle around the entire planet to either kill or befriend other species so you can enter the
Tribal stage, where the game shifts into an RTS, and you and your new tribe must become buddy buddy with or invade to then become a civilisation
Civilisation stage, which is quite similar to the tribal stage, but instead, you and your new technology must race against other civilisations to become king of the world
Space stage, the biggest part of the game, where you can fly around in your new spaceships to colonise other planets and meet other space civilisations.
The end of the game is still unknown to me, if there is one.
I, personally, loved all the stages, and there you have it.

I have mixed feelings.
It's a generelly nicely immersive game with some great voice acting, interesting characters and clever writing that begs for a continuation as the game ends with a cliffhanger.
You control a robot suit that is supposed to be piloted by a human person wearing it. From space you violently crash into some planet's surface diving some dozen meters below into a cavern. With the human operator unresponsive and possibly seriously injured the robot suit's A.I. takes control of all movements attempting to reach the surface where it hopes to find medical aid for the pilot. Along the way the A.I. intentionally puts the pilot at even greater risks to gain access to otherwise unauthorized systems of the suit, fighting off other robots that don't take too kindly to her presence (or, at least your A.I. is voiced pretty greatly by a woman), solving puzzles, discovering a bit about the domestic robot production facility she'll soon stumble into and even more about herself raising philosophical questions for example about humankind, artifical intelligence, obedience and empathy.
The gameplay can be a bit tedious. What may look like an action platformer at first sight is for most parts actually a sidescrolling, puzzle-solving adventure game. There is combat, but it feels tacked on and as similarily stiff as it did to me in "Gemini Rue". The game could easily live without it, though a gun with an attached flashlight that is aimed down in the eerie dark to examine things probably begs to be fired.
The middle part where you are supposed to do what felt like petty errands in order to "graduate" as a "domestic robot" in that abandoned facility didn't feel as enjoyable, though I suppose oldschool adventure fans will love the dozen item-world-interactions and backtracking you'll have to do (I did look up a walkthrough because I got stuck several times and wanted to speed it up). Story-wise I guess these parts fit, but the general philosophical message that comes with them probably could have been expressed just as well without dragging on for as long.
But perhaps I'm biased. I almost naturally prefer less puzzling/adventuring and more of an interactive/cinematic experience when it comes to games that are as immersive as this one as I like to stay "in flow". Here you'll inevitably stumble a bit unless you are a puzzling pro or have a walkthrough/a Steam guide at your side. I don't remember the puzzles as being illogical but things are rarely plain obvious either. No handholding here, Telltale friends.
It's a genuinely interesting title that feels somewhat bold and ambitious, but I'm not entirely sure if it wants to or should be a puzzle-solving adventure game or a more direct/cinematic action title.

I usually never write reviews (I know, it's a cliche) but I had to write one for this game, is very fun, especially if you love cladenstine/hacking type things, if you played Hacknet (which if you like hacking games it is a must, super fun and mostly realistic) it is like that, but you move around and aren't just using a terminal remotely, you go fromplace to place using your terminal on the fly and after each location (each location has 3 jobs in it) you get new gear to help you along) the story so far is fairly good (I am not far so I cannot say much about the story) the game is very "figure it out, do it however you want, there are no guidelines" style, which works phenomenally.
