Another indie dev (basically one guy) designs a simple, yet gorgeous Metroidvania game with a strong Zelda 2 vibe. It does have the graphical look and musical persuasion of Fez, however, I would argue that it is nowhere near as insidiously cryptic. This game will challenge you, yes, but will reward exploration - the clues can be found and decyphered - *cough, La Mulana.
Pros:
- Metroidvania - duh
- Zelda 2 - duh
- Great exploration opportunities
- Neat mechanic allowing unlocking of secrets through musical sound
- 8-, 16-bit homage
Cons:
- Because of the 8-, 16-bit retro feel, the controls (fully gamepad-compatible) can feel a bit wonky. There is a lag to sword swiping in the air after jump (and especially double jump). Spoiler - Once wall grab is obtained, the jump, double jump near walls can convolute with the grab and confuse what you had originally intended. Ok, basically, this con is criticizing its intentional retro control design, but, I grew up with crappy controls due to these limitations - no big deal.
- Spoiler: After all the orbs are obtained, a new level is unlocked that basically yields a health upgrade - there is a treasure chest as well. However, one of the levels in this level is so exponentially more difficult than the other aspects of the game that it's almost a game breaker. Again, this level is optional, and only rewards with a minor upgrade, but completionists may be disappointed. I'm all for challenge, but one particular section of this level within a level fights the control mechanics offered. It tries to be Super Mario, but without the superior twitch control necessary.
In summary, the game is a gem, especially for the price. I don't know why it didn't get more press or notice - I believe it's available on 2016 gen consoles. It can be a bit challenging, but nowhere near as difficult as Cave Story+ or Valdis Story. The game's exploration, again, rewards with upgrades that can greatly benefit near-endgame play. Definite buy!

Chronicles of Teddy has the makings of a good game, mostly in its graphics and sounds.  But the current gameplay is an uneven, frustrating mess in need of retooling.
The mechanics don't mesh, so the gameplay falls apart the more you progress.  Right off the bat, your ability to push small pots serves no purpose outside screwing up your ability to break them.  The double tap run makes you prone to accidentally running face first into a shielded enemy.  Gaining the wall jump frequently screws up your double jump and which way you were facing.  Get the ground pound and it goes off by accident when you least want it to, sending you down a chasm or leaving you pinned to the ground in front of an enemy.  I get what they were aiming for in a Metroidvania, but what it adds up to is highly unpolished.
Enemies lodge their loot in walls to make them unretrievable, and artificially ramp up the difficulty with cheap abilities like "turn invincible wherever and whenever for however long where you get hurt if you hit them." Or they just sucker punch you from out of view, and the lack of mercy invincibility gets you dominoed into a bunch of attacks and fall off a cliff to repeat the process.  One monster can continuously spit spikes from across the room for half a minute while you're stuck in stun lock until you die.  Things get very luck-based the further you go.  Fighting bosses means a lot of standing around waiting for long periods until they become vulnerable, sometimes by sheer chance after several minutes.  Battle only gets more unrewarding and tedious.
Then there's the musical gimmick.  It does its job when you're just unlocking chests and gateways by song.  But early on, there are platforms you must unlock one at a time by going into a menu and picking two notes from a list.  Then jumping on the platform and reopening your menu to pick the same two notes again for the next.  And the next.  And the next.  Seven Platforms in a row.  There are 4 such chains fairly close to one another, and they rear their ugly head again from time to time.  Those sequences aren't difficult, but they might just be the worst, momentum-wrecking chore brought to platforming.  Aside from the invisible collectibles you hunt by sound, which have long periods of silence so you can walk right past them unless you spend even more time just standing still on every spot in the game.  Of which ther are 50 to find, so if you miss one, you'll have to obsessive compulsively re-explore every map again as a cruel joke.  They really should be marked on the map.
The game has all the assets to be good, but there's a lot off in its direction and execution.

Nobody owes you an argument or "proof," and you sure didn't supply the latter just by making your own claims.  I don't enjoy wasting more time on games I don't like, but I do enjoy making fun of horrible people on the internet.  And you've certainly qualified, so I'll step up.

"As for the fireflies, you want hidden elements to be marked on the map? Dude, wtf? That one doesn't even compute."
Several treasure chests are out of view "hidden elements" the programmers themselves marked on the map.  Even they don't follow your arbitrary rules. There are no respawns, you crash and the race gets reset without you. Accidentally turned the corner too tight and your back wheel touches the inside edge of the track? The race resets without you. This may seem harsh but getting the skills to actually finish the race without messing up makes it feel extremely authentic. As for the rules of bumping other riders sometimes you feel cheated when an AI slams into you and you go flying towards the barrior only to see that rider not get punished. However other times it will punish riders by taking them out of the race and keeping the person who crashed in it.
All in all if you're on the fence about trying this speedway sim I'd highly recommend it, feels like a slice of the real deal.

NEON STRUCT is a stealth espionage adventure using very basic block style graphics, but doing so in a way which really fits the setting. It isn't a difficult game to complete, but it is difficult to perfect it. Each level you are tasked with a number of objectives, but there are also 5 geocaches hidden on each level, which encourage you to fully explore the environment.
At the end of most levels, you are rated on: Undetected, No harming anyone, No bodies found, No alarms tripped, All geo caches discovered. To get a perfect rating on a level is very challenging!
When hacking computers/cameras/etc. you are presented with a small breakout style game. It seemed weird at first, but quickly becomes a really fun part of the game. If you sneak up to stand beneath a camera and start hacking it, you don't just have to worry about the hacking, time hasn't stopped, so a guard patrol could come by at any moment, adding a sense if urgency to the hacking attempt.
GRAPHICS: Wonderful use of basic block art, with neon trim.
MUSIC: All original, I believe, and fitting in a 90's electronica style.
SOUND: I found it difficult to identify where footsteps were coming from sometimes, but for the most part the sound effects work as expected and keep you in the fantasy.
STORY: The story fits in well with current espionage/conspiracy type theories, and comes to a satisfying conclusion. Although some parts are predictable, it flows well and I never lost interest.
REPLAYABILITY: Definitely. Not only do you make decisions during missions that will affect the outcome of the global story, but you also have the targets to perfect a mission.
SUMMARY: I loved this game, and will be playing again to try new decisions, and to try to perfect the levels. In addition, there seems to be a thriving mod community for additional stories. If you are a fan of stealth/espionage games, buy this game today!

This was hands down THE best game I have played this 2k16, and was possibly the best puzzle/adventure/hacking game I've ever played. If you had asked me a day or so ago what my favourite puzzle game was; I would tell you the portal series. Now, it would be Quadrilateral Cowboy. no question.
The story was simplistic, yet beautiful and oddly touching. I felt myself grow attached to my group of friends,  though a single word was never spoken.
The "Hacking" mechanics were easy to use, and even easier to learn. Unlike a majority of well known hacking games, you actually type commands, rather than 'click' them. Don't expect these commands to come in handy in real life, but in the context of the game it felt empowering and, well, awesome.  The gadgets were simply F***ing awesome, and some of the 'abilities' you pick up later on are pretty cool too. My only complaint was that the game ended feeling too short, even though in truth I had played for 7 hours. I suppose that is the hall mark of fun, though. Time flies when you're having it.
The technology had a retro feel to it, which was, to put it simply, delicious. I've never had more fun typing on a clunky old keyboard, inserting cassette tapes, or hooking a telephone line to my laptop.
If you haven't played this yet, do. You won't regret it.

Once upon a time, in a tiny town far far away there was a man who's friend told him to buy a little game called Mount and Blade Warband. The man bought the game, but forgot to play it. One day, when the man looked for games to play in his Steam Library he came across the game and found out that he hadn't actually played the game. So he pressed play. He had heard that it was some kind of medieval/rpg/strategy game and since he loved all of those things he figured that he would like this game too. But it didn't stop at liking, no, he started to love the game. And so his story began.
This game is pure
. Personally the only con I could come up with whilst writing this story are the graphics, but since the modding community is extremely active you can just fix that to your own liking. Talking about the modding community: Do you want to play in the Roman times and command legionaires? Then there's a mod for you. Do you absolutely adore The Lord of the Rings and have you ever wanted to play a game that let's you fight on a battlefield against a horde of Orcs with many troops under your command? Then there's a mod for you.
Talking about the troops that you have under your command. In the game you can hire or recruit certain warriors for your party. Your party has a morale and needs food or they'll desert. You can level them when they've gathered enough experience points which will make your party stronger. Furthermore there's a Renown system. The more renown you have the more people know of you.
The land of Calradia is continually in a state of war between all of the different factions. You can choose to join a faction or you can make your own faction. In your faction you can manage whom you go to war with and which of your companions gets which fief.
The final point I'd like to talk about is the combat. Because the combat in this game is extremely good. You have 4 different attacks with every weapon (with an exception for throwing weapons and bows). You can choose which attack by moving your mouse in a certain direction. The blocking works the same.
I've probably missed lots and lots of things, but I believe that if you aren't convinced of buying this game right now, well then you'll probably never be convinced.

The further you get in survival mode, the better the AI gets, the stronger mechs they have, and the more you really test your limits with your response time and weapon management.
My only complaints are that the lock on system for the normal machine gun is a bit cheap on early waves and lesser enemies in general (this goes for the Campaign mode as well). Sometimes you move a little too fast and that can be a problem if you're around buildings; your speed can be more a of problem when it comes to escaping missiles being locked onto you while trying to maneuver around tall buildings. The camera seems a bit hectic as well. While you are more focused on the enemy at hand, the way the camera moves with you can cause a person to get a little disoriented (at times it gave me a headache).
Never has a game made me want to be a mech pilot as much as this title does. I'm very eager to see what the full game has to offer.

Well, here I go to try and write a review. ;)
Heroes and Generals is a Free to Play, First Person Shooter/Real Time Stratigy game developed my Reto-Moto, which is based in Denmark. The FPS and RTS are tied together by the gamemode, War.
The FPS side of things starts with 3 guys. A Russian, German, and American. All your guys start out with a Semi-Automatic rifle. SVT-40,(Russian) Gewehr 43 (German), and the M1 Garand (USA). Make no mistake, these guns are very good, though they are your starter guns. They can be modded it 2 hit kill, and fast firing. But I would not recommend doing this until you have a larger income, because the repairs will take away some of your earnings.
The game has a wide range of weapons, from S-A rifles and bolt actions, to Submachinguns and Assault Rifles.
You progress by getting XP on ribbions, and these ribbions progress through levels, at which on each level you may unlock something.
I can not really say too much about the RTS side of the game, as I've just started to play it, and as such am figuring it out . ;)
There are two kinds of currency in this game, Credits, and Gold. Gold is bought with real life money, and Credits are earned through the FPS side of game.
ingame can be bought with credits, Even Veteran (Premium) memberships. You earn credits by hour, so time in battle, not just in the spawn menu, but actually in the battle.
As you gain a higher rank soldier you will get a higher salary, thus earn more money.
.) The match maker is unfair.
No, its not really. In staged, both teams have the
same things availible to them. Same number of tanks, planes, infantry, paratroopers, they all have the same. So why do I end up ingame agaisnt a team with 5 tanks, when we have 0 you ask? Nobody has used them. Its that simple. Both teams have the same thing open to them, but its up to the players to use them. So if somebody has a tanker, but does not use it you won't have tanks.
.) Its P2W (Pay too Win)
I would call it P2P: Pay too Progress. Anything, anything ingame, can be bought with credits, meaning that its not P2W.
Always remember, the strenght of a player lies not in the weapon, but in the seat. To roughly quote a person on the forums.
.) The grind is sooooo long. I've seen a person with 3.2 hours say it take eternity to get something. Well, in a way. I won't lie to you, the grind is long, it is hard, and it will take a long time. But once you have that new gun, tank or what ever it is you want, it all seems damn worth it.
.) This game is full of cheaters and hackers.
It was. Once. But the Devs have done a good job of weeding out the bad, and keeping the good. Many people call hacks simply because they are not very good at the game. I once had a newer guy tell me that he was worried he would be accused for hacking because he was 12-5. It is sad when people are afread of being reported for a simple thing like that.
Don't get me wrong, there are some hackers out there, but over 900 hours, I have only seen 1, maybe 2. Most people are just really good.
.)The game is unfair once I reach level 5.
Once you reach level 5 you will be thrown in agaisnt the very best. Tanks, paras, recon with 1 hit kill rifles, fighters constantly dropping bombs on your head. It will all seem very hard, and it is a learning curve, but give it time and stick to it, and soon you will be one of those vets that others complian about. ;) Once you hit level 5, you WILL die alot, but its a game, try not to rage too much. Just respawn and try again.
-Its free
-Not P2W
-Has a lot of stuff to chose from, like Paratroopers, Tankers, Recon, Fighter Pilots, and General. (NOTE: General can not play FPS side of game)
-Balanced
-Still activly being developed
-3 factions to choose from
-Long grind
-Will die quite a bit
-Quite a bit of whiny people who can't handle getting killed. ;)
-It has a few bugs here and there
-Flight controls feel a bit off to me, but I never got used to them
-Explosives, and weapon mods are a bit expensive to maintain until you get a higher rank.
.)Don't come in as a know it all.
Just because you might play games like CoD and CS:GO does not mean you know all there is to know. This is a different style of game, slower and more realistic.
.)Listion to the veteran guys.
They have more time played, and are better at it. If they give you advice, take it, try it, and if it doesn't work for you, thats OK. And don't be afread to ask for help either.
.) Always remember its a game, and should not interfear with real life duties. Nor take it to hard if you die.
.) Please, when disscusing something about how hard something is or all that, remember that
of us where there, all of us were "noobs".
.)Respect the devs, as they put a lot of work into this, and none of us really can say that they are doing a bad job, or need to do this or that fully, because almost, if not none of us have ever made a PC game like this.
.)Don't act like a know-it-all.
Have a nice day, and I hope this was of help!
~CaptainRA11

Chronicles of Teddy is good but not great. I wanted to love this game but after putting about 6 hours into the game I just lost the will to continue. But don't let this make you think the game is not worth purchasing. Those 6 hours were an enjoyable experience and an experience quite unique.
The graphics are beautiful. I love the art design.
The music is pretty good; it's like zelda where each area has its overarching theme and dungeons have their own as well.
The combat is fun too.
My big gripe, and the reason I lost interest, was the music system. In this game, the puzzles revolve around this musical language you can speak; you collect different runes and must use them to open doors etc.
I hated having to remember the runes and I found it took me out of the game; for the majority of my playthrough I just pulled up the guide and did what it said with regards to the music puzzles. I did not find them fun or creative but rather monotonous because it seems in every dungeon you just explore to find these secret music words. After collecting enough you can finally open the boss' door. It ended up feeling so formulaic it took me out of the game.
Worth trying though, I don't want to minimize the awe and intrigue I felt going into the first two areas of the game. The 3rd snow area is great too but the dungeon really made me question this game's design.

After 30 minutes of play, this game sets a pace that I'm not interested in continuing on in.
The interesting visuals and dramatic first 5 minutes of the game did a good job of setting an interesting tone for me. I was excited to see what the game actually had to offer.
Then 15 minutes later, I was still wondering when the game would start.
The introductory "graveyard" level is too long, relies too much non-imaginative platforming (one area feels like bad rip from the first level in Mario 2), and doesn't offer anything but a possible feeling of suspense based on how quiet it is. But that suspense never gives way to anything -- Only the next empty area: a boring labrynth of dead-ends in the "library."
After searching the Library, you eventually find your way to the first actual level of the game - the forest. Experience riviting pleasures as you wander through a seemingly endless collection of random doors and caves, opening treasure chest after treasure chest, collecting countless items that mean nothing to you as the player.
After meeting a large creature that expected me to play it a specific song to communicate with it, and it killed me for answering wrong too many times, I didn't have the urge to continue.
Overall, this game has some setbacks that don't grip the interest of the beginning player: the pick-ups give a sense of pointless collect-a-thon meets scavenger hunt, and the level design gives no real feeling of excitement, adventure, or familiarity. Even with a map, it felt like a confusing collection of randomly designed rooms thrown together without much forethought.
Perhaps this game picks up if you give it more time, but based on my first 30 minutes, I can't recommend it. Which is a shame, because I love the visuals, theme, and proposed genre of this game. The gameplay just didn't do it for me.

The game is a pretty good bit of fun, but a huge issue is that literally 90% of the game is dice rolling. And they don't pretend to hide it either. Basically the entire strategy of the portion is to limit the dice rolling to be in your favor as much as possible or to try and avoid it alltogether OR to stock up on rerolls. Now again, the game is pretty fun, when things work out in your favor. But it can be incredibly frustrating when playing a neck and neck match with someone and then losing your entire turn the first move because you failed a dice roll.
There's also some serious balancing issues with several races being incredibly worthless and a few being super powerful and still easy to play. Regardless, the game is an interesting take on a 'fantasy football' (Yes, that's what I'm going to call this) type of game with some amusing commentary... for the first 3 matches. For a game that's been rereleased a dozen times I'd expect it to be more polished, but if you want about a few hours of enjoyment from a unique turn based strategy game then you can't really go wrong here.

All the levels are simple and focused on 1 to 2 of the avialable mechanics. The rest is either not used at all or simply taken away from the player, sometimes for 1 mission and other times forever.
Because of all this, the game became way too easy later on. Instead of having puzzles to solve, you just go through the motions. Click this, click that, go here, go there. Some timer here and there. No challenge whatsoever. Not to mention you can 'cheat' your way though a lot of the levels.
The final mission tries to bring some stuff toghether but it's just not enough.
I played it again with the developer commentary on and he talks about world building a lot but the story didn't grab me at all so it's hard for me to care about the game world. In the end I felt like the story was very basic, obscure and just patched up with some 'gags' here and there.
I thought this was going to be a great game, but it turned out rather bleak.
I was going to say it was too short (4h is pretty much all you get), but that might have made it better here. At least I didn't get bored of it before the end.
I liked previous games from Blendo but this one was a huge disappointment.
All in all I don't think it was worth the price of $20.
EDIT: Since this review got so much votes I feel like I need to make some things clear. The weak puzzle design is what disappointed me the most in this game. The mechanics are great. Amazing even. They're just never used to their full potential.

A simple, 80's retrofuture stealth game that draws inspiriation from Thief and Deus Ex. I wish more games purposefully chose art styles that utilized low-poly level design. Maybe it's just me, but there's a weird calming effect with environments that are scaled too big and free of static mesh clutter.

Much like in Thief or Dishonored, if you're KOing every guard you see then you're basically saying "this stealth is too hard and I'm a big baby, etc." -- and if you're trying so hard to depopulate and simplify every level, then you don't get to complain that it's too simple. (advice: if you've played a Thief before, play one difficulty above Normal.)
The operative word here is "minimalism"... the levels aren't too big nor too small, and all the spaces have good logic to them. The whole campaign has a nice rhythm to it actually, alterating between mansion heists and small city hubs. There's also some nice bits where what you do in the towns seem to affect what happens in a mission, e.g. you carelessly talked to someone you shouldn't have, and they ratted you out, and now there are more guards, etc.
The soundtrack is 10 steps above most video game music. Like, it's actually listenable as real music that real people listen to. What's weird is that this game gets oddly quiet sometimes, like 50% of the game is pretty much just footsteps and no NPC dialog, which is a shame, I wish there was more to the NPC sound and world soundscapes, but I guess when you gotta ship you gotta ship.
Anyway. This is a really nice homage to Thief / Deus Ex / some Shocks, and it respects your time. I recommend it.
(disclaimer: I know one of the dudes who made this, and I presented on a GDC panel with him)

I am a big fan of Eldritch, especially the stealth system, so when I heard that Neon Struct was a first person stealth game running on the Eldritch engine, I could hardly contain my wallet. Anyway, here is a list of Pros and Cons of the game:
PROS
-Good soundtrack, if a tad repetitive at times
-Runs very well
-Good characters
-Decent amount of gadgets to use
-Good missions, and small side objectives occr very often, which are extremely satisfying to fulfill
-For the completionists, there are collectable geocaches and a rating system to help motivate you
-The hacking mini-game is pretty well made, sure it is a breakout clone, but the fact that the game does not pause while you are hacking adds to the suspence
-Good level design for the most part
CONS
-Bad ending. A very big anticlimax. I am not going to tell you how, but you will understand when you get there.
-AI can vary between laughably stupid and incredibly hard from time to time, which may annoy fans of other stealth games. I though it added to the charm, but I can see it being frustrating.
-Feels like it was originally going to be bigger, but was cut down. A few levels feel really unique and interesting, and then the likes of them are never seen again
-Short. I beat this game in 4 hours, and although I will be coming back for more, the campaign is very small. You can download new levels over the internet, but this game has a tiny community.
-LEVEL EDITOR NOT AVAILABLE FOR LINUX OR MACINTOSH
Here is my final grading
Story: 6/10 It is good until the end, where it begins to suck.
Gameplay: 8/10 Excluding a few AI hiccups and the lovable wonky physics of the Eldritch engine, its good.
Replayabilty: 6/10 Same levels over and over again, some side objectives, but not as much as its predecesor, but honestly, no game can beat Eldritch's replayabiity so I won't judge it too harshly
Atmosphere: 9/10 Exceedingly good atmosphere, you really feel like you are living in a Cyberpunk society.
Total: 7.25/10 This game is good. A little pricey, but definitely worth your time. I would love to see a Neon Struct 2 as well as MAC AND LINUX COMPATABILITY FOR LEVEL EDITOR AND STEAM WORKSHOP SUPPORT EEEEEEEEEEEEEE (edit: Apparently the level editor is not available on any platforms yet, so it is entirely likely the level editing software will come to all platforms at roughly the same time/)

Okay, what?
Imagine a game where you are the chosen one!
Imagine a game where you go on a great adventure quest for wealth and glory!
Imagine a game where you make the peasants bow to their king!
THIS... IS NOT... THAT GAME!
No.
Instead, you're a homeless schizophrenic who gets woken up on a prison boat taken to the worst place in the world. Morrowind. A humid and mosquito-infested rotting bog, full of Ashlanders, or Ash-trash, as they're called.
As you get off the boat and look around, all you see are sorry poor sods who drink and do skooma all day, while they fish their butts off to make some money as imperial wage slaves. All they want is a life in peace, but they're too much of a bunch of passive trashlanders to do anything about it.
You're then shoved into an immigration office, where you'll meet a sorry old oaf who stares blankly at you with a suicidal glare from shipping human garbage like you into Morrowind everyday. After you pick "Custom Class", because you're a waste of human resource who can't get a real profession, you're met with an unenthusiastic "Interesting", and get kicked out into Seyda Neen.
All you're given is a moldy ring, a rotting note, and a "package". The note gives you directions to Balmora, which, according to the architecture, seems to be in Afghanistan. You then spend the next 4,000 hours reloading your save file due to getting murdered by Cliff Racers, having their annoying screech stuck in your head to haunt you for the rest of your miserable life, while getting xenophobic remarks from everyone and everything, until you finally reach Afghanistan. To the far south-west part, you'll find a topless old creep who'll let you sleep in his bed with him. You can also pay him so he can teach you wrestling. No, he's still topless.
You then drunkedly scribble down his directions in your journal, which are visible by pressing "J", to see where you're supposed to go. I'm sorry, what was that? Quest markers? Fast travel?
Now those are four words I haven't heard in a long time...
After you've wandered around for 600 hours with animations that look like you've pooped your pants and are trying to unstick your buttcheeks from the poop, like every other NPC in this game, you end up figuring out that you can choose to become the "Nerevarine".
The Nerevarine is supposed to have intercourse with Vivec, a "Chimbucha" addict, and save Vvardenfell from some dude called Dagoth Ur, who apparently was his ex-boyfriend. They broke up after having a threesome, or something. I don't... I don't want to know.
So anyway, Dagoth Ur is trying to make the volcano erupt and swallow the continent whole. Because Morrowind hates you and everyone in it hates you, but to me that the beauty of it,you are forced to work your way up slowly, you are forced to get people to like you and you are forced to figure everything out yourself and that is one of the things i like about Morrowind; It doesn't hold your hand and it trusts you to be intelligent enough to play it. The magic system like you can collect spell effects and make your own spells, you can do so much with it, and in what other game do you get to fly and turn invisible? I also really really just like the island of Vvardenfell like its so rich and detailed there is so much to it, its just so alien and unique that you just want to explore it, But you can't! Morrowind is the indirect sequel to the 1996 game, Daggerfall. Morrowind is widely recognised for having one of the first hand-modelled open worlds in gaming. How does it stack up? Well, spoilers, but it's good.
Morrowind follows the questing style of Arena an Daggerfall, in that there are no questing markers, and no fourth wall-breaking journal entries. You will get directions to your quests, that's it. This adds to the feel of immersion in the game. FInding areas without the help of a quest marker was a satisfying feeling. The directions given by questgivers were almost never tedious, and are descriptive enough to make you feel like you are getting real-life directions to a town or area. In typical Elder Scrolls style, there's a silly amount of quests, and every one of them feels unique enough to keep you interested for a good long time. The DLCs in particular have some engaging and immersive questlines. You never feel like the hero the world needs. In a similar fashion to Dark Souls, you feel like many have come before you, and the world isn't owing you any favours.
This land is very compact. You can go anywhere at any time, uninterupted. However, in a similar fashion to Zelda, there are certain places you can only go off of your own accord once special circumstances are met. The world feels very alive, there is very little empty space in between the towns and cities. This felt like a true RPG, in every sense of the word, and was even better when you knew it wasn't holding your hand in any way. Elder Scrolls is known for its charming characterization. Not every NPC is just a copypaste of the last. They all have unique dialogue, names, questlines and personalities. This is taken to the extreme in Morrowind. Even bandits who you will be doing nothing besides killing have names and different traits, I feel this went on to inspire games like Shadow of Mordor in the future. This world felt real, with real people, both good and bad. This isn't to say that the world is perfect. while all areas are loaded, crossing into different regions triggers a very small loading message along with a very brief pause, this was obviously to stop lag on ye olde machines back in the yesteryears, and isn't needed now, but is hard wired into the game, and can't be removed, sadly. The dungeons suffer from "Elder Scrolls-syndrome" of being a little repetetive, but the before-mentionned characterization makes them feel unique enough. There are so many random events in this game. Becoming too popular? Someone might try to bump you off. Taking a stroll in the woods? Watch out for that wizard falling from the outer atmosphere. This game had so much content for the time.
Morrowind's combat system is pretty bad. Even for the time. The first three Elder Scrolls games use RNG to determine if you can hit enemies or not. This will lead to you flailing your weapon towards enemies, even right into their face, dealing no damage at lower levels. Thankfully, this can be modded out, but I reccomend playing on a higher difficulty if you do, as it becomes too easy. Skyrim's combat was just clunky. Morrowind's was bad. But you know what? It didn't hinder the massive sense of immersion. This was the Skyrim of 2002. And that's why Elder Scrolls fans revere it so much. Rightfully so, too.
Morrowind is one of the best RPGs of all time, hands down. There has never been a higher sense of immersion in an open world game. It may be somewhat dragged down by the out dated mechanics, but you know the Elder Scrolls modding community always has your back. This is my favourite Elder Scrolls game, and for many good reasons. Not only that, but it's one of my personal favourite games ever.

a fantastic re-release for 2015 of the gamecube remake from 2002 for the original resident evil on playstation from 1996.
seriously though, while that sounds like the most cynical and lazy move capcom could ever pull, this is a legit fantastic version of a groundbreaking game with some serious work done to it. the game runs in the MT Framework engine now which means the looping videos that allowed faked real-time lighting from the gamecube is no more, replaced with modern lighting effects. some of the rooms in the game are even completely rebuilt from the ground up in service of the new lighting! the character and item models have gotten a *massive* boost in detail, with the character models in particular being redone from scratch.
however, some of the pre-rendered backgrounds in some areas look like total garbage with lots of image artifacts from being upscaled to a resolution that was unheard of in 2002, also, the pre-rendered cutscenes have *not* aged very well and seem to be just blown up to what ever resolution you are running the game in. there have also been some complaints about serious slowdown on more underpowered machines, which results in the game running in slow motion due to the way the engine works. i had only a few instances of slowdown on my card (GTX 970) but none of them seemed repeatable. so be aware of all that going in!
sound and music has also been upgraded to support 5.1 systems (i have no idea if the original GCN remake supported that or not) and it sounds *incredible* on a good set of headphones or on 5.1 speakers. also, the controls have been redone to offer a different take on the famous clunky controls, but some of my friends who are RE purists think it ruins the flow of the game and makes it too easy, so YMMV. support for widescreen resolutions is also accomplished in a curious way, with the camera panning up and down the original 4:3 assets to give an illusion of widescreen, not too disimilar to pan & scan in old moves on VHS. it's hard to articulate and you can switch between the original 4:3 aspect ratio and original controls at any time, so the point is moot anyway.
the gameplay is still rock solid once you get your feet wet, but it did take me a little while to find my balance in the game before i had a smooth flow going. basically, don't play as chris your first time through.
the script and dialogue is still pretty much pain-inducing. i wish part of the HD remaster included a second pass at the script and VO but you could argue that is part of the charm and to change that would change the feel of the game.
all in all, i highly recommand this remaster. now, to wish for capcom to make REmake 2..

First, the most important thing you need to know about this game righ off the bat: It's fun. The weapon systems of your mech are well thought out. All have their merit, and while some are more powerful than others, there is no one weapon type that works for every situation. You'll need to make ample use of every weapon type, even (or especially) your close range machine gun. This is also a pretty darn fast game, so if you're expecting Mech Warrior style slowmotion or even Hawken style gameplay, this is not at all the kind of game this Project Nimbus is. But don't let that scare you off. If you lose your bearings, it'll only be for a moment. Especially since every Weapon has a lock on function that helps you keep on facing the enemy. However, just because you're locked on, doesn't mean you're going to hit your target. Missiles can be evaded by moving away far enough, or via flares or via the funnel weapon (little interceptors that fly around you and that can also be used to attack, very powerful). Everything else needs to be evaded manually and works fine most of the time.
You'll most likely breeze through the first 4 or 5 missions or so, learning about the weapons, reveling in your massive fire power and perhaps asking yourself where the challenge is. Especially since you get to pilot a really nice mech and you're fighting against all kinds of simpleton mechs or stationary weaponry that really isn't all that big of a threat. But as you near the end of Act 1, you'll have your work cut out for you. You'll be forced to pilot different, lesser mechs as well as fight pretty darn dangerous special boss mechs with potent entourages that will shoot you down in mere moments, if you don't know what you're doing or just aren't careful enough.
I'm no expert on the game yet, but keeping your distance is often a very good idea in this game ;)
All in all, it's a fast paced, arcadey Gundam Mech Shooter. It's easy to get a handle on, and you'll be having fun from the moment you start. I got this via Steam Christmas Auction and wasn't expecting too much, but it really surprised me and got me hooked.
Only real downside is that there's only Act 1 to play so far. That'll give you around 2-3 hours game time, depending on how good you are (I have 2 missions left). And there's a survival mode that's pretty fun, that'll keep you occupied for 2-3 runs. As it stands now, it's a good game to spend 15 - 30 minutes on (especially after you've finished Act 1) before doing something else. However, if you're looking for something meatier, I'd wait until they finished the game.
I'd definately recommend it for anyone looking for a fun arcade shooter. Because in essence, that's what this is.

So, I finally got off my♥♥♥♥♥long enough to hop back onto Project Nimbus, only to find it to be a chaotic mess. Good gods, the second act starts off with the Chinese, then gravitates a little towards the Americans, then forces you into the Russian's side of things, and finally brings you back to the first girl from Act 1. I don't know, folks. If there was a "Meh" rating, I'd give it instead of saying yes or no in recommending the game. I'll keep it at a "Yes" for now, though, but my personal rating for the game dropped to 6/10 for lack of character development.

Simply put, it's a 2D puzzle platformer about ARID, an artificial intelligence piloting a suit. As many have said before me, the story, voice acting, and visuals are fantastic. I won't go in to the story too much (since plenty of reviewers have already explained it better than I could), but I will say that the game made me think quite a few times. The controls aren't too bad once you get used to them, but a few of the puzzles are so "how-was-I-supposed-to-figure-that-out" levels of obscure that I found myself enjoying the game a lot more with a walkthrough at my side. It is a bit short (only took me 3.2 hours,) so you might want to wait for a good sale before picking it up.
All in all, you mostly come to this game for the story, not the gameplay, and while the story is amazing, it is still unfinished, with the game ending on a big, fat, "To Be Continued" screen, which saddened me deeply. I'll definitely buy the next part, but if it's as short as this one, I'll probably just hold out for a sale.
Oh, and don't be suprised if you develop deep emotions for the AIs you meet. I certainly did, and I loved every minute of it.

The Fall seems to be the first episode of ARID, an AI in a military suit programed to protect their pilot who has become unconcsious from the sudden fall from space. The rest of your journey follows ARID as she embarks on a journey to get medical attention for pilot Joseph. Along the way she meets help from the mainframe, and an opposing force in the Caretaker. It is a harrowing adventure posed with danger and many hard decisions, but ARID is willing to go through everything to save Joseph.
The game is pretty short, but the ending is quite satisfying in leaving a want for sequel. Gameply wise it isn't anything too difficult, but one can argue that the puzzle solving isn't too straightforward and may turn into a guess and check. The shooting is straightforward as well, but I do recommend that you only go for headshots because the enemies can be quite difficult. Overall it is just a side scroller puzzle adventure game with some shooting elements.
The story is definitely  the strongest point in the game, and charater growth is something that becomes so powerfully moving. When you see the mainframe in danger you do feel angry at the Caretaker and it drives you to hunt him down. As you see what lengths ARID is willing to go, you can't help but sympathize with her strength to make tough decisions.  And as the mainframe tries to help ARID you feel this strong camaraderie from him. The ending as I said before gives the short story and nice bow to wrap everything up. Would definitely play a sequel if it comes out.
The Fall is a great story based game that for some will demand a sequel, but some may not be influenced enough to look past the simple game mechanics which would also be fair. The Fall looks great and will in fact create the mood of exploration and impending doom. It is a little bit guess and check with the puzzles, but that can quickly be overlooked with the setting as stated before. The shooting parts are actually a fun reprieve from the little exploring and puzzle solving you must do. A fun little game that should be on your list of purchases, sale price or otherwise.

Once upon a time, in a tiny town far far away there was a man who's friend told him to buy a little game called Mount and Blade Warband. The man bought the game, but forgot to play it. One day, when the man looked for games to play in his Steam Library he came across the game and found out that he hadn't actually played the game. So he pressed play. He had heard that it was some kind of medieval/rpg/strategy game and since he loved all of those things he figured that he would like this game too. But it didn't stop at liking, no, he started to love the game. And so his story began.
This game is pure
. Personally the only con I could come up with whilst writing this story are the graphics, but since the modding community is extremely active you can just fix that to your own liking. Talking about the modding community: Do you want to play in the Roman times and command legionaires? Then there's a mod for you. Do you absolutely adore The Lord of the Rings and have you ever wanted to play a game that let's you fight on a battlefield against a horde of Orcs with many troops under your command? Then there's a mod for you.
Talking about the troops that you have under your command. In the game you can hire or recruit certain warriors for your party. Your party has a morale and needs food or they'll desert. You can level them when they've gathered enough experience points which will make your party stronger. Furthermore there's a Renown system. The more renown you have the more people know of you.
The land of Calradia is continually in a state of war between all of the different factions. You can choose to join a faction or you can make your own faction. In your faction you can manage whom you go to war with and which of your companions gets which fief.
The final point I'd like to talk about is the combat. Because the combat in this game is extremely good. You have 4 different attacks with every weapon (with an exception for throwing weapons and bows). You can choose which attack by moving your mouse in a certain direction. The blocking works the same.
I've probably missed lots and lots of things, but I believe that if you aren't convinced of buying this game right now, well then you'll probably never be convinced.
Thanks for reading this review.

Quadrilateral Cowboy is a retro-cyberpunk heist/hacking game. If you want to compare it to something, think Thief and Uplink meshed together.
As with all Chung's games, it's got a quirky, simplistic aesthetic that lends more focus to the narrative than the environments. The game is set during a retro-futuristic 1980 with airships, space elevators and oversized ventilation shafts.
The basic gameplay consists of lugging around a chunky Osbornesque "portable" computer and using it to hack into security systems to open doors and windows, turn off laser grids and cameras, and so on. The computer lets you set up sequences of commands to create small scripts, optimally letting you simply walk through a building while doors and alarms toggle around you. I'd loved if this concept had been explored more, since only the last mission starts to approach the complexity I expected.
.
I chalk this down to the game being too short. Chung's games tend to go in the "short and sweet" category, and narratively Quadrilateral Cowboy works perfectly in its three-to-four hour playtime. Mechanically, I was left wanting more.
The story is fun, the characters are quirky and characterful (despite not saying anything), the gadgets have great potential that isn't fully realized, and there's apparently mod support out of the gate (makes sense considering the engine is open-source).
I tihnk the mods might make this game really great. As it is now, it's simply very good.
It's a Brendon Chung game. Buy it if you like his game. Buy it if you liked Thief or Uplink.
Basically buy it. It'll only get better.

"Whenever you mention this game,someone,somewhere,will reinstall it." -The Internet as a Whole
This has been said many times about many games. Vampire: The Masquerade. Deus Ex. Thief. Morrowind. That last one is the focus of this review. Is this game old? Certainly. The Game of the Year release came out in 2003. I originally played this on the original Xbox. Has the game aged well? Arguments can be made in either direction; I personally think it didn't age well,but it's still serviceable. Is it fun to play? Depends.
Morrowind does not give you a dense tutorial. All Morrowind does is give you the bare basics,and an in-character journal. No compass,though you do get a minimap with a radius of about fifteen metres. No objective markers. No point-and-click fast travel. What does it have? An assortment of spells to aid in mobility; Water breathing,water walking,and levitation from the Alteration school of magic. Mark and recall,ALMSIVI and Divine Intervention from the school of Mysticism. That journal? It can record entire conversations,if you need it. Your character will note down the important details entirely in the first person,as well. All of this encourages you to explore,which is something that point-and-click fast travel and objective markers rob you of. You're told to kill some poachers at a nearby mine? There's a tomb along the way,and you just know you'll be tempted.
And that's what brings people back to Morrowind; The joy of exploration and discovery. The thrill of stumbling upon something unpleasant in a poorly lit space. But,exploration alone is not enough to keep most gamers,myself included,hooked. Morrowind truly shines with the writing. True,the game,for the most part,lacks voice acting. But,for a game of this scale,back then,such an undertaking would've been cost-prohibitive. But,almost entirely through text and environmental storytelling,Morrowind will spin for you an entire library's worth of thrilling tales. From in-game books (Try the 36 Lessons of Vivec!),to numerous great questlines (House Hlaalu gets niftay!),to one-offs (Naked Nords!),expansions (Welcome to Mournhold!),and even incidental characters (Thanks for the ring,Fargoth!).
Morrowind is a game of stories. A game of plots. It is a vehicle for delivering to you,the player,a story. Or more. If you come into the game expecting flawless gameplay,fluid animations,and a game where you can't cheese the system,you'll be sorely disappointed. The game is far from perfect. But,if you can look past the flaws,you'll find some of the best stories ever,or never,told,and some of the greatest music to ever by produced by Jeremy Soule. And,to cap it all off,Morrowind is made for modding. The Nexus Mods Network started with Morrowind,and has expanded into what it is today.
If you want a great story in an alien world,you'd be hard pressed to go wrong with Morrowind.

Clustertruck is a platforming game with very simple mechanics. You can sprint and jump by default, and your goal is to hop between trucks while avoiding pretty much everything else - making a dash for the goal on each stage.
There are 90 stages currently in the game, plus 10 stages for the Halloween update (for 100 total). There are 10 stages each divided into 9 worlds in the base game, plus 1 world for the Halloween update.
Each world has its own theme and its own set of obstacles to overcome, such as lasers in the "laser world," or various swinging hammers and such in the "medieval" world. They are fairly well varied, and make good use of the concept of jumping between trucks. Each world also has its own unique soundtrack, which in my opinion makes it very easy to get lost in playing this.
There are also a number of "Abilities" you can unlock, and you can equip two at any given point.
Examples of these abilities are a temporary time-stop that freezes everything around you while holding down the right mouse button (by default), or a dash that lets you jump a little bit further forward to close a gap (left mouse button by default). You unlock these abilities with points gained by simply doing the levels, and I've already unlocked about half of them as of this writing. They are fun to use, though for those who prefer to avoid them, you can get an achievement for beating the game without using any abilities (I am in the process of aiming for this myself).
You can aim for a high score by performing tricks (such as having high air-time, or jumping between trucks that are in mid-air). Or you can aim for a fast time. There are leaderboards, which you can filter by friends and such to compete if you so desire. Though the "world high scores" have the typical hackers at the top, with names such as "end me" or "ban," a problem that seems to plague this sort of game.
All in all, it is a very fun game, and the platforming mechanics work very well.
They take time to get used to however, and for those without the patience to endlessly repeat a stage until you finish it, it may not be the game for you.
That, and the fact that the game can be beaten in less than 3 hours (took me just about 3 hours exactly to beat every stage, including an infuriating final boss that requires a lot of trial and error to figure out the mechanics to), make this game really for those who love the idea of fast-paced platforming games.
To compare to other games I have played, this game reminds me of Super Meat Boy primarily - a platforming game where you will die a lot, but you always can restart the stage immediately, so the frustration at losing can always be quickly forgotten by simply trying again.
I'm still expecting to get a few hours of enjoyment out of this game, so it was worth the price to me. Mileage will depend on the individual of course, but this sort of game is right up my alley for quick fun when I'm not feeling like doing anything too mentally taxing.
I recommend this game to anyone who loves fast-paced adrenaline-filled platformers.

I originally bought the game of the year edition of Morrowind when it was first released in stores. I can honestly say after playing HUNDREDS of hours on Skyrim and Oblivion, this title still earns its stripes. I would recommend this game definitley.
Here are some notes about this game for new players:
-There is no quest marker in this game telling you where to go and what to find. You must read and listen to everything people tell you. It makes the game more challenging and also more rewarding once you solve riddle, ciphers, and accomplish tasks. It puts you and your brain into the game more than the other titles, and your journal is your best friend. Ask lots of questions to get the most information possible.
-Combat in this game is a little dated now, but you get used to it pretty quick. You do damage only when you land a hit on your opponent. At first you will have low skills, so don't expect to land hits when your swinging your blades or shooting your arrows. Magic is different however, as it will always hit....because it magic of course haha. The last thing to remember is that you see a man out in the woods wilderness.....he could kick your a$$. The opponents can be weaklings, or pretty strong adversaries, so it is best to think frist before you strike and choose your battles.
-Graphics in this game have aged, but there are some nice "visual enhancements" out there if that is your thing. IMO this world feels the most unique and alienated of the series, and the graphics support the vibe and general sence of feeling.
-The expansions are great! You can choose to jump right into them if you wish, but you should build your character first and save some coin. They expand the map not once, but twice.
-You can kill ANYONE in the game, and it is perma death. This includes people that hand out side quests and main quests. If you happen to kill someone that happens to be linked to a main quest....sorry brother, tought luck that quest line is DONE. Choose your battles and think before you act. This is why I like this game personally.
-Good music & there are strip clubs in the game! Heck yea!
-Player customization and weapon maitanence is bar none the most diverse out of all the games.
-This game can run on any PC and Laptop that exisits now, so you can play on the go! *Bonus*
Have fun out there! Cheers

I have played Elder Scrolls games my whole life and I can say with complete confidence that The Elder Scrolls series is by far my favorite collection of games. I started off with investing thousands of hours in Oblivion then moving on to Skyrim. I actually had not played Morrowind until recently. I decided to visit the game soley to experience the story of the Nerevarine and I had heard nothing but great things about the game.
first off the game is beautiful considering it's age (I had expected it to be much worse). From the moment I started the music, environment, and NPCs instantly drew me in and immersed me in the way all Elder Scrolls games have in the past. The lack of fast travel was a refreshing change... for a while. Although there are "taxi" services you can make use of so it wasn't a huge issue. The Wonderful graphical affects (with all things considered), Peerless storyline, many customizations, and the freedom that all Elder Scrolls fans enjoy are all fantastic things to look forward to in this game.
With that being said, the game is not without it's major flaws. Like I said, I got the game to experience the story, but I didn't get to experience any of it first hand becuase the combat system is abysmal and made it so difficult to advance through the game and made exploration impossible without being mercilessly slaughtered by a wild rat. The combat system is unlike anything I have ever encounterd in an Elder Scrolls games (and that is NOT a compliment). The combat robs the game of all strategy and makes it impossible to play a mage-class character.. At least early on, I hadn't gotten too far in the game before rage quitting because I had been killed by the same rat 5 times, because the mana does not regenerate and my dagger just WOULDN'T ♥♥♥♥ING HIT the little ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥. The chance based combat is so repulsive and an insult to the Elder Scrolls series. The best part of an Elder Scrolls game is going off the beatin' path.. Don't even try it here. Before you know it you'll be up to your balls in cliff racers and out of mana and a 20% chance to hit with a melee weapon.
Before you think to yourself "I won't die over and over and over, I'll just run away". Well your dead wrong. Sprinting in this game is about the same speed you would move if you were sneaking in skyrim and just barely pushing forward. Walking is intolerable.. Running is a joke. This is so incredibly frusterating when trying to flee from enemies who are twice as fast as you and made doubly annoying that there is no fast travel. Traversing the terrain is a huge pain as well. Getting stuck, falling to your death on level ground, and the ungodly slow rate of travel makes just walking around a serious chore.
Horrific combat, intolerable travel, copy-and-paste NPC formats that make interactions so impersonal.. For all these reasons I cannot recommend the game. Most people who give it a 10/10 perfect, flawless, "Best Elder Scrolls game" review are people who started Elder Scrolls with this game and had it as a kid and are simply fondly remembering days gone by. Don't get me wrong it's story and landscape are breathtaking and I do love the game in my own way, but it most certainly is NOT the best Elder scrolls game and I cannot recommend playing the game for the combat or "rich and immersive" NPC interactions alone. 6.5/10

The original Resident Evil was remade for the Gamecube. This is an HD remaster of that remake. Even though it's been many years, this game has not lost a single step. I fell into the world of Resident Evil big time with the Gamecube remake and this HD remaster has drawn me back in. This game reminds us of what Resident Evil should be. Not some Gears of War rip off with laughable characters and designs (Jessica Sherawat) and linear stage-by-stage progression. No, instead we're taken back to the glory days with a giant free-roam area. This game sees us enter the fabled Umbrella Mansion. Sure, the dialogue has barely (in some cases, not at all) improved but we need to remember that this was a Japanese game translated to English in the 1990's. That rarely went well, especially in film. The dialogue needs to be overlooked. Accept it for its cheese factor.
The gameplay is your standard RE stuff. You have tank controls which means you move forward, cannot strafe and have to turn left and right. This is not RE 5 or 6. You only have a few inventory slots and the only way to drop items is to find a safe room and use the storage chests which are all linked unless you play the locked mode that makes the game harder. Monsters may seem slow and stupid but if you go into a room and don't take them seriously, you'll get overwhelmed. They did change some things. If you kill a zombie and do not blow his head off, he will turn into a Crimson Head and get back up later, then chase you down and he will be much faster and have claws that do more damage. There is also a new flask that you can put oil in and burn the corpses. Doing this or killing zombies with the incendiary rounds will prevent resurrection. There are other types of monsters but I'll not spoil that here.
Some might complain about the controls but I'd argue that the fact you have to be super careful with the limited ammo you find, the limited inventory space you have and the fact you have limited control over your character and zero control over the camera makes the game more challenging. You will have to plan everything you do, from what items to carry between visits to chest to what ammo to use. The problem with modern RE games is you have too much control. Over the character who you can move any which way, the camera... even being able to piledrive zombies. There is no challenge, you're never scared of anything because you're too powerful and you have far too much control over any situation. In RE1 HD, you are the prey, not the predator. You can play with alternate controls akin to modern RE games but going into different spots changes the camera angle and disorients the character movement, so I don't recommend it.
There is a ton of replay value as well. Beating the game in certain ways offers new unlockable content and you can even get different endings based on your choices. You have the option to play as Jill or Chris, both lead you down varied paths. There are even mods you can experiment with. Definitely a buy for this price. Capcom is obviously trying to make up for its mistakes and we, the fans, are grateful. 9/10. This is survival horror at its finest. Now if we can just get RE2, 3 and Code Veronica remade...

A game that is overshadowed by it's own creators failings. Fable did not end up the game that we were promised all those years ago, but this remaster proves that it is still a great classic even today. It is a simplified or introductory RPG at its core, placing a much larger focus on dodging and attacking than on level ups and strategy. The shining points of this game are in it's lifestyle gameplay mechanics. Fable manages to add realistic elements to the game without it feeling out of place or panderous. This is the type of game that has as much focus on questing as it does on buying a house, finding a wife, getting fat and kicking chickens.
Because these things are not forced on you in anyway, your decisions and action affect the character in a believable way. If you eat too much food you get fatter, if you need money you can rent out a house that you own. Doing a lot of evil deeds will make your character appear visibly more hideous and accomplishing more in game quests and side quests will begin to age your character and show how they have grown throughout the game.
This remake includes not only the original game but also all of the content in the lost chapters. It has its moments of imperfections but they aren't an overall detriment to the enjoyment of the game. If you are a keyboard and mouse player however the lack of options compared to the original steam release are dissapointing.

This review is basically an overview of the game and the differente stages that you go through in it, along with my opinion of the game
I bought this game because I read some good things about it online, I got it in the winter sale along with sims 3, thinking sims 3 would be my main game to play and spore would be a nice fun game to play a bit when I got bored of sims.
Oh boy, I was really wrong lol
The best way to describe this game is as a REALLY complete experience, you start off in the "cell stage" where you are basically a really small fish in a giant sea who has to find food to survive and grow, the stage is really short but really fun to mess around with. Once you become the biggest fish in the tank, you move on to the creature stage, one of the best parts of the game. Here you are a basically a monster, with legs and arms and all that good stuff that you can edit to your liking, you can make it a dragon looking thing, a ♥♥♥♥ing monsters inc thing, or just some abstract♥♥♥♥♥♥that you think of, it really offers a lot of customization and it's really cool if you're creative... in this stage you also get upgrades that give you social skills or combat skills depending on if you want to make other creatures go extinct or if you want to make allies to survive in the wilderness...
Next is the tribal stage, which is a MOBA sort of game, only with AI tribes instead of players and some funny♥♥♥♥♥♥to play around with, here your species learn to use fire and tools to cook food and make shelter out of the resources you can find. Once again, you can choose to be passive with other tribes and be an ally to them by using musical instruments to partner with them or just destroy their village and completely erase them from the map.
Once your tribe has mastered the use of tools and is pretty much dominant in the tribe game, you'll get into the civilization stage. Depending on your actions in past stages, you will become a religious, economic or military nation. (Economic is sort of hard mode, military is ez mode, religious is inbetween). Other nations are born while you are growing your city by adding houses and turrets and vehicles and other cool things to make it stronger, and once you get the economic resources you need, you go all in for world domination, using your best troops to beat down every nation in the world until the planet is under your control.
Last, but DEFINITELY not least, is space stage, the most different, lenghtier, and bigger out of all stages. After civilization stage, your planet basically gets to the point in technology where they can develop a spaceship and launch a space program, where you become a space empire. You get to explore an entire GALAXY, going from star system to star system, from planet to planet and maybe even into black holes as you wish and as your resources allow you to. You basically look for other life forms in different star systems and you choose to destroy them and keep their planet and star system, or ally them and gain some support from their empire. You do missions, going to different sectors of the galaxy and adquiring upgrades for your spaceship while you gain allies, enemies and territory. You get badges for doing different tasks, and those allow you to rank up and gain more "respect" from other empires, as well as gaining more stuff to upgrade your ship. Btw, I highly advice to go all the way to get to the center of the galaxy, you'll find some cool stuff there, but you'll need a heavily armored and upgraded ship to get there.
So yes, in this game you go from a random cell lost in the sea in a random planet all the way to an omnipotent empire that dominates everything in the galaxy.
This game is really, REALLY fun, it is a very complete experience since you're basically getting a completely different experience every couple of hours you move on to the next stage, it's a really ambitious game in which a lot can be done and a lot of hours can be invested. I can't recommend this game enough, do a favor to yourself and buy it if you haven't already!

It's not an easy game to master, far from it, but the simulation mode is where you'll get the best feeling of actually riding the bikes and being out there on the track. Persevere on simulation and you'll get a surprising amount of satisfaction from even finishing a race due to the difficulties of holding a line and finding good grip around the bends. You'll find yourself crashing into the barriers more often than not for the first few hours but the hardest part is riding with three other riders who want the same thing as you do, to win. After a while you'll get used to what you need to do to avoid the other riders and to get good speeds out of the bends and compete.
Default settings for your bike may have it set a little to quick with lots of torque and high rpm so I would advise turning both these down quite a bit while you are learning the game. About half of what they are set on default will help you to finish the races and still compete with the other riders. I also found putting the AI onto Hard difficulty was a help when it came to staying on the track. They stay at a good speed and are subsequently easier to avoid yet are still beatable with good riding.
If the devs keep on improving this game then it will become a classic for fans of Speedway and hopefully over the years to come we'll see more content added. For me it was well worth the full price admission.
