The art style is nice (although honestly, I couldn't really tell that everything was made from "real" materials) and the music was decent as well, but that is where it ends....there is no content and very sloppy controls.
PROS:
-Nice art.
-Nice music.
CONS:
-No content (first level is basically the entire game; there is no boss)
-Controls are sloppy
-Weapon upgrades just cause more damage. They don't change weapon behavior in any way.
-No powerups, modifiers, mini/full bosses, or really anything else to vary gameplay. The basic shooting you see on level 1 is all you get.
-No enemy variety (there is a new enemy type introduced in level 3, but it is too little too late). The few enemies that exist are very bland and similar
BOTTOMLINE:
The art assets look good, but it seems like too much time was spent on that and not enough on the actual game. This might have made for a great (actual) arcade game, but you will lose interest after a handful of playthroughs due to the extreme repetition and sloppy controls.

So, first negative review. Although to be fair, my technical first was for a game that's since been removed from Steam, so that's another story for another time.
The Blue Flamingo is a prime example of "style over substance." Yes, the game is very pretty to look at, I will give it that much. It definitely fits the bill of the "Eye Candy 2" Humble Bundle I got it in. But that's where my cheers for this thing end, I'm afraid.
At it's core, the game is astonishingly mediocre in terms of content and originality. You fly across the screen (we'll get the that bit), you try to shoot stuff, you earn money to upgrade your plane in arbitrary and quite honestly hard-to-notice ways, and repeat until you crash. Which you will, because you don't recover damage in between levels for some asinine reason.
Your weapons feel very miniscule in comparison to your targets (that is, I felt like I was pumping several seconds worth of rounds into any given enemy on screen). Not to mention that nothing seems all that impressive about your arsenal save for the bombs, and I've seen better examples in a host of other games; there's nothing that made me say, "Oh wow, that was neat" or anything along those lines.
Then there's the four ton white elephant in the room: the controls. Any miniscule movement you make will send your plane shooting across the screen with little control over it. This will cause you to be hit by kamakaze pilots, missiles, death rays (just go with it), or any number of other obstacles you will see if you have the patience. At the moment, there seems to be no way to adjust the sensitvity, meaning that I'm doomed to either keep crashing on the first couple levels or leave it be and hope that the devs fix this problem eventually. That factor simply makes the game frustrating to play, and a chore to leave open while I wait for the trading cards to come in.
To be fair, I was using an Xbox 360 controler for this, and can't say how the keyboard controls are (although other reviews claim that it's even worse with the keyboard).
I'm glad I got this as part of a Humble Bundle. That is, I barely paid anything for it, and plus I'd feel guilty if I gifted this to one of my friends. Don't let the amount of time I spent playing this fool you; I've played enough of this game to completely condemn it.
*UPDATE* It dropped a foil card, which makes the experience worth it in my book.

This is probably the only time I've ever wanted to give a game a "maybe" rather than a definite yes or no.
Reveal the Deep is a 2D platformer set in the ruins of a shipwrecked steamer so big it must have given birth to the Titanic. You play a diver tasked with exploring the wreckage.
Gameplay is essentially a 2D walking simulator. You walk across a big empty room, find a trinket with some backstory written on it, and move on. Along the way, there's the occassional puzzle. Most of these puzzles rely on a game feature where some rooms can be specially illuminated by turning off your lantern. Unfortunatley, this has the same problem as that Silent Hill game for the Wii, where twin worlds to explore just means you need to explore everywhere twice. Additionally, the ship is simply massive and is designed to have unlockable switchbacks, which only complicate an already dark labyrinthine layout. It doesn't make the game harder or scarier, just stressful.
I won't spoil anything, but the story isn't especially interesting, even for a walking simulator. The game spends the entire first chapter building a mood and introducing a monster hiding just outside the ship and it ultimatley amounts to a series of monsters that are more silly than scary. Additionally, enemies aren't hunting you and are delegated to a single axis in particular hallway encounters. That's not really a problem with Reveal the Deep, but rather 2D dungeon crawlers as a whole; The Final Station suffered from the same problem.
Though the game is short, it's tightly knit. We learn about all the characters and the ship's backstory through the previously mentioned trinkets and it all works pretty well. My one complaint about story may be that it's a reverse bait and switch. The first chapter leads you to believe the mystery is something really interesting and then you read the two sentences explaining the story at the finale and you're like "that's it?" The truth about writing is that no matter how small your team, as long as you have talen you can make a good story. It's true for every b-movie, every blog, every short story, but I feel like this story ultimatley fell flat.
I acknowledge this game was made by two people, but in this cambrian explosion of independent game development, it doesn't really matter. Papers, Please was made by one person. The Walking Dead was made by about 400. Staff size doesn't matter. Effort and gameplay experience for the player does.
On the one hand, I recommend it because it's a cheap, short, almost Lovecraftian walking simulator. On the other hand... the story isn't great, the enemies are boring, the environment is overly complex, and the game suffers from the curse of 2D claustrophobia.
Consider this a 51/49 split.

There are no markers and I have to remember where to go, who to speak to, and what to do. When I complete a quest it's more gratifying in the long run. I spent two days looking for something and when it was found there was instant relief. I love how the game hasn't aged over time, and though there are new mods out there to make it look and run better I am just enjoying the whole aspect of the environment and expanding my imagination to fill in the details. Speaking of details ... the LORE in Morrowind is absolutely breathtaking. All I ask for in a game are three things: Depth, Environment, and Freedom of Choice. Morrowind fills in all three. I'm going to try something with this review for The Blue Flamingo that I've never done before: write it from the beginning of my experience with a game. Perhaps the MOST honest appraisal will be a the result of discussing TBF AS a new player, updating as my experience grows. (My considerably longer offline play is NOT calculated.)
TBF is quite possibly the MOST beautiful game I've played. My understanding is that the DEVS actually built physical aircraft models, and it shows. It's a fairly small game, so great care can be applied throughout at reasonable cost. What I don't understand is how the beauty of the landscapes matches the beauty of the planes. It is BETTER than photo-real because of the artistic touches applied. The colors are SO vibrant, the explosions so realistic. The night skies, the desert landscape, the cars passing below all add SO MUCH to the game.
Admittedly, my first impression was "Great. Like I NEED another PONG....". And in a very broad sense that's what it is. They come at you, you shoot at them as you move from side to side and front to back. BUT.....
The Blue Flamingo is a fairly hard game (so far, for me), and if there are hints or instructions, I haven't found them. I've made it as far as level 3, shot down over 1,500 craft, and I still DON'T even have a score! I don't know how far I'll have to get to be able to regain health, but until I do I'll be crashing ad infinitum. So far, goal #1 is MAINTAIN HEALTH! But simply avoiding bullets and explosions won't do, and wouldn't be much fun. (Blowing up a plane in close proximity=BAD NEWS.) What's obtained as enemy(?) craft are shot down are points (as money) and coins to be grabbed swiftly resulting from special... somethings. At the end of levels they can be exchanged for guns or bombs, but not health. At least not as of Level 3. Money NOT exchanged increases according to the interest rate, a feature new to me, and possibly an intriquing twist yet to be explored.
The variety of planes (or whatever term might best be applied to the aircraft) and their movements makes it almost seem as though they convey personalities, and THAT'S what elevates this far beyond PONG type arcade games. I expected to be bored after 2 minutes. NOT EVEN CLOSE! Between the bullets, the screen-clearing (and limited) bombs, the new enemy craft and weapon varieties on each level, and the end-of-level target practice, player skills can be felt growing with each attempt.
(I've had no experience with the control issues I've read of.)
Hopefully to be continued....
(Be aware that I'm using a mouse and keyboard. I can only imagine the game would be even more interesting with a more appropriate controller, such as XBOX. Hopefully I'll report on that as well.)
(4JJ)

Kind of hard to figure what the audience of this was.  The shoot'em up elements are very simple and easy and won't satisfy most shoot'em up fans and the boring gameplay won't draw in casual fans of the genre and the visual design is disappointing.
Definitely a pass.

"The Blue Flamingo"... a survival shoot 'em up I got in a bundle, so can't really complain, but... I can't recommend it regardless.
Non-existent, besides a few lines explaining why you fly your plane and why you shoot stuff coming at you.
Nice, but repetitive. All the objects in the game were conceived using real-life models. It looks neat, but you only get two levels (so far as I've seen), and the only difference is you play them at various times of the day, and under different weather conditions. I
be mistaken, but in that case the levels all look alike. Aircraft and enemy models also lack variety and become extremely repetitive.
Probably the only saving grace of this game. The soundtrack is fantastic, if you like the kind of easy-going rock music. But since the soundtrack has only 2 songs and is 7 minutes long in total, it's not really worth getting the game for (at least not at the regular price).
Laggy. Boring. You can forget about precision-controlling your plane. You want to squeeze just in between those tow parallel shots the enemy sent at you? Well, you're gonna get hit. There's a slight lag in response time when you press the button, and the there's a slight delay when you release the button. The movement is kinda floaty.
Other than that, you gain money by beating levels, you buy one of the two available upgrades: a machine gun, and a bomb. Can't say I saw much of a difference after upgrading the MG a few times. And there's all there really is to this game.
Half an hour of this game, and I had enough. The only time I recommend buying it is in a bundle, and then only if you get the soundtrack alongside it.

Bad Hotel was another "but, you know, it's indie and stuff" game that failed miserably to be anything more than a way to get a few cards. American-made shmups suffer from a lack of understanding of what makes shmups fun: tight controls and more than a few enemies, not live music from your brother's ironical surf rock band. I have played less than an hour of The Blue Flamingo and it was enough for me to never have to revisit it.

The very detailed 2D environment surprised me, since I had only barely heard of this game prior to buying it, and as 2D indie games go, I expected bland and low fidelity visuals. The protagonist is an AI called ARID, so the slightly wooden animations fit perfectly.
The already mentioned dark atmosphere gets complimented by the sounds and music, which are very subtle most of the time.
Voice acting is pretty good, and it is a joy listening to the robotic voices of AIs.
I wish I could tell you all of it, but I do
want to ruin the game for you.
"The Fall" does not bring a lot of new things to the table, but both the new and the old are executed neatly. Most of the game is a side scroller adventure game, with a few puzzles to solve.. You look around by illuminating your surroundings with a torch attached to a gun, which brings us to the slightly clunkier mechanic: Shooting in the same 2D side scroller environment. Firing your weapon works fine, but the cover system is a bit confusing. At the beginning of the game it is not 100% clear behind what objects you can take cover, but it is pretty easy to figure out. Finding the exact right spot to press the "take cover" button, whatever that may be for you, is a lot more difficult. It happened to me more than once, that I wanted to hide behind cover, just to be slightly off and just start leaning against a wall. The final part of the gameplay is the Dialogue box, where you can choose different questions to ask, or different "buttons" to press. Worked perfectly, which is to be expected of a story driven game.
In conclusion, I would recommend you buy this game, if you love thinking about the morality of artificial Intelligence or love relatively short ( I played 3.2 hours, but I am quite daft from time to time) and relatively easy ( I got stuck only once) adventure games, or just love compelling stories.

"[...] part 2 [...] will be done in about april [...]", is what I wrote in 2015, january, if I am not mistaken.

If your looking for a review on this game you've come to the wrong place, but if your looking for an outstanding pie recipe you've come to the right place.
Ingredients:
1. 6 tablespoons unsalted butter
2. 1/2 cup white sugar
3. 1/2 cup brown sugar
4. 1/4 cup water
5. 1/4 teaspoon cinnamon
6. 1 pinch salt
7. 5 apples - peeled, cored and sliced
8. 1 pastry for double-crust pie
Directions:
1. Preheat oven to 425 degrees F (220 degrees C).
2. Combine butter, white sugar, brown sugar, water, cinnamon, and salt in a saucepan over medium heat. Bring to a boil, remove from heat and set aside.
3. Roll out half the pastry to fit a 9-inch pie plate. Place bottom crust in pie plate; pour in apple slices.
4. Roll out top crust into a 10-inch circle. Cut into 8 (1-inch) wide strips with a sharp paring knife or pastry wheel. Weave the pastry strips, one at a time, into a lattice pattern. Fold the ends of the lattice strips under the edge of the bottom crust and crimp to seal.
5. Pour butter-sugar mixture over top of pie, coating the lattice, and allowing any remaining sauce to drizzle through the crust.
6. Bake in the preheated oven for 15 minutes. Reduce heat to 350 degrees F (175 degrees C), and bake until the crust is golden brown, the caramel on the top crust is set, and the apple filling is bubbling, 35 to 40 more minutes. Allow to cool completely before slicing.

This game is one of the finest RPGs ever made.  I place it in the top-3 RPGs of all-time along with Ultima 7 and Baldur's Gate 2 on my personal best list.  Even though quick travel (although there was a mass transit system that allowed you to travel to villages and cities) did not exist in its original release and now the graphics are very dated (check out the graphical overhauls to fix this), there was incredible mystery and world immersion that really isn't there for me in most modern day RPGs.  Breadcrumb trails don't exist here and you had to play this game with the world map at the ready (a physical one in my case).  Morrowind's magic system allowed the player to make and craft their own spells and bind them to everyday objects like lockets.  You could create a powerful Jump spell and then use a magically crafted amulet that had a Feather spell.  With such a spell you could, for instance, vault yourself over a third of the map and then Featherfall down to the ground.  You couldn't really do anything like this in Oblivion or Skyrim.  In fact, the magic systems of the subsequent Elder Scrolls games seemed to really be Nerfed in relation to Morrowind.  You also could rise to be more powerful then the gods in this game.  In the Tribunal DLC add-on, there was a moment where I could literally kill the other gods, and the game would accomadate it.  The lore in this game was fantastic and the story was top-notch.  Much of the game centers around you fulfilling prophecy set down eons before your time.  I was struck by the story's scope and it felt like every nook and cranny had some new adventure to be found.  This game is a masterpiece, and for me, the new Elder Scrolls games lack this games immersion and freedom.  As someone who has been playing computer games since their infancy (i got my gaming start around 1980) this truly is a classic that every RPGphile should experience at least once.

The Blue Flamingo is a visually very pleasing game and could have been a really good shmup, but in this genre you need perfect controls without any lag, and there it fails.
The Blue Flamingo definitely has an interesting art style. All the aircraft, missiles, laser platforms and other things you encounter are actual models, and all the explosives etc. are also made from miniature pyrotechnics. You're also flying above what looks to be model landscapes as backgrounds.
The music on the other hand is uninteresting and the soundeffects are decidedly standard, but not to the point of annoyance.
There are too few enemy variations which is perhaps understandable since everything had to be photographed from actual models but worse is that they all use the same patterns. The challenge in most shmups comes from the variance in enemies and their different patterns, here the challenge is simply increased by giving you more enemies to deal with at the same time.
That in itself is not a big issue, worse is that like any shmup, The Blue Flamingo lives and dies by the accuracy and responsiveness of its controls. That is where I have issues with this game. Controlling it with an Xbox360 controller works decently enough, but several times I got damaged or lost because I ran into a bullet or missile which I was sure I had dodged -- and I had, but the control was a little laggy in registering.
This will not be much of an issue for the first two levels or so and you might not even notice it but as soon as the sceen becomes busier, you will begin getting annoyed by how unresponsive your ship feels.
If you get this at a decent price, TBF may be worth your time if you want to check out a unique visual style, but I cannot recommend it to people looking for a serious shmup.

If you humor me, I will attempt to describe the emotions that I feel when I play Clustertruck.
First, there is elation. The level spans far out in front of me with trials and tribulations to conquer. Second is determination. "I am going to beat this level and make it my term for female dog."
Third is terror. "Oh sweet jeezus watch out for the cannon shooting trucks at me!"
Fourth is moribund. "Oh sweet god I need to use slow time and nail this jump gggnnhhhhh!!!!"
Fifth is acceptance. "I'm screwed."
Sixth is fury. "F--- this and everyone that made this! My controller isn't working! There is a delay and obviously the game is a cheating McCheaterton!"
Seventh is denial. "I can do this, just concentrate and don't make the same mistake."
Finally, eighth is madness. "Son of a -----,  I died in the exact same freaking spot and same way!"
Rinse and repeat.
While this roughly rounds up just how I feel about Clustertruck, that wouldn't make much for a review right? So let me starting by saying that this is FAR from a game just about jumping on trucks, it is so much more then that. The overall idea is getting from point a to b true, but the game plays almost like a puzzle game as much as it does a first person platformer.
Clustertruck's focus is on high replay and speed running. There is no story to speak about here and this game feels geared towards video makers and streamers. You spend the entire game hurling yourself over obstacles ranging from simple pits, to dodging lasers beams. Death is quick instantaneous, actually. There are many ways to die and a simple misstep will more than likely get you killed. Fans of games like Super Meat Boy can expect the same level of brutality when it comes to how precise the game expects you to jump. Needless to say, frustration and rage come hand in hand with these types of games and should be expected. I found myself having to walk away a couple of times and come back later to play this game.
The game starts off rather light in the first ten levels, after that the difficulty and tricks start ramping up rather quickly all the way to level ninety. Clustertruck is a game that always had me on the edge of my seat and I never knew what to expect next. This constant anteing up of obstacles makes the game ludicrous but hilarious all at the same time. I genuinely laughed when suddenly a giant boulder was rolling down the hill at my sad truck army. Basically, don't take the game too terribly serious, mmkay?
How does one go about conquering lasers, boulders, missiles and more? Power ups and sometimes luck. There are a large range of power ups, ranging from jet packs, double jumps, grappling hooks, time control, and some others I don't wanna spoil for you. You can attempt to the beat the game without any of these powers up but you would be considered a masochist and must love fail screens.
The game doesn't always play fairly and this is kind of my first gripe with the game. There are rare times where you are going to fail a level completely, not because of your own skills but because the game simply didn't chaotically align the way it was supposed to. This unpredictable nature makes the speed running aspect difficult. as you never know what you might get from one run to the next.
One particular level that highlights this chaotic nature was Steampunk eight. The floor is sending everything forward incredibly fast and trucks are constantly colliding and exploding. By the end of the level you may not have a truck to land on near the goal, and you sit there with nothing to do. There are some power ups to counter this but I didn't have one that at the time. It was frustrating and felt as if I had been cheated.
I could've gone back and earned up enough points to buy the power up, but every level can be beaten with no power ups. So after an hour, I finally got lucky and trucks aligned the right way for me to complete it. Keep in mind this is a minor gripe, the game is very tongue in cheek and really just wants to make you laugh and rage a bit. This is more a warning to speed runners and people who may take the game a bit more seriously.
Once you do manage to beat all the levels in the game, the fun is far from over, as the game features steam workshop support. Insane Mario-esque levels and more await players and gives the game another truck of life. The content creator is simple enough and lends itself to just about any creation. If I had the patience for that type of thing I would've made one myself.
Aesthetically Clustertruck runs par for the course. It isn't the most gorgeous game in the world and sound wise there is nothing to write home about. They are well done, mind you, but nothing that is going to blow your mind. The level design is something of note though and the themes change in fun and dramatic ways every ten levels. Something to keep in mind is that touching the edge or even a sliver of any corner, may lead to a fail screen. Certain bulky square levels can lead to some serious frustration.
A strange thing, which I had a hard time believing, is that I found this game WAY easier to play with keyboard and mouse than with a controller. That is unless you have giant fingers and are proficient at pressing five buttons independently, all at the same time while moving the directional stick and moving the camera. You are moving so ridiculously fast in a forward direction, that moving side to side is extremely difficult with a controller. You may have a different experience than I did, but I found the controller to be very awkward and clunky.
Is the game a revolution of gaming mechanics? No, but it is sure damn fun and very good at distracting you.
While playing Clustertruck, such strange sounds and profanities escaped my mouth that my wife hired a young priest and an old priest. Not many games incite such rage in me and still let me have fun at the same time. You're going to get plenty of bang for your buck and there are plenty of levels being made by the community. Little things like Supertruck mode and "Coal" make this game worth it.
So have fun with it, don't take it terribly serious and enjoy dodging missiles, cursing like a sailor and the sweet, sweet, screen of victory.

The Blue Flamingo developers spend their time and money making fantastic graphics reminiscent of old Flash Gordon movies from the Golden Era but the controls are terrible.
On touch of a key on a keyboard sends your ship zooming from one side of the screen to the other, making Blue Flamingo impossible to play with any sort of accuracy.  A controller is a little better but you still can't make fine adjustments to movement.  You're still sliding in whatever direction you move in and likely straight into an enemy.  The best thing they could have done was allow you to move your ship with your mouse but that's not an option.
It's a fantastic looking game but it's rage-inducing when you play it.  Avoid unless they fix the ship movement.
Edit:  Since the original review in 2014, there has been some work to fix the controls.  Ships no longer slide from all the way to the edge of the screen when you press a button which is a major improvement.  Still, the controls aren't "tight".  The game seems designed more for a gamepad and I would say Blue Flamingo is at least playable now if you have one.
In spite of the beautiful top down graphics, the controls matter to me more in a shooter and I'm still not recommending this for WASD movement.  It's too bad they didn't let us use a mouse to move the ship.
It's obvious effort went into making this game, but the controls are just too imprecise.

I bought this game after listening to Giant Bomb's Game of the Year podcasts, where they named it Best Story and soundly spoiled a twist or two, so I went in with expectations. And, to be honest, neither the storytelling nor the story lived up to their high praise.
It starts off really, really good. The first 30 minutes *is* outstanding: mysterious, menacing, brilliantly told and stunningly visualized. If there's one thing this game nails it's robots talking to other robots, and it offers perhaps the best representation of robot 'culture' (if there is such a thing) in sci-fi that I've seen. The world is weird, the characters are weirder, and the atmosphere is thick throughout.
But then you run into the puzzles. I'm not an adventure gaming veteran or anything like that - I've played a few in my time - but the puzzles in The Fall are *so* obscure, *so* out-of-left-field and backtrack-y that it immediatly halts any momentum or goodwill the game conjures up in the first 30 minutes, deciding instead to take a hour long detour into pure puzzle-solving that feels like fluff to a game that's already achingly short (my steam time is 2 hours). Here, the story not so much evolves as mutates, getting sidetracked from the initial danger and wonder of that first half-hour. It continues to explore some interesting philosophical approaches to robots (though not particularly unheard of ones), but starts loosing its footing quickly.
The ending is a little stronger, buoyed by more directive and a brutal ending, but too many of the motivations behind characters are left unclear and combat - while unobtrusive but never exceptional in the earlier parts of the game - starts to become an annoying crutch. Since you are so fragile and your combat options are so limited, throwing more enemies than you can handle coupled with bad controls was incredibly frustrating in the final 20-stretch. By the time the game reached its climactic confrontation, I just wanted it to be done.
Luckily, about five minutes later it was. Both a blessing and a curse, The Fall's 2 hour run-time gives it a pleasant short-stort feel while still leaving questions open for the next two chapters. However, it's too short to give one character in particular much interesting motivation, which isn't great because there are only three in the entire game. The story itself is...unexceptional, though, for the most part, well told. The main character, A.R.I.D., and a friendly (or is it?) computer AI she meets along the way are both well voiced and written, and the world they inhabit is always fun to explore, if not being the most fleshed-out. Some character beats, however, fall totally flat - mainly one weird 'morality' choice near the end comes out of nowhere and means next-to-nothing.
Did listening to the Game of the Year stuff bias me against this game? Maybe. Probably. But in a year where we had good, emotional storytelling it The Wolf Among Us and This War of Mine, The Fall barely holds a candle to the rest. It didn't hit me as particularly better than other indie-sci-fi games (if you want a great one, go buy The Swapper). Overall, it just didn't feel that special. It never could live up to those first 30 minutes.

I won't go into too much detail about The Fall's storyline, as you can check the store page for that if you haven't already.  Instead, I'll talk about the rest of it so far as January 2015.
This game is thankfully uncomplicated in its control scheme and gameplay mechanics, and the atmosphere of it is seriously tense and dramatic - perfect for dystopia effectionadoes.  The game is quite reliant on problem solving, and many of the methods for dealing with situations have results that seem a little unorthodox - which, while fitting the theme and story very well, can leave one rather frustrated.
However, for those of us who don't want to miss out on the rest of the story because of one little puzzle, there's thankfully a number of walkthroughs out there that can help you.  Alternatively, since there isn't much that directly hinges on doing things in a set order (that I know of anyway), the tactic of brute-force use-everything-with-everything and do-everything-again-just-to-see-what-happens thing can work.
The combat system is fairly decent too, and while currently lacking in variety, due to the relatively low health and shields of your character it can be rather intense.  Also, quite fortunately, there are frequent saving points before combat situations so that if you die, you won't be too far behind.
All in all, I like this game and I recommend it to anybody who's got a bit of time up their sleeves and an itching for a gritty and dark puzzle game.

The Dating-Sim aspect is really tongue-in-cheek and takes itself about as seriously as it does the player. It really plays it up for laughs. Also it features a slightly larger than average board for these kinds of games which might not sound like much but it immensely rewards careful planning.
The characters you meet are absolutely 1-dimensional but the twist is, they seem to know it! I have been playing this game before it was released on steam and whilst watching it grow, i would have to say it has come a long way but is yet to be a polished, all-round decent game. It does have mostly pros but the cons are what drag it down from being enjoyable across the board. This review is based on my expiriences and suggestions on what is missing but take it as a grain of salt if you will and try the game out yourself, don't read the negative reviews, its a free game... give it a try!
Pros+
+Decent graphics, textures and colors are very nice and realistic, really captures the essence of WW2 for me
+Great variety of weapons and vehicles, enough to satisfy any WW2 fans
+Good Ranking system, fairly standard for the genre but worth grinding for (most of the time)
+Great weapon upgrade system- very in-depth
+Starter weapons are not overly underpowered, you can outmatch newbies who paid for their scary LMG's with the basic rifle if you have practiced and possibly picked up a few upgrades from grinding
+Nice layout of classes and weapon slots, easy to navigate
+Load times are not very long (excluding queue times for servers)
+Good FPS game gameplay/controls (just let down by a few cons)
Cons/suggestions-
-very basic server structures and are lacking in other regions (mine being Australia)
-Additions of new weapons and vehicles throws the game's balance around which is annoying
-FPS character controls and navigation are a bit floaty and with bad connection, extremely frustrating
-Hit Detection is sometimes poor unless your ping is good
-Bugs which have been popping up from time to time need to be constantly ironed out
-Balancing is mostly good but sometimes swings the matches favor to one team to quickly

If the goal of a first chapter is to get the player interested in buying the rest, then this one has failed.
- Every adventure game has at least one obscure puzzle, but there's usually some kind of hint if you think about it long enough. The hint system is a good idea (as is it's time delay), but it seems like it's made the designer reduce the in-game prompting as to what to do next.
- There's a few animation glitches where the character ends up on the ceiling. The double click fast travel was a good idea, but I couldn't get it to work reliably.
- Hitting the same option 7 times to progress the story is bad design. At least change what the character says so we know we're on the right track.
- Context dependant pick ups aren't a bad idea (the medicine was a good one) but when a nessecary item is next to something that we're literally told is useless (like a pile of trash) it's frustrating.
- The voices and english are a little off. Since this wasn't originally in English, this isn't something worth marking the game down for, but I think I'd find it better with text only if I played the next part.
Lastly, there just isn't enough information on the setting to pique my interest. Something about an explosion and a coup? Everyone seems to avoid telling you things, presumably for the sake of a reveal later on, but the purpose of amnesia characters are to justify the big exposition dumps needed to catch the player up. There just isn't enough there for me to put money in and find out.

This game is one of the finest RPGs ever made.  I place it in the top-3 RPGs of all-time along with Ultima 7 and Baldur's Gate 2 on my personal best list.  Even though quick travel (although there was a mass transit system that allowed you to travel to villages and cities) did not exist in its original release and now the graphics are very dated (check out the graphical overhauls to fix this), there was incredible mystery and world immersion that really isn't there for me in most modern day RPGs.  Breadcrumb trails don't exist here and you had to play this game with the world map at the ready (a physical one in my case).  Morrowind's magic system allowed the player to make and craft their own spells and bind them to everyday objects like lockets.  You could create a powerful Jump spell and then use a magically crafted amulet that had a Feather spell.  With such a spell you could, for instance, vault yourself over a third of the map and then Featherfall down to the ground.  You couldn't really do anything like this in Oblivion or Skyrim.  In fact, the magic systems of the subsequent Elder Scrolls games seemed to really be Nerfed in relation to Morrowind.  You also could rise to be more powerful then the gods in this game.  In the Tribunal DLC add-on, there was a moment where I could literally kill the other gods, and the game would accomadate it.  The lore in this game was fantastic and the story was top-notch.  Much of the game centers around you fulfilling prophecy set down eons before your time.  I was struck by the story's scope and it felt like every nook and cranny had some new adventure to be found.  This game is a masterpiece, and for me, the new Elder Scrolls games lack this games immersion and freedom.  As someone who has been playing computer games since their infancy (i got my gaming start around 1980) this truly is a classic that every RPGphile should experience at least once.

I loved this game when it first came out on Xbox and put many hours into it; I enjoyed this ported version (supporting gamepad input) just as much, and it gave me a chance to play The Lost Chapters expansion. Definitely worth playing! *****

This game has a very specific character. On the one hand, it displays a dorky, sometimes childish type of humor (fart joke level), on the other hand, it gets really dark at certain points: I am talking about villains slaughtering helpless civilians, torturing children and murdering hostages in front of your eyes.
There are summarizing scenes at the end of each story chapter in a seriously epic tone, presenting you as the heir of a mysterious power and saviour of the world from the rule of demons and the undead. In contrast to that, you can donate books to a school and watch the little ones recite the lines on stage, giggling at the mature content, or you can go to the beach and participate in a competition called Chicken Kickin' (yes, the name is a literal description!). And it is not just comic relief, the overall atmosphere, at least for the most part, is playful and self-ironic. Slay an ugly monster, then take its head, go to the next town, and run around showing it to everyone to enjoy the applause. Choose a fabulous nom-de-guerre, like "Liberator" or "The Hood", and listen to everyone you see talking about you until you cannot even hear it yourself anymore. Find a sick child in the poor quarter of a town, learn that you need certain mushrooms to save it - then get one of those by performing a Russian style dance number in front of a woman to make her laugh and give you the shroom as  a reward... These examples should give you an idea of the vibe.
The production value is undeniably excellent: The artstyle is captivating and flawlessly executed, in all departments from graphics (both environment and animations) via sound (atmospheric and beautiful music, the voice acting always top-notch!) to the writing (actually interesting lore-texts,  diversified quests with creative solutions and twists) - I feel that a lot of love went into these aspects.
The character development I find a little unbalanced. You have access to high level gear pretty early, and then, armour and weapons don't change that much any longer. Other games have succeeded to give you more intermediate goals to work for. Also, it does not help that the title everybody knows you under (like "Liberator") is not earned by heroic deeds, but purchased from a trader after you have become tired of hearing your default title all the time ("Chicken Chaser"). Nevertheless, I appreciate that you see your hero growing up from his traumatic childhood experience via the training as a youngling (which is, at the same time, the tutorial thus integrated in your personal story - kudos to whomever had that idea!) to the point where you are a grown man and a famous hero in the end. This organic development of your story is a big plus.
There are a few annoying things though:
- The inventory is divided into different parts and subparts, which makes sense somehow, but you need many clicks and scrolls when you want to find a specific consumable or tool.
- NPCs are only available during a limited part of the game day, and there is no "wait x hours" function, which makes you run around and look for some public mattress with a suspicious blanket to sleep in - it is not only kind of "ew" and underwhelming, it is a lot of unnecessary running.
- Some quests give you too little choices; e.g. I wanted to complete the game as a noble hero, including the charitable task of collecting books for the local school - but you cannot do that legally, you have to steal certain books from the houses of people who just welcomed you with cheers of love and admiration; that bothered me a little.
- There are too many loading screens!
- Also, I never like it when enemies respawn endlessly, it belittles the achievement of having defeated those enemies before and encourages farming - a technical, non-immersive form of playing an RPG. But that is a matter of taste.
The combat is not very well designed in my opinion. It is interesting for a while, specifically when you are still discovering all the new types of enemies, but after the waves of identical opponents in the Arena quest, you have seen (almost) everything and can only expect repetitions of the same patterns while you mash your buttons. The most annoying thing about the whole game though is the ease with which enemies stagger you, even if you parry and wear heavy armour. Some types like trolls, nymphs and the final enemy of the main quest send you to the ground every few seconds (!) because they spam unblockable power attacks from a distance. That does not feel good, you don't feel powerful and heroic at this point, and you don't feel well entertained either when you constantly watch your toon picking himself up. I think this is a cheap way of adding artificial difficulty and takes away from the immersion and the fun.
Still, there are many features to enjoy: Minigames within the game like the aforementioned Chicken Kickin' or the numerous cardgames in the taverns, the various demon door riddles you can solve for bonus loot, or the challenge to buy and upgrade houses in all the towns, maybe even marry one of your nameless, but quite attractive groupies...If you don't take this game (or life in general) too seriously, you will get the most out of it.
Bottom line: A game with character and a lot of creative content, some (mostly technical) flaws, but nevertheless good entertainment; overall a 7/10.

Clustertruck is a very interesting take on what I like to call rage 3d platformer. In clustertruck you jump from truck to truck and try to get to the end of the map.
Sounds easy right?
Yeah not so much!
Levels go from pretty simple with a few obstacles to dodge to massive explosions, gigantic rolling rocks, on coming traffic, roads that just bloody disappear, vents that literally blow you away, and other devious implements of salty rage perfection.
While completing levels you manage to acquire "style points" I'm pretty sure style points are a tracking system devoted to your screams and the squishing noises you make when impacting the ground at hundreds of miles an hour.
These upgrades allow you to change the game by adding double jump, slowing time, and many more!
Not only that you can compete with your friends and the world for the best time. Even get a ghost ball to show how they schooled your butt in real time.
All in all I really enjoyed the game and for a low price of 14.99 I think its definitely worth it!

When it said that the covered tiles were 'asleep,' I though that was a cute euphemism, but they were actually asleep. Clicking the wrong animal would give you a snoring sound and zzzzzz's. The quality of life adjustments in the game make it very playable. The gameplay flows smoothly. A dog will match any dog, and the same with cats and ducks. Not worth buying.

Anime is not something I will often watch except for notable examples like Cowboy Bebop, Code Geaus and Full Metal Alchemist where the prepubescent problems of pre-teens becomes something more elaborate and complex with adult issues beyond simply violence. Violence isn’t a problem as I play tons of violent games, yet anime often will make talking the filler in-between budget cuts for fights or make fighting a simple solution to more difficult obstacle with a inane moral behind it.
Ghost in the Shell: Stand Alone Complex Season 1 does away with all the pre-teen nonsense by making a truly adult world with tons of subtlety and a tastefulness of violence that often is more haunting to imagine than horrifying to watch. Without having watched the original film nor read the manga, I can appreciate SAC as it manages to introduce the world and history in a smart way by connecting story-arcs that more people who are interested in crime-fiction will truly appreciate the craftmanship of the whole season. Watching this show in order is vital to enjoy the series as the connections made between episodes are what makes this anime more rewarding to watch on repeated viewings. It's these qualities that make the SAC series is without a doubt my favorite anime of all time.
Seeing as how I often purchase games on Steam, I am not familiar with the standards of movie service on the platform. However, I felt it was necessary to describe the quality in detail for anyone interested or dissuaded by other commentators as I don’t find any technical issues with the service.
The obvious thing to mention is that you are purchasing the season, not renting it, though I have had some friends were confused. If you are interested in the SAC series, there are technically three seasons on Steam. Season 1, Season 2 (2nd Gig) and Solid State Society (post-2nd Gig film).
The service itself had little, if any hiccups, on a stable internet connection with multiple quality options to choose. My usual quality rate was 1040p with lower options available. There is only the default (Japanese) video-track with English, Italian, German and Japanese audio options. The only commentary provided is in English with options to determine the font, size and color to minimize its obtrusiveness if you enable it. The only negative I can state, though it might be my hardware with 5.1 Surround Speakers, is the audio quality can seem a little too low and inconsistent between episodes.
While I cannot decry censorship of any kind, I did not feel any lines were tampered with as I could hear lines like “Major She Ape”, though perhaps the commentary obscured that line. On top of the 26 episodes, the first season comes equipped with all the Tachicomas snippets at the end of every episode and the interviews after Ep 26.
What really hooked me on SAC was the developing complexity of the season from seemingly unrelated threads linked together to create an elaborate story-arc that feels complete from beginning to end. Many shows handle this poorly by withholding clues or plot-points until the “Ah-hah!” episode whereas in SAC the plot mainly develops by reexamining each previous episode in a new light such as The Laughing Man. Not every episode, thankfully, spends its time to reflect on the same facts or the same story, and right when the overarching threads like The Laughing Man become stale is when the show moves on to something else to give the viewer some time to breathe.
Sometimes these breaks will be used to draw interest into individual members of Section 9, or they will be used to connect previous episodes considering their future events. No episode ever feels wasted despite not all of them always being at their best.
This is perhaps why each episode, even when it’s not great, makes it worthwhile to watch from beginning to end, though there are noticeable “meh” episodes such as the very first one when followed by great episodes like the second episode. The problem with the first episode isn’t that it isn’t entertaining; it’s trying to cram a lot of story in one episode, and it manages to do it succinctly yet not without confusing newcomers. It may take a few viewings to absorb the significance in every episode, yet that is why the show is so endearing to me as there are always questions upon quandaries, moments foreshadowed early and events to reconsider in light of new facts. Simply watching this show is an engaging experience in an equally thrilling and terrifyingly all too real world of an encroaching society that has more in common with today than it did previously.
Though the 2nd Gig perhaps has more to resonate with the immediate present, the themes of SAC: Season 1 still retain their value in an era and generation fostered by the internet. Perhaps even more so today than the time of its creation, especially for a generation that has been born into it.
This idea solidifies itself in the episode titled, “Memes,” which explores the idea of the Laughing Man who was introduced in previous episodes in context of the culture he has created, the copycats he has made under the guise of anonymity, and the propagation of the myth and the meanings associated with the Laughing Man in an era of information. This is also important in terms of a stand-alone complex, an accidental creation of a collective made up of detached individuals that appears to be an organized conspiracy, yet it remains detached from each other and its origin.
It’s these ideas and the depth of their exploration that truly makes this show worthwhile for adults as well as teenagers who perhaps have similar thoughts. Most episodes retain this level of thoughtful discussion as well as high-intense action through seemingly unrelated cases, events for individual Section 9 members, and other types of moments that are hard to define. Sometimes the discussion turns into transhumanism, morality, or more down-to-earth matters like greed or love that seem more (or less) human due to the changes of society. It’s all these compelling ideas that makes up the breadth of SAC, and the show isn’t too afraid to use a lot of books as references from J.D. Salinger to Richard Dawkins.
Even the action has context and purpose beyond their spectacle, which makes those slow-building moments intensified by the realness of the world and the likelihood that any character at any point might become disposable. The added visual and musical accompaniment to smart storytelling makes this show a sublime experience and food for thought, and it easily overturns any fears of the mature themes becoming too much or the strange oddities such as the Major’s clothing or the Tachichoma’s childlike voices becoming obtrusive. (I imagine there are reasons such as the Major’s enjoyment of her female body type or the innocence of the Tachichoma AIs.)
In the finale, the season wraps up its remaining threads succinctly for the next season to continue on with new concerns, retaining all the moments of SAC: Season 1 into a finished story that retains all its purity without a lacking sense of closure tarnished by modern stories in films or in games.

Let's talk about
. Well, you can already see that I recommend it, but here's why:
There's no better setting for a spooky atmosphere than the deep sea. Darkness everywhere and more importantly the fear of the unknown are both concepts, which get explored in
. However I have to say, that the horror-tag might be misleading. It's true that eerie music, low visibility and the general fear of being stuck in a sunken ship, do their job to creep me out, but once the game got its handful of jump scares out of the way, it loses its scary aura.
There's no map, no journal to re-read entries or even see how many can be found and overall no additional gadgets. You walk, jump, crouch, turn your lights on and off and activate/read on your way through a sunken ship. That's it. Even the story is optional, if you're willing to reduce the game to a mindless journey from A to B. In a world where games, more often than not, advertise how you can do everything in them, I like to relax with such a simple game, with simple rules.
The story gets told through a series of notes, sketches and letters. You may find reviews stating that the story could be more present or better explained, but I'd disagree. The journey wouldn't be as interesting if you reveal everything from the start and since those little snippets of information are the only motivation to explore the whole map, it'd also make this aspect of the gameplay obsolete.
I don't want to spoil anything, so don't expect me to go into details, but the plot reveals itself at a steady pace until the very end, but still leaves some room for interpretation.
One thing the game lacks is difficulty. I'd even say that remembering the ship's layout is the hardest part of the whole game. Puzzles are a rare sight, since I don't qualify pushing a box across half the  screen to get to a higher platform as one, but perhaps that's just me.
Also rather strange for the horror genre:
I like the overall bad visibility. What I don't like is having to go another round across the whole map to reach an optional room, because I couldn't tell whether or not there's another platform under a drop-off.
~) There are a lot of people out there who can't start the game. Mostly Linux and Mac users as I understand, but some people also experience problems under Windows. I use Windows 8.1 (64-bit version) and Java Build 1.8.0_141-b15 myself and didn't experience any problems.
~) It took me not quite 3 hours to complete the game. However that includes exploring the whole map and finding all entries (whether story related or not). So basically 100%ing the game.
~) It's a short game, yes, and personally I don't have any problems with it, but it's noteworthy that
doesn't have a save function. Once you start a chapter (1 out of 3) you either finish it or start all over again from scratch. However during a session it has save points.
In the end I really like
, which is a pleasant surprise, since I only got it as part of bundle. Perfect for everybody who wants to kill a few hours, but I wouldn't recommend it for anyone who wants a challenge or a true horror experience.

If your looking for a review on this game you've come to the wrong place, but if your looking for an outstanding pie recipe you've come to the right place.
Ingredients:
1. 6 tablespoons unsalted butter
2. 1/2 cup white sugar
3. 1/2 cup brown sugar
4. 1/4 cup water
5. 1/4 teaspoon cinnamon
6. 1 pinch salt
7. 5 apples - peeled, cored and sliced
8. 1 pastry for double-crust pie
Directions:
1. Preheat oven to 425 degrees F (220 degrees C).
2. Combine butter, white sugar, brown sugar, water, cinnamon, and salt in a saucepan over medium heat. Bring to a boil, remove from heat and set aside.
3. Roll out half the pastry to fit a 9-inch pie plate. Place bottom crust in pie plate; pour in apple slices.
4. Roll out top crust into a 10-inch circle. Cut into 8 (1-inch) wide strips with a sharp paring knife or pastry wheel. Weave the pastry strips, one at a time, into a lattice pattern. Fold the ends of the lattice strips under the edge of the bottom crust and crimp to seal.
5. Pour butter-sugar mixture over top of pie, coating the lattice, and allowing any remaining sauce to drizzle through the crust.
6. Bake in the preheated oven for 15 minutes. Reduce heat to 350 degrees F (175 degrees C), and bake until the crust is golden brown, the caramel on the top crust is set, and the apple filling is bubbling, 35 to 40 more minutes. Allow to cool completely before slicing.

As a long-time fan of the Resident Evil series, to the point where I once assisted with the infamous plot analysis FAQ, I am one of the few who consider CVX as the end of the series proper.  Not there's anything wrong with 4 or 5, per se - though there is something seriously wrong with 6, WTF - but the good ol' haunted house/city simulator died with the penultimate Code: Veronica X.  However, no matter how much time has passed since the original RE/Biohazard introduced itself to us on the PSX, there has always been a certain charm to its obtuse puzzles and B-movie cast of characters, which is why I think Capcom has once again revisited the first title, despite RE2 being arguably the best of the series.
Of course, most of the work was already done for them as this is an HD port/remaster of the original Gamecube release (the sole reason I even own that paperweight, mind you), but it has always been a title that has sat in the back of my mind, constantly beckoning me to return to the mansion and have another go at it.  So it is that I no longer have to dig out that cube-shaped machine to play this, as one of my favorite titles from the entire series proper makes its way to PC and consoles with a nice new shine on it.
As I said, this is a revisit of an original Gamecube release.  While character models have been updated and re-textured to look nice at today's resolutions, the pre-rendered backgrounds didn't get a whole lot of work on them and a lot of the cutscenes are blocky and chunky, just like mama made it.  As a result, the game has lost a lot of its pizzazz, but it makes sense that they wouldn't go back and re-render all of the backgrounds.  Still, I often find myself thinking, "this looked much better on my Sony CRT," but games always look better in your head than they actually did when you played them.
For those familiar with the original release, perhaps intimately so, rest assured that Capcom did not muck with the formula one bit.  The game is exactly the same and you can enjoy it like you always have, including all of the fun sequence-breaking that's available to you.  For those on the other side of the fence, this is one of the most important remakes in the history of the industry because it not only legitimized the first game as something "unstupid", but it also greatly expanded on it and tied it all into ideas that made themselves apparent in the sequels.  For conspiracy theorists, it doesn't get better than this (really, check out the plot analysis FAQ).
The greatest treat of this game was for people who knew the original or director's cut inside and out.  Those who really spent the time with the first game to know its every corner and dark little secret were in for a few surprises when they got their hands on this one.  This remake went through a lot of trouble to play with fans' expectations.  I distinctly remember saying, "...there wasn't a door here before," when I popped it into the GCN, making the familiar unfamiliar, keeping fans on their toes.  Moments like that are abound, so if for some reason you never got your hands on REbirth, there's no better reason than it's available now and in HD... -ish.
With the obvious out of the way, you should know - especially if you've got anything else from them on Steam - that Capcom really stinks at PC.  I don't know what it is, but they have no idea how to work with them.  A quick scan of the forums will tell you how many issues people are having with the game, but solutions are being found and if you can get them in place, this game runs like a dream.  Framerates inexplicably drop, like in other Capcom titles, and audio goes out of sync.  A little fiddling, though, and you're off to the races, but for those non-technical people out there, just know that you might require a little elbow grease to get this port running the way it ought to.
At the end of the day, this is the perfect excuse to revisit the remake or experience it for the first time.  Like I said, I think it's one of the most important remakes ever because it just does everything right - it keeps things the same (because fans really hate change), but expands the original just enough to keep everyone on their toes.  Despite being over a decade old, the game is still a wonderful romp through a creepy house and it gives you the very tip of the Umbrella conspiracy iceberg.  This game needs to be played by everyone and for the record, I LOVE the tank controls. :P
Now, Capcom, where's that Resident Evil 2 everyone wants, hey?

This is a really enjoyable game throughout. I played the original on Gamecube and it's definitely fair to say that the graphics have aged well. A nice HD polish-up certainly does the vision of the game great justice. The sound design is as good as ever; every zombie moan and footstep still feel as inherently creepy as ever, and the music is perfectly placed and atmospheric. Gameplay wise, I'm a supporter of the old method even though there is an enhanced control scheme available, the clunky controls are as integral to the experience as the zombies, and everything is suitably creepy and uncomfortable.
In terms of pros, I would say that the game's graphics are great, its sound is fantastic and it's overall a triumph of design; this is how Resident Evil should be. The atmosphere is only helped by the remasters and the improvements and it's still by far the brilliant remake it was. It also runs well, I have a very weak laptop, but it runs this game perfectly without even trying. I tested my comp on Can You Run It, and it said I couldn't, but my laptop more than managed it. It's fairly generous in terms of system requirements and if you just take a look at the specs and use common sense, it is probably quite likely your computer would run this smoothly and with no problem.
However, I did find the 60FPS mode seemed to run in slow-motion, which was probably due to the weakness of my laptop, but it was still frustrating considering otherwise it can run the game on very high settings.
Cons, I would say that the game has a HUGE filesize for what is essentially just a HD reskin of a Gamecube game. I find it hard to believe that it wasn't possible to cut the game down from the massive 16.8GB download that it turned out to be. The controls are not for everyone either and the story is still on the wrong side of cheesy, though it's arguable that this is the point of Resident Evil (I personally enjoy the story). I would also say that while it is an improvement on the original remake and a very well-made remaster, I wouldn't say this is that much of an improvement to be shouting home about.
Still, it looks beautiful and this is certainly the best version of the REmake out there, I would easily recommend this over the Gamecube or Wii version of this game. I would recommend this game to anyone who likes atmospheric scares, some action and those who are interested in seeing one of the biggest influences on the zombie genre. It's a good price at £15.00, so I think it's more than value for money. This is simply a game that, if you're a fan of horror, you must play.

Most people I know got their introduction to the series with 2008's Fable II on the Xbox Tree-Sickidy. From what I remember, it's not a bad game, but it was a bit of a step down from the original. And the third and final entry was even worse. I believe Fable / Anniversary is the only truly great game in the series. Truly a one-hit wonder.
Why? I guess it just has a charm that it's sequels did not possess (as much), from the characters to the world to the soundtrack. And the sequels were also too simplified, especially the last one, from the breadcrumb trails to the combat. Still, it's a shame Lionhead shut down recently, so there doesn't look to be a chance of a redemption for the series. Even the cancelled Fable Legends didn't look all that promising in my opinion.
At least before Lionhead went out with a whimper, Anniversary was released, a remastered version of the original game. Being an Xbox hipster when all the other kids had PS2s, I played it back in 2005, not long after it's release. I remember actually not being too keen when I first started, what with starting as a kid and having to earn money to buy your sister a present. I thought, wow, how lacklustre is this... And the world and goofy-looking characters with thick-accents I found somewhat freaky.
I didn't play it for long, and lent it to my brother to play at the hospital where he was staying with hella-bad tonsilitis. He played a ton of it and convinced me it was a great game, so I tried it again, and got very much into it, eventually falling in love with it. And I fell in love with it all over again with Anniversary.
The world is a medieval interpretation of Britain, of course with the addition of magic and the threat of dark forces and whatnot. So yeah, sounds pretty darn familiar. But this exceeds with the way all that is portrayed. With colourful charm and humour, the choice between a good and bad alignment, either which alters you physically and changes the perception of those around you, and easy accessibility (but not too simple as it's sequels, as I said).
You start as a little boy, scatting about your nice little town trying to get money to buy your sister a birthday present. And the choices start here. Do you earn that money with good deeds (i.e watch a bloke's barrels for him while goes off for a♥♥♥♥♥♥ or earn it with bad deeds? (agree to watch those barrels but then smash them and earn the approval of a little shitbag trying to peer pressure you). You get many of those choices throughout, some harder to make than others.
Bandits attack your village, and♥♥♥♥♥♥goes sideways. You are rescued by a member of the Heroes Guild, where you begin training as said Hero, and grow up there, eventually leaving as an adult. As it goes in video games, whatever alignment you choose, you still end up saving the world from the big bad guy.
In games with moral alignments, I tend to stay on the good side, because that's just me. And I did when I played the original. But this time round I became as evil as possible, doing bad deeds, assisting bandits, betraying my family and murdering innocents. Either side of the moral spectrum grants you exclusive items and weapons. I was so evil I grew horns, had red eyes and skin like a zombie. I looked awesome.
On the higher end of the light side you have nice skin, a halo above your head, and all the people love you. And if someone loves you that much (you can further earn their affections with gifts and flirtatious gestures), you can ask them to marry you; man or woman. Pretty impossible to earn trust and affection if you're evil though. Everyone just screams and runs away. Just like me in real life ohhhhhh!
All in all do I recommend this? You bet your big♥♥♥♥♥I do. The thing to take into consideration though, is that while this is an RPG, it's not entirely open-world. It consists of many individual chunks of areas, many with very narrow paths. And there isn't a colossal amount of things to do, once you've unlocked and collected everything. So those who are more used to the gargantuan games of today (i.e Skyrim, The Witcher 3) with literally hundreds of hours of content, stunning graphics and modern mechanics, might not be so impressed.
But there is certainly enough to keep you going for a good 25+ hours or so. Especially now as it has achievements, and some rather amusing ones at that, like getting a headshot with a crossbow while dressed as a woman, farting while dressed as an assassin, and choosing whether to explore every single region or just get fat (they unlock the same achievement).
A personal niggle from me? It's possible to miss one of the silver keys out of the thirty you can collect. If you leave it too long before starting the fishing competition, the NPC you talk to can disappear forever. As an achievement geek this♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥me off. You have to get all thirty keys in one playthrough for an achievement, and I have twenty-nine... So to get it again I'll have to start again and get the thirty all over again...
Still, I gotta give it full marks for everything else.

First I would say this game has quite a learning curve. I would consider 30 hours a "college try". So If you're trying to get into the game it has some commitment to it.
Pick your race, which has benefits/weaknesses, pick your major and minor skills, which decide how fast/slow you level and progress. Melee combat may seem dated but is a very complex system based on dice rolls factoring everything from your fatigue when you swing to the condition of your weapon before it calculates damage. Magic system is leagues above future titles(looking at you Skyrim) with thousands of spells that you can create. Tons of gear choices with 3 classes of armor and unarmored as well. Lots of skills, some of which are more rewarding than others. The game is less balanced than future titles but thats part of the charm.
Quests and travel really set this game apart from most games. No hand holding here. You really have to read and comprehend your goals before you can set off acomplishing tasks. There is usually several ways to organically complete quest, for instance one of the first quest in the Thieves guild has you stealing a diamon from a local shopkeeper but you can just purchase it and lie to the guild when you turn in the quest.
Graphics are the most dated part of this game, but there is good news. Its an Elder Scrolls title which of coarse means MODs! One in paticular called Morrowind Sound and Graphics Overhaul or MGSO for short is a complete package of graphical updates with loads of bug fixes added as well. The Installer for MGSO is fairly simple and I've recommended it to several people (including a 51 year old computer illiterate co worker) and they havent had any trouble installing it.
I love Morrowind and recommend it fullheartedly. 9.9/10

Those who haven't previously played
or
need have no fear of starting
without familarity with the series' lore.  The conclusion of this epic trilogy (please let there not be another) allows new players to dive right in without issue thanks to that hoary gimmick, the amnesiac opening.  Yes, you start the game not knowing who you are, how you came to be where you are, or what's going on.
You end the game that way, too.
All you ever know in
is that you are in a bucolic rural setting, with a lot of tile-matching puzzles to solve that, while not being Mahjong in the strict sense, are based on Mahjong mechanics.  Tons of those puzzles, in fact, which is good, because there are no random layouts here, so a puzzle once solved is solved forever, unless you want to go back and try to do it a little faster.
As a Mahjong-like game goes, this is a bare-bones experience, without any bells or whistles beyond a few static background images and a bouncy folkish theme tune that loops endlessly.  Not even achievements to collect.
The final two level sets of the game are a little surprising because they suddenly introduce an entirely new mechanic.  Suddenly the tiles are suspended in space, facing in all directions, and you need to rotate the mass around to find matches.  In this mode nothing is blocked from the sides, so your only challenge is to locate matches as quickly as possible.  It's even less Mahjong-like than the base puzzles but it is kind of fun.  Had the idea of Mahjong just been abandoned altogether, this puzzle mode could have been developed into something interesting.  As it is, it's still simple, with no challenge to offer besides racing a clock.
Bottom line: there's no shortage of Mahjong-based puzzlers out there, many of them are free, and most of them are better than this.  Don't bother.

The Blue Flamingo is a neat "art game" that has a unique artstyle created by actually building the terrain and all the ships in miniature and then converting photographs and video of them into the background and sprites used in the game. Somewhat defying the tendencies of "typical" art games, it's actually a shoot-'em-up, rather than a puzzle platformer or walking simulator.
Unfortunately, that's around where the neatness ends - it's a fairly short score attack game, where you play through more or less the same two levels repeatedly, just getting slightly more difficult each time, with very clunky controls. The shortness in terms of content is likely due to the limitations of the artstyle, which constrained them to only having one model for the terrain because building an impressively detailed 32-foot-long model is hard and only so many models for enemies, as those too had to be hand-built and hand-painted, but the loose controls are less forgivable, as they combine with the lack of ability to restore your health to make a game where you're rewarded for playing very conservatively, which ends up feeling rather boring.
In the end, I can't really recommend The Blue Flamingo because ultimately it doesn't hold up as anything except a neat visual experience.

3 out of 10

While it is pretty to look at, The Blue Flamingo is rather underwhelming as a game.
1) Control lag and movement inertia.  I hope you don't like having fine control over your ship.  It makes the game vastly less enjoyable to play as a result.
2) Enemy design is incredibly basic.  There's a lot of the same enemy from the last level, who flies the exact same way and shoots the exact same way, over and over, level after level.  There are even enemies that litereally do nothing but take a bunch of hits.  Nothing remotely interesting starts to show up until you've looped the game around six times.
3) Weapons are dull and uninteresting.  Leveling up your shot only increases fire rate.  No shot type selection or variety to choose from.
4) Color selection.  In most games of this type, certain colors are reserved for important information (such as enemy bullets), so they are always visible and clear.  The nighttime cityscape background breaks this basic design rule, as bullets and enemies blend seamlessly into the background colors.  Lucky for us enemy fire is absurdly predictable.
5) Menus ignore your button config; you always have to press enter to do anything regardless of what you set for your action buttons.  Also they use blinking text to show what you are highlighting, meaning you have to wait a second just to see what you're actually selecting.
In conclusion, The Blue Flamingo has sloppy controls and uninteresting gameplay.  Not recommended.

I got this game for Christmas, so I checked it out even though I didn't expect much beforehand. I was quickly hooked by the fascinating premise that starts off the storyline: An unknown soldier crash-lands on an unknown (but sinister) planet for unknown reasons, and is left unconscious and likely heavily injured. So the emergency on-board AI of the soldier's futuristic combat suit activates, programmed with the mission to try and save the life of "its human". You, the player, take on the role of this AI...
In order to find out where you are, what happened, and how to get your human to medical treatment, you'll have to overcome both your own pre-programmed limitations and the obstacles imposed by the dystopian environment and by other machines who are stubbornly following their own programming. You'll have to act in the face of insufficient data and moral dilemmas, and figure out whether to "follow protocol" may require you to bend or even break it...
A cool concept would not stand on its own; Luckily, this game has a really well executed atmosphere - both visuals and voice-acting are very polished for an Indie game.
Most of the core gameplay consists of aim'n'click puzzles. Even though I usually find point'n'click style games off-putting, I had no trouble getting into the gameplay here, probably because:
The puzzles tend to be things that make sense for the character to do as part of the storyline (rather than just arbitrarily tacked on), and some were even used as set-ups for later revealed "character developments", which felt pretty satisfying. However, the difficulty was a little uneven - some puzzles were no-brainers, while other seemed unreasonably hard to figure out.
The "side-scrolling shooter" gameplay parts are too easy for my taste, despite the fact that some of the controls there felt a little clunky/unreliable. Since it's not the main game mechanic, that's fine though.
All in all I feel very positive about the game, except for one big downside: It is short and unconcluded. When I was getting close to the end after 3 to 4 hours, it felt like the end of a prologue or "chapter 1" would feel in a game of traditional size, and I was pretty disappointed when instead of transitioning to the next chapter, it showed "To be continued..." and rolled the credits - with the storyline wide open and many questions unanswered.
I suppose splitting game releases into separate single-chapter titles is a reaction to the fact that many gamers are no longer willing to spend more than a few bucks per title, but Steam should at least be honest about it when a title is merely a first chapter rather than a full game in the traditional sense. Also, games like Aquaria are proof that even tiny Indie dev teams can create big game worlds, so I don't think we should accept "Indie" as an excuse for unreasonable brevity.

Stick RPG 2: An impressively overpriced experience.
Now before I delve into the game itself, let me say that I played this game heavily when I was younger on sites like Kongregate and XGen, so much so I unearthed some forgotten memories of the game, like which jobs got you the most dosh and so on. And when I saw this game on Steam, I jumped at the chance to relive those memories of my childhood I blew on Flash games like Stick RPG 2. And those memories came back, for the first hour, the next two were slowly realizing this game's critical flaw.
There's one issue with this game: You can play the same game for free, still on those sites. In fact, the only thing this "Director's Cut" adds is an entire small area with a whole 3 different jobs, a few combat zones and a small plot involving murder. It also gives you cheats of varying utility, mostly making the grind easier to pull off. But everything else about this game is stock standard from the free online game, in fact too much is.
I blew 2.99 on this game, and that's the lowest I've ever seen it go and I still wasn't satisfied. This game needs a lot more content to differentiate itself from the online version, and it doesn't. It's still in the same resolution with the same annoying XGen save system, the same incredibly outdated memes and the same music. It's a incredibly painful port of the game onto Steam in an attempt to revive nostalgia in people of the original game without much attempt to make it better than the free version still available to play on every flash game site on the Internet.
My advice: Play the free version online and leave this overpriced port to languish in the same hell that all bad ports sink into.
