for the amount of money that goes into this game through method II, there is surprisingly little content being produced. from what I understand, there is only a small team developing this. they have in the padt deveoled titles such as the Hitman series, which i have heard good things about, although havent myself played.
for this reason, i doubt it is dev incompetence, but poor management ruining the game. the company is based in Copenhagen, Denmark, and from research into universities over there where i will probably end up studying at, they have a vast talent pool available to choose from. they just dont. management is♥♥♥♥♥♥

What many of the positive reviews here don't explain is the scale and excitement of the battles that happen in this game. If instead of just growing your star collection you give attention to your planets and their fleets, you will eventually wind up with an impressive space empire, each planet spawning its own fleet of tiny battleships. Having this empire of yours roam around the galaxy and war with other star systems is like watching thousands of years of galactic history pass. Like those golden moments in really good space opera where the scope of the whole drama really comes down on you.
Well there isn't so much drama here as scope, but the battles can be pretty exhilirating as your little ships lure the adversary's forces into range of your planets' guns, or use as a weapon some budding planetary civilization you'd picked out just for that purpose - smashing it into the enemy's bristling homeworld in the hopes of knocking it free from orbit and stealing it for youself. Meanwhile nomad fleets hunt through space looking for worlds to plunder, and sometimes they see an opportunity in these system battles and become involved also. Watching these subhuman filth destroy each other while you gather million year old civilizations and harvest them for resources is far and away the most satisfying experience life has to offer.

Okay yes, I have only played a couple minutes of this. I just wanted to get a feel for this. I have however played every LethalRPG game I could find online. I have to say, While the combat system is nice, It feels more like a spiritual successor rather than an addition to the saga that was going on. Considering no one else has brought up the series, I feel theres no problem with what I am going to say but if you really don't want to see it then SPOILERS:
Still here? good. Okay so the Lethal Rpg series is about a knight, not his name at first, He served his kingdom loyally, but eventually, after they were done with him, they got rid of him. A Wizard came along and saw the wounded warrior laying there. He fused him the warrior with a magical orb, which formed the man the series knows as Lethal. Immediately, Lethal wanted revenge, so he went along, conquering entire islands by himself, getting more powerful the more souls he would take. Before he could challenge the king himself, Lethal was taken down by an adventurer. But that didn't stop him. He just went and beat Death itself to come back, more angry, and more evil. This time nothing stood in his way as he murdered the king, and world domination was his. But the wizard grew angry, as he wished to control Lethal for himself. Having failed at that, He split (or cloned, I never got full details on this) Lethal into another being, Fatal. Fatal destroyed the planet itself, and sealed Lethal away in a tombstone, a mere wisp of his former self. Fatal went on to terrorize the rest of the galaxy (yep this went a bit SciFi) as Lethal watched one. He began to see the truth of his ways as he had witnessed the destruction of his home and now the galaxy itself was at risk. Eventually, a rebel happened by the planet, and Lethal offered up his powers to the rebel to help take down Fatal (in the game it was mostly a transformation to Lethal) Finally, working with the Rebel, Fatal was finally taken down. Remorseful with his evil ways, Lethal went to sleep. Promising to wake up when they needed him again. Eventually, a long time later, he was woken up again, as Fatal's cult had begun to seemingly attempt to bring Fatal back. Lethal fought, with two adventurers, to stop it. They chased the cultist into hell itself. But they realized too late that the cultist weren't trying to bring Fatal back, They were bringing back a greater evil, which sealed the opening to hell which Lethal and his team had gone through.
And thats where the story left off. I can say the game is great, but to go to that deep a plot (yes parts of it are missing, I play the series 2-4 years ago, I can't exactly be expected to remember the exacts of a forgotten plot) and then to come right back to the beginning with this game, I just can't recommend it. Go play the other games in the series, I'll look the titles up and add them to this review. Let me get one thing out of the way before continuing with this review. As of this review's publication, only Part One of this game is released. If you do not wish to purchase only a portion of this game for full price, wait until the last two parts are released. As such, this review will only concern Part One of The Fall.
The Fall: Part One puts players in the role of an A.R.I.D. AI unit on a mission to rescue her human pilot after the two crash land on a planet at an abandoned droid facility. Gameplay is very similar to that of a "Metroid-Vania" style, with a large influence on puzzles. This can be problematic at times, as the game involves backtracking for a majority of its puzzles, something I for one do not particuraly enjoy.
Combat is fairly responsive, with battles with hostile droids verysimple and non problamatic. However, these encounters are EXTREMLEY predictable, as spawn stations that will deploy them are visible far before these conflicts.
While Combat is very repetitive and Puzzles can be a bit too complex at times, The Fall's story is where this game truly shines. Sure it's not a GOTY type story writing (IE The Walking Dead or other story-driven games), but the character development A.R.I.D. goes through is very deep, and makes players question whether or not following the rules is always the right thing to do.
Overall, The Fall: Part One was a  satisfying game story wise, but had a semi good combat system and a few overly complex puzzles killed the mood for me at points. Kf you are one for puzzle/story games, this one's for you.

Machinarium is a beautifully done puzzle adventure. Not as long as games like Myst, but the journey is a wonderful experience full of unusual thinking and robotic conundrums. The characters are cute, and well made, as well as full of personality which is rare for a puzzle game. The presence of a hint for each area is helpful for those who get stuck, and if you really want a solution you can work through a mini-game, moving a key through a side-scrolling maze while avoiding the spiders (or shooting them) and not touching the walls or bricks, until you find the keyhole at the end, which unlocks the walkthrough book and shows you a page for the area you're in with a step by step picture guide of what needs to be done. It thoughtfully avoids any spoilers, and has a few surprises for those who explore possibilities aside from those needed to directly progress. A good game, with fun and cute characters, a fantastic style, plenty to see, and a great ending. It's worth the price.

The concept of Clustertruck is very simple. Its basically a video game version of "the floor is lava" that pretty much every kid played once. The goal of the game is to reach the finish line of each level wihout touching the floor, the only thing you can stay on are trucks. You progress through the levels by jumping from treuck to truck and thats basically the whole game.
While the concept is very simple the different levels offer a great variety, both in obstacles and looks, and it never really felt repetitive. Every level is well thought through and you can see that the devs put a lot of time into designing them. If you are concerned about not enough content, there is also the steam workshop which has tons of levels to try.
The soundtrack, which varies from level to level, fits the fast pace of the game well and adds to the overall feeling.
Overall i really enjoyed the game and even beat it without using abilities to add some extra challenge. I can recommend this to anyone who likes fast paced and/or movement focused games.

Probably the definative version of the game, but still suffers from some issues (most which were already present on the original gamecube release).  Its the best "modern" Resident Evil game but still falls far short of the first three games on the original playstation and even RE:CV IMO.
The bad first -
1. The characters control like they are moving underwater.  Gone is the tight, percise control of the original tank control fixed camera angle games, and capcom even changed the controls for the worse in the remaster edition, (right trigger to shoot ?  WTF ?)
2. The mansion looks like something that was built in the 1860's, not the 1960's.  The "lab" looks like a converted dungeon that the nazi's would be using in a wolfenstein game.  so much for a state of the art bio-weapon research facility.  The PS1 game did both better even considering the graphics limitations of the day.
3. Why is Umbrella now an evil quasi-cult organization instead of simply an amoral, money hungry coporation ? (this was made even worse in RE:Zero).
4. The added backstory of the Trevor family felt shoehorned in and added nothing to the story or gameplay.
The good -
1. Graphics look nice with the "HD" upgrade and the widescreen option is well done.
2. You don't need a gamecube or backwards compatible Wii to play the game any more.
3. Its not an over the shoulder TPS action game like the more recent RE games.
If you liked REmake then i would recommend this version, or if you wanted to play it but missed out on it the first time around its worth a purchase.  If you were "meh" about REmake back in the gamecube day like i was or already have the original GC version, this really dosen't add anything groundbreaking and you might want to pass.

Fantastic game, very unique and well worth the recommendation. Despite a few minor gripes with some of the puzzle mechanics, everything about the game was solid. I'll break it down here:
- Graphics and art looked extremely polished and well designed. I really liked the 3d graphics with 2d platforming, which can be tricky to get right. The dark lighting really added to the atmosphere, but the silhouetting made sure you know where your character is at all times. The textures and models beneath the lighting looked really nice too; when you fire A.R.I.D's gun, it illuminates the whole area for a split second, allowing you to glimpse the hard work that's gone into the it all. The animations were solid and convincingly robotic, and the backgrounds were just awesome.
- Sound design and music were also totally solid and really fit into the atmosphere of the game, adding an eerie and arid (heh) ambience without drawing too much attention to itself. The voice acting was pretty fantastic too, well recorded, well acted and well edited, it just blends right in.
- The story was great too, maybe inspired by Isaac Asimov? I won't get too much into it, but if you're into sci-fi, you'll love it. The dialogue was really well written, the story progressed at a steady pace, teaching you more about the characters and the facility. I was hooked. My only criticism is the mainframe A.I. seemed a little too human. He seemed to really care about A.R.I.D. and the other robots (great job on the voice actor's part), but I think he should have been written to seem like he was feigning affection.
- The gameplay was really unique, I love the twist on the point n' click puzzle solving, and the combat really broke it up and made the whole thing more exciting. The devs' choice to display a list of the suit's extended functions like 'unlockable abilities' that unlock when the suit needs them, but not giving access to all of them (because the suit didn't need them) was very clever indeed and added a lot of realism. Criticisms here would involve some of the puzzles and how their solutions were illogical, a common gripe I have for the genre. Why did I have to find and crush a gold coin to make a wire when there were plenty of other wires I could break? Why couldn't I just smear the fish guts on myself? Some solutions needed a lot of walking back and forth and looking for something that I hadn't found, which was a bit annoying, but other than that, I still loved it.
Thanks for an awesome game guys, can't wait for the next one!

The Fall has a lot to say for a game that doesn't want to tell you what it is.
It wraps its narrative up in the pretense of AIs attempting to work within protocols to protect the humans they serve, but digging deeper it's not very hard to apply its underlying themes to areas outside the field of technology. Taken in a different light, The Fall is potentially a dialogue of the dangers presented with the necessity to work within societal rules and expectations; to be who you were created to be, and serve the ones who made you without question of their intention or if it is indeed "right".
Matters of the value of one life over another, abusing a system you've been placed in for your own needs, and whether the end really can justify the means are presented in such a way as to never be the sole focus of the story and pull you away from the task at hand, but they're there, in the background. It's entirely possible to go through The Fall and enjoy it as solely what it appears to be: an engaging sci-fi plot of a crashed pilot only barely hanging onto life, requiring his suit's AI take control and attempt to find him help. But it's the subtlety of the narrative that really stood out to me and made me pay closer attention and try to pry away at the layers concealing what the game was trying to say to me.
Ultimately it's almost always yet another question. For all of The Fall's heavy societal and possibly theological musings, it never quite arrives at the point of clarity. It made me think but at times I wondered if even it knew what the end result of all these ideas was, or if there was supposed to be one at all. And that's perfectly fine, but at the same time there's this feeling that it's possibly trying to cram too much into a short experience and perhaps becoming a little bogged down as a result.
Of course this can all be waved away with the presumption that this is but the first part of three and everything The Fall wanted to say, or the things it didn't quite get to finish elaborating on will all become clear in those ensuing games. There are parts of The Fall that were a little profound to me as I directed my character through desolate environments, flashlight barely cutting through the impenetrable atmosphere as weird shapes seemed the move in the background as sounds echoed around. They're the moments that had me entranced with my monitor; the ones that made me glad to have took the time to solve the occasionally convoluted puzzle to arrive at the moment I was currently in. They're scattered about and can sometimes seem exasperatingly out of reach, but when you get there, they're always worth the investment.

While The Fall makes a good attempt, it is unfortunately not a smooth, seamless game and it lacks certain critical cohesive elements.
Pros:
+ The story CONCEPT
+ The voice acting (it's actually quite good)
+ Auto-saving and reloading
Cons:
- The details and unfolding of the storyline
- The movements and animation
- The combat
- The controls (oh my god, the controls...)
Details:
Someone started this project with a good idea.  It was simple enough to execute while still being interesting and strong.  The voice-acting for the main characters is well done and helps to make the dialog very engaging.
However, the game suffers from a lethal combination of unwieldy controls and a very disjointed telling of the story.  Many of the tasks and intermediate goals (including the combat) are not only difficult to complete due to arbitrary object/action associations, but also seem completely unrelated to the main objective.  This makes the game disjointed due to seemingly random tangents and it quickly starts to feel more like work than something intended to entertain.
Although the heart of a good story exists somewhere in here, I honestly cannot recommend this game (even on sale) since the frustration and boredom greatly outweigh the fun.

All in all, Stronghold Legends is OK. It's not the greatest RTS out there. I mean REALLY not. The original is a classic, and it has its design quirks too. In some ways though I feel like Legends takes a few steps backward from its predecessor, i.e. there are inuitive design features I feel like I need that are missing. Stuff you would expect out of an RTS from 2006.
There are also a smaller variety of units (unless you get characters), and a smaller variety of buildings, which is disappointing. Again, if you want something more in depth, a true castle simulator, then you'll want the original Stronghold. It's sad to say, but it's very true.
The game has a lot of character and flair I do respect. Every mission has a voiceover and artwork I love. The problem is that the actual gameplay is missing any of its character.
Try as I might, I can not recommend this game. That hurts because Stronghold was my first computer game with my buddy. I wanna like this game, I do, but it's severely underbaked, and after my short time with it, I feel like I've seen all it has to offer.
Sorry Stronghold. I do love you guys.

So if you don't like micro-managing a town while fighting another lord, then this is your game.
But, if I had to rate it on a scale of 1 to 10 it would definitely be a solid 7.5. It's not quite there, but it's more there than Stronghold 3  and Crusader 2.

What do you call a game that had amazing potential really nice designs and an awesome story like with good old RPG elements in it that the developers never realised? A sad story, and thats exactly what this game is a sad sad story.
To begin with the positives the gameplay is nice units get some pretty nice upgrades when they level up and you can use a lot of different army compositions in this game. The heroes (or generals) also have some really nice specialities the wizard for example is adept at killing big masses of enemies in a split second or changing the weather in order to stop contain certain types of units from dealing massive damage to his army, the champion is really good in being at the front lines hack and slashing your enemies and providing CC to help the whole of his army maneuver or flank your enemies and last the warlord is...what one would expect, a good old classic general buffing his army and providing support for units while also fighting in the front lines. The units are really interesting, there are a lot of different upgrades for your units to check out and all of them have their uses and you can customise your army in any way you want.
So thats all nice right? A rather nice game with interesting gameplay and storyline a few puzzles here and there etc etc. Well yes, untill you realise that some units are just broken some certain builds have by far the strongest units the wizard class is just hands down over powered and you can also bring more generals along if you so desire allowing you to decimate entire armies while keeping your spell shield so strong that the enemy wont be able to cast a single spell appart from a few supportive ones. The cavalry just crushes everything they find in their way with enough momentum and suprise suprise they have a skill that maxes it instantly, monsters are kind of useless (archers and spearmen make short work of them due to the extra damage spearmen have and the damage archers have the ability to rain down on them in combination with wizard heroes in your army monster are just big fat masses of flesh that die before they manage to reach your light infantry which they are expected to take care of), there is absolutely no reason to upgrade any of your castles since you will never fight in them even if the enemy attacks you while you are defending them, you can not create more armies than what the game gives you, for example you get pendragon morgana and lancelot. THE END no more armies even though the game gives you somewhat about 12 more heroes. The strategic map has no value any negotiations with other kingdoms are 100% worthless and overall all there is to do is the quests... Thats it, you do the main quest choices do not matter appart from the ones that give you points towards you religious believes and wether you are considered a tyrant or not and thats it, anything else is compeletely pointless and if you want to do it you do it just for your own personal reasons like roleplay etc. they provide you with almost nothing appart from different looking units and thats it...
Over all this game could potentially be a great one it really is a shame because I wanted to see this game becoming great the ideas in it are really nice and fresh, it's just a shame that the developers stopped supporting the game...Lets hope creative assembly makes a good job with their warhammer title.

First off, I haven't had any issues with the game crashing, not loading, etc. From what I can tell from other reviews, this game plays similar to the Total Wars series. I can't say since I haven't played them before, but I have played the first King Arthur. This game plays similarly to the first game with a few exceptions. The developpers have tried to make a few balance changes from things that generally seem overpowered in the first game; namely magic, cavalry, and archers. There's now a magic shield that helps prevent your units from getting completely mashed before they even make contact with the other team, along with cast times for most spells. Cavalry now actually gets mashed by spearmen instead of the other way around, but they still pretty much trample everything else. Archers have a much lower starting accuracy, and you can't get skills to prevent decrease in shooting distance to take advantage of combinations such as Storm of Avalon to counter cavalry. Of course, by the end of the campaign, all of these points are moot anyway because units level up to 15 and destroy pretty much everything regardless.
The campaign has an interesting story, but runs into the same issues of the first game after a while. Namely that auto-batlle becomes an extremely appealing option regardless if it causes more casualties to prevent the tedium of fighting the same battle over and over again. This is especially an issue since you can only have 3 armies by the end of the campaign, thus giving you little room to vary your tactics.
All in all, it's a fun game, especially for the price during sales. I enjoyed the story and the puzzles in the campaign, but should probably have stretched out the game a bit more so battles didn't become a chore.

Unfortunately, a number of the units are unbalanced, and so the combat can take a lot longer than it should.  It adds spells, which I found to be an annoyance, as my archers were always literal lightning rods.
The overarching strategy seemed deficient as well, as there aren't many ways to get gold so tech, infrastructure and army all suffer.  It also limits the number of armies that you can have roaming around, so wandering armies just take over buildings of mine, which admittedly didn't seem to affect me at all.
As far as the RPG factor goes, it again struggles.  For some reason the player is fighting Irish demons.  You don't get to see or use King Arthur, and end up killing multiple knights of the round table.  Other knights don't even appear, which would be understandable for most, but they cut out Gawain, and left in Agravain?  A lot of the leveling really didn't feel like it mattered for heroes.
Overall, depending on what you want there are games which do what this game does, only much better.  I can't recommend this game.

EDIT: I've decided to make this an actual review after binge playing this game for a few days straight and I've come to realise some issues that I have with the game itself
Let's start with the Pros
-You can play the game in multiple ways giving it a huge replay value
-You can level up your character, build huge armies, become king of a faction, take over factions to instill rightful heirs, etc.
-You can get many hours out of this game just playing through a single character
The game itself is so well molded. I love the social and politcal micromanaging, yet I like the macromanaging too. You have to take care of your troops, your heros, your towns, and eventually your court you can really come to love this game. There are cons however
-The native game seems to lack in a few departments, yet there is a workshop to kind of cover those bases. Vexed is a great mod that really beefs the game up where it needs to be beefed. It's easier to make money, become a lord of a faction, manage large armies, level up. Things like that are kind of difficult in Native but not impossible.
-The game seems to be a bit buggy at times, AI is kind of all over the place, Characters can get stuck on objects or behind walls or trees. Raiding castles and villages is a good example of this because you may not be able to even get to the top the characters just plow in up the ladder. Heros sometimes disappear and can't be found again even if you ask a traveler. Sound bugs, graphical glitches, basic bugs are present.
-Trying to build an army after defeat can be hard as stated before it's harder to make money in Warband Native so if you are captured by a lord or lose a battle defending a castle, you had better hope that they don't take much of your cash. Sometimes recruiting from villages only yields a handful of people at a time so it's much easier to buy mercs.
-After a while you may reach a dead end and have to restart and make a new character.
I still enjoy the game and find it very fun. I just hope bannerlords fills in the holes that Warband has.

Considering Lethal RPG's origins as a Flash game, it's actually pretty darn good but it's one patch away from being great.
You're given eight playable characters to add to your team.  However, only a small number of combinations are actually worthwhile.  For instance, having the mage in your team is absolutely essential.  I found the solider, berzerker, and assassin to be of far less utility.
There's a nifty crafting system that's driven by loot from tons of optional bosses and sidequests.  Upgrading your equipment visually changes your characters, which is a nice touch on a game at this price point.  Yet, the distrubtion of crafting items is frustrating.  The game desperately needs some manner of exchanging crafting supplies, especially since the money you earn by completing battles is nearly useless.  For instance, by the end of the game I had several hundred leathers but had to spend significant time grinding for linen and silk for the necromancer and mage.
The random encounters are too difficult and the bosses are (for the most part) too easy.  It shouldn't take 8-10 rounds to decide the outcome of a random encounter.  One the up side, the encounters are placed on the map so you get to decide when and where you fight.   The boss encounters are much easier and generally follow the same formula: stack DoTs, heal and regen mana.  The bosses telegraph big attacks a turn or two in advance, so throw in a well-time defend command now and then.  The multitude of bosses look cool and are animated well but don't differ significantly in strategy.
It sounds like I'm being harsh on the game but I really did enjoy it a great deal.  It was a nice break from the generic RPG Maker games that litter Steam.  If you're looking for a low-priced RPG to kill a weekend on, this is it.

The Fall is a disturbing sidescroller story-driven point-and-click puzzle game.
Phew, that was a mouthful.
You take on the role of A.R.I.D., an artificial intelligence onboard a high-tech combat suit. The suit crash-landed into an unknown location, rendering the pilot unconscious and likely unstable, activating A.R.I.D. From then on, the player is left on their own to figure it out.
The world in The Fall is horribly dark. I don't think I've experienced something like it before, which makes this a hard thing to review. Personally, I am easily terrified. Movies that are not intended to be scary end up keeping me up for nights on end, sometimes fueling nightmares, so I always avoid games such as this. I received The Fall through a bundle with other games, and I forgot about it for quite a while. A friend of mine wanted to ask my opinion of the game, but I told him I hadn't even played it yet, so I jumped in without knowing what to expect.
Truth be told, I could only get through the first half of the second section before I had to stop. I seriously could not keep going for fear of what lied ahead. If you are into this kind of thing, you may find The Fall more tame than other games or movies with similar styles.
However, The Fall also requires that you be familiar with the mechanics of point-and-click puzzle games, as these mechanics override everything else. You have to have your flashlight on almost constantly. It's not that it's bad, but if you're not a fan of point-and-click, this won't be for you.
The sound and the graphics absolutely fit the game, and the sound design is partly what made me stop playing because it was so powerful.
If you like games like LIMBO and The Swapper, if you like dark and disturbing plots, if you like point-and-click puzzle games, this is definitely something to check out!
Somewhat on the short side, though the developer has stated there will be a second and third part. Some of the puzzel objectives could be a little clearer, other than that, a great game.

At first glance, I thought The Fall would lean heavier on platforming and action. But it's more like a twist on the point and click adventure formula. It's mostly story and puzzles, and it does a good job at both. It’s about AI, and how they bend the fine rules of their programming to achieve the bigger objectives they were made for. You get the impression it's inevitable that they start bending the rules, subverting their original meanings in order to achieve what they believe is the greater goal.
This is a sidescrolling puzzle game with light combat elements. As with so many other puzzle games before it there are sections with pixel hunting, where you’re blindly combining every inventory item on every object in the world just in case that progresses the game. A couple areas I’d argue are poorly designed, as they are almost impossible to see, even when you’re taking it slow. But I guess we have walkthroughs to solve that problem. On the whole, it’s good, and not even close to the level of frustration 90s adventure games had.
I had a great time with The Fall. The writing is smart, the aesthetics are great, with just a couple questionable design decisions. Like why can’t you reduce gamma? It pops up a calibration screen when you start the game, and the default setting is at the bottom of the scale. That shows to me that the creator doesn’t realize that a lot of monitors are incorrectly calibrated out of the factory to be set too bright. Too dark gamma is rarer than too bright. The game also has a transparent texture overlaid over the game at all time which consists almost entirely of banding artifacts. I cut the game some slack, as I assume the developer only had mediocre uncalibrated monitors as reference. You'd only miss those artifacts if you were using a monitor with black crush. There’s some room for improvement here in the future installments which are apparently on the way.
The Fall achieves all the most important parts of what it set out to do. The combination of story, animation, and audio makes the game cool. It reminded me of Flashback. And it has a really good ending. Even though sequels are planned, this game stands on its own. Well worth playing at some point.

Reveal The Deep is an amazingly atmospheric game, but unfortunately falls short to unaddressed launching issues and its length. Not too bad for the price, though.
In Reveal The Deep, you play a diver who explores a shipwreck, uncovering the story and fate of the ship through notes and logs left by its former occupants in various rooms. You also have the ability to somehow
to a less derelict state of the ship, revealing books, items, and the like, by turning off your headlamp which activates lamps in the ship's rooms. Needless to say, you aren't exactly alone once you get to exploring.
Having dived into little wrecks myself, I'd say the game pretty much captures the general uneasiness that I would personally get when underwater: the uncertainty of whatever lies beyond the void untouched by my light, the confusion that you would get finding your bearings, which makes it much more difficult in real life to navigate underwater, and in-game a little more challenging to solve the little puzzles, being that I found myself often unsure whether I've been in a particular room before (or that might have just been the game toying with me). The little puzzles themselves aren't that challenging to begin with, but with the tense atmosphere around you, you might not want to get too ruffled anyway. The story is great, interesting at the very least, and the variety of notes that you get to encounter are good little reads that flesh out more and more of the story.
Where the game fails are on more technical issues. It's been stated in the update logs that patches have fixed startup issues on several platforms, with the last patch (as of this writing) being released in April 2016. Now nine months after that, I was surprised to find that I still had launch issues via the Steam app! The fact that it's been so long since this was properly patched is a very worrying sign from the dev for me. Fortunately, getting around to launching the game was little more than a minor annoyance (you have to navigate to the game's install directory, open the 'Linux' folder and run the .jar file. You may or may not need the Java Development Kit; in my case it ran right off the bat. YMMV), albeit leaving a pretty bad taste in my mouth.
It's also short. Only three chapters, and the long wait since the last patch really makes me doubt that the dev would add anything more, if not in a sequel. For the price, however, you might consider it worth at least what you pay for it.
For this cheap, it shouldn't hurt much to give it a try. However, given its current state and lack of any recent updates (for a game released just last year!), I'd pass on this one if ever I'd buy it again.

To quote the masterpiece itself, "Fear doesn't kill you, but..."
All features from the Gamecube re-release are retained:
Limited saves - Collect Ink Ribbons to save your progress, only a set amount within each game.
Defensive items - grab knives, tazers, grenades, etc. to use as a defense when grabbed.
You must either decapitate or burn downed zed's so they don't come back as Crimson Head's later.
Environmental and puzzle differences from 1996's release.
The Lisa Trevor subplot is lovingly kept, ready to scare the bejesus out of you.
More secrets, more costumes and more endings.

Choose between classic full screen or cinematic widescreen that scrolls the camera with your movements.

Easy, Normal, Hard difficulties from the start - Very Hard and more modes unlock upon completion:
Real Survival - Complete the game on Normal. In this mode, the item boxes are not linked.
One Dangerous Zombie - Unlocked when you complete the game with both Jill and Chris on Normal. It can't be turned off. In this mode, Forest Speyer comes back as a zombie with bandoliers of grenades strapped to him. You cannot shoot him without setting them off, if you do, the explosion will kill you and end the game.
Invisible Enemy - Unlocked when the game is completed twice on any difficulty. Like the name of the mode implies, every single enemy in the game is invisible.

Two storylines to play through each with their own differences in plot development, skills and objectives - Jill Valentine and Chris Redfield.

At the moment of writing this review it's ​09.15.2014. And now, at this moment, I'm gonna give the game a thumbs up...
Let's first talk about bad stuff, then the good, then I'll try and explain the overall impression and why I've given it positive grade.
The game has many things against it - the voice over is bad. The char's are flat and lifeless, and translation is abysmal with lots of non-sequiturs and seemingly butchered meanings, but which uninterrupted went on to voice actors, to sound mixers, to testers. Easily it could have been done far more satisfactory. The graphics are simple and remind me of late 2000s flash animation style. There is no option for full HD resolution. Even in my full HD full screen, there are black borders, the game doesn't scale up. There's not much music, nor sound effects. UI is clunky with option wheel which has to be pressed for a second to open, and no way to change default function (there's only three - look, talk, use/take) and always use the same click for it.
But what's good with the game? The setting is unique in more than one way - not just that it's set in Argentina, Buenos Aires, but in the future of the city where some cataclysm devastated the city and supposedly made an independent militia controlled city-state of it. Even in this golden age of indie development, it's extremely rare to experience something which isn't centered in standard circle of western culture in adventure games. It's either some traditional western(ised) setting (say US, New Orleans for Gabriel Knight, Paris for Broken Sword), or some extremely exotic setting like dungeons, far future, or jungle temples. Usually it's completely ignored that there are millions, if not billions of people living in some different urban settings which aren't either New York, or, say, far east. This game allows me to experience different culture. So that's a great plus in my books.
The standard adventure gameplay mechanic flows nicely. There is a hint function, so I was never stuck for long. Usage of objects is logical, there's no "use brick on tin can to squish it open and then use antique wig to gather the tomato sauce"* nonsense, even though actual intentions and objectives could have been expressed better. As said, hints keep the game going nicely. And it's short and sweet having no delusions of grandeur. It's an indie game through and through. More importantly, even with that about shortness said, the sense of mystery and adventure hits the precise spot I had from the days of the Curse of the Monkey IslandTM. I want to explore further, I want to learn the story and the world. I want some answers goshdarnit! Big plus there!
But what's the most positive sign, and the reason I've started this review with a date of all things - is the price. The first episode is free on Steam. Second episode is out and I got it in a humble sale. I started playing it, but quickly the same sense of mystery forced me to download this one and find out how the story started. There are lots of negative reviews, here on Steam, but now, at this date, with these conditions, there's no reason why you shouldn't try the first episode. It's an adventure snack. I actually waited for some other game to download and ended playing it till the end in 66 minutes.
I remember the time not so long ago people said adventure games are dead. This isn't the game that will singlehandedly save the genre - it's the proof it's actually so much alive that the games are vital enough to develop in non-standard settings and tell non-standard stories from small developing teams who don't even bother to translate their official game blog to english.
It is what it is. And, considering the price, yes. You should try it.
*NOT an actual example!

Related to the previous point, theres no "leave to menu" button in general. The only way to access the main menu is to close the game.
For some reason the same save file I loaded up seems to be missing a lot of progress even though I clearly remember unlocking the Castle and having a bunch of other job paths opened and maxed out.
Also if you forget your account, there's no "Forget Password?" button so have fun figuring out your username/password or restarting from scratch all over again.

Stronghold Legends has great medieval sights and sounds...esp the music. Totally fitting for the period. The gameplay? AND, it's on baby-level easy difficulty! The balance between me and the AI limits my  games to about 20 minutes...no casual planning and admiring your castle that you worked so hard to  build, the enemy will show up when you are a quarter/halfway into your building and, from there, it's a frenetic battle that leaves little time for me to enjoy the game..I spend the time putting out fires. Maybe it's me, but I've completed Stronghold where the difficulty was gradually increased. Legends has me feeling so incompetent it's maddening. These are my major gripes, though....if the AI didn't have all their stuff researched and produced at warp speed, this would be one of my top ten games. I still recommend it, though...a Monarch should be proud, but not SO proud that he dismisses, outright, any incompetent behaviour on his part. No, no...a great leader is more realistic and contemplates his incompetence and, thus, can learn from it.
In my opinion, the pro's outweigh the cons.

A short platformer with only three chapters, yet it did its job splendidly. The sound effects constantly had me on edge, and I certainly was not expecting light mechanics aside from your average "flashlight". One of the only major gripes that I have with the game is a block-pushing segment in Chapter 2 that was a slog thanks to my body blocking the block's light, forcing me to constantly stop and turn around to not get killed.
+ Length of game fits its price.
+ Sound effects were on point.
+ Interesting usage of a toggleable light source.
+ Only rarely resorted to jumpscares.
+ The location of the final journal entry blew my mind given how deep I thought I travelled.
- Block-pushing segment in Chapter 2 becomes a slog if you're unlucky with enemy placement.
- Some instances of cheap enemy placement; impossible to see before falling into their hurtbox.
- Block-pushing sound effect has an obvious point where it loops.
- A few glitches and bugs, but nothing gamebreaking; jumping in a tight corridor and on top of some rising blocks will keep you in the jumping animation, forcing you to jump again in a larger room in the case of the former or land on solid ground in the case of the latter to resume your usual animations; had one case where trying to walk underneath a rising block with spikes underneath it killed me out of the blue.
All in all, I would recommend giving this a try if you have some trading card money to spare and fancy a short horror experience.

This is a decent little budget title that I won't describe much past its technical aspects. If I lift the curtain on the story for you just a bit, I doubt there will be anything left to reveal because... the game isn't very deep. Irony, maybe? Anyway, Reveal The Deep is a short, atmospheric, adventure puzzle-platformer.
Pros:
+Somewhat creepy. Not a horror game, but it does have some disturbing vibes. The sunken ship setting meshes with the minimalist graphics and sound. Good atmospheric ambience.
+At $1 off-sale, the cost/gameplay ratio is reasonable.
+I did enjoy what little there was of the storyline. The puzzles are an important aspect of reading through the narration, which I appreciated.
Cons:
-The story is thin; it could have benefitted from a slightly more fleshed out scenario. Although the game doesn't necessarily feel like it plays fast, it is over before it feels "complete." I don't feel cheated by any means, but a little extra polish would have helped.
-No replay value whatsoever. You just uncover the mysery and that's it. A coin-operated weight scale in a public bathroom has the edge on this point.
-The headlamp is a good idea for a gameplay mechanic that is underutilized. I understand the desire for simple presentation, but this is one of only a handful of ways to interact with the environment, and is the most interesting.
-No native controller support, keyboard only. Not a deal breaker, just inconvenient and mostly pointless to bother mapping keys to a gamepad for this game.
Despite my initial reaction to the ending, I felt the experience was worthwhile. Well, at least 50-100p worth. 6/10 Recommended for bored, cheapass hipsters who would rather be telling their buddies they beat this game already.

You take the role of a diver as you explore the sunken ruins of a sprawling ship in order to find out what led to its demise. The story is progressively revealed through the discovery of diary entries left behind by various of the ship's past passengers and, to my surprise, it was actually very interesting and disturbing. Its 2D pixel graphics work wonders in reinforcing a constant sense of threat and solitude as does its lack of music, solely focusing on natural sounds of the deep. Its platforming sections are mostly basic, focusing on jumping and pushing crates, but it does have a very interesting "light" mechanic that I had never seen before and found quite refreshing. In a few words, by pressing the "space" tab on your keyboard, you toggle your light on and off which, in some spaces, reveals much more that you might originally had thought was there.
There is really not much else to say about it. It took me about 2 hours to beat with every achievement, but for the price of 0.49 that it cost me (50% off), it was worth it (although its 0.99 euro full price is also not that much). If you enjoy games that focus on exploration, where the story is slowly revealed to you but is well worth the wait, then I highly recommend this. I enjoyed the atmosphere of loneliness that it evoked, as well as the horror-themed plot which I found quite engaging and sorrowful.

Over the past few years, I've played a good 90 hours or so, mostly through borrowing my friend's xbox. Over that time I went back and forth on my opinion of this until I finally managed to settle on a solid answer: This game is worth the money. However, you may struggle a bit getting into it. SInce I'm not going to compare this to the other games in the series, I'll just give a pros and cons list and a summary.
Pros:
1. Interesting story.
It's not always easy to find an rpg with a good story. I can safely say that Morrowind does a decent job with this, and it tells a compelling story.
2. Real RPG mechanics.
As much as I sometimes have trouble with it, the hit/miss system is much more in line with a tabletop rpg, which I feel like bethesda was going for. take this one as you will, as it isn't for everyone.
3.Vast and creative world.
This was one of the first games I came across when I was younger that actually had a unique world, immersive lore, and sheer size to it. Even after all my time playing I still haven't explored everything, and that's part of the fun!
4. Mod support.
I don't know about anyone else, but I love mods! They have the potential to breathe new life into older games through many means such as dlc-like quests, new armors, graphical overhauls, and even sound packs! Some even give new playerhomes and worldspaces to explore. If you don't mind searching through pages of cringeworthy nude patches on the Morrowind Nexus, this is a huge plus!
Cons:
1. Dated graphics.
I get that this was top of the line when it came out, and honestly it doesn't hold up too poorly, but these can be an issue sometimes. not being able to tell if what you're looking at is an argonian or a bunch of triangles can be pretty jarring. If you truly can't stand older 3d graphics, stay away from Morrowind.
2.Real RPG mechanics.
"But you put that in the pros column! How can it possibly be bad AND good?" The answer is this, my friends: inflated difficulty and painfully slow traveling! The hit/miss mechanics are genuinely more like tabletop RPGs, but there's a reason they aren't commonly used. when you're in a 3d world space and you stab someone in the face with a sword, you would probably expect the sword to do damage when it actually visibly collides with the enemies' face. In Morrowind, actually hitting them only gives you a CHANCE to hit when this occurs. This makes for an insanely difficult beginning to the game, so be warned. Also, YOUR STAMINA DEPLETES WHEN MOVING!
3.NO NAVIGATION
I know that a lot of the hardcore fans of the game love this aspect, but the map of Vvardenfel is really bad, there's no fast travel (which to be honest isn't all that horrible,) and there is NO compass to help you through questing. A lot of the Morrowind fanboy crowd would say "You don't NEED a compass, the quest givers and NPCs will give you directions! It's called immersion!" But the problem with this oh so horrible excuse is this: Npc directions are frequently wrong! I don't know if this was an intentional "Immersion" trait, or if the devs just typed it wrong, but there are numerous quests that have no correct directions, making it nearly impossible to find the objective! Quest markers were added for a reason, people! Mod this in!
Summary:
The Elder Scrolls III: Morrowind has its flaws, but it makes up for them in creativity, exploration, and just downright fun! As long as you can find where you're going, the game is really good and worth every penny!

Worth playing, I guess. Though the writing's okay - what you see of it  that is - the menus are terrible, I don't like the fonts, the way they display messages, I don't like the controls, I don't really like the graphics, I don't like some of the weird messages the game offers you (for instance "the radiator looks broken" like, really, not like I haven't already passed a dozen of those), I don't like the monsters...
I don't like the way that when you take a hit, you just... get set back to a very specific location. You don't even die. It literally just sets you back. Oh. Except that's only the very first time you 'encounter' the monsters. Every other time they just stop you for like half a second and plays an annoying sound. What's up with that, huh? Oh, I know what is up with that. This was a game made by uni students as part of a course they were doing. They couldn't get it working, or couldn't be bothered, or thought it was too hard, so they didn't get a proper health system, live system, or save/load system going. So when you take a hit during that first encounter, the game makes an annoying sound, you get set back. Then later on, when it becomes too much of a chore or something, they said screw it, nobody will care, just don't even penalize the player in any way.
I also HATE the fact that it seems the developers did EVERYTHING IN THEIR POWER to try and let players backtrack to the start of an area, or at least the start of a 'puzzle' area, or whatever. This is NOT NECESSARILY A GOOD THING. YOU DON'T NEED TO GIVE PLAYERS THE OPPORTUNITY TO GO BACK AND MARVEL AT 'HOW FAR THEY HAVE COME' OR WHATEVER THIS WAS. I spent at least 10 minutes total just wandering around, backtracking, going through 'puzzle' areas all over again just because I accidentally dropped somewhere, took a ladder up or down, or because the only notable objects in this game get reused over and over again, I managed to walk down a corridor I had already gone down.
If you are NOT going to have a map system, what you NEED is to have are landmarks, you need to have doodads, stuff you look at and go "huh, I will remember this" because otherwise, you're gonna get confused, especially since you can barely see anything in the first place, even if it's something stupid like a BIG rock. This game has none of that.
The game has a kind of Lovecraft feel to it, so I was super disappointed by the fact that instead of creepy fishmen or something, we get... black blobs. Black, ♥♥♥♥ing, blobs. With arms and legs and a big cute round smile. Like, wow, guys. Super disappointing.
The sound design was okay, I guess. Not great, it's not all muffled, but some of it is...? I mean, come on guys, Duke Nukem 3D back in the day even had muffled underwater sounds.
Despite all that, sure, why not, I'll follow the herd and recommend it.

is an indie horror game that puts the player in the role of an explorer of a sunken ship. This game was super intriguing. For such a cheap game (I got it on sale for less than .99) it really was worth a dollar for me. I wouldn't venture to say it was worth $5 and definitely not $10 or above, but for it's price it's super worth it.
There were cons, as are in most games, and I often found myself confused for quite a long time just figuring out where to go. A simple thing that could have helped this game was a map-- even one very simple such as the one in Claire. Just something to be able to keep track of the rooms so that you don't get so confused. The way it's designed kind of looks like a platformer, and the awkward camera angles makes it really hard to see (and not in a tense, scary kind of way). As far as the scares go this game didn't do it for me. The atmosphere was there, but no real jumpscares or really anything to keep me tense. Also, I knew nothing about the main character. I'm all for silent protagonists (Isaac Clarke, Link, etc) but I didn't have a name, a story, or any reason why my guy was there. As such, I coudn't feel all that tied to him. However, I kind of felt like that might have been the designer's intention-- to make a protagonist you can just dive into and explore. Although, I would have liked to at least have a motive.
Regardless, this game was good in it's own right. The game was kind of short, but I think the length was just long enough to tie in all the elements into the story. The exploration of this game was really invigorating,and every time I found a new area I was super excited to explore-- ready to figure out what notes and clues I would find to tie into the story. The characters you read about as you read the notes gave you a true sense of the passengers of the ship, and makes you really feel for them. The puzzle at the end was very involving, and I just really loved how they ended the game. The story was great, for what it was worth, and the concept and imagery-- the crushing atmosphere of the dark beneath the sea-- really made this game worth it for me. Also, as a final note: POOR TOM! I wanted to cry so badly after seeing him... but his image and words really made the ending to this game so much greater.
So, in conclusion, if you like dark themes, intriguing stories, and exploring deep, dark coridors, then this is the game for you!

Over the past few years, I've played a good 90 hours or so, mostly through borrowing my friend's xbox. Over that time I went back and forth on my opinion of this until I finally managed to settle on a solid answer: This game is worth the money. However, you may struggle a bit getting into it. SInce I'm not going to compare this to the other games in the series, I'll just give a pros and cons list and a summary.
Pros:
1. Interesting story.
It's not always easy to find an rpg with a good story. I can safely say that Morrowind does a decent job with this, and it tells a compelling story.
2. Real RPG mechanics.
As much as I sometimes have trouble with it, the hit/miss system is much more in line with a tabletop rpg, which I feel like bethesda was going for. take this one as you will, as it isn't for everyone.
3.Vast and creative world.
This was one of the first games I came across when I was younger that actually had a unique world, immersive lore, and sheer size to it. Even after all my time playing I still haven't explored everything, and that's part of the fun!
4. Mod support.
I don't know about anyone else, but I love mods! They have the potential to breathe new life into older games through many means such as dlc-like quests, new armors, graphical overhauls, and even sound packs! Some even give new playerhomes and worldspaces to explore. If you don't mind searching through pages of cringeworthy nude patches on the Morrowind Nexus, this is a huge plus!
Cons:
1. Dated graphics.
I get that this was top of the line when it came out, and honestly it doesn't hold up too poorly, but these can be an issue sometimes. not being able to tell if what you're looking at is an argonian or a bunch of triangles can be pretty jarring. If you truly can't stand older 3d graphics, stay away from Morrowind.
2.Real RPG mechanics.
"But you put that in the pros column! How can it possibly be bad AND good?" The answer is this, my friends: inflated difficulty and painfully slow traveling! The hit/miss mechanics are genuinely more like tabletop RPGs, but there's a reason they aren't commonly used. when you're in a 3d world space and you stab someone in the face with a sword, you would probably expect the sword to do damage when it actually visibly collides with the enemies' face. In Morrowind, actually hitting them only gives you a CHANCE to hit when this occurs. This makes for an insanely difficult beginning to the game, so be warned. Also, YOUR STAMINA DEPLETES WHEN MOVING!
3.NO NAVIGATION
I know that a lot of the hardcore fans of the game love this aspect, but the map of Vvardenfel is really bad, there's no fast travel (which to be honest isn't all that horrible,) and there is NO compass to help you through questing. A lot of the Morrowind fanboy crowd would say "You don't NEED a compass, the quest givers and NPCs will give you directions! It's called immersion!" But the problem with this oh so horrible excuse is this: Npc directions are frequently wrong! I don't know if this was an intentional "Immersion" trait, or if the devs just typed it wrong, but there are numerous quests that have no correct directions, making it nearly impossible to find the objective! Quest markers were added for a reason, people! Mod this in!
Summary:
The Elder Scrolls III: Morrowind has its flaws, but it makes up for them in creativity, exploration, and just downright fun! As long as you can find where you're going, the game is really good and worth every penny!

This is third person adventure/action game combined with RPG and the premise of: Will you be a hero, or a villain?
Indeed, the choice is yours to do whatever you want to do. Kill villagers that are traveling to the city to buy stuff and steal their precious posessions? Go for it! Want to defend the poor villagers from robbers? Oh, you sure can. In fact, lots of missions can be accepted in 2 ways, example being 2 missions that are either; robbers that need help stealing from a farm and will hire you to defend the farm, or guards needing an extra hand with the security of said farm. Now, actions have consequences, if you're truly bad people will be afraid of you, your skin will shatter and horns will grow out your head, and if you're good, your eyes will turn blue and a halo will be put above your head. Of course, it's not as simple as good or evil, your choices have direct impact on your character and they'll show a bit of horns if you're just being a bit evil. Also, want to mention about dying; if you die, you'll forever receive an scar in a random place in your body that is impossible to remove.
The story is alright, you're a kid with a great family in a village, and you start the game in the birthday of your sister, you need to buy her a gift, which is a chocolate box if I don't recall badly, that is 5 coins of gold, and you need to get 5 coins, and this is basically a tutorial that doens't feel a tutorial at all, you can choose a few things to do. You will see a woman angry that her husband isn't home, and you need to find him, and then decide wether or not to be good or bad (I don't want to spoil), and then twist! You're in a hall of heroes, and you'll need to train and grow up to be a hero, and then choose your path.
Gameplay is not really dated, it feels great to use your bow to kill enemies from far away, and with a simple touch of a key, you're holding your 2 handed sword ready to blow them off, or you can always use magic. Lots and lots of magic abilities to choose from, leveling up is so good because as I said, actions have consequences, and the more strenght you put in your character, the more he'll look like a bodybuilder, and there are quite a few secrets in which you'll need certain amount of strenght/speed/magic abilities :).
Sounds and graphics are nice, nothing extraordinary, they're excellent if you think of a game that is this old, but they're only good if you take into acount that we're in 2016 already.
Overall; buy this game and feel for yourself what everyone has been speaking about for years. You WILL have fun.

I got it for four dollars, I'd put it's value at anywhere between 5-10$. So anything in that range or lower during one of Steam's various sales - I'd say nab it.
It's a simple game where you flail around four maps findings things to do. Slowly working up your cashflow, grinding out some stats that ultimately unlock more things to do. It's a neat distraction and functions as any browser-based flash game would. A simple distraction before work, or something to do with Netflix on the side. It's simple and fun, and there's not too much left to say.

Don't get me wrong, I absolutely love Stick RPG 2.  It was one of my favorite games back during high school, and while I don't think it's held up as much as some other online game classics, there are still a lot of things I really like about it.
I highly recommend trying Stick RPG 2, but I wouldn't recommend this version.  And here's why.
My major problem is that this game is in no way shape or form a $20 game.  I personally think it's barely a $5 game.  The features exclusive to this version add little to nothing.
This game has given me months of fun and I'm really happy I was finally able to financially support it in some way.  But there just simply isn't enough new content here to justify a $20 price tag.  If you can get this game in a sale or in a bundle, I would say go for it.  Otherwise, you're better playing the free version on XGen Studios' official site.  I recommend this game, just not this version.

I like this game because it triggered all my fond memories of addicting flash games from the early 2000's on Newgrounds.
It's not worth full price, I don't know if it's even worth the few dollars I put into it, but out of respect and nostalgia to the original Stick RPG and the good old times with similar flash games inspired by it- a couple bucks was fair to me personally.  It's worth mentioning that you can still play games like these for free on Newgrounds, so to drop actual money on this or not is totally your prerogative.
As for the gameplay you should know what you're in store for if you played the original Stick RPG.  You wake up, go somewhere in the city to click on a dialogue option repeatedly until you've increased your stat/money quota for the day, head home, sleep and repeat.  It's mind numbingly dull but oddly relaxing if you're in the right mindset.  This game hit the spot for me at a time where I was so record breakingly lazy that any and all other video games on Earth seemed like they required too much effort to play.
The resolution is terrible and there's no way to modify it.  Fullscreen mode looks ugly.  You have to go into this game wanting it really bad, or having brain damage like me, otherwise you're probably going to throw up.  The bright side is that Stick RPG 2 a finalized product and not another Early Access game stuck in purgatory forever.
I think the creator and I would get along really well, his humor is as unfunny as mine.  I like that.

Back in 2007-ish Stick RPG was one of the best games that has ever been developed by XGen Studios. Though fairly simple and short, Stick RPG was a great game for its time. However, when Stick RPG 2 came out, it has improved upon evry aspect of the previous game.In case you might not have known, there are two versions of the game; There's the free browser version and the "expanded" Steam version. Though both have similar features, the director's cut gives you access to another area to explore, more jobs, full access to cheats that you would otherwise have to pay seperately for, etc( All the info is in the game's description I'll make it simple and list off the pros and cons of this game:

Cons

If Stick RPG 3 is a possible thing in the future, I hope that XGen Studios can improve on making it even better than this installment.

The Fall is well written and povoking game. In addition to being about an AI trying to save its human, there are constant questions about logic vs intuition, service without purpose, and the nature of intelligence. The game looks beautiful and has some excellent puzzles. Buy this.

Wow - I just finished The Fall a few minutes ago, having started it this morning, and wow, what a game!
The biggest reason to get this game is definitely the story. A.R.I.D, the AI controlling the suit, and her driving motivation to save the man inside, provides an extremely interesting main character that is surprisingly human for being such a convincing artificial intelligence. One of the most interesting aspects of the story is how far an AI should be willing to go to perform its primary function, an example being A.R.I.D breaking several of her protocols in order to indirectly further her cause of protecting the suit's occupant, and her interaction with other AI not so willing to do the same. Overall, the story is very intriguing, with a small but extremely likeable (or, in some cases, frightening) "cast," with some great voice acting and a tremendous cliffhanger.
The gameplay is also extremely well-done. Light plays a relatively important role, and the flashlight on your gun must be used to reveal clues or enable actions in order to continue. Doing this is the majority of the game, but doesn't feel repetetive, given that the main purpose is exploring, and this is how you explore. The puzzles are very cleverly done, but sometimes /too/ clever, and can take a long time to solve. Also, given that every clue can be interacted with generally and individually with every item in your inventory and you have no idea which one, if any, is the correct solution, after being stuck for a while, I started trying everything with anything that was remotely promising. Obviously this is not intended to be done, so I would recommend trying to avoid it and to think the puzzles through as much as possible, but sometimes the solution can be really obscure. Combat can be intense and difficult, and has been done pretty well. I preferred the smaller fights with a gun that needed a second or two to charge before firing early in the game more than the more frantic fights later on, but it was all good, and the final boss fight was epic!
The graphics and sound effects are amazing! Graphics are really well done, especially the lighting effects, and the animation is strong as well. It's not perfect, and there are times when one animation visibly skips to another, or you can see outside the map, but these issues are minor and won't hurt the immersion unless you let it. The sound effects and music are well done and spooky, and, especially when using earbuds/earphones, really capture the mood.
Basically, this game is amazing! Short, yes, but there's more to come to finish the fantastic story, which I can't wait for! If you like immersive games, difficult puzzles, an amazing story, and especially AI, you will absolutely love this game. Ten dollars may end up being a bit much if another ten has to be payed for the next two parts as well, but I'm not sure that it will, and even then it's probably worth it. If it's on sale, though, seven dollars or under, don't hesitate to buy it!
TL;DR - Buy it on sale to be joyful.

A fun and thoughtful little game, with excellent voice-work and a good, well-presented narrative.
However, it must be said that THE FALL’s strong points are mainly visual or relating to the atmosphere of the game .The overall experience is hampered by an underlying mystery that is frankly quite obvious from the start, while other questions remain unanswered even at the end of the game (two additional episodes might be released in the future). The game’s puzzles are usually solvable without Walkthrough assistance, but it is not always clear ”why” something worked. Especially around the mid-part, there are some typical examples of Moon Logic with solutions that defy common sense or seem needlessly complicated. The game is short – possible to complete under three hours – for which reason I cannot recommend a purchase for the full price of 10 €. Wait for a steam sale.
Still, I really liked THE FALL so I’m going to recommend it. It has a great feel to it and it generates some interesting food for thought. At its core, THE FALL seems to be a story about an AI (ARID) interacting with other AIs, struggling – however superficially – with questions of raison d’être, behavioural limitations and the relationship between objectives and the means to realise them. These essentially human questions find an intriguing context when presented to beings which are not human, but are forced to behave as such when finding themselves in a dark unforgiving place, cut off from their makers.
Is it perfect? No. Is it worth your time? Yes.

The Fall is an atmospheric 2D platformer. I highly recommend it, although episode one was relatively short, it still had a great sci-fi vibe with a dark sense of humour and intriguing plot line. The visuals were good; the silhouette style did make it difficult to find certain clues but ultimately it added to the ambience.
Not all of it was great; the controls did feel clunky at times and occasionally the puzzles were frustrating but overall it was enjoyable for the price.
TL;DR - Great Sci-Fi with trust issues, minimal combat and lateral thinking puzzles.
Some of the puzzles are really obscure. But the amazing story totally made up for it.

is a very good game with a few faults. I'll talk about it in a bit of detail and sum up my feelings on the last paragraph for those who want to skip a bit.
To begin with the good bits I'll say that it's so good that it prompted me to write what I believe is my first review on Steam (maybe it'll provide the push to write a few others). The game looks very nice: dark, atmospheric and pretty. I mostly found the puzzles to have balanced difficulty and a few were pretty creative.
The story is where
shines. You play the part of the AI of a combat suit, basically a robot whose main objective is to protect your unresponsive human occupant. For reasons you don't know you've crashed into an uninhabited maintenance facility in a distant planet an must do whatever your programing will allow to protect your human. Intriguing and mysterious I didn't stop wanting to know more about what had happened before the story begun and what would happen next for an instant. The few characters are interesting and very well acted by the voice talent, who did the most with the already excellent dialogue. Very smartly written stuff. It plays a bit like an old Lucasarts adventure game, only side-scrolling instead of point and click, with a bit of very simple combat thrown in.
While I mostly really liked the game I have a few complaints, which I'll talk about in increasing order of importance. Firstly, the combat bits were so simple and undeveloped I wonder why they had to be in the game at all. I don't think they detract from it, but they certainly don't add much. Relatedly, the controls felt a bit dodgy throughout. Due to the nature of the gameplay and to how fast our character moves, this isn't a major complaint, but I'd really have liked it a lot more if controls were smoother. I only experienced one bug while playing this, but it was pretty major - near the middle of the game, after solving a puzzle I went forward following a route the game didn't expect. Because of it I didn't trigger a cut-scene very important to the story; to make matters worse, when I'd almost finished the game I passed through this area and triggered the cut-scene, which at that point made zero sense storywise. If I hadn't had to use a walkthrough to solve a puzzle which had made mention to this cutscene I would have been very confused. This leads to another complaint: while I mostly enjoyed the puzzles and found them to be logical and creative, a few times I had to resort to a walkthrough because I hadn't seen some object or element necessary to the solution or because they'd used absurd "adventure game logic". That said, this kind of puzzle solving has never been a strength of mine so YMMV.
My last and main complaint is major enough I'll give it its own paragraph. This is an episodic game and here you only get the first part of a multi-part story. The game is very short, around 2 hours for me, and ends very abruptly. I was left feeling very frustrated and eager to find out what happened next without the means to do so. I had read reviews of this game and taken a look at the store page before buying and hadn't seen any indication of this, so it came as a very unpleasant surprise.
In conclusion, I'd recommend
, mostly on the basis of story and atmosphere with a couple of major caveats: this plays a lot like an adventure game, so people who dislike that genre are likely to dislike this game and, most importantly, this game is very short and only the first part of a story. If you decide to buy this knowing what you're getting I don't believe you'll be disappointed.

This review won't be popular but I'm just giving my opinion.  I am a massive Resident Evil fan but I only got into the franchise in a big way from Resident Evil 4.  I had previously played RE Nemesis and Code Veronica on the Dreamcast.  I have played RE4/5 for 100s of hours and completed them numerous times (my RE4 hours on Steam are only a fraction of my total hours, I played the 'original' PC version previously), also RE Revelations is excellent, and I've also played RE6 a bit although I am not too impressed with that one.
I was excited about getting this game.  It runs flawlessly for me on i7 4790K and gtx 750 Ti.  Although it IS very demanding indeed despite its modest graphics.  I've tried it on my laptop (AMD dual core 3.2GHz with Radeon 7520G graphics) which is capable of running the modern RE games decently, and it is too slow to be playable, even on the minimum settings and resolution!
I have played this game for a few hours now and I cannot get into it at all.  I am not enjoying the experience.  There is a complete lack of direction for the player to know what to do.  You can wander around all of the unlocked rooms, examine every object, and find yourself stuck and having to go on google to find out what to do next, only to find loads of other people have done the same thing.  I never got stuck in the modern RE games.  I found them challenging, and I might have died or needed to replay sections to get through them, but I always knew what to do and how to do it.  The player should never be left dangling and directionless.
The game mechanics and camera angles are extremely dated and if this game had just come out as a new game in 2015, rather than being a 'classic', I wonder if it would have the same high ratings.  Judged purely on its own merits, it's medicore.  It isn't fun.  The enjoyment of a game should come from playing, you should get enjoyment all the way through, not only when you complete it.  This game feels like work, like a chore.  I never felt like that playing the modern RE games (well, maybe RE6).

I really enjoy this game and would definitely recommend it to my friends.

Reveal the Deep is a short gaming experience. It took me approximately 3 hours to finish. The atmosphere of the game is very well constructed. The SFX and focus on lighting are the strongest contributing factors towards the lonesome and (occasionally) fearful emotions this game invokes. There is a very minimalist combat system with a unique twist, and the level design feels well paced. The plot starts out a little confusing, but if you stick with the game, answers will come!

Pros:
+Turn-based combat
+Surprisingly fun
+Combat  and enemy designs are interesting
+Lengthy story.
Cons:
-Combat can range from frustratingly difficult to absurdly easy within a battle or two
-No random encounters
-Story is cliche-riddled and very derivative
-Attempts at humor fall VERY flat
I've played about 6 hours so far, and have to say that I enjoy it. Despite its flaws, it's a very fun little RPG. It is one of the few games that make you think the price it's sold for is too low.
It may be done in 2D pixel art but the way the devs implemented the sound and the lighting gives it a very unique atmosphere. I will go so far to say that in terms of atmosphere this cheap little 1€ game manages to give quite a few triple-A titles a run for their money.

You can field 3 characters at a time in the party but as you do the campaign you unlock more members to choose from. I was very impressed at the depth of the game for being so cheap. It is a simple no brainer to be sure but you can tell by playing it someone did alot of work and this was a product of love. Someone put a lot of effort into this game for its price. I reccomend this game to anyone who like TBS / RPG games if they are looking for a totally mouse driven, simple point and click adventure that isn't hard to learn at all. I finished the campaign in 20 hours and after that had the option to re-do the campain keeping all my characters and gear from the 1st run-through and yes the enemies scaled to our levels ... got my butt kicked in the 1st fight of the 2nd run through not thinking I would need the mage / healer and took in the orc berserker ... oops ... got slaughtered with no healing present because the formerly noob zone mobs were no longer noob mobs lol. Even for the full price of 5 bucks .. worth every penny
