A mix between RPG and RTS, this game shines with its immersive adventure quests, yet technical problems spoil the fun.
This review was written February 8, 2012. It is based on about 20+ hours in the main campaign, and 20+ hours in the prologue (dead legion DLC). I will update this review when I beat the game if it changes anything.
THE GOOD
- Text adventures make a welcome come back; they are pretty well done and are the main element that gives KA its flavor and uniqueness.
- Voice acting has improved since KA1, at least this voice seems deeper and better at reading the text without rushing it. Sometimes however the voice acting becomes very bad, especially when the same actor tries to voice other characters (women, monsters) while telling a story.
- Big improvement on the graphics, especially on the campaign map which is a lot more detailed, believable, and immersive. (Especially in the prologue DLC.)
- New spell protection system is a welcome addition, no more having multiple stacks getting decimated in a blink because of one well-placed spell. Addition of a casting delay to spells helps by giving you a chance to react.
- New diplomacy system with other factions. It adds some welcome depth to the game.
- Pacing seems better than in the original. At least I didn't see any enemy going into an army spawning frenzy, or what the community called the "whack the mole" mechanic in the first game.
- Estimated play time seems decent. It should take you about 40-50 hours on a challenging difficulty, maybe less if you auto resolve a lot of the battles. There is some replay value since you can do the text quests again with different decisions to see what happens.
THE BAD
- Horrible performance even on beast machines. I was getting 9-12 FPS on high settings (on a 6 core 3.2gh), and finally managed to get 20-25 with everything on lowest possible. At lowest settings problems surface like being unable to see clearly which units are selected, winter time turns into a white light mess, and so on. This might be a deal breaker for a lot of people.
- Loss of the province management aspect. No more management of gold and food incomes. In fact there is no more food in the game, and you only gain gold from quests and battle loot. Other elements like natural disasters (floods, plagues, etc.), and all the laws and decrees are gone too. As a result the whole "kingdom management" aspect of the game is mostly gone and reduces the depth of the game.
REVIEW
King Arthur makes a comeback, and the result is overall "good enough" by being neither great nor bad. The text adventures are still fun as ever, adding a wild card to the gameplay which puts you in a wide variety of situations, and gives a unique flavor to the story telling in this game.
The biggest change seems to be the simplification of many aspect of the game, which results in a clear loss of depth and replayability, but at the same time makes the game more accessible to casual players. The first King Arthur was a trinity of battle, management, and text adventures. King Arthur 2 is a duality of battle and text adventure only since the management aspect is mostly gone.
Even if regrettable, this change isn't all bad. The campaign seemed to have more "flow" to it than in the previous game. You will find yourself passing the turns faster since you don't have to take as many decisions, the game is now more comparable to a relaxing read of a book than a struggle to expand your realm, fight the enemy, and deal with the random events and quest spawning frenzy. In other words, the kingdom management is gone but the game is now a more refined adventure game.
Unfortunately some of the more serious technical shortcomings present in the first King Arthur are still present. The random crashes seem to be mostly gone; thankfully I only crashed a couple of times so far. But the extremely low performance and framerate problem is still here. I also found quite a few bugs, like having the narrator reading the wrong text for a quest, campaign map objects flickering, reserve units disappearing, and archer upgrades from buildings affecting their melee damage instead of ranged damage, etc. Also I encountered 2 game stopping bugs myself, and other players reported half a dozen game breaking bugs just days after release.
CONCLUSION
Your experience with the game will vary wildly depending on the performance you get. If the game runs well, you will probably enjoy it as it is a very charming game, and even if it has lost some of its depth I feel the game gives enough entertainment value for its pricetag.
On the other hand, if you are getting bad to horrible performance, the game will be near unplayable and it might be a deal breaker for you. I highly recommend you try the demo to see how the game runs on your machine. The first KA still gets 12 FPS on my machines after 7 patches, so if history repeats itself as usual a quick fix to the performance problem is not going to happen. However it is worth mentioning that the Neocore team is active on the forums and seems to be working actively on fixing bugs.
Of course if you consider yourself a fan of the series, you will probably want to buy the game and play it even with the bad performance and the buggy release. I know a number of people will do this, as I did myself since the game is somewhat playable for me (25fps) on minimal settings.
So the bottom line is:
1) If you are a fan of the series you will want to buy it and be patient while bugs get fixed.
2) If this is your first King Arthur game you might want to wait for a couple of patches or a sale.
3) In all cases trying the demo first is highly recommended since the performance issue is probably a big, if not the biggest factor in your purchase decision.

Greenlight, Indie, Horror walking simulator - Immediate question was it worth playing? Answer - YES.  DEFINITELY YES. Was it worth the $1 US? It is definitely worth more than that actually.
Storyline: In 1901 the passenger/cargo ship Eurydice sunk with everyone on board and no survivors.  What happened on board and why is that diver even there in the first place is the big mystery. (Unlimited oxygen supply since the player is in a dive suit walking around this dilapitated wreck going deeper and deeper into its bowels searching for answers.) Besides just who is that diver? (No spoiler, I will let the player figure it out.)
While playing my son asked curiously, "What are you playing?"
"Reveal the Deep" I reply, without thought.
"You DO realize that is a horror game?" he remarks incredulously.  He knows I hate horror games.
"It is?" I replied totally shocked.
Yes, actually this is a horror game, psychological terror would be more precise.  The reviews comment on how scary this game is.  It is scary, very scary in fact, with a couple of very good and well placed jump scares.  However, unlike most people I did not play with headphones on, in the dark, and in the middle of the night.  With headphones on at night in the dark, the combination of the creaks and groans of the ship, the occassional almost heard talking of many people, the thuds and thumps of unseen unknowns, the general decay and terrifying atmosphere of knowing one is not alone certainly has that terror factor well and truly targeted precisely.
This terror factor really goes into effect as one explores since the player had limited visibility due to only being able to see what the flashlight on the dive helmet reveals in a vertical maze of corridors.  Also if the player taps on their helmet one of two things happen 1) most of the screen goes dark except for the helmet (truly all alone in the dark ... maybe) or 2) alternate time occurs (shown in an eerie red light).  (I could debate future time as well as past but that is for the player to determine.)
According to the developers each chapter (3 total) should take approximately 20-30 minutes to complete.  If one looks at my time it was far longer then that. (Minus the idle time to make dinner, do errands, repeating a chapter or two, I would say my actual play time was around 3 - 4 hours.) I would say unless someone is every good at completing mazes in the dark, while solving some quite intricate puzzles and later fending off things that will kill you, I doubt this 20-30 time frame is accurate for a first time playthrough.  I estimate about an hour for each chapter, assuming one does not get stuck and have to start the chapter again.
About that - starting a chapter from the beginning.  There is no save feature mid-chapter.  So if the player leaves the game the player must begin at the beginning of the chapter they were on.  The player is warned about this, so no crying.  However, if one dies, there is a feature where the player begins at their last hidden "save" point - basically a safe place before death occurs.  That is very useful when one accidently dies (especially late) in a chapter or when trying to survive while figuring out where to go or what to do.
The game is relatively linear, though the player does not necessarily have to find everything there is to find, and the path is generally coaxing the player along from one puzzle element to the next (and through the storyline).  It is an exploration game after all.  The player can find snarky comments, interactive places, along with Isaac's letters, Beatrice's diary pages and Tom's journal entries all of which tell the tragic tale of the horrible fate that befell the ship and all those on board. (Look for those (!) exclamation points.)  The ending made perfect sense to me, but then again I actually read everything I could find.
One last item to touch on - glitches, glutches, and oubliettes - This game worked fine for me.  No problems.  Even all the achievements popped for me.  So I can only assume of as July 6, 2016 the developers have fixed all those little nagging problems that have plagued many players causing them to express their displeasure.
In the end I recommend this game, and for those who like horror do play at night, in the dark, with your headphones on.  I am sure you will appreciate the skin crawling effect the sound track has and as for those jump scares - careful not to tip your chair over.

Pro's
.Massive galaxy
.Alot of custom alien races
.Various play styles
.Terraforming, including plant and animal life.
.The ability to raise tribes and civilisations to galactic stage, via monoliths
Con's
.Grindy
.Grox empire is giant, and as above, grindy to get through.
.Limited audio (voices)

Overall, Spore is worth it. It has replayability to, I would say 4 or so times, minimum. (1 herbivore route, 1 carniverious route, 1 omnivore route, 1 mixed).

Its a card game. If you don't like sometimes losing because you draw a bad hand, you shouldn't want to ever play card games. Well, Spectromancer is a bit different.
There are 4 basic elements and 1 special element depending on your mage. For each element, there are 4 cards you can play costing various amounts of mana. These cards can either be spells or monsters. These cards are reused throughout the entire match. You don't get to choose which cards you get, and you don't draw cards. You may get a different combination of cards in different matches however as there are more than four cards in each element.
You can have up to 5 monsters on your side of the field. Normally you get one of each mana per turn, but some spells give mana and a few monsters boost mana generation.
I believe you start with 20 hit points and you can play a single card per turn. Gameplay is generally fast paced. You can die in a couple turns if your generated cards are weak against the enemy's. Since you get mana every turn, you can play several weaker monsters while waiting to cast a strong spell or monster.
Balance between monsters is pretty good. Some are virtually unkillable with regeneration, some hit the entire enemy row, some are immune to magical spells. Spells can range from healing the player to wiping the entire field.
There are quite a few deck strategies to use, but since you don't pick you cards you generally decide the strategy on the first turn.
Cards that enhance mana generation are generally weak, but are very powerful in combination with monsters that grow stronger based on that type of mana.
Use tanks to hold the line while nuking your opponent's life directly.
Rushing the enemy down with swarms of low mana monsters. This isn't as strong since there are several spells that do damage to multiple creatures. It could be used to safely bring out a stronger monster once your opponent has nuked the field.
The campaign is pretty fun the first few times you play. The opponents start off fairly easy and then get pretty brutal. Different decks help keep the game fresh, and the random combination of cards means you can't rely on solely one combination of cards to win games.
I haven't tried the DLC, but they seem to add new mage types. These mage types represent the fifth element of mana. They are the unique cards that add even more depth to the game.
I believe this game has been in an Amazon bundle recently. Therefore it probably stands to reason that if you have a backlog, you can probably wait for the eventual sale to buy this game. With Hearthstone coming out in the future, I can't see much reason to buy this game. But since that's not out yet,  you should pick this up if the game goes on sale. I would like to present a strong reccomendation for Spectromancer, its multiplayer in particular. I don't have much opinion on single player, as I was drawn to duel games right away. But let it be said that there are several varying game modes in addition to a campaign.
Multiplayer duels is what made this game for me. There are no cards to be found or unlocked through winning or other achievements, no grinding. You have all the cards available to you right away (with an exception of expantion pack cards, which are additional entirely new decks).
Cards are dealt randomly, but within a predefined system, to keep things balanced. From then on, one gathers mana each turn and it's up to the player which cards to spend and when. This is a brilliant mix of luck and strategy, but with the point that you still have a chance of winning if you got bad luck. There are ways of bluffing your opponent, trying to outsmart them, manipulating them to reveal their hand, and various other tricks.
Through the two years that I have played this game, servers always have been populated enough so I would rarely have to wait more than 1 minute to find an opponent matched approximately to my level.
It must be one of the best confrontational card games. Unlike MTG, there's no deck-building, but prudent calculation is needed.

Spectromancer is absolutly fun. It's got a unique take on the way you play.
It's a little old now due to current titles coming out, but none the less, it's very fun to play.

Spectromancer is paradoxically both too simple and too complex. Each match starts with you being shown your entire 20 card deck (no randomness here), and each turn you choose exactly one card to play that you have enough power for. That's the extent of your interaction with the game. You don't control who your monsters attack or block (they just attack directly in front of them), nor can you move them to a different column. Your opponent then does the same.
Each of the twenty cards in your deck has some different effect. So do your opponent's cards. The winner ends up being the person who has the right one card in their deck of twenty to counter the other player's attacks. These sort of "I Win" cards are a problem in games like Magic, but at least you know they aren't guarenteed to be in your opponent's hand at all times like in Spectromancer.
There's a lot more to a good digital card game than the matches. Unfortunately, Spectomancer is lacking in these areas as well. From the stock sound effects to the mundane card graphics, this is a very severly budget effort. The campaign consists of reading a page of fantasy trope nonsense, and then competing against your opponent.
With so many other great digital card games, including free ones like Duel of Champions, why play this one?

First off, buy the BASE GAME + the GATHERING OF POWER expansion. It includes all the features and content of the other two DLCs and it's a very naughty move on part of the developers to still sell the older two expansions on Steam, potentially making you pay $30 to buy all the expansion content, when you can be buying it for $10.
With this unpleasant situation out of the way and despite it, I still highly recommend the game. It is co-developed by Richard Garfield of Magic: The Gathering and Netrunner fame. The game uses many concepts similar to MTG but is presented in a more casual framework. The major differences from MTG are: a) no card draw or deck but a set of semi-random given cards that don't 'run out' and are always available to cast if you have the mana, b) slot-based battlefield with two lines of 6 slots in which players summon creatures.
Spectromancer is far easier to pick up and play compared to MTG. As there is no deck building, gameplay offers more limited options but the game livens things up with its unique class system, with each class getting its separate set of cards. Creature interplay is far more important and summoning order and spell support often require as much strategy as a game of MTG.
Multiplayer, a very big factor for Spectromancer's appeal, is still alive and well, with available players at all times and lots of replayability given the large number of classes available.

This review primarily focuses on the Multiplayer component of the game with brief mentions of single player content. Review code was sent to me by the developers free of charge.
Mushroom Wars 2 is a very simplistic RTS title that is finely tunned into an incredibly addictive multiplayer game. The goal of the game is to conquer your enemies through the use of your mushroom men and your hero powers of which there are several in an all around pleasant RTS title.
Gameplay:
Basically, you have several types of buildings that your army uses. Towers, which attack enemies. Forges, which provide one incremental upgrade per forge on the map for your troops. Finally, you have mushroom homes/hovels which slowly build up your army. You can upgrade your towers to do more damage and your hovels to hold more units.
The gameplay is very simple but there is a degree of mind games going on. The single player doesn't quite have this mechanic. In the single player campaign (which is essentially a bunch of skirmish maps VS the AI) you get alerted when the enemy AI is sending units to the base, highlighting that specific base that is about to be attacked. In the multiplayer, there is no alert or highlight. You have to carefully guess and reinforce the building that you think is going to be attacked based on how the enemy has been mobilizing their troops and how they have been watching you move your troops between buildings in addition to the location of the building(s) being attacked in question.
The game is based on numbers. When you overwhelm an enemy position with more units, you win. It doesn't happen instantly (unless you have a hero power for that) and you have to navigate your troops across potential hazards like enemy towers or fire pits. Meanwhile, when you attack an enemy, the defending enemy base gets stars based on defending successfully (beating your troops and holding the position). As the enemy gets these stars, their defense rating goes up. You could send 100 troops to attack a 50 troop home and if the enemy has enough stars they can slaughter you without even needing extra troops from other positions. The game discourages early game rushing because of the way buildings generate troops but it also discourages late game all out attacks unless it's pure desperation. This leads to a lot of very mentally intensive matches despite the game being relatively simple. It's all about what your opponent is thinking. This is all on top of all the unique hero abilities allowing for sneak plays and big comebacks. This is easily the games strongest point and with matches lasting less than 5 minutes on average you get that “just one more game” feeling.
Art & Sound:
The music is nice. Orchestral and thematic. Unfortunately, there isn't a whole lot of tracks and you will start to hear them repeat very early. The art is very colorful, gorgeous at times I'd even say.
Content:
The game has a good multiplayer community with features such as ranked 1v1, unranked (1v1, 1v1v1, 1v1v1v1, 2v2), a replay system as well as a profile.
The game also features a large pool of maps. The biggest letdown is the number of game modes. There are only 3 and you're mostly going to be playing each game like conquest (kill the enemy outright). It does make up for this with a good selection of characters and special abilities
Unfortunately, the campaign is the weakest portion. While custom games does allow for some offline content with friends (up to 4 player local multiplayer here with controllers), the campaign VS ai removes the mind games and manipulation the main game is known for. I haven't played it a ton so it might get interesting later as I have read things about "boss fights" but that might just be character vs character powers like you have in multiplayer. The other big issue that draws away further value from an offline experience is the controller support. It works but there is no way to rebind your controller and the controls for it are generally poopy and take time to get used to.
Conclusion:
This is an incredibly simple yet solid RTS polished to a T. As you can tell by my hours, I got hooked on it and I am excited for some of the tournaments the developers have been doing. I don't see a massive lasting appeal unless new maps and heroes and balances are implemented in (fighting the same heroes in the multiplayer meta gets a bit tiresome). The single player is the weakest part so far so I would keep that in mind when making a purchase. Even though I got the game for free I'd certainely have gotten my monies worth.

So where do i start with Mushroom Wars 2, where indeed. When you think of real-time strategy games, tech trees, tank rushes and turtling all come to mind, not bands of mushrooms warriors running back and forward. However, you don't need gameplay mechanics like those in Dawn of War III or StarCraft: Remastered to have an engaging RTS experience. In fact, sometimes the simplest games can have the most engrossing gameplay. Zillion Whales has taken this concept to heart with its recent release of Mushroom Wars 2, a game that's simple to learn, but has a surprising amount of complexity and replayability. As a result, you can pick up and play a level or two for a few minutes, but feel thoroughly entertained. The gameplay is easy to pick up, Once the directional arrow is shown, you have the option to send a quarter, half, three quarters or all of the troops from one location to another by hitting one of the four face buttons. Clearly, it's up to you to make the decision as to how many soldiers you want to send, but each structure that you're trying to capture has varying levels of resistance, regardless of whether they're a neutral structure or held by an enemy. If you don't send enough soldiers, you'll be repelled and the building won't fall under your control. Send the right number of troops or more than enough, and you'll see the structure change colour. Mount & Blade: Warband is an action / role-playing / strategy / medieval simulation - game developed by turkish developer TaleWorlds Entertainment.
I personally love this game and spent way too much hours on it, while never having stopped to have fun with it. Let me start off with the world map, which is pretty decent in size and variation. At the beginning of a new game the world, named Calradia, is split up in 6 factions: Kingdom of Nords, Kingdom of Swadia, Kingdom of Vaegirs, Kingdom of Rhodoks, Khergit Khanate and the Sarranid Sultanate. Those six factions are able to wage war on any other faction, even if the player doesn't take part. Every faction has it's own ruler and vassals, which can also change (I'm not sure about the ruler, but I've never seen him change). You start off alone in one of the big Cities and meet a merchant right at the beginning of the game, after you've been ambushed by a few bandits you can kill pretty easily. He gives you a quest to gather a few fighters in order to rescue his sibling, who is held captive in a nearby bandit camp. That's how you're thrown into the game. Now you have the choice what to do, you don't even have to help that guy. You could choose any faction you want and join it, as soon as you fulfilled enough quests for the respective leader of that faction and your party is big enough. You can expand his kingdom and hope to get some villages or even your own castle, if you're a very good fighter you may even get a whole City. But if you don't want to fight for a permanent income (Or you want to just invest in the future) you can also get a few businesses in some cities. Depending on what the surrounding villages produce a brewery for example can give you 400+ denars (the currency in the game) per week, or even cost you some money. Trading is part of the game and in every city you can go to the market for a few hours and just listen to the merchants and find some profitable trading routes for yourself.
But you may ask yourself now what the actual goal of the game is? Well the answer is pretty easy...
Conquer EVERYTHING.
Build up your party, while being vassal for one of the rulers and if you feel strong enough tell him to f*ck off and then you start conquering every castle and city for your own kingdom. You can also promote your companions to vassals or "steal" some from other factions.
Or you help one of the throne claimants (every faction has it's throne claimant), but I never tried this so I sadly can't tell you anything about it.
To be honest, this game has pretty damn ♥♥♥♥♥♥ graphics, but at least it will run on a toaster from 1990...
The audio is acceptable and the soundtrack is very enjoiable, but is not guaranteed to run the whole time it should...
The controls are easy and you can get fast into commanding your fighters in the battle.
All in all this game definetly has more potential, but is astoundingly good and a deep medieval simulation, but the sequel (M&B II: Bannerlord) promises to give us everything that is still requested. If you think you could like this game, get it. It probably still is a long time until Bannerlord is released, since it's release is to be announced...

First off, I should at least mention that I'm not a huge platformer fan, but occasionally when I come across something that looks like it might be up my alley, I don't mind taking a punt. I'm very glad that I did exactly that after watching the trailer to Lazy Monday's, Reveal The Deep. Over three chapters, all of which come with the purchase of the game, the player explores the sunken remains of a Victorian-era cargo ship which has met its mysterious demise. As seems to be the current norm in independent games under $2, Reveal The Deep uses pixel-style graphics. In this case however, the story-critical information is fed to the player in a series of short handwritten letters and diary entries, supplemented with hand sketches of the various characters and their discoveries. The plot threads are evenly spaced enough to keep the player engaged in the story, and do a good job of breaking up the rather nominal difficulty of the gameplay. Indeed, Reveal The Deep is far more of a walking sim than a true platformer, and not being particularly fond of platformers, that was something that delighted me. I hate being punished for a poorly timed jump, and I certainly don't like to be rushed when I play games for enjoyment; so I was in fact, relieved when it became clear that I wasn't going to have to repeat the same sequences over-and-over because I'm more like Woody Harrelson than Wesley Snipes, and that I was actually going to be allowed to enjoy the premise of the game: To explore a shipwreck.
Lazy Monday have done a great job of capturing the romance of being an explorer at the turn of the last century. Considering there is no voice acting or narration, no flashbacks or cutscenes, they have still been able to paint a wonderful picture for the player despite the minimalistic approach to the inclusion of text in the game. Anyone who has read a bit of similarly-themed literature, will understand what I mean when I say that what Lazy Monday have done is to include only what is needed. And in my mind at least, there is a very subtle art to that that really should be appreciated and applauded.
Normally one of the things that I get excited about when I play indie games is the soundtrack, but Reveal The Deep instead does something that makes a lot of sense for an underwater exploration game. Rather than trying to tell the player how they should be feeling using music, the lack of it in this case gives the game an unnerving quality that suits it very well. There are some very contrasting moments in each chapter that utilise this to great effect, and all the while the player is hearing the muffled sounds of their own breathing and heavy footsteps against the protesting groans of the sunken wreck. Again, the Developers have made a great choice to leave something out rather than put something in as a matter of course. I think that the only reason to use a soundtrack in this game would be to take it in more of a horror direction, but doing so would only serve to pull Reveal The Deep more into the mainstream, and thereby do it a great disservice. Indeed, I would much rather have seen a little more creativity in the use of lighting than any type of accompanying soundtrack, as the former would have added much more artistic value to the game, and added yet another layer to an already enjoyable game. If you want the full diving suit experience, be sure to put on a good pair of headphones, they really do make a huge difference to the amount of immersion you can draw from this little gem.
With their debut offering, Lazy Monday Games have delivered something that emphasises how keeping it simple can often yield the best result. I'd love to see what they can do with a bigger budget, because there is a lot to like about how Reveal The Deep has been produced. I just realised today is Monday, how strange...

I wouldn't recommend this game to anyone and here are a few of the reasons:
- The puzzles don't make any sense - there's no indication about what you are supposed to do next, so you spend all the time clicking objects around the room randomly, picking them up for a later use, without having a clue how they fit in the story. I must say that this is the first game I've played for which I needed to check a guide at almost every step.
- Sometimes you need to repeat the same action several times until it unlocks the next step - which I find very annoying.
- The mouse cursor doesn't change when you hover an object of interest or a person to talk to them. There are options to inspect objects, take them and talk to persons but those are enabled only if you click the right item.
-  The inventory is opened in a separate window that covers almost entirely the game area. Every time you need to use an item from the inventory, you need to select the item, close the screen and only after that use the object with the desired target. I consider this to be a very bad design decision since the objects that are ment to be used together (from the inventory or from the scene) need to be visible all the time.
- There is no option to skip the dialogues.
On a positive note, it's a short game (around 1h of game play) with very easy achievements - in a single walkthrough you can collect all the achievements except one (that requires a second play through); although keep in  mind that some of them are known to be bugged. Nevertheless it's a very easy game to max out for the achievement collectors.

This is not a TCG (trading card game) and that's what makes it so great.
There is no card collection or deck building, each game you get a random selection of 12 basic cards out of the game's pool of 48 basic cards and 4 special cards from the class of your choosing.
"So what if I get completely screwed over and only get bad cards?" - That doesn't happen because a) the game is incredibly balanced, every card has its use and strength b) the selection isn't totally random, the game makes sure that you have 2 healing cards every game and that it's a fair mix of low and high cost cards ad that you always have board clear cards.
So to get back on point what makes the lack of deck-building great is that you have to adapt to your cards every game. Do i try to get an advantage by being more mana-efficient than my opponent, do I try to win via board control or do I just rush my opponent? If you want to win you have to play to your decks strength. Also a big part of the game is reading your opponent and predicting what cards he has.
One example: I'm ahead in board control, my opponent just played a very low impact card and he has a lot of fire mana saved up, that means that he is probably preparing to play Armageddon which deals a lot of damage to all creature on the board. So if I correctly predict this I can take advantage of it by not overcommitting and not playing any expensive creatures next turn because they'd probably die.
Advanced players will use this to bluff you. e.g. a player might save up a lot of air mana which makes the opponent afraid of the spell Lightning Bolt, which deals massive damage to the enemy player's hp. So the opponent may waste his turn by casting expensive heals even though it was a bluff and the opponent doesn't have Lightning Bolt.
All this predicting and bluffing wouldn't work as well if the game didn't have a limited number of cards.
Oh I almost forgot the most important point about not being a TCG, the game isn't pay to win, it's all about skill.
Other important points:
- The game has still an active online community even though the game is 5 years old
- The computer AI is really clever and good at predicting your moves, so if you don't like online play, it's never boring to play against the computer
- The campaign is pretty okay, every fight has special rules, so it's nice and varied, though as I said the best thing about the game is the online play
- you can get a lot of value out of the demo. I played like a hundred online games before I bought the game (but a year or so ago they added a 5 games per day restriction to the demo)

By the guys who made Magic: The Gathering.  Really fun, and not a huge time sink!

When the original Magic: The Gathering was created by WoTC, they never expected it to be so successful. It not only captured the hearts, minds and wallets of nerds everywhere who can't get enough of it, it made the founders wealthy beyond dreams of avarice. Just like the Federal Reserve convinced everyone that paper money was better than Gold, Wizards convinced nerds everywhere that cardboard was better than paper money. One day Wizards had an epiphany. If the Federal Reserve can print unlimited amounts of money, why not print unlimited amounts of cardboard? And so they did. In a perverted form of Magic Quantitative Easing, the printing presses ran non-stop. A litany of problems symptomatic of rush releases and lack of playtesting soon plagued the game: endless erratas, rule changes, Bannings, etc... The game slowly transformed from Magic: The Gathering into Lawyer: The Travesty. A game only someone like Phoenix Wright Ace Attorney can appreciate and Barristers play as a warm up to litigation. Co-created by legendary Wizards of the Coast founder Richard Garfield, it is not surprising that Spectromancer bears some resemblence to Magic. However there is no deck building and no rare power cards to 'collect'. The rules are simple and skill plays a bigger role than luck. A fun casual fantasy card game that can be enjoyed by people other than Rules-Lawyers.
Simple but smart. Each round lasts for 5-10 minutes, so it is very good choice to those who wish to relax in between any personal tasks or "big and heavy" games.

The original Resident Evil, a game that started an entire genre. You play with either Jill Valentine or Chris Redfield as your special forces team is investigating strange occurrences happening in the outskirts of Raccoon City, and is nearly all wiped out, ending up in a huge mansion.

While I still enjoy the modern Resident Evils, they aren't really survival horror games, but more action focused. In this Resident Evil there is no coop, resources are really scarce as defeated enemies do not drop any loot and the game is very difficult and tense overall. The story unfolds in slightly different ways depending on your actions, and there are six endings for each character, which adds to the replayability.
The port is also very good with plenty of options to customize your experience and mostly bug free. The remaster also retains all the music from the original, but in better quality, while the voices and dialogues have been entirely redone. Besides the clear visual upgrade, many new things have been added such as new game modes, new enemies and new locations.

Resident Evil is an absolute classic and whether or not you have played the original on the Playstation or Sega Saturn, you should get it to experience what a true survival horror game used to be.

I remember playing
on the PS2 and attempting to jump from vehicle to vehicle in quick succession, similar to how I tried to replicate the idea in later games like
and
. However, I always imagined the concept to work better in a
game... But no.
Instead, Clustertruck delivers a polished concept of what I previously attempted in other games and offers 90 exciting  levels designed to test your reflexes and challenge your thought process by jumping from truck to truck to get from point A to B. While trucks wobble along a straight path, you are expected to predict every truck's movement to create your own path to the end goal without touching the floor or most parts of the environment, much like playing a first person 'floor is lava' game.
Upgrades are available which offer different advantages to playing levels. You can only equip 2 at a time, so there's some strategy with what upgrades you choose. To unlock them, you must acquire skill points by performing stunts, beating time records and completing levels. Replaying levels is necessary to unlock every upgrade, but that's no issue because this game is a heck of a lot of fun! Not to mention, some upgrades offer really silly ways to play the game!
The speed your character goes is incredible when you use momentum to your advantage, throwing yourself off the side of trucks forward to gain better upward force or simply jumping smoothly from truck to truck. However, the game is actually, surprisingly easy until half way into the campaign levels. I only found challenge later on. Then again, the learning curve is very well done, since casual gamers may be attracted to the simple (yet good looking) graphics and appreciate a slower paced challenge progression. Afterall, there is a lot of spacial awareness being used in this game that can drive some people insane without patience.
Thankfully, there is a great FOV slider, and the ability to download custom maps from the Steam Workshop is a great treat. In addition... THE SOUNDTRACK IS SO GOOD. This is super important, since the game needed a fast paced soundtrack to keep up the hype of completing a level in the coolest way possible.
Now for the bad stuff. Playing this game with Vsync off made for a stuttery experience for me, so turn that crap on. Secondly, playing with TSAA on makes for a blurry visual experience, but offers motion blur as well, which makes the game appear faster than it actually is, which also helped me focus on trucks better once I approched them at high speed. Also, the level editor is super annoying to use, with glitches and physics based malfunctions happening a lot. I really wanted to create my own level, but got too annoyed by the fact I couldnt click on a lot of objects without my click being registered. Finally, the 90 levels go by too quickly. It only took me 6 hours to complete them, with the final boss (yes, you heard) only really taking a few attempts to defeat.
Nontheless, each level is created brilliantly, with some levels begging to be replayed over and over again just ebcause they are so much fun to replay! This game will thrive more once the Workshop is full of greatly made levels and I will play this game more and more the greater the amount of levels there are to play.

Growth/Stages:
In this game, you start out as a small astroid. You grow by slamming yourself as hard as you can into other astroids. As you do this, you avoid planets and stars. If you hit one of them, depending which of them and how hard, you die. You also avoid small white and red fighters, which we will get into later. This stage takes about a minute if you're quick enough about it, and comes with about 9 missions which are fairly easy.
After you have become best friends with enough astroids (by pummeling their surface with yourself) you become a small planet. This time it's different, not only because you are bigger, but by the way you collect mass now. Now, you have to get an astroid to orbit you and then absorb it. You do this by getting fairly close to one, and watch as your gravity pulls it in and around. This is also where is gets somewhat problematic: you have gravity. This means, if you can't get an astroid to circle around you, it will hit your surface as you pull on it more and more as it gets closer. There's a small penalty for getting hit with an astroid, but it's enough to make you not want to get hit again. You still avoid stars, other planets, the occasional black hole, and fighters. There are 9 new missions that will be accessible by this stage and the next, but are somewhat heavily leaned toward the next stage.
After you have absorbed enough astroids to give Cell a run for his money on things you absorb, you become a life planet. This stage is where things start to get a little more complex. You gain mass the same way, but there's a mixture to the formula: life starts evolving on your planet. After about 15 seconds, life has evolved on your planet, and your planet starts building small, green fighters, a shield around your planet, an turrets. The shield, amount of turrets and amount and quality of ships is all varied by EXP level, which is essentially aided most by kills. What you do to get kills is find another planet, or a group of nomads, and watch as your fighters waste them. Your shield will protect you from damage, but one shot to the planet itself and life restarts on your planet. All of your experience will disappear and you have to restart. There are 4 levels; you start on level 1. The kills to advance all 4 levels is relatively low, and if you find yourself in an intsense battle with another planet, you'll most likely reach that 4th level fairly quickly. I will also mention how there's 3 types of fighters: The regular fighter, the missle cruiser, and the destroyer. More or less, the fighter is just a standard fighter that does single shot damage. They become nearly obsolete once you get the other two. The Missle Cruiser fires missles that cause an explosion has area of effect damage or splash damage. The explosions do massive damage, insta-killing fighters and other missle cruisers, and causing heafty damage to the shield. The destroyer is like the fighter, bigger, and can shoot multiple shots at a time while rapid-firing... So it's nothing like the fighter. These, while they don't cause the damage of a missle cruiser to the fighters, are devistating to the planet's shield. Even a level 4 shield can be taken out fairly easy by the destroyer. During this stage, you also have planetary turrets which fire lasers and ships, but only ships. They are fairly powerful and good at defending, but the most you get is 4... Until later. Once again, the 9 missions from last stage are still avaliable to do in this stage.
These next stages are pretty much the same stage, but I'll give the differences once I get there. There are 9 missions total that can be completed in all the stages These are the 4 star stages:
Small Star
Medium Star
Big Star
Neutron Star
After you've absorbed more astroids, you become a small star. You gain mass by absorbing planets in a similar fasion to how you absorbed astroids as a planet. Except... You can make a planet orbit you, have it collect astroids and absorb it, and make it a life planet to protect the entire system. Yep, you can have multiple planets orbit you and have life on them. You also get a shield around your star if you get enough of them. Here's where the differences with the stars come in:
Small Stars - These have a low gravitational pull and can only sustain 4 planets orbiting them. They are relatively small.
Medium Stars - These have a medium gravitational pull and can sustain 6 planets orbiting them. Relatively medium.
Big Stars - These have a large gravitational pull and can sustain 8 planets orbiting them. Pretty large.
Neutron Stars - These have a massive gravitational pull, but can only sustain 4 planets. They are small.
So, this stage is collecting planets, absorbing them, and gaining mass... Unless you want to grow your empire, which in that case, grab the planets, convert them into life planets, and make them all level 4! One would ask, "What if a life planet absorbs enough astroids to become a star?" Great job Timmy, that was actually my next topic. You see, when a planet orbiting you gains enough mass to become a star, your system will become a binary-star system. In other words, there will be two stars orbiting around a center of mass! With a binary star system, your planet capacity becomes 10 and your gravitational pull is far greater than even as a neutron star. You can get even more stars in your system, but it won't do any more than a binary system.
And the last stage... You become a black hole and suck in everything, including other black holes that are smaller than you. That's the stage, and it's fairly exciting. You suck in EVERYTHING. Once you've sucked in everything you suck in the entire universe and then!... You become an astroid again.
I won't say much more, I won't talk about the final boss or God powers, but you'll figure out as you go.
The question on everyone's mind... Is it worth it?
Well... Sorta. My thoughts on it are:
If you only have 60 dollars and you want to get a game, there are some really good options that'll use up those 60 dollars, but this is not one of them.
If you have some money laying around and are just looking through for games to try on Steam, I'd pick it up... Actually, that's kinda how I picked it up.
It definitely kept me for the 13 hours I've played so far, and I'm sure it'll captivate me again in the future. Either way, It's a relatively good game that has a price barrier that isn't too good for some.
For the gameplay that does exist, I'll give it an 8/10

First off, this game is short. Like, beat it in 4 hours short. In addition to that, the combat isn’t great and the controls are a bit clunky, feeling like you should be using a gamepad when on KB/M and vice versa.
Great, now that we’ve got the bad stuff out of the way, let’s talk about why this game is good and totally worth your money.
Most of the puzzles are interesting and some can be difficult, but in the standard adventure game style they can be overcome as long as you have a sharp eye and creative mind. I don’t, but this aspect of the game was still enjoyable.
The two things that shine the brightest in this game are the writing and atmosphere. The portrayal of AI as a concept was very well done, and all the robots you meet were interesting and not outright good or evil, not even the antagonist. The environments are all sufficiently creepy, and everything ties together into a world that feels subtly dystopian, but not in an overt ‘everything sucks’ kind of way. I felt very immersed in the world as I played, and they managed to do that without an oversaturation of books or text logs scattered about like in many other games. Oh sure, there are some, but not all over the place. So kudos for that.
All in all, I enjoyed the experience I got, and look forward to playing any continuations of the story.

Stick RPG 2 has two different sides to the game.  One side is a time management sim featuring wild goose chase quests, and the other side is a top down arcade brawler.  Both sides completely different from each other, and both are necessary to master to complete the game.
As a sim, your character has to make money through working jobs, gambling, and performing various tasks.  Doing favors (quests) for individuals will help you aquire different tools, which will ultimately lead you to the game goal items.  As for time management, you have to decide what jobs and tasks are worth your time to work to build up your bank and character stats.  You can also develop a love life interacting with potential mates.  You also sometimes have a choice on how to accomplish certian tasks, but there are very few choices offered throughout the entire game.
As a top down arcade brawler, it feels very similar to Hotline Miami, but everyone has a life bar, and you can't pick up weapons off the ground.  You can build weapons through quests, shop at the weapons store, or sometimes even win them as fight rewards.  Some battles will only allow you to fight with your fists, but there are also battle grounds where you can exploit all your weapons.
As far as the overall experience goes, it feels really unpolished and unfinished.  Prices of various items and services are very inflated, forcing you to spend a lot of time working jobs to develop a solid bank account.  It is also frusturating working a job and losing stats on a bad shift (on the job accidents, with no insurance options).  You also can have lucky days where you get a substantial bonus on your shift, but you can't adjust the odds in your favor for these events.  On a funny note, your strength stat will make your firearms stronger for some reason, and you have unlimited ammo, so running blindly with a machine gun or flame thrower on full auto is an acceptable tactic.  As fun as it is the first two or three times, it gets old really fast.
The game feels more like a prototype for something really awesome, but definitely lacks a lot of ambition, and needs to be tweaked.  I do recommend it to hobbyist level game designers who want ideas for implementation, but need some direction.  For everyone else, pick it up as cheap as you can (I got it for $1), and waste a good 4 to 6 hours before you give up on it.  It isn't so bad, it just isn't all that great either.

This is my first review of a game. It's more an appreciation for what Capcom have achieved here (I try not to lick their ring piece too much in this review).
For the TL;DR, please skip to the bottom =).
I grew up with Resident Evil. I was terrified, amazed, addicted and in love all at the same time with the franchise.
I played the very original around the age of 6. It was iconically memorable and ingrained in me the love of Survival Horror; that no doubt my fellow players would appreciate. I put a good chunk of time into that gem.
When REmake was announced, I was so damn pumped. I purchased a GameCube for the [b}sole[/b] purpose of REmake. Playing it was mind-blowing. The love and work Capcom had put into upgrading
aspect of the game was clearly visible. New mechanics such as Defensive Items, Crimson Heads (
) and new jumpscares were tied together very well and felt a great way to step up the fear factor, without intruding too much on the core of what makes the game amazing.
Graphically, the GameCube version, IMHO, has stood the test of time. For the time, the visuals were fantastic to observe. You truly felt frightened when roaming the run-down, dusty, mansion: the atmosphere was an enemy all-in-itself.
The game featured unlockable items and rewards for completion of the game; dependent of course, upon how well you did time-wise. This was even more incentive to replay the game. This one time, at band camp, I missed unlocking Barry's Samurai Edge by a minute! Salty, I ran back through the game and smashed that time by half an hour. Excuse the brag.
So now we come to
. REmake with a face-lift that looks natural. Woah...
I couldn't have imagined this game looking better. But Capcom pulled it off. Player models, enemies, items are all crisp. The environment is polished and is highly detailed. My only frown on this version would be that there are some graphical tears here and there. If the player model is far from the camera, I noticed a slight jolt and tear: but it's not game-breaking. Some texures are smudged and stretched, but not very noticeable. These aside, the game looks brilliant

Bartering? I like this a lot, you can actually barter and raise the price you are selling for or decrease the price you are buying for and see whether merchants will accept your offer.
Visuals? Mods work, but still nowhere near on par with Skyrim if that's what you were expecting.

Medival knight simulator. Imagine Heroes of Might and Magic 3 with single hero moving in real time on the map and real time battles, in which your hero participates. As the result, you get a mix of strategy, role-playing game and Third Person Shooter - although shooter is here not an accurate word, as you mostly fight with melee weapons (unless you decide to use bows and crossbows). Other than that, the game is a sandbox - you can do anything you want with this world. You can become a mercenary and fight for one of the existing kingdoms, eventually becoming a knight or even a lord, who can get married with some lady. You can become a thug, robing caravans, killing peasants and plundering villages. You can support one of the usurpers and start a civil war in some kingdom. Or you can take over some castle or town and start your own kingdom, if you feel like it and become the king or queen yourself.
There are some options I miss like ability to marry the queen, once you help her reclaim her throne, but those are added by mods.
Mods - there's loads of them and they deserve to get another word; there's one that turns the world into the one known from Game of Thrones/Song of Ice and Fire TV/book series. Multiple mods making the game more visually appealing or making politics more complex. Lot of others.
Try it yourself, it's really worth it.

Solar 2....what is there to say about it.... A lot. Strap in ladies and gentleman as I take you through this awesome indie space game. I'm going to talk about this game in grave detail and also add stores of my gameplay. I've only played for a couple of hours but the fun is instant. This review is gonna be rather long so if you aren't into long reviews i'll have a summary for you at the bottom :)
First finding the game on store: I stumbled across this through looking at my recommended "praise gaben!" and instantly was intrigued by the screenshots and the introduction video; an added bonus was the sweet glorious blue text saying "very postive" this is a must for me as reviews determine whether I buy or not...That's why it is my duty to make reviews for the kind people of the master race so they don't miss out
Downloading/ loading up: Okay let's get back into the review, As soon as solar 2 popped up in my libary I was ready to go, lava lamp setting the mood give a sci-fi feel to my room (I love to get lost in games...setting the scene beforehand helps ;) ) The download was very quick and i was in. You are thrown right into the game with the press of your enter key.
Gameplay: You start of as an asteroid with one simple goal...To grow! This is done by travelling at breakneck speeds and colliding with other lonely asteroids...It is a little tricky as the pesky asteroids would move at the last second allowing you to shoot past them with a firm middle finger plaved in their direction. The priciple is the same from there, you collide into asteroid after asteroid until you've gained enough mass to officially be called a planet. This is not good enough however, you must get bigger, stronger and most importantly you want to host life!
Features: The main feature of Solar 2 is the life that forms on your planet/planets once you've growed into a big boy planet. You grow to either love or hate these people and trust me you get mixed feelings. You see, once lifeforce has evolved on your planet, this takes a couple of minutes if that, the people of your planet start installing defenses and firing space ships into orbit. These ships often fly behind you or circle around the planet and take down aliens or other planets. The main reason you may grow to hate your people is these ships....yes they are good defense but when you're a planet you still require asteroids to absorb...these ships however destroy most asteroids before you even get to them causing mass frustration...luckily you can full on smash into these little ships teaching them a lesson...as well as exploding them causing insta-death for the ship...but they deserve it! muwahahahaha-sorry
Story time: So he's the little segment I like to call "story time" in which I tell you something that happened to me in my travels through this game...Todays story is about my first time becoming a star... So once you've become a planet that holds life what's next? Well, becoming a star of course. This is where the awesomeness is truely revealed. I named my sun The Milky Sun (Sadly you can't actually name it in-game) and I set off In search for planets to defend me. You see, once you reach star level you need to consume whole planets to progress to the next level but you can also keep some of these planets so life can grow on them to defend you. The first planet I found was a gem, it already had life on it and they were pretty advanced meaning I had a good defensive force. I pet named the planet Milktopia. Now me and milktopia had good travels together, I gathered other planets but always consumed them to become bigger. The story gets interesting when I  became a medium star which can hold 6 planets in orbit; I had all 6, 3 with life, 3 without. Then aliens...flipping aliens surrounded my solar system as I ventured into their teritory. Queue the badass music. 100s of little ships fired out of my 3 advanced planets attacking the alien invaders head on and the cannons based on the planets blasted away. I felt like I could rule the world...galaxy. I was wrong...so so wrong. The aliens kept on attacking and I wandered where they were coming from; I moved to the orgin to find a big♥♥♥♥♥star with roughly 10 fully armed civilized planets. My pants filled with crap. I instantly fled but the aliens were stubborn. They kept on sending waves and waves of ships after me. One of planets exploded, then another one by one my planets were dying. I managed to escape as the aliens tired of chasing me...all that remained was my trusty pal milktopia. His life was sort lifed however as I traveled into a asteroid field, milktopia took heavy hits and exploded leaving tears rolling down my face...RIP milktopia RIP
Summary: This game is fricken awesome and if you're a fan of sci-fi or general space game then you should definitely try it. The music also adds to the sweet badass feel and the gamegenerally is relaxing as you drift through space. Controls are really simple even a monkey could play it (no offense)

Gripping and challenging, The Fall is an awesome Sci-fi puzzle/horrorish game (with no jump scares!) that I HIGHLY reccomend if you like AIs or AI theory.

The game is worth it on sale price, but only for the story and atmosphere. The gameplay is more or less a point and click adventure disguised as a platformer. The "puzzle" elements are not very good, nothing is hinted at and there isn't really a way to beat the game without either a guide or extensive trial and error.
The story is good, and was the only motivation to beat the game for me, but the ending falls a little flat since they plan to make this game the first part of a trilogy. I don't plan to buy the next game in the series, despite the ending or the overall story.

Though it feels like a game that take only 4 hours of gameply to complete should get some backlash, The Fall manages to sidestep that completely and make me want more from another installment. The puzzles are well-designed which can befuddle you for a time without being excuciatingly difficult and the gameplay is imaginative.
While the plot itself is slightly predictable, I would heartily recommend this game should there be more coming from Over the Moon. This game has clearly been designed with sequels in mind and The Fall is a brilliant start to this franchise.

What I like about Morrowind is how intelligently they treat the player. Directions and riddles are given rather than a waypoint arrow that you can't miss. There's always the option to go into areas early with an underdeveloped build, or even kill characters pivotal to the main story, forcing you to find a difficult, hidden path to completion.
So what's so good about a game that allows the players to royally screw themselves over? Well, the answer to that is that Is that it creates a living, breathing world with tons of freedom and creativity.
People often say that player choice is an important thing in games. And never is this more pronounced in morrowind. Because it's not just important for the story, it's important for YOUR story.
That's right. If I wanted to create the most powerful sword in the game, I would start by reading in game books about various types of daedra monsters, then ask around in taverns for where all the daedric shrines are, then make the journey to the shrine, fighting all the wild monsters along the way and restoring my health with potions made from the various herbs and monster drops. I then do battle with several dark elven, nord, and orc daedra worshippers, first casting various buffs and then funnelling then into a chokepoint where I can fight them one on one. Next it's time to go deeper into the shrine, where I fight a daedroth. Fortunately I have several cure poison potions with me and a spear to strike from long range. At this point I take a brief rest, repair my armor, and restore my health. Now I search around for a daedra lord, kill it after a difficult battle, and escape!
After that I carefully save up every bit of gold I have by completing quests and selling illegal drugs to khajits. Then, with a visit to the enchanter of choice, I combine the sword with the best soul gem I have, and create a terrifying weapon that can do whatever I want!
With Morrowind, the game doesn't treat you like a child. If you want it, you have to get it. There's no easy fast travel system, no quick magick and fatigue regeneration, no invincible companion to serve as an item dumpster. When the player accomplishes something in this game, it's because they combined knowledge of the world with planning and patience.
And my goodness, can you acomplish a lot. You think the dragonborn is powerful? Hah, he can't even touch me when I'm 60 metres above the ground and 100% invisible, summoning dremora lords and golden saints to my aid while casting down deadly fireballs. You think Kratos is powerful? Pffft. I've abused the potion system to give my little elf 36 676 strength and endurance. He can kill Kratos easily, and throw him next to a dead Chuck Norris.
This was all done without any game breaking bugs, glitches or cheats. It was done because the player wanted to play the game this way, learned how to make the world of Morrowind work for them, and become this powerful.
I guess the point I'm trying to make is that Morrowind is the closest any game will get to making you feel like a true adventurer. It isn't dumbed down, it isn't limiting, it doesn't break the mood. Dungeons are like real dungeons, labarynth nightmares full of locked doors and twisting passages, and hidden treasures, rather than just a single linear passage and boring loot galore.
If you are able to look past the outdated graphics (or get mods), get used to the wierd combat system (or get mods), and are tired of games with excessive handholding, I can confidently recommend Morrowind. It's atmoshpere is through the roof, it's world is massive and alive, and the feeling of satisfaction is unlike that of almost any other game. Because the choices you made didn't just matter to the story, they were the story.
Ummm I guess it also has a cool main quest. But yeah.

Fable Anniversary is a fully remastered version of Fable: The Lost Chapters. It features a graphic overhaul, new save system and incorporates achievements.
And well, that's it. And that right there is the problem.
The reason everybody loved the first Fable was for it's slapstick humor and eccentric characters. But the game aged pretty badly. Sloppy animations, simplistic combat, stiff and eerie looking characters, finiky movement, oh and don't forget all the bugs..... So when Lionhead announced Fable Anniversary I was pretty stoked and could not wait to play a remastered and polished version of Fable.
However, even though the visuals got an upgrade, characters, animations, movement, interaction, combat, etc. all remained the same. I've played through the entire game and nearly 100% completed it, because I do love the world of Albion, but in the end there's more to a game than nostalgic value. And this game delivers no more than that. I would only recommend getting the game if you are a fan of the original Fable: TLC.

Reveal the Deep is a very atmospheric game that takes place in a sunken ship at the bottom of the ocean floor, and your job is to find out what secrets lay at rest, along with passenger's logs giving clues as to what exactly happened to their dear ship.
I genuinely liked Reveal the Deep. The sound design was fantastic, as the creakings of wood, doors closing, and bubbling sounds truely put me in the dark underwater caverns. The level design and puzzles were nothing too fancy, but they were something to get your mind thinking. The story is basically placed in logs and letters written by past passengers in 1901, and the progression of the horrors that the ship contain show in the letters they write, clearly showing fear of the unknown.
This game isn't exactly "scary", in my terms. Granted, there are a few times when enemies are present, and in turn can give one a jump. However, they don't pose so much as a threat, and more of a way to stress the player (watch their back), or to find a way to solve a puzzle to continue the adventure. It's mostly just the sound design that is meant to place you in a real sunken ship, and it does a very good job.
Minor things such as controls, art design, and playability are all totally fine. In general, Reveal the Deep is an interesting 30 minute to possibly an hour game that has great potential, and shows it very well. It's simple, but brings interest well enough to keep the player emursed, and it's just a handful of fun, and for a good price.

A game where you play as a sentient space mass that roams the galaxy in a sandbox type of way. You start out as asteroid that can magically move around using some short unknown force, your 1st goal is to build mass to progress into latter stages of space mass ingame. You progress into planet which eventually leads into being different stages of stars until you each being a “Black Hole”. After being a becoming a black hole, you get to suck up the galaxy and other blacks holes you’ve meet along the way until you reach critical mass, this is the technical ending to the game but there is still more to be done.

After unlocking all the stages of being space mass (which you can now access at any time), you can now tackle the missions within the game which mostly involve doing stupid tasks for the “All mighty being” of the universe. (There are also survival challenges which I still need to dip into)
The graphic quality of this game is very well done for the time when it was made (expect really good space backgrounds) and the gravity/physics engine functions more or less what you can expect from being in space. The physics engine has less effect on you though (by default) to prevent you from getting frustrated by being so easily suck up/destroyed by bigger masses than you. (Yes, you can mess around with the gravity properties after a certain point ingame if you want to)
Probably the game’s biggest selling point or what I think is the most wonderful thing in this is the soundtrack. IMO It perfectly captures what a space theme soundtrack should be
Although some of the soundtrack additions are better than others, there are enough goodies in there to warrant ripping the OST from the game files and listening to it when you need to kill some time.
As to go for buying this game, I would personally price it around getting it around at least < $7 sale, on the bearing on how good it is for what you are spending.

The Infinite Black is one of my favorite games of all time.  I've been playing it for 4 years on its mobile platform - well before the game was introduced to Steam.
This game is an open-story sandbox MMO RPG, so the "fun factor" lies more in the social and political aspects of the game than in the actual game play.  Still, there are some in-game tasks that require proper planning, quick thinking and excellent dexterity.  The main goal of the game is to help your Corporation become the most powerful in the game by aligning itself with up to 7 additional corporations.
There is also the daily Hardcore XP contest where you are always at the edge of your seat, knowing that the next sector could be stacked with hostile players from enemy alliances.  Die once and lose everything.  Climb to the top of the leaderboard and earn spiffy high-level gear, all in a day's work!
Getting started can be tedious, but outgoing social players will enjoy the camaraderie.  The best groups will join up with new players and help them explore the map.  The deeper you get in the game, the more possibilities that are open to you.  Players can switch "classes" quickly by equipping different sets of gear to handle the task at hand.  There is no getting stuck as a particular class of character only to realize that you want a different gameplay experience.

This game would be suggestable to new comers of the adventure genre who really don't want to spend five bucks on Myst or Secret of Monkey Island until they know its a worthy investment.
As one such new comer, there were some puzzles in the game that took atleast a little thinking out of the box, but not something too far out. However, for the most part, the puzzles are easy to piece together and require little out of the player except for a little bit of short term memory, making the game extremely short (about one hour on the first playthrough, without hints, and twenty minutes on my second). Some of the puzzles are oddly specific, though, requiring you to click on specific things, things that the player can figure out without the narritive aid of the character, which can be irritating.
As for the animation and graphics, I kinda liked the visuals, as I liked the emphasis of things on characters, such as a large gut, but it was obvious that the animator had little work when it came to walking, as most of the time, the character slides across the floor. Also, some of the animations just look silly or are just cut out, maybe to spare the animator from animating something a little harder.
The voice acting is horrid. The main character has little expression in his voice and after a first playthrough, it grates against your ears, at least in English (the game was made in another country, most likely Argentina, so Spanish would likely sound a lot better).
The sound design is pretty alright. There weren't any out of place sounds, and I kinda sorta liked the main menu theme, though it sounds a little out of place at first.
Overall, the team could have done a lot more polishing to their game, but I would be willing to pay for another chapter of this series if they stepped it up a notch in all departments. For the modest price of free, and considering that you are intrested, check the game out.

: Clustertruck is a 3D Physics Platformer where you jump from truck-to-truck while avoiding obstacles. The levels get harder and harder as you go advance through each world that has it's own gimmick, such as lasers, cannons, flamethrowers, etc~
: The soundtrack is mostly synthpop with light electronic sounds mixed in, it fits well as background music. But that’s really all it’s worth for.
Art and Design: The design for Clustertruck is very minimal and basic. Levels lack colour in order to not distract the player. However the majority of them are very white, which strain the eyes sometimes and can be distracting if you have gunk on your screen.
. That’s how Clustertruck works. Each truck is completely random with where it’s going to go most of the time. Most of the traps and obstacles are random too, activating whenever they want. This is a
for a Platformer that requires tight movements. The game punishes you for things that you can’t help, such as randomness. This would be okay if only
levels were dedicated to Randomness. However, the majority of the levels are completely random, which is just annoying trying to learn a pattern for a level just to have your timing ruined by something random going on.
. There’s a few very bothersome collision issues with the trucks and some levels. It’s very common during the Medieval World where the buildings hitbox is bigger than it appears to be. That and it’s also possible for you to get lodged inside the bonnet (That’s the front of the truck for Americans) if you jump as the truck moves over a small bump.
. The soundtrack, while good background music, is nothing too impressive. It’s not repetitive, which is nice. Although I don’t see myself listening to it casually while not playing the game. But that’s just me. If you enjoy it, more power to you.
Watching others play this game is sooo exciting and fun. It’s hilarious how popular Youtubers and Streamers react. Even more hilarious when the developers butt in and personally mess with the game while the Streamer tries to figure out what’s going on.
The game also has Twitch-Intergration that allows viewers on Twitch to vote for different abilities for each level. Which means that if you’re watching a stream, you can directly affect the Streamer’s game. That’s awesome.
The developers are also some of the coolest indie devs out there right now. They're a great bunch of people who know when to joke and how to take criticism from what I've seen. Good on you guys, if you're reading this.
The idea of Clustertruck is also a pretty good one. Jumping from truck-to-truck while dodging insane traps, pretty neat!

A collectable card game that isn't a collectable card game! Instead of creating your own deck, each player is given a random set of cards in 4 houses (Earth, Wind, Fire, Water) and 1 specialty house of their choosing. A set of draw rules is in place to determine which cards each player gets, so it isn't imbalanced. It may sound like pure chance, but it's quite possible to predict your opponent's cards and moves and generate some strategy off of that.
There's also a solid AI opponent to practice with. Fans of CCGs should check it out.

I finished this damn thing back in June, and I still find myself thinking about it, so I figure, sure, I'll write a review.  Might as well, since that'll probably boost it's visibility on Steam.
So first of all, this game has pretty much everything going for it on an aesthetic and narrative level.  While not treading on wholly new ground, it handles its story very well and manages to be effective despite being composed of very familiar elements.  The same goes for the art style.  Harsh shadows, sharp angles, and cool colors are all very common in indie science fiction games, but they're done as expertly as possible here and they really add to the mood.  Finally, the sound design is top-notch.  Some stellar voice acting sets the standard easily lived up to by the eerie ambient sounds, all mixed to perfection for evoking the sense of isolation this game wants to acheive.  The only area I wouldn't praise so highly is the music.  It works and provides a good backdrop, but there's nothing incredibly standout or memorable.
The real pitfalls for this game lie in, well, its gameplay.  Many have already pointed out the clunky shooting mechanics, which don't kill the experience entirely, but can be rather frustratng at times.  However, I would also argue that some of the puzzles tread into "jump up and down with your finger on your nose five times and rub a dead spider on the window to activate the disco ball which you then shoot down to make a hole in the floor" levels of obtuse.  It's infuriating and legimtately detracts from the overall engagement.  Not all of the puzzles are this way, but enough of them are to get on my nerves and I suspect quite a few other people's nerves as well.
However, I think that what this game does right honestly makes up for the qualms I have with it.  It's far from perfect, but it's a fairly unique experience and one I thoroughly enjoyed having.  I can only hope that future installements live up to the promise shown here.

The visuals are pretty, the game runs surprisingly smooth on my cruddy computer and okayish laptop (at least with graphics settings set to performance > quality). But honestly, you're here for a cluster♥♥♥♥ of trucks, not a cluster♥♥♥♥ of particle effects.
Graphics: Who cares, it's trucks
The controls are very smooth and responsive, although sometimes you can slip and slide around on trucks instead of landing and jumping off of them because the game doesn't detect you achieving a "landing" state on them, which can get a little annoying. But it only happens if you're going really fast and on sloped trucks.

The game features 80+ levels spanning across many worlds, which is honestly pretty short for it's price point, even if I did preorder it for $12. As for the gameplay, I haven't had this much fun playing a game since Super Smash Bros 4 came out. It is extremely fun to play with, and once you get the hang of it, it's super difficult to break the habit of flipping around and jumping off the sides and backs of trucks at high speeds, especially when you nail that golden angle and complete the level in a stylish way. Makes me wish there were replays of some sort.
Oh, and did I mention that the game doesn't have a Y axis lock on your camera movement? You can do frontflips, backflips, and even play a level upside down while facing the wrong way if you wanted to.

You spend the mana points to use spells or spawn out monsters that have a cost in the top right corner, attack power at the bottom left and health in the bottom right.
