I wanted to wait a bit before writing a review.  This game does take a while to get used to, after all.
So far, this is one of the best games I have played.  I have played Skyrim for several hundred hours (maybe not too "impressive," but still enough to have an informed opinion of it), and Oblivion for around 50.  Morrowind blows both these out of the water.
Maybe it is partially the jump (for me) from console to PC.  Maybe it is just my mindset at the moment. But Morrowind makes its sequels look ... lackluster.  You begin the game with a vague idea of what you're doing and no clue who you are.  And truthfully, I'm not much farther than that in the main story.  And I am completely okay with that.  This game immediately makes you want to explore all of it.  It starts you off in a little town and teases you with these big names that are not so far away.  And, yeah, you can take a silt strider to them.  But frequently a quest makes you leave the big cities. And it is then that Morrowind shows it's true colors.  I walked out of the first town, no idea where I was going, and came upon a man falling from the sky, screaming, with a few scrolls on him that begged to be tried out.  And then I, too, was falling out of the sky.  I later came across a woman who had fallen in love with a man who had stolen her jewels and begged me to find the thief for her.  I walked into a strange-looking edifice and found it filled with high level dremora who quickly taught me that I was not yet welcome there.
Save frequently, get a few mods (like the Real Signposts mod.  It truly is a must for navigation. And a mod to make you run faster will keep the game from seeming so slow.), and buy this game.  If you are a fan of the Elder Scrolls, or even of RPG's in general, you will not regret it.

One of the best games in the series (coincidentally the first one) gets a major HD update. Fans of the original collectively wet their pants when they heard Capcom was doing an HD retexturing. REmake was beautiful when it came out in 2002, but this version is just godlike. Same gameplay, same style, just updated HD textures. Forget about the new control scheme, it's garbage. Thankfully Capcom left in the tank controls that the series originally shipped with.
If you're new to the old-style RE games, do yourself a favor and familiarize yourself with the tank controls. The new one is horrible. Since the new controls depend on where you're at on screen, when you change camera angles it gets all sorts of messed up. I tried the new controls and found it impossible to dodge enemies that I had no problem dodging before. In certain areas it might be beneficial, but who wants to keep switching controls over and over again during gameplay?
Enough complaining though. My one complaint is negated by the fact that it's moot if you choose an alternate setting. Either way enjoy the creepy ambiance, beautifully rendered scenes and hordes of twisted abominations gunning for your throat.
Here's hoping Capcom does the same thing with RE2.

So far I have completed two out of the [I think] three chapters, and I absolutely love this game thus far.
Pros:
- Really good story (if you read all the notes)
- Scares are EXACTLY how I like them i.e. no popups; instead there is sound, atmosphere, and fear of the unknown
- The sound has been used VERY effectively
- Atmosphere is amazing
- Helmet light mechanic is cool where you can see stuff how it was before the ship sank
- Puzzles are a perfect difficulty level
- Game design is good: you can go back to the start anytime you want inside the level (which is good incase you missed a note)
- Super cheap price - ITS WORTH - the time it takes to beat the game is two hours-ish
Neutral:
- Graphics are pixelated (in my opinion that is effective in a game like this, but some people don't think so, so that's why it's a neutral point)
- Pace can be slow sometimes, but in other times there are adrenaline rushes, which makes this a neutral point
Cons:
- No in-level saves, and the level takes about 40-ish minutes if you play at an enjoyable pace collecting all notes
- Can't change window size/resolution (no fullscreen) or graphics quality -- don't really need to, but still
Overall Rating: 9/10 Strongly Recommended

I played the original Lost Chapters on the PC, saw this in the steam summer sale and thought I'd give it a go. TL;DR Can recommend! (Runs fine on Windows 10 btw)
Pros:
-Fantastic dialogue and humour, you will appreciate this even more if your British as a lot of regional accents and stereotypes are used.
-Very well done linear RPG of old. It's easy to navigate around and you always know where to go. At the same time there are some nice touches on thi sides such as buying a house, getting married etc
-Game looks beautiful. The unreal engine really brings this vibrant game to life, some of the old characters look a little weird at first but you'll get used to it.
-Good/Evil decision making split. I played this game years ago and then transistioned into The Witcher Franchise.  Your choices have an impact and make the story consequences split, as well as how towns folk respond to you.
-Combat is fast paced and satisfying. Hurling your sword around smacking foes feels great, at the same time there's a nice mixture of spells to choose from too
Cons:
-Little buggy here and there. Had 1 CTD throughout the whole thing which is fine. But sometimes, particularly at the start some NPCs bugged out and wouldn't attack me.
-Shows its age. If you played Skyrim and Witcher 2 & 3 get ready for a step back. Game is still fantastic but respect the fact it came out 10 years ago.
-Sometimes you accidentally attack friendly NPCs mid combat when using the lock on mode, NPCs are quite patient and forgiving but still kinda annoying.
I heard some people moaning about keyboard controls, can't say myself, I used an Xbox controller throughout and the button set up "Traditional" was great for me.
Overall smashing game worth a pick up!

I usually won't write a review for a game but for this one, I thought it was nesccary.
Fable has always been a game that I've liked, It's a good series of a games, even if they're not the sprawling epics usually promised there usually always solid games.
Fable Anniversary is no exception.
First, Every action having consequences is a bit of an oversell. Every choice has immediete consequences, but  that doesn't mean every choice changes the world. in fact very few choices actually change the world around you. You'll get bounties for committing a crime, and people may react to your characters differently, but your actions don't change much how the story goes.
An example of this is, in one quest you're given the choice of killing or sparing someone. If you kill them they're dead you never see them again in the game. If you let them live, you get a few moments of dialouge with them, than they leave Albion forever so you never see them again. The choice's don't have any real weight, except affecting your players look and how npcs react to you.
The Combat is solid enough, although it kind of punishes you for not being a Jack of all trades. I would never suggest only doing Will or only doing Skill or only doing Power, All 3 are needed for combat (Although skill less so) You will likely be fighting with a mix of Power and Will. Skill is alright for bosses but the time you'll need to charge a bow makes it almost usesless against the regular mobs of enemies you'll face.
The Social and Property side, If you're coming from Fable 2 or 3 you know how much the Social skills and Property are important. In this game not so much. You have about 1 house per town you can buy without killing the owners and the Social actions are not nesccary at all if you can get a certain level of atractiveness, Seriously I don't think I used a Social action once in the game but I had a full level of affinity with every elegible bachelor and bachelorrette.
Game time, I currently have 14 hours, that's what it took to beat this game (Both Main game and Lost Chapters) while also doing Bronze quests and most of the silver quests except 3, The last 3 were basically quests I couldn't see a Good way of doing so I skipped them. It's short for an rpg but it's fun enough to make up for it.
What does Anniversary add? Now I haven't bought any of the anniversary DLC so I don't know how good the weapons are it adds, but what I do know about are it's Steamworks compatibility and Graphic/Audio remaster.
Steamworks: Definately in it's infancy, there are not a lot of mods and a lot of them are Heavy Weapons guy at the momement. If playing as heavy weapons guy with a Heavy Weapons hammer and Shrek wasps sounds good than this is the game for you.
Graphic/Audio remaster: It's amazing, the whole thing looks like a brand new game, on my machine enemies with a bit more detail like the White Balverine or Twinblades, too a little longer to render but for the most part it was seamless.
What would I suggest you pay for this game? 15-20 dollars. While the Remaster looks like a brand new game it's really the same Fable The Lost Chapters you can pick up for 10 here on steam. However I definately think it's worth an extra 5 or 10 dollars, but don't buy it for the full 35. However if it's on sale I'd say pick it up in a second. If you're a Veteran of the Series or a new player Fable Anniversary is a solid game that will give you at least 28 hours of enjoyment (14 for Good, 14 for Bad Charachter)

Armored Gear is a indie game where you run around a map shooting up tanks and sometimes buildings with a tank on your own. Feels like bomberman with guns or something like that.
Pros:
It's actually a little fun for the first few minutes.
Cons:
1. Misleading tags.
"Strategy": There isn't any strategy involved in this game. If I may say so, there's hardly even any thinking involved. You get the hang of it within a few minutes and the rest of the game is simply repeating the same thing over and over; flank the enemy tank, spam your cannon to take it down and repeat until you win the mission, then do the same thing again and again.
"Great Soundtrack": The soundtrack isn't bad, but putting "Great Soundtrack" in the Tags is ridiculous. We have games with awesome soundtracks like Sang-Froid Tales of Werewolves and they don't even have the tag.
2. Pixelated Developer Splash Screen
I've played a lot of games; good games, bad games, average games, whatever and I've never encountered one where the developer didn't care about putting up a good first impression; no matter how bad the game was, chances are they put considerable effort to making sure their brand didn't look terrible. It tells players that "Hey, I put in effort." no matter how bad the game is.
It was considerably disappointing to boot up the game and see a splash screen featuring a *very* pixelated image of the developer's logo. It was clearly not a design decision as the rest of the game graphics wasn't even close to being that pixelated.
3. A lot of bugs.
The game's got a lot of bugs. They aren't game breaking, but they can be quite annoying. You can boot the game and the text can be glitched up so bad you have to reload it. The game can crash when you try to continue from where you left off. Your movement can glitch up. You can end up stuck on the upgrades page etc etc.
4. Repetitive gameplay.
The game is very repetitive. You can play it for about 20 minutes and you would have experienced most of what the game has to offer. Dodge slow bullets and shoot slow bullets at tanks, watch them explode and repeat with other tanks. Worst of all, there's no timer, nor any sort of indication of your progress on that mission which means that for most missions (save the ones where you just have to destroy a building or two) you're probably just shooting everything you see and *hoping* that the mission ends so you can carry on to the next. Which is pretty much the same mission on a slightly different layout.
5. Room for improvement.
5a. Make things more interesting faster.
Fighting the same tanks with the same AI for 3 or more levels in a row gets boring real fast. Fighting new enemies like the tower, the boss, the rocket tanks and the infantrymen was a breath of fresh air but they got stale real fast too after you realize they either only appear on one level and then don't appear anymore (or too seldomly), or they just keep using the same boring AI.
5b. Make the levels more different.
Levels start out with different layouts, but with so many destructible terrain everything just end up blown up and it feels like level 1 again. The goal usually feels the same, too. Destroy ? tanks until you complete it.
5c. Tell the user how far he is into the mission.
Which brings me to my next point. At some point into the mission, I'm just shooting tanks up randomly hoping that I'll progress. It'll much be better if I had a sense of achievement, a sense of moving closer to the goal completing a mission with every tank I destroyed.
Conclusion
Meh.

Mahjong is one of those games that I always come back to, like poker or Klondike solitaire. It's casual, yet still challenging. However, the challenge has to be built within the rules of the game, not artificially added as is the case with Pretty Girls Mahjong Solitaire (and its sequel, "Delicious! Pretty Girls Mahjong Solitaire").  As with many solitaire mahjong games, tiles can and will appear directly on top of each other, making a board impossible to complete. This would be fine, were there options available to shuffle the remaining tiles and/or undo moves. Unfortunately, PGMS doesn't offer those, so be prepared to play the same boards over. And over. Another big problem is that tiles that are "trapped" vertically somehow are removable (they shouldn't be), while tiles that are trapped horizontally work according to the game's rules of being inaccessible. It's all a bit of a shame, because mahjong otherwise works really well in the standard Pretty Girls environment of unlockable girls/levels. The usual lack of options are here (for example, windowed vs fullscreen), along with simplistic, but servicable, music and sounds (although the moans that occur when you make a move are just silly).   For my money, the benchmark for Mahjong games is still Cyna Games' Kyodai - a game which is 20 (!) years old, but still plays beautifully, even on Windows 10. As for PGMS, your time invested is not worth the frustration you'll experience.

Lionheart is a monument to grind. It loves nothing more. If there’s a goal to obtain, an obstacle to overcome or a secret to find, the answer is--universally--that you need to grind some more. Nothing gets done without grind. Want to do something other than advance the plot? Perhaps you'd like to see a bit of character development? Sure, that’s an option... but it lies behind the grindwall. Think it’s time to put to use some of that gold you’ve obtained through your countless hours of grinding? I mean, you could. But not for something useful like better armour; you’ll need to collect items you can’t buy for that. How do you get those items? Through grind. As in all RPGs, your characters gain experience and grow in strength, which is accomplished through grind. That’s standard, but do you also want them to learn new, powerful moves to complement the stat-buffing level gains? Those don’t grow organically with levels. You need special items to trigger instances that teach your crew those advanced skills. Those special items first have to be built. And how do you get the items you need to build them? Grind, grind, grind.
Because there’s so much grind, Lionheart is a long game topping at 100 hours, should the game's promotional blurb be believed (though I logged a little under 40). There’s a story behind it all, one openly trope-reliant that contains--and stop me if you’ve heard this before--a young, naïve farm boy coming to the big city in the search for adventure! Who (and what are the chances of this?) also happens to be the son of a once-famous mercenary, now looking to continue Daddy’s legacy. Crikey, if only there was a stoic guardian figure, or a disinterested love interest, or a ditzy support character, or a tomboy princess. There are all these things. There are all these things and more.
Lionheart is unapologetically superficial. Though it adorns itself in JRPG trappings, it also unashamedly borrows from visual novels. So, all that grind isn’t tapered with exploration like you’d normally expect. There’s a winding labyrinth you’ll need to conquer before you see endgame. That much is true. There’s also a plethora of side locales that either need to be (or can be) explored on your never-ending grind to collect stuff from which you can make more stuff. There’s a mine you can grind ores from, and a haunted forest lousy with enchanted wood. Or a plateau where you can hunt boar and sentient wheat (which you use to make packed lunches), or a lake you can visit to batter mermaids to death and steal their scales. But you only visit these places in the shallowest of senses; there’s a static hand-drawn background and a progress bar. You press start and a counter moves through the bar, going from start to finish. There’s a boss battle, or at least a bulked-up fight to look forward to at the end, where you progress the plot or earn your crafting McGuffin upon victory. Then you do it over and over and over again.

With 2017 already fulfilling its unspoken promise of delivering a deluge of delectable games I will probably never be able to finish, it does become difficult to limit my commitment or even outright pass up on a particularly interesting find. Smaller projects especially seem to have this hold on me. Lionheart, a visual novel/RPG hybrid developed by doujin circle Shiisanmei is a fine example of one that is engaging, but a joy to come back to between play sessions. Players take on the role of Leon, a young man dreaming to be adventurer. After a chance meeting with a young woman named Maria, she enlisted his unique abilities to explore the Magic Labyrinth, “Libra Corridor.”
In many regards, when it comes to tone, Lionheart does put me in the mind of plenty of old-school RPG’s that comes off with a straightforward and neutral voice. That is not to say that it doesn’t contain any moments of levity or earnest, but it is difficult most of the time to tell what is going for. Of course, with the comedy being far more prevalent, players will probably find themselves chuckling most of the time at the endearing and sometimes frivolous humor. In particular, Maria pretty much made the game for me, her standoffish and deadpan personality clashing nicely with Leon’s oblivious behavior. Along the way, other members are added to the team such as: Leon’s guardian, a nun of the church, greedy merchant, samurai nekomata, naive princess and more that are not only valuable party members, but also lend a hand into the brand of humor and storytelling. The narrative is by no means great, yet serviceable for what it is and gets the job done.
Where most of the time will spend spelunking and exploring the Libra Corridor as far as the storyline is concerned, you will have the chance to visit other areas in order to gather much-needed resources, train, and learn new skills (if you have the required material). As far as dungeon exploration goes, it is a very simple affair where players are given a map and get to choose the movement speed. Depending on the speed, you may run across resources more frequently or enemy encounters. The quickest option will usually prompt more battles as the slowest and normal options will yield more resources, but not a guaranteed outcome. When entering combat, battles are turn-based allowing you to use up to 3 members in battle. One of the things that I like about the battle system is that it is reminiscent to the “Mana/Atelier” franchise that allows you to swap frontline and backline party members, yet makes it more necessary especially in fights where enemies can take a more of a beating and players need to recover HP and AP in order to perform special skills or even wait out their emblems (magic abilities) cooldown period. With their being 3 difficulty levels to choose from (can be changed at anytime), you will most likely find yourself using these strategies often on any, but a great deal more choosing the “Heroic” mode that doubles enemy damage. My only complaint about Lionheart’s battle system is that there is no way to speed up battles. This is especially noticeable going into the aforementioned optional areas to grind for material only to get greeted with back-to-back encounters of annoying foes that you have no choice than to whack with normal attacks if you don’t feel like letting your emblems recharge over and over. The game does promise 50-100 hours of gameplay, however wouldn’t be surprised if a good 10-15 hours of that is counted toward toiling through optional areas.
For game that was produced by a fairly small team, the production values for Lionheart looks great. Background and foreground environments are somewhat bland, but the character artwork and designs easily makeup for it. I am also impressed that the game does contain Japanese voice acting in various parts – a feature that wouldn’t be missed, but nice to have nonetheless. Being appreciative for the work that has gone into the game to fit the experience, it is very regrettable that there are some technical shortcomings. One in particular, the game is not very response on the world map, usually taking a few seconds or clicking elsewhere for it to show the drop down for areas that have more than one section. Another issue regards saving that takes a minuet or two before it actually does. With Fruitbat Factory being stellar with the titles they publish, these are problems that surely will be resolved during the full release and nothing that seriously impacts the game enjoyment factor.
Having plenty of other games waiting to be started or finished this year, Lionheart is another delightful title I’m proud to add to my playlist. From the spread of characters to easy-going storytelling, I would be simply remissed to understate how much amusement I was able to get out of it and still have a few more hours left to pour into it. For those that enjoy the grassroots approach to RPG’s that you can only get from the indie scene with a splash of old-school style coupled with modern sensibilities, I do highly recommend giving it a chance. Seeing how Shiisanmei seems to be at work with a sequel, I can only hope it won’t be too long until I can join Leon on his next adventure.
——————————————————————————————————————
Pros: Entertaining cast of characters, simple and solid combat system, adjustable difficulty settings, a lot of optional events.
Cons: A few minor technical issues, no way to speed up or skip combat animations.
Final Verdict: Another satisfying and engaging RPG that should be able to offer plenty for fans of the genre craving a meaty experience.

So, this review is more of a first impressions kind of review. I'll get to a full review after I finish this, but I think I've played through enough of the game to talk about it some.
Judging by the kind of games Fruitbat Factory puts out, it seems they prefer doujin titles that nobody would otherwise recognize or purchase. I don't mind this, since many of them are good games, but occasionally you get a game that's more hit-or-miss in terms of appeal. I knew from the screenshots and promotional material that this game wasn't exactly going to be my cup of tea, but after winning a key, I thought I'd at least try it out.
Lionheart, at its core, is a visual novel pretending to be an RPG. This is in due part to the fact that it's built on the popular KiriKiri engine, which gave us splendid titles like Fate/Stay Night and GaoKao.Love.100Days. Quite honestly, this game has some elements that could make for a great visual novel. High quality art, a script with decent font and no perceivable grammatical mistakes, pleasant music...there's some good stuff under the hood.
Unfortunately, I can't help but be bothered by other elements that aren't as good. The sound mixing isn't quite the best, as the voice acting is just a little too quiet compared to the music (I put both at the highest settings possible). Many scenes in the game aren't fully voice acted either, which is honestly more of a nitpick, but the inconsistency bothers me. The effects and transitions aren't terribly impressive, which is a shame because I know the KiriKiri engine is capable of some great effects.
Now, that's all for the visual novel side of things. As far as the RPG stuff is concerned, there's little that impresses or engages me. I'm not a big fan of Dragon Quest-style battles (with Dragon Quest VIII and Undertale being rare exceptions), and this game does very little to spice things up. Three party members are allowed to battle at a time, although party members can be switched in between battle rounds. Oh yeah, battles are split in two phases in this game, which I will call preparation and combat. During the preparation phase, you have four options:


In combat phase, battles work for the most part like a Dragon Quest game, with some minor cosmetic and mechanical differences. A turn order akin to Final Fantasy X's can be seen on the bottom left of the screen in case you're wondering what's coming up. I wouldn't say the battles are difficult to figure out, although I only played the game on Normal difficulty. The harder difficulty doubles damage dealt by enemies, which I can see getting tough for a variety of reasons. Healing items, materials and even money are hard to come by if you're not playing on Casual difficulty. Add to that the fact that some areas are restricted to you unless you have a specific item and you have the makings of a slow, tedious experience.
In short, even with some saving graces, this is about as generic a VN/RPG as you can get. Some people might find mileage in that somehow, and that'll be beyond me, but if you're looking for a turn-based RPG you can get invested in, I'd suggest saving your money and buying Trails of Cold Steel when it comes out later this week. Just sayin'. :P

-Very open ended world, you can flat out fail the main storyline by killing important NPCs

Cons:

This game is what Skyrim promises to be. I love all the Bethesda games, even Fallout 4, but there's no denying this is the best Elder Scrolls made IMO. Daggerfall is too archaic for me to want to pick up, and while I recommend the Morrowind Overhaul project, I'm playing through for my first time using only a mod to fix the resolution and loving it.
You can craft spells with EIGHT DIFFERENT EFFECTS. Want a spell mixing multiple elements and area of effect damage? You can do it. Want to summon 8 Daedric Beings with the press of a button? You can do it. Want to create a spell that heals as much as it damages, allowind you to indefinitely practice your magic on one enemy? You. Can. Do. It. All the systems in this game are about as deep as that, and alchemy requires FOUR different machines to properly do it.
The two biggest barriers to entry are the graphics and combat. Morrowind Overhaul fixes that completely so that's squared away. The combat is purely stat based; I do more damage with a mid range sword than the best most OP axe in the game, because you'll miss your swings with a weapon you have no knowledge of how to use. Also WATCH YOUR FATIGUE. % chance you hit is based on how much fatigue you have, don't be like those dumbasses who mash left mouse and wonder why they miss every swing.
Pros-
In depth lore and a wide variety of topics to ask NPCs about.
The best magic system in any game I've played.
Free form quests- I have a sword powered by the soul of a god I slew. Nobody told me to do that, Morrowind merely provides the weapon (Daedric Shortsword) the soul (not gonna spoil which god) and the means (in depth enchanting system) to do it.
Wide variety of locales and quests.
Good storytelling that isn't always spoonfed to you. To cure vampirism without looking it up online, you need to read a couple of books and figure it out yourself. As far as I know, it's impossible any other way besides discovering it by dumb luck or google.
Truly an RPG. Very easy to stick to your characters beliefs, unlike in Skyrim where the story makes you a good guy no matter what you do because you saved the world from Alduin.
Cons-
Somewhat obtuse mechanics. Once they're learned they're badass, but hard to do so. I recommend looking up how to do alchemy, enchanting, etc. as the game expects you to have an instruction manual.
Some bugs. Morrowind Overhaul fixes thousands though.
Personal Preference-
I think having to read to figure stuff out without the game just telling you is awesome. Some might not.
No quest markers. You get directions, and late game are in unexplored areas and have to go off of handwritten maps.
Conclusion-
10/10 best RPG I've ever played. Quite a challenge, but if you're up to it, it's the most rewarding game I've ever played.

To start: I used to add a header to these reviews, but since it far too often made reviews too long to submit (an unfortunate consequence of my sometimes very verbose method of writing), I've instead decided to leave the header on my Backloggery.
Gameplay: I picked up The Fall when it was on sale, and if you're anything like me, you no doubt will have picked this game up based solely on the trailer. While this trailer does somewhat sell up the game, it is by no means a disappointment. We'll talk more about the trailer in the story section, though. The gameplay of The Fall is one of a rather esoteric genre known as the Cinematic Platformer. Two sterling examples of this kind of gameplay are Another World/Out of this World and Flashback (the old one). However, if you remember particularly frustrating moments from the former example; do not worry. This game has no absurdly precise platforming in it. Truth be told, this game doesn't have much platforming at all, but that's perfectly fine; it doesn't need it.
Rather, the core of the gameplay plays more like a traditional point-and-click adventure game in which you will sometimes be able to cleverly figure out the puzzle and other times just spend five or ten minutes just rubbing objects on other objects to create success. Yes, this game does have some Sierra logic here and there, much to my dismay. Also, due to how dark the game's presentation is, it is sometimes more challenging to even distinguish what you need to be clicking on. You can only interact with objects by shining the flash light from your gun on said object, so you don't have to worry about accidentally using things over and over again, but considering how dark the game is, it sometimes becomes a task of flailing your light everywhere in a desperate attempt to find something that you can rub against something in your inventory. Yes, the repetition of the word something was intentional in that last sentence.
Much like Another World/Out of this World, there is some element of gunplay. Don't worry, though; your gun has infinite shots, so you won't be screwed over by that. You only really fight one type of enemy throughout the game, but once again; that's not that big of a deal. There are also some abilities that unlock as the game progresses, but not all of them are available by the end game. I was confused by this until I found out that this game was meant to be the first in a series. Considering that, it is in a way no surprise that the game's platforming and combat felt inconsequential at times.
Overall, the gameplay isn't the most brilliant aspect of this game. The puzzles can be alright at times but othertimes completely obtuse; the platforming and gunplay are rather insiginificant at times; however, they do their job to keep this game from just being another walking simulator. 7/10.
Story: I mentioned that I'd be talking about the trailer here, so I most definitely will be. The "Conform" trailer represents this game as being mainly about an AI's crisis of identity as it gradually gains more and more of a simulacrum of what we humans would call a true consciousness. While this is a core theme of the game, there is more to it than that. There aren't many charcters in this game; in fact, there's really only three characters including the enigmatic Caretaker. They all do their job serving the plot and the dialogue is really the main presentation vehicle of the themes. Just the way it should be in my opinion. I don't want to spoil too much, obviously, but just know that this game has some very excellent writing behind it, and if you've not already pored over the idea of the technological singularity, this will certainly be some very interesting philosophical material. Also this is part one of a series. The game does wrap up conclusively, but I'm very excited to see where the game goes from here. 10/10.
Graphics: Again, the trailer could be a very big selling factor on this front. This game has an excellent art style, and the animations are all very very fluid, save for instantaneous turning around and all that. That's a minor detail, though. There also appears to be a sort of "light filter" always on whenever you're playing the game, which unfortunately doesn't have the greatest color depth (it looks patchy). That's a bit of a disappointment, but not too much of a mood killer. Obviously, this game doesn't need too terribly intense of a computer setup to run, so if you can run Windows 7 with Aero on, you should have no issues running this game. Apart from those two minor issues, I really don't have any other complaints about the graphics side of the game. Ther is the issue with interactable objects being hard to see, but that's more relevant to gameplay, since HUD elements appear showing you where the objects are whenever you run over them with your flashlight. Yet another example of why style trumps substance. 5/5.
Sound: There really isn't much in the way of music here, since it is all ambiant pieces. However, it's
ambiance. This game has one hell of an atmosphere, and that is thanks mainly to the soundtrack. Excellent stuff. The voice acting does a fantastic job as well, eerily portraying AI constructs gradually gaining a semblance of humanity, be it intentional or unintentional. Yeah, there really isn't much else to talk about here other than the sound design and voice acting is top notch. 5/5.
Overall scores are: 7/10/5/5; cumulative score of 9.0/10. Definitely worth the $10 if you've got the $10 to throw down. Not much in the way of replay value, and the game is rather short, but the quality of the adventure more than makes up for it. Better to have a short, really excellent adventure than a long, doldrumic one.

My all time favourite indie game. Its a simple side scroller puzzle game, with short bursts of combat here and there, and its absolutely outSTANDING.
You pay as an Autonomous Robotic Interface Device (ARID) on board a Mark-7 Combat suit that has crash landed on a mysterious planet. Your piolet (the actual human inside the suit) is unresponsive, and it is your duty to get them medical aid. However, you have no idea where you are, and there seems to be very little signs of life around you.
Its a puzzle game, so that parts pretty self explanatory. You need to navigate your way through this unknown environment, and as you progress, the story just gets more and more convoluted as the puzzles get more and more difficult to solve.
One of my favourite things about the game is your characters attitude. You'll see what I mean, they are just fantastic.
No spoilers here, but trust me when I say, whatever you THINK is happening... its not.
Play the game.
Save your piolet.
But remember to follow the rules.
You must ALWAYS follow the rules.

An engrossing story with a side of hard sci fi in the tradition of Asimov. Interesting characters, an engaging, somewhat creepy atmosphere and setting and extremely good pacing make this hard to put down. A few unexpected moments of humour also fit surprisingly well. The small number of choices present are well written, though the options are occasionally ambiguous. It also handles philosophical concerns in an unpretentious manner that's not clear-cut, adding to the story rather than coming off preachy. All in all I loved it, though it is a little bit short. P.S. loved the ending, hope they do more in the future :) Seriously thinking about replaying immediately.
EDIT: Just found out that this is only the first of 3-parts (next part in 7-8 months according to developer's Youtube comments) courtesy of DjSF's much more comprehensive review. Also, forgot to mention that the menus are awesome - they help tell the story and engross you in the world.

The good: The writing is amazing, developing new and interesting tropes and taking the narrative to places I've never been before. The voice acting, sounds, and art are perfect and establish a wonderfully dystopian mood. The advancement of your character's capabilities is done in a very clever manner that I've never seen used in a video game before.
The bad: First of all, I didn't see anything suggeting that this is the first part of an episodic game, so when the conclusion failed to explain many mysteries, instead saying "to be continued" it was a surprise. The controls are strange and hard to get used to. They're also not super responsive which can make combat occasionally frustrating. The puzzles are much more difficult and obscure than I would have liked. They tend to be of the "go everywhere for no reason and rub everything on everything else for no reason until something randomly works" type. They don't require cleverness to solve but rather dogged persistence. A strong ability to memorize the slightly complicated map will assist you also as the map is a vertical maze and many of the areas look kind of similar. Generally the puzzles get in the way of the wonderful writing rather than augmenting it. I enjoyed the game much more once I found a walk through to get me past the more obtuse puzzles.
But all in all, good writing can overcome a myriad of sins, and this writing is great. I strongly recommend The Fall.

Although the game is pretty well polished and starts off with an interesting concept, I'm not sure if the follow through is what I was expecting. I would still recommend it because it is certainly a unique and passionately crafted game, but keeping that in mind, there a lot of reviews outlining the good, so I’ll be focusing on the aspects of the game I found a little bizarre. Here’s my good bad review?
While determined to finish Mystic Destinies, the frustration built up to a point that I took a break from playing the game a couple of times and I had to wonder if there were others who felt the same as I do.
Visually the game is rather appealing. The character sprites are very beautiful, although I have to say the men do sometimes look a little strange. I’m also pretty sure everyone is wearing full on lipstick at all times, which I guess… why not? Rock that gold lip gloss Shou. The CGs are also a little hit and miss: some are very sweet and beautiful, while others are blurry and visually inconsistent character-wise.
The music is nice – it changes up a lot to fit the mood, nothing too special. Actually, the nicest piece of music is probably the main title song, it’s kind of melancholy and atmospheric, but I can’t recall hearing anything like it in the main game.
The characters are all pretty interesting and I especially would have liked to see more of the side characters have their moment. Some more levity and fluff would have also gone a long way towards world building, developing characters and relationships, as well as just breaking the story up. On that note, it is a little frustrating being handed small snippets of magic-world stuff without ever diving into it fully. So many conversations start with "So that power your using, it's suuper dangerous like you're gonna expl-" or "Oh yeah your mum was-" and then it's suddenly interrupted by "anyway we should focus on this relationship/ mission/ crisp packet." Yes, this is an otome game, but some of the best VNs I’ve read have been effortlessly immersive and I so wanted to learn more about this secret society and it's magic.

The love interests are a combination of uniquely appealing and strangely stereotypical. What I really mean is that the characterisation is a bit dodgy. To me, most everyone seemed just shy of being 3 dimensional; there were a lot of inconsistencies and sometimes a general lack of personal investment that prevented me from ever really getting a strong grip on who they were as people. Despite what I said the focus is very heavy on the guys and their issues. This is all well and good if utilised properly, but not only does the game often put the protagonist almost totally on the backburner, there are a lot of missed opportunities to explore the LIs as people instead of “they did the difficult thing and then it was good”. It’s this double whammy of not much development on either side and everything just felt very circular.
Finally, the protagonist is very unlikeable. I’m sorry, but as I read route after route I couldn’t help questioning what it was she wanted. She has very little in the way of personality, humour, motivation etc. and I couldn’t believe how her role in the story just sort of fizzled out in most routes. The prologue is a little rushed, but it also had one of the most interesting
ever. I thought it was fantastic and I really felt for her. I was so excited to see how the game handled this trauma: how the characters would react to it, how she’d grow as a person, how she’d deal with being
, would she learn everything she possible could etc. I was pretty disappointed to find out there are only brief mentions of vague “studying”, a couple of small magical outbursts (quickly forgotten) and brief emotional venting (also quickly accepted in a sad-backstory-bro way) to keep us going.
Her magical journey of self-discovery is more like the convenient journey of plot discovery and her personal growth felt kind of minimal. She spends entire chapters bumbling around in awe, making stupid decisions, reacting in ways no normal person would react to things, and just generally lacking in all self-restraint and tact (but not in a funny, satisfying way). Also, I noticed that the ‘right’ choices for happy endings are often “be quiet and let man do the thing”. She has some of the most interesting abilities and yet seems to have very little interest in learning about them or sorcerers in general;
.
Not to mention, the entire time, information is kept from her to an infuriating degree and she never pushes further. She studies business and plans to take over an international company as CEO but frequently can’t manage to remember a single fact or put two and two together? Is this girl ok? What is happening? Why does everyone blow her off? Why do a least three separate guys suddenly have crushes on her when all she’s done is be emotionally distressed? Why isn’t she asking questions? WHERE IS THE UNABATING RAGE? After everything that has happened to her, my favourite part of the game is when, in most epilogues, the protagonist says something like
That, and the part where college students drank beer out of glasses instead of bottles – totally ruined my suspension of disbelief.

Huniepop is a misunderstood game. Underneath all that sexual contents lie a relatively fun puzzle game. Think of it as Bejeweled, with sex. Basically all you need to do in this game is to match tokens. The more tokens you match, the better, as it will net you more score and, and sometimes a power up token, which if broken can net even more score. Some girls prefer different type of tokens, which will net you more score if matched, though they may dislike certain tokens, which if matched, won't make you lose your score, but you will get very little points for doing so. There are also penalty tokens, which will reduce your score if matched, and some power up tokens, which provide some bonuses to the tokens matched, or allows power ups to be used.
Other than the puzzle aspect, there is the dating aspect, where you need to buy stuffs for whoever you are dating. Some girls like certain types of items, which will help you in terms on improving your traits. Some items, if given to certain girls, will net you a present in return. This present will contain an item which will help you in your dates (aka some power up used for the puzzle sections mentioned earlier). Some power ups are useful depending on your style of playing. Once you have dated all the girls, you may unlock another mode, where the difficulty keep on increasing. Basically the date never ends (three cheers for endless polygamy and dating behind the girls back).
There are many types of girls you can date. You can choose the girl net door, the Asian, the MILF, the cougar, the mega betch and so on. They have different personalities, but this does not really affect the gameplay aspects of this game. It's mostly on your preferences on who to date, though note that under certain circumstances you may unlock additional girls to date. Once you reached certain amount of..... love meter, you will get to sleep with them if your date at night is successful. This will consist of another puzzle game, albeit without the penalty tokens mentioned in the usual puzzle games. Keep breaking them and you will hear the girl moan a lot, once you filled up the meter, you will get to hear the girl reach her climax, and a CG image of the girl naked (or semi-naked). Yay.
Overall, if you like puzzle games and massive fan services, you may enjoy this game. Just don't play this game in front of your parents or children. They may think you are some kind of a weirdo. I know I am one.

Spore is by far one of the best sandbox evolution based survival games I've played. Given that I haven't heard of any other games that pursue this kind of playstyle, my review may be slightly biased. You will start off as a single cell that has been brought to your planet by a meteorite. You can choose between playing as a carnivore or an herbivore. In the first stage (Cell) the carnivore is argueably the better choice because there will be plenty of creatures to eat, and you get parts to add to your cell faster this way. The currency in this stage is DNA points, which can be gained by eating plants (herbivore) or meat (carnivore). Once you have filled the progress bar to full, you will advance to the creature stage. In this stage, your cell evolved into a creature and migrates onto land with a group of your species. You are able to add legs and arms in this stage, and can add a filter mouth or jaw in order to make your species into an omnivore. I highly recommend this because you are not stuck with being forced to find animals to kill or migrate to find more fruit to eat. The currency in this stage is the same as the currency in the cell stage, however is gained by allying groups or destroying them. Once you have finished the creature stage through defeating or allying other groups of animals, you will transition to the tribal stage! In this stage you band together with your group and make alliances with other tribes or exterminate them. There is a wide array of tools available to choose from in this stage, from fishing spears, to stone axes, to healing rods. All of them serve various functions and your main currency to purchase these buildings is food. Which can either be gathered from the wild or plundered from enemy villages. Once you have finished the tribal stage, you will advance to the civilization stage! In this stage, the tribes you either destroyed or allied will band together to form your first city! You get to design a lot in this stage. The town hall, factories, houses, entertainment, boats, cars, airplanes! It's all at your fingertips! The main currency in this stage is called Sporebucks. This is earned by selling spice, the hot commodity in spore, which is produced by geysers on your planet. Eventually, other groups of your species will arise with their own cities. You can either choose to ally them, purchase their city through economic means, convert their city through religious means, or force their city into submission through military means. How you played each stage determines which kinds of special abilities that you have. In the civilization stage, the way you played the tribal stage determines whether you are a militant or religious city. How you caputure an enemy city determines its specialization. Or for instance you capture a military city by religious means, you can choose whether it is a military city or a religious city. Once you have achieved total global domination, you will advance to the space stage! Most people dislike the space stage because it's "boring" or "too different from previous stages". I think it is the most fun stage because you can purchase star systems, plant colonies, craft planets to your liking, discover other empires, destroy lesser empires, uplift a species in a lower stage to a higher one, terraform planets that were 150 degrees Celsious to a comfortable 22 degrees, control the spice empire through taking ownership of the high profit spice planets, defeat the evil Grox empire guarding the center of the galaxy, and so much more! People dislike it because it takes so long, but that's the fun of it. You are but a single planet in a galaxy of tens of thousands! Have fun, explore! They've even included the Solar System for you to find (I've found it)! After playing this game for over a week now, I've expanded my empire to a measly 30ish systems. I look forward to conquering the Grox and expanding my fruitful empire to the farthest reaches of the galaxy.
tl;dr A great game with tons of customization as you expand from a cell to a galactic superpower.

Pros:

-Cool large world to explore, one of the more unique locations of the TES series
-Complex mechanics (this could also fall under cons for younger audiences, but it's a pro to vets)
-Interesting characters (that walk like they have to take a♥♥♥♥♥♥:-P)
-Very open ended world, you can flat out fail the main storyline by killing important NPCs
-Very rewarding character progression. Go from a physically disabled manbaby, to a God far greater than mr. Dragonborn

-Sometimes confusing quest locations (I personally very rarely get lost, but sometimes a quest cave isn't exactly where you're told)

All in all a solid 9/10 RPG.
A tip I'll give to newcomers; your starting weapon skill MATTERS. Going with Long sword skill but not Short sword, matters. You most likely will get the♥♥♥♥♥♥beaten out of you by those pillow noming rats if you go in with a weapon you didn't set for you to be skilled in. If you end up wanting to level different weapon skills, practice on lower level enemies slightly later on, it'll make it less of a headache. This game is what Skyrim promises to be. I love all the Bethesda games, even Fallout 4, but there's no denying this is the best Elder Scrolls made IMO. Daggerfall is too archaic for me to want to pick up, and while I recommend the Morrowind Overhaul project, I'm playing through for my first time using only a mod to fix the resolution and loving it.
You can craft spells with EIGHT DIFFERENT EFFECTS. Want a spell mixing multiple elements and area of effect damage? You can do it. Want to summon 8 Daedric Beings with the press of a button? You can do it. Want to create a spell that heals as much as it damages, allowind you to indefinitely practice your magic on one enemy? You. Can. Do. It. All the systems in this game are about as deep as that, and alchemy requires FOUR different machines to properly do it.
The two biggest barriers to entry are the graphics and combat. Morrowind Overhaul fixes that completely so that's squared away. The combat is purely stat based; I do more damage with a mid range sword than the best most OP axe in the game, because you'll miss your swings with a weapon you have no knowledge of how to use. Also WATCH YOUR FATIGUE. % chance you hit is based on how much fatigue you have, don't be like those dumbasses who mash left mouse and wonder why they miss every swing.
Pros-
In depth lore and a wide variety of topics to ask NPCs about.
The best magic system in any game I've played.
Free form quests- I have a sword powered by the soul of a god I slew. Nobody told me to do that, Morrowind merely provides the weapon (Daedric Shortsword) the soul (not gonna spoil which god) and the means (in depth enchanting system) to do it.
Wide variety of locales and quests.
Good storytelling that isn't always spoonfed to you. To cure vampirism without looking it up online, you need to read a couple of books and figure it out yourself. As far as I know, it's impossible any other way besides discovering it by dumb luck or google.
Truly an RPG. Very easy to stick to your characters beliefs, unlike in Skyrim where the story makes you a good guy no matter what you do because you saved the world from Alduin.
Cons-
Somewhat obtuse mechanics. Once they're learned they're badass, but hard to do so. I recommend looking up how to do alchemy, enchanting, etc. as the game expects you to have an instruction manual.
Some bugs. Morrowind Overhaul fixes thousands though.
Personal Preference-
I think having to read to figure stuff out without the game just telling you is awesome. Some might not.
No quest markers. You get directions, and late game are in unexplored areas and have to go off of handwritten maps.
Conclusion-
10/10 best RPG I've ever played. Quite a challenge, but if you're up to it, it's the most rewarding game I've ever played.

Contrary to what the trailers (and, at first, the interface) suggested to me, The Fall plays like a point-and-click adventure game. Maybe you're better at watching trailers than I am and interpreted it better, but I was really expecting much more of a Metroidvania than I got. I'm not about to complain, though. The game that The Fall turned out to be was, I think, a much better game than what I was expecting when I bought it. However, I do have to agree with other reviewers on one point: It's pretty short. I beat it in about three and a half hours and I wasn't even particularly bright about it.
You are A.R.I.D., the artificial intelligence aboard a mark-7 combat suit, activated in order to ensure the survival of your comatose pilot. You run swiftly up against the limits of your own programming, and as many of the game's puzzles involve circumventing internal obstacles as external ones. It sets up an exceptionally well-written narrative as A.R.I.D. interacts with the bizarre underground facility it finds itself in, and the people that live there. Do note on that point that The Fall is the first game of a planned trilogy; the story ends on a maddening cliffhanger with fewer questions answered than not, and I can scarcely contain my anticipation for the second installment.
Gameplay sits comfortably between the likes of a point-and-click adventure game and a cerebral, puzzle-heavy platformer; kind of a
meets
. Combat, I'm sorry to say, is nowhere near as interesting as the trailer seems to promise. You're given a handgun with a flashlight which allows you to examine your surroundings, and soon the option to switch to lasersight mode to shoot, though you'll spend a good 80% of the game in flashlight mode. With the exception of one sequence near the end, the shooting parts can typically be solved by strolling forward and aiming loosely for heads; though the cover tutorial section promises otherwise, your foes are largely too few, too far between, and far too inept to be terribly threatening. This is to The Fall's credit, I think. Despite being a combat AI loaded onto a suit of power armour, fighting isn't really what you're doing here.
Special mention needs to be given to the dialogue. The writing is outstanding, and the voice acting is some of the best I've heard anywhere, indie game or otherwise. A.R.I.D.'s voice actress is particularly superb, which you might not expect from the flat monotone of the trailers. I can't expound particularly on that point without risk of spoilers, so you'll just have to take my word for it on that one.
TL;DR: If you're into thinky adventure games and don't mind waiting for the other two games, this is well worth picking up now. If you're not patient enough to wait on the plot to resolve itself, wait on it a bit, but absolutely get it later when the other two come out. And if you don't care for story or puzzles, give it a pass. In the interests of disclosure, I picked it up in a Humble Bundle; I didn't want to pay full price for it at the time, but after having played it I'm convinced it would've been worth it.

I got this game in a bundle, and it has easily been one of my best bundle grabs. Keep in mind that this is a three-part game, and - at the date this review has been made - the next installment is projected at ~12 months. Also be aware of the shortness of the game, it is beatable in one sitting - I completed my playthrough in less than 2.5 hours, proceeding at a leisurely pace. That being said, if you are interested in a well-written, well-executed story revolving around an AI protagonist tasked with protecting its suit pilot, this game is more than worth the playthrough.
If you like atmospheric puzzle games, space themes, and a good storyline, then you should really enjoy this game.
The aethetics are great - the details add nicely to the dark atmosphere. The presentation of the AI interface (when you press ESC to go to the menus) is really cool. The startup screen mimics the faceplate of the pilot, and the cracks are a foreshadow for the story (and you also have a cracked screen effect whenever you are low on health/shields). The sounds and music are both very good and do a great job of creating a gripping vibe.
The controls are very simple, and the tutorials are quick and helpful whenever a new mechanic is introduced. The learning curve is minimal to moderate, depending on your experience with puzzlers/point-and-clickers. Most of the puzzles are intuitive, and can also be solved with a bit of trial and error. There is also a combat element, and this part is fairly straightforward and not very challenging.
For the ahievement hunters, you MUST do a second playthrough to get 100% completion (and if you do everything correctly the first time around, this will be for a single achievement). I am currently contemplating whether or not I should do a speedrun for that 100% game completion.
The gameplay thus far has been pretty good - I really enjoyed experiencing your suit "upgrading" (or "unlocking," to be more precise) new abilities as you progress through the story. Most of these unlocks occur due to threat to the pilot's safety (ex: you unlock stealth capabilities when a sentry gun locks sights on you), and the small ways these can influence gameplay is great (ex: you later unlock semi-automatic fire - which decreases your damage, encouraging you to use more cover/stealth to protect yourself from incoming fire). You will be moving back and forth between areas to solve many of the puzzles. The map is not too large, and enemies do not respawn.
I really enjoyed the dialogue and dialogue options - the AI protagonist reminded me a lot of GLaDOS from the Portal series. A.R.I.D's (the AI) development over such a small amount of gametime was refreshing to see, and I look forward to seeing how the next installments play out.
Admittedly, the ending reveal of The Fall was much more obvious/predictable (at least to me) then, say, The Swapper. This does not, however, make the game any less valuable or fun to play.
If you are interested in atmospheric puzzlers with a good storyline, definitely check this game out. For it's current price ($9.99), I would suggest waiting for a sale, considering the very short gametime (unless of course, you are really dying to play this game).
Highly recommend!
Cheers,
DJSF

Reveal the Deep is a very heavily atmospheric game that knows how to squeeze out the feeling of dread throughout its 3 chapters.
No mistaking, I finished the game in about 2 hours, but not a moment went unappreciated. From the incredibly dark corridors of a shipwreck, you explore the notes and story of a group of various travelers while on an expedition and discover what occurred.
I was impressed by the shadows in the ship as you moved about, the delay for turning the helmet light on and off always had me holding my breath as the light dims to almost pure blackness, while also waiting for the light to return and expose what, if anything, was lurking in the dark as it was off. Small details like pulling the camera in very closely while exploring small spaces to really exacerbate the claustrophobic feeling really impacted my experience in the entire game.
The sound was on point, delivering creaks of the ship, whispers and general unnatural noises  that made every step forward a test of courage. Having consistent screen tremors as you explored gave the sense that you were not on safe ground, as if the ship was being swallowed by a creature unseeable by uncorrupt minds.
The experience is fairly linear with branching paths and shortcuts out becoming available, but there's generally a good indication of where you're supposed to go throughout without the use of a map, which was pretty impressive to me, given that it certainly feels like a game akin to the "Metroidvania" design with its presentation and the entirety of the paths you explore certainly feel long and winding.
A few simple puzzles are in place during the chapters but they weren't difficult to solve as they mostly consisted of pushing blocks into positions, using various means. This is not a bad thing, as the story was the main focus for me and that was very well done, in my opinion.
A few control issues such as getting off ladders sometimes causing simple transitions onto a platform to fail, but this never once caused any kind of progression blocks. While not a real issue considering the length, the lack of saving was noticable in one or two sections of the third chapter, so if you have to stop in the middle of one, just be aware you'll start at the begining of that chapter.
Over all, Reveal the Deep is a short but very sweet gem that, with a price of $0.99, is worth every cent.

I don't often get dollar-store games from Steam because they tend to be often underdeveloped products and/or not worth my time. Reveal the Deep is something I would consider underdeveloped, yet I felt my time was respected. (For the most part.)
Price is something I don't often take into consideration for reviewing the game's quality. However, I do think for an indie team's (or lone developer's) first game on Steam, the price point is low enough that if the game doesn't interest you then you won't have much buyer's remorse.
With all that being said, I hope Lazy Monday Games learns a lot from this project to create something more substantial gameplay like The Swapper while also keeping all the great aspects made in Reveal the Deep.
Unlike games like Home where it has more left to the imagination about horror and the gameplay boiling down to one or two choices, Reveal the Deep has some gameplay and horror elements into its gameplay design. None of which make this game into a full puzzle game, yet it's more enjoyable to play than to watch.
The best design decision for RD is how levels/chapters give the impression of free-form exploration without feeling more linear than it actually is. Messages, items, new pathways that lead back to previous areas, etc. improve an otherwise boring experience of going down a linear corridor with horror-ish moments.
On a second playthrough, I would probably find the level design more linear than first impressions; however, that's okay because exploration is all about the sense of discovery, which is what the game excels at for its short time.
One huge oversight in exploration is how areas are split into chapters. There is nothing of a Metroidvania design between each level nor any reason to replay a past level for deeper insight into the narrative. It also means when you want to quit you'll have to restart the area you last played, which is mitigated by how small these areas are when you rush them. So you'll only have to replay 10 mins at most.
The other downside to Reveal the Deep's core gameplay is that other than the exploration there's little else to keep your interest. The puzzles are far too bland and simple to keep you engaged.
The game's biggest problem when it comes to its puzzles is not that the ideas behind them are terrible; the problem is that they have nothing unique to them or added to make the conventional puzzles act differently.
RD's main puzzles boil down to pushing/interacting with blocks either by pushing them or turning on and off your light source. Other puzzles with light horror elements involve using the headlight to fend off monsters. Lights also seem to have a space-time effect for revealing new passageways to explore or notes to read.
The light gameplay gimmick could've been enough to make these puzzles more interesting on their own, but the game never commits enough to the idea to make them original. (Similar to a game like Glare that uses the light-mechanic at the start and then completely forgets about it.)
This issue is why, if the developer(s) took some lessons from The Swapper, they could center a main mechanic for an entire game as well as giving more playtime for their product while not artificially expanding the game. They could also offer a greater sense of challenge, exploration and character to the gameplay.
They could also learn some ways to avoid some of the obvious pitfalls for storytelling in these exploration, horror, puzzle-games that have become all to common tropes now to be avoided.
I won't be mentioning spoilers in this section. These are rather criticisms I noticed by how the game reveals its narrative, mechanically as well as the content you find. I'll try to limit my examples to the most obvious problems with some specifics mentioned.
The biggest trope this game stumbles across is the same thing you have to ask yourself with H.P. Lovecraft's work: Who is taking the time to draw/write out these notes? Many messages you come across have some detailed images of horrific situations (or make the reader question why are they writing this stuff down) that get in the way of the story. It's easier to swallow when it's some crewmember bored out of his mind doodling some of the crew but harder to accept when tragedies occur.
On a similar point, some of the written material is weird. The ending line for all of Isaac's letters is hard to ignore when the events become more immediate. Context clues you find from exploring can be pure nonsense. One example is a random note you'll come across, "The dinosaurs used to have ears--something that is forgotten by fossil records." Most of the early clues you find, either environmental designs or the protagonist's thoughts, are relevant to the story in some small way. This is in a stark contrast to these meaningless thoughts.
Those are problems I can point to as objective faults of the narrative's design. They don't need to be overhauled, they just need to be handled better so every detail is important and there's just enough explained to keep some mystery in check. (For example, why is it that turning off the light seems to take us back in time? The game never explains this in any way.)
On a more personal note, I would advise not following the staple "Mind is superior to the body; spirit is stronger than physical means" meaning you find in a lot of artsy games. I've yet to find one game where the handling of that idea wasn't pretentious and it wasn't at odds with what the rest of the game is focused on. Unless there is an immense amount of theming into that idea, then adding it in for the hell of it is worthless.
My advice to create a game with meaning is simply this:  Stick to creating a story that has details hidden beneath the surface, leave some details open to the imagination, then let the reader/player come to the conclusions of their own. Those types of stories will ALWAYS be more impactful to the reader, and you won't come off as standing on a soapbox; you'll be making people believe their own messages through your game.
All these criticisms are said with admiration for what has been achieved so far. I am more often not a fan of horror games, and even the staple jump-scare tactics were effective here as well as the atmospheric horror of the unknown. So coming away from this game with a positive outlook has to mean something from me.
In the end, Reveal the Deep is a game you won't regret purchasing if you have some level of interest for its narrative. It won't end with a satisfying conclusion but the hour and a half of playtime you'll experience will be sublime with the feeling of exploration.
Even when restarting a chapter, you'll probably beat this game under two hours, which makes me worried for the developers' sake. This is another reason why I think they should take the ideas that work here and make a full-blown game to warrant more purchases as well as people retaining their interest with it.
Quality made games like this one need to be commended more often, especially when they don't waste the player's time.

I have been playing this game for 2-3 years so far, and I would highly reccommend trying it. I'm going to be fair and try and give perspective to everyones expectations.
The Infinite Black (TiB) is a lot of fun for players who want to meet new friends. In my opinion, this is what the game is about. It is an extremely grindy game, and though you might see you can purchase special currency to augment your gear, there is nothing you can do for levels, and a level 30 in all ultimate gear is nothing to a level 200 in all legendary gear.
The Reality
This is a 2D Space MMO game. The graphics are not meant to be state-of-the-art, layered and shadowed. If you are wanting to play a game to immerse yourself and get lost in a space sandbox, discovering new planets, don't even expect that from this game. This isn't that
Don't expect this game to be easy to noobies. It's not. You'll see a lot of negative reviews about this game after somebody has played 1-2 hours, and they haven't even began to actually get into what this game even is about.
This game is about community. Corporations/Alliances are the end goal here. To get the absolute most out of this game, it is about networking, friends, and socializing to create bridges. This is what the end game looks like, along with a few things I'll list below.
What I enjoy about the game
Besides the social aspect (which is #1), there is a lot of variety in builds/strategy. You essentially have 6 things to do in this game.
1) Farming (main source of leveling/gaining gold)
2) Hunting (Up to 20 ships diving in and out of invasions/rifties looking to pvp and gain combat points)
3) Rift/Black Invasions (PvE, up to 20 ships, Great source of BDs/XP/Gold)
4) Garrison Busting (End Game stuff, done with 15 ships to essentially take out enemy HQs)
5) Garrison Defending (Also end game stuff, done with 10 ships, to defend your HQs)
All of them are fun, but as you see, this isn't Elite: Dangerous.
As I previously stated, I've been playing this game for years. Moderators have always been excellent and helpful, the community has always been helpful, and even guys that have been life-long enemies, there is a mutual respect there where we enjoy figuring out new ways to destroy each others ships or garrisons.
If you do play this game, my suggestion to you is that you go into it knowing that it is a very grindy game. It's versatile, however. Got 30 mins at work? Log on your phone and join a hunt team for a bit. When ya get home, farm up some credits to buy the new piece of gear you want.
My main piece of advice for anyone who tries this game is MAKE FRIENDS. JOIN A CORPORATION. When you do this, you're joining a group of players who are out to help you. Why do they want to help you? Because the stronger you are, the stronger the corrp is as a whole. Corp members can farm together, hunt together, bust garrisons together, rifty/invy together.
If you're looking for a game that takes meticulous hand eye coordination and immersion, this isn't your game. Come here and make friends, join up and have fun. This game can cater to people with 10 hours a day to play, or only 1 hour. It's a lot of fun once you have people to play with. The community is really what has been bringing me back all these years.

I have had this game for about a month, yet I've played as much as did with TF2 or other games that I have enjoyed and owned for more than 2~4 years.
It's as if I've departed this world to live in Calradia instead.
This game may be close to 6 years old, it may look outdated (which it is), and even though I've missed the sale and bought this game at a full price: the only regret I have is that I've spend so much time playing this game and probably that I'll continue to do so. (Can't do anything else!)
Yes, this game has flaws. AI is rather dumb, exploitable in some cases and screws you over in other. Some quests instructions aren't immediately intuitive. FIghts can get a little repetitive, yet auto-resolve functions is as good as "I forfeit button" (Yes, auto-resolving can be seen as cheating by some, but I'm not saying it should give better results than you playing yourself).
But, those flaws are like a barely faint itch you feel once in a while.
Mount and Blades Warband is a new open world you can live in. Skyrim is good, but Calradia (I dare say) is better. It doesn't have the beautiful scenery of the newer games, but Calradia gives you a different sense of wonderlust. I just can't pin point an aspect that makes this game so immersive and interactive.
You end up liking your hero companions, the fellow nobles of your country, as well as some enemy lords you just happen to develop liking of. Of course you make enemies once in a while and have to run after them until you have them locked up in your dungeon. (Keep your petty ransom, He's rotting in there until the war is over!)
I guess one of the best thing about the game is the difficulty. It constantly challenging. It does get eaiser with time as you build a bigger and better army and you and your companions get stronger. However, defeat is always a possiblity and you learn how to play safe and when to tug tail and run. But you eventually find a way to break down the enemy army; and pick the ground where you know you can make a stand and win.
Calradia is riddled with towns and villages and castles. Yet, I also ended up developing affection for my fief. Dumped troops onto it to keep those filthy Swadians away from my land. (Screw you Harlaus!) Those that raided my village got chased, hunted, defeated, and locked up in my dungeon.
There is so many things in this game that can make you love and hate, both in good sense.
Calradia is an ever changing tempest of wars between factions, you ride the shifting tides, get lost in it and enjoy every moment of it.
I do not think it is too late to buy this game now. It is worth every penny (or nickle for us Canadians) even today I'd say.
P.S. - Get Diplomacy Mod, it adds rather critical functions to the game play and interface. Although vanilla is good, it gets better.

Clustertruck is a fantastic idea on paper. You scoot around at incredible speed and jump from the backs of one truck onto the next truck. The Trucks behave somewhat randomly, and explosions and truck crashes happen.
However, I found the gameplay loop to be predominately about repeating mundane jumps over and over again hoping that the truck RNG allows one to be positioned somewhere you can go. Even in the earlier levels trucks randomly swerving sideways without warning (while you're droping onto them), sudden truck pileups on even the slightest obsticals, and my personal favorite of the player's momentum not working quite properly as they slide right off of the truck they tried to land on, all contribute to a solid MEH experience.
Frustration is based almost entirely on two factors: 1. not being omnipotent about the level design coming ahead (leading inevitably to a repeat) and 2. The RNG stranding you on a truck that is driving off map into the far distance or directly into a game ending obstical.
The platforming is floaty but rewarding at first, and the difficulty creeps upwards at a modest pace. However, the RNG is what determines a good run vs a bad run, and you're going to have levels where you repeatedly end up playing again and again and again. Sliding around, falling in gaps, and hitting questionably sized hitboxes on obsticals leads to many repeats and it starts wearing out the game's intial charm very quickly.
There is an Upgrade system, however you'd need to play enough of the game at a decent technical proficiency and with good RNG to successfully get any of the upgrades within your playtime. Also, the Double Jump is just pathetic. Aside from that, it appears that the online leaderboards are jacked up- or I didn't get far enough to unlock the ability to have a clear time of literally 00:00:00.000.
In short: Floaty platformer with indie charm that relies too heavily on RNG to make its rudimentary platforming interesting. Upgrades contribute to some continued enjoyment, but the game itself is mostly cute rather than serious about keeping its playerbase. If rated on a scale of 1 to 10, with 1 being nonfunctional garbage and 10 being some kind of gaming revolution, I'd give it about a 4. It's not offensive, but just doesn't seem to work that well for anything beyond the charm of RNG-AI Truck Based Platforming.

Curse of the Old Gods Curse could have been a fair throwback to likes of early MacVenture series, had its otherwise decent writing and fair puzzles not been buried under indistiguishible swathes of magentas and blues.
The story is somewhat reminiscent of Sierra's Laura Bow (Dagger of Amun Ra) and manages to be quite entertaining if a little too linear. Presented puzzles aren't by no means original, but fairly accessible and woven well into the games narrative.
It's undeniably mountainous task for single developer to do all the games art, music and code while keeping up with a reasonable release schedule; and quite understable to be tempted to cut some corners. Overimposing fixed CGA pallete over digitized images may look like a good idea in theory, but sadly does not translate well in practice. It does help a great deal for all the different source material to blend in quite nicely without too many touch-ups but the resulting lack of detail would have made the game utterly unplayable had it not been for the hotspots toggle conveniently added to the top right corner.
Had the developer chosed either true EGA* (16 colors out of EGA 64 color pallete) or 256 color VGA and spent a few extra weeks on touchups, dithers and outlines, the game's visuals could have easily matched the estethics of early Dynamix games such as Rise of the Dragon or Heart of China which took similar approach of using digitized video as a baseline for ingame art.
In overall, Curse of the old Gods is fair choice to be made for its asking price, but it is competing for your attention with much more polished games from late 80's and early 90's being re-released on digital platforms in the very same price bracket.
A lot of mechanical aspects haven't aged well but I'll be daedra damned if it still isn't one of the best adventures out there.
