Alright, so first off, I didn't really think I'd like this game as much as I do now that I've played it. I didn't really care that the graphics sucked, since it is a pretty old game, but I did hear some new Elder Scrolls players say they didn't like how dramatically different it was compared to the newer games (I'm fairly new, since the first Elder Scrolls game I played was Oblivion). Even though this game is nothing like the newer ones mechanic wise, it's still an amazing game for multiple reasons.
- This game is pretty realistic in multiple ways. When you do quests, you have to ask around and find things out in order to complete it, since there are no quest markers. When you get a quest, the quest giver gives you the place/person, but might not go into specifics on where at that place they are (if they're in a town), or they might not even know the name of the person. Everything you know goes into your journal, and you're sent off to complete said quest. If the quest is set in a town far away that you have to get to, there are multiple ways you can do it, since there is no fast travel. You can pay someone to take you by silt strider or boat, or you can go the long way and walk there, depending on where it's at.
- The weapon variety is also realistic, along with the way armor is set up. Morrowind has all the basic weapons the newer Elder Scrolls do, along with some others. Staves have been in all the Elder Scrolls games I've played, but they haven't worked like they have in Morrowind, since you can actually attack people with the base weapon along with tossing magic at them with it. You also have some other weapons that haven't made an appearance in the newer games, like Tantos, Wakizashis, Spears, Halberds, and various throwing weapons, such as throwing knives, darts, and throwing stars. With the armor, you can basically have a layer under your armor for normal clothing, and you can put different armor pieces on at the same time.
- Many different types of spells and enchantments exist in Morrowind, more so than Oblivion and Skyrim by far, ranging from your usual elemental spells, healing spells, buffing and weakening spells to teleportation and levitation.
- The lockpicking and smithing mechanics are very different, with lockpicks and smithing hammers coming in different levels of efficiency. As you level up, you end up finding better lockpicks, but the chance of you picking a lock depends on the efficency of the lockpick if you are a low level in lockpicking. If you are a high level, however, it seriously doesn't matter what lockpick you use. I haven't really dealt with the smithing hammers that much, but I assume it is similar.
- There are a ton of guilds that have a bunch of nice quests that you can do, yet they have favored attributes that you need to have at a certain level to progress in the guild. Basically, they favor certain character builds, so if you aren't built for the guild at first, you need to work a ton in order to perform well in the guild, which is realistic.
- Morrowind features many intresting and unique creatures that vary in difficulty, but they do not level with the player like they do in the newer games, which can be frustrating to some, but pleasant to others, depending on who you are.
All in all, this is the best game of the series and the game that is truest to the Elder Scrolls universe. I completely recommend it to anyone who is willing to give this game a try.

The infinite Black review
I am going to start my review with multiple points on why I enjoy the game, then I will go into more detail if anyone cares to read more about those points.
Versatile gameplay/strategy in how to play.
Teamwork oriented (But not necessary)
Simple gameplay mechanics, but more complex strategy in how to equip your ship for different purposes.
Large objective events
Not an open-world necessarily but a large one none the less. Lots of space to kind of roam on your own and do your own thing (But it is pvp in these areas so sometimes groups can come in and try to kill you)
One of the most helpful communities I have come across and generous
One of those games that has many layers that you can't fully appreciate until you become more experienced
Versatile gameplay/Strategy: While this game does not have a straight forward objective or plot it offers the player many various play styles because this is so loose.
So in my experience someone can focus on "roiding" which is mining asteroids in the pvp area. In the game it is usually not safe to do this because the map is visable by other players and if they see asteroids disappearing it can give away your position leaving you open to be scouted and hunted. But if you equip you ship with fast gear so you can out pace your hunters it’s a fun strategy that keeps you on edge with nice rewards. Plus this area is filled with abandoned goods sometimes.
Another play style is a farming one. Where you go with alone or a small group, maybe even a large group and hunt down tough npcs and collect material and low level items. Your numbers can help ward off smaller hunting raids so it’s usually a safer option. You can equip more of a sustain build than a speed build.
Then you can form large fleets and go after large objectives such as invasions, or raiding other people’s garrisons (Corporation HQ) In these builds you usually get the standard team builds of a healer(tech), tank, grapplers, dps, and standard builds, and you go out and try to take these things out for grander rewards.
You can place bounties on people, therefore you can be a bounty hunter. But this is difficult unless you are strong enough which can take a while.
There is more but I am still new to the game so I am not familiar with other game play aspects so I don't feel comfortable writing about them.
Teamwork oriented: I kind of hit on this in the point above, but joining a corporation is hugely beneficial, as experienced players know how to help new players and they are good guides and can help carry you or even protect you in bad situations that come up. But I received great advice from my corporation when I started which has given me a solid foundation.
Another big thing about corporations is you can help fund yours allowing your corporation to undergo research which then gives your corporation specific bonuses. Your corporation can join an Alliance which then gives you more protection, and more players available to work together. Often times multiple players from different corporations in my alliance get together to conquer an invasion and we split the rewards. Or donate them to the alliance.
It is a lot of fun going out in groups to achieve certain things. Or when people try to hunt you you can scatter limiting their success at hunting. Kind of like a school of fish strategy.
Simple game play, complex gear: So battling is pretty straight forward you click on the enemy you want to target and your gun will fire at it based on its cool down. So groups have different strategies on who to target first but I won't talk about that. But this makes it nice for the phone and for talking about what needs to get done since you can worry less about fighting mechanics and more on how to conquer a base and who needs to transfer metals to who. It is nice on the phone since you can just click with your thumb and do not need the dexterity of a mouse or wasd.
But what’s fun for me is there are a lot of equipment slots; weapon, armor, storage, engine, special, computer, harvester. Each piece of equipment will provide different advantages and in some cases disadvantages. Some ships also have different abilities. For example if you have a carrier and you follow the carrier your movement speed is now based on the carrier and not your equipment. So this can be used to your advantage because you can equip that bulky gun and armor and not worry about your movement speed (just your evasion probably). But if you were solo in black, and hunted that equipment is now fatal as you can’t run away and are outnumbered. But to get more to the point is you can equip your ship to have a wide variety of bonuses or disadvantages that work in your favor based on what you are trying to do. Because this game doesn’t pigeon hole you down one path you can be as unique as you want and test out different things. While by this time many people have come up with many viable builds it’s really up to you which play style you like.
I mentioned this before in team work but there are large objectives that have high rewards and its fun taking a fleet of your friends and conquering these things.
Large map. The map is a grid system that you have to explore to discover the different paths. Not every dot will connect to those around it. Outside of the earth is the gray where beginners can farm, then you have the much more expansive black(pvp, harder npc, invy locations, sometimes garrisons). You have to farm in the black lvl 15+ so you can venture out to safer areas with less player traffic and have a good time. But closer to the gray you will often see hunting parties roaming around trying to pick off people. What I like about this is the risk reward aspect. You have to be able to deceive these hunting parties, or path in a way that you aren't found. While it sucks being hunted and killed, (especially since your equipment’s durability goes down) it is a big thrill running away and surviving. As well as find a bunch of mets(metals) or material in the middle of nowhere that you can $$$$ in. The map is large enough where it can facilitate a nice ratio between lone farming and hunting parties finding you. It isn’t enough where it is a constant threat, but just being in the black in the first place is a threat and it gets your adrenaline going haha. Sometimes it’s really chill and you don't see anyone and you have a nice relaxing time. Other times you get hunted three times in a row.
This community is very helpful whether you are in their corporation or not. I had ppl in another alliance even giving me good beginner gear to help me lvl up faster. And I have had very generous people in my alliance give me good prices for ships that they take a hit for. But because alliances rely on the abilities of those in the alliance it really favors generosity which is a really nice change from other games. That is because teamwork is necessary for large event that alliances can take advantage of. And defending your garrison from others.
There are a lot of little things to this game that you don't realize are there such a "spaceball", "skulls", and a bunch of other stuff. There is also stuff like the rift that you can’t take advantage of until you are a higher level so it has nice late game stuff too. People lvl 80 can battle with ppl lvl 15 it isnt an unbalanced game. Until you get outnumbered but there are plenty of strategies so the grind really doesn’t feel bad or difficult in my opinion I have played my fair share of grindy games.
Anyways those are my thoughts and if i didn't enjoy the game I wouldn't have taken the time to write this. Anyways I hope this helps give a good feel for what this game has to offer.

So I'll get this first part out of the way for everyone who's already played REmake for Gamecube/Wii: port runs great. There's an issue with some Nvidia/AMD cards that runs cutscenes in slow-motion, but you can fix it by setting the framerate to variable, and turning off vsync should help as well. More fixes are addresses in discussion.
For those of you that played RE back in the PS days but never owned a Nintendo product: REmake is worth your time and effort, the differences aren't just cosmetic, Capcom tightened up gameplay and enemy types to make sure you're not having an easy time.
And now for those of you who've never played Resident Evil: I'm not sure how best I can put this to you, but I think this gets the point across: This game is one of a kind.
There was nothing like Resident Evil before 1996, and despite the fact that was the first game to be classified as a 'survival horror', despite the fact that hundreds of horror games have come out since then, despite the fact that the market today is flooded with games of similar eerie atmosphere and setting, there hasn't been anything like RE since. Except of course for its sequels, until the remake came out in 2002.
This game will scare you and you will still want to play it. You'll figure out how to dodge zombies, drop attack dogs, kill giant plant monsters, fry spiteful fish, and you'll feel good about being in control for a few minutes, but then it's back to the mansion, back to running into something that could kill you unless you use your precious ammunition. There's something around the corner, you can hear its breathing. You don't have the advantage of moving the camera around so that you see it before it sees you, you're bound by the beautifully composed camera frame. The music is haunting and will put you on edge, but the alternative is no music at all, just the sound your footsteps in an empty room. Those *are* your footsteps, right?
You will learn not to shoot. You will learn that two guns mean two ammo types and maybe that crappy knife is better for your inventory. You will learn to look at a map and know instinctively which hall, room, balcony or yard that shape represents. You will learn not to pick up every item you see, even health and ammo. You will learn that never using the kerosene will cost you dearly. You will learn how to survive.
Or you'll die, a lot, and you'll learn not to do what you did next time. The point I'm getting at here is, rotate your saves.
Enter the Survival Horror c:<

This game is the definitive Resident Evil experience.
Set back in the original Spencer Mansion, ground zero for the zombie outbreak, that consumed Raccoon City. Plot is basically non-existant, but RE series was never known for good plot or story telling, if anything I prefer the setting where almost nothing is explained, you're not halted every few steps to talk to someone cliche or uninteresting. Dialog is for the most part atrocious, but as I sad with it being not the main point of the game, I can forgive the cheesy lines of voice over actors. It leaves the player to his/her own imagination, to find out what happened in this mansion and it's surrounding areas, It doesn't give you big pointy glowing arrows for objectives, so that might be discouraging to same players that have never tried playing the original games. The game just explains what it is through atmosphere and tense encounters with deadly monsters and the documents you find in the enviroment.. Only thing that will take more time than running around and cleaning B.O.W's, is puzzle solving. Really refreshing to finally see some interesting puzzle solving, that seemed to evaporate, the further the series went into B-Grade action crapfest. The game is not new, so I can't give too many points for crafting interesting puzzles, because this game is from 2002, back when cryptic gameplay wasn't frowned upon by reviewers, simply because it encouraged thinking and solving them, sometimes even under pressure. Graphics are nice, the enviroments look great, but they were supposed to, because it's all pre-rendered and the fixed camera angles make it easy to show that shine. Character textures could be slightly more high quality, but I'm not complaining, in due time modding can take care of that issue. Controls work well, there are options to satisfy both, the serie's purists (tanky clunky controls) and more modern spin of tanky controls, where it's slighly simplyfied to fit modern needs of common gamers. Sound design is amazing, though personally I think that it still lacks the certain eerie score that for ex: Resident Evil 2 had. Gun sound effects feel meaty and powerful. Zombies moan, groan, slither in the mansion halls, with equally terrifying shadow and lighting effects.
I'm really hoping CAPCOM begins to understand, that to make something good, you need to comeback to it's roots. I definitely would like them to re-release more older Resident Evil games with HD textures and better visuals, while retaining the same charm of the series that gathered the massive fanbase, but I also want them to make new entries in the series, without losing what this series was known, and is known worldwide.

Solar 2 is a simple sandbox with not a lot to keep you compelled. Gameplay revolves around smacking into things to grow (asteroid and black hole stages) or get things in your orbit so you can press some keys to grow (planet and star stages). Missions and challenges play around with these goals, mostly by telling you to avoid contact with most things and not grow.
Some people say that the game is relaxing, and it can be if you don't care about doing anything. If you want to see anything new in the game, you will have to fly through 2D space and hope that the strange physics doesn't impede your progress. I can accept being attacked by spaceships and having to avoid obstacles, but my biggest issue is that pulling an object into orbit has a bad habit of rubber-banding the object into you, reducing your mass. So the method of growing your planet or star can randomly decide to remove your progress just because the programming has clear-cut orbit paths with the first object being yanked to the closest orbit.
Even the black hole stage is underwhelming, HOW could they mess up something that should be total fun to let loose and eat everything! Once you reach black hole stage, other black holes begin to appear, although they never spawned in the previous stages of the game. These other black holes can take objects from you, and if you hit a larger black hole than your own, you are forced to restart the state with no progress. This restart is made more terrible as black holes have a nasty issue of failing to pick up many items. Apparently entire stars and systems can fly around a black hole and not actually be swallowed.
I remember liking this game originally, but I only played for about an hour. The game has definitely become dated and feels especially mediocre now. Controls are weak, physics are annoying, and the gameplay is a repetitious grind full of elements that impede your progress. I believe I got the game for cheap in a bundle, but I wouldn't really recommend it for even $2. It's a time consumer, but similar games could be found for free. I'd recommend just playing a game you know you like, as this won't last long for most players.

I hopped into the world of Solar 2 prepared to have a super fun sandbox experience of messing around with stuff in the big realm of space.
Wow that just simply didn't happen.
Solar 2 has fair music, fair sound effects and overall okay design. The sandbox design of it isn't particularly fun. Even if you're trying to build a giant solar system it is not fun.
All you can do in this game is absorb planets/stars/asteroids in your system and move around. Now that wouldn't be so bad if so much stuff was just so out of your control. Sudden planets out of no where destroy your planets or level down your "evolution" from the next object you could be. I mean you can have your planets and your star(s) and you could suddenly be destroyed by stars, asteroids, planets, evolved life that lives on planets. It would be fun if you weren't always being punished while you're trying to just build your systems. That is what annoys me.
The missions are okay. They're sometimes a little bit too challenging for the controls or are far too confusing. Some are just plain unfair. And most of the time for combat missions I found that just having a giant system and then saving it to my Solar system files and then proceeding to absolutely brute force my enemy into submission and then reloading the system before I did that is probably the best and easiest way to victory with no damage after the reload.
I really don't like how the game shoves missions down your throat either. My goal in the beginning was to just become the big crunch (a black hole) and eat absolutely everything. But I had to do that with mission markers on my screen that would never go away unless I beat them. I looked for a button to turn those off, but it was nonexistent.
I expected the things you can do, the systems you can create to be much more vast and interesting and expanse with new things to adopt into your system. But really it was just nothing but asteroid, planet, planet with life, and then just stars. It wasn't fun, it was disappointing.
Overall, with such minimal amounts of things to do "sandboxy" wise. It wasn't very fun, the missions weren't fun and pretty much a lot of things weren't fun. Nothing in this game really made me really dislike it except when planets or systems I was working on just get crushed in an instant just because a random solar system came wizzing my way.
Other than that, the game isn't bad. It's just painfully mediocre, but mediocre games can still make you smile, this one though, doesn't. It's just a timesink where you're sinking time just because you have time to kill. It won't make you enjoy your time in it, and if it does. It will be very briefly.

So, where do I begin with this game? That it's from a relatively small Turkish developer? That it's a sandbox, singleplayer, and a medieval battle simulator? Seriously, I don't know where to start with this awesome (I mean awesome as in AWEsome, not some weak equivalent of "cool") game. Well, I guess I'll get down to the nitty gritty first off.
Mechanics
==========
This game operates on two separate principles. On one side, there is a strategic map of the entire continent, complete with castle locations, town locations, village locations, what have you. This is also where your character is allowed to travel, making their path over the bridges, around the mountains, and through the sprawling plains of Calradia. Apart from the strategic map, there is the third/ first person walking camera. This is when you arrive at a destination or battle and decide to stretch your (or your horse's) legs. To swap between these alternatives in generally TAB for swapping from walking-strategic, and selecting an option when arriving at a location for strategic-walking. Battles are fought in walking mode, unless you simulate the battle (I'd suggest never doing this, unless you're okay with losing a few troops. Simulation is more risky than fighting the battle yourself.). Markets are accessed through menus and exploring the streets may lead you to find a village elder or guild master. The battles control alike, yet differing from, standard configurations. The combat is quite realistic for a game of this genre, and controls are unique as opposed to other games. Unless an option is selected to auto-block, blocking and swinging are controlled by moving the mouse in a direction and right or left-clicking. As an example: an enemy is swinging at your right side, you'd move your mouse to the right and right click simultaneously to block him. The same applies when attacking, just move your mouse in a direction and left click. The combat system is refined and complex, with many ways to diversify your strike patterns and make your own martial style. While in battle, one can command his/her troops with the f keys at the top of your keyboard, from there, you can command your troops to charge, hold a specific position (Hold f1 to command them to a position other than where you're standing), advance/retreat ten paces, hold fire, open fire, etc. Your troops will fight to the absolute death, unless outnumbered something terrible (like 50-3) so pretty much everyone is a coked-up maniac with a bloodlust as unquenchable as CommentEtiquette Erik's thirst for boys that can take a good bouncing. (ily if you got that one). So yeah, hope you got all that, onto the next topic.
Also, there's no linear story, because why would there be? It's a sandbox.
Basic Lore (Some Conjecture for Effect)
===============================
This game, being as small-budgeted as it is/was/whatever, has some pretty decent lore. There are feuds between individual lords that you can take part in, politics that you can manipulate, and kingdoms to crush left, right, and center. Ready for some pro immersion? Here goes nothing. The sparse and brutal land of Calradia, land of kings, of fallen emperors, of a fractured whole that needs uniting once more. In years long gone by, Calradia was a continent under a single banner, ruled by an empire destined to stand the test of time. But time had taken another path with the land of Calradia, and long ago, the empire fell into a spiral of glorious decadence. The men of Calradia were no longer toughened by drought and scarcity, as all was plentiful. The glorious legions of the emperor were no longer battle-hardened veterans, but show-pieces of a bygone age. Foreign slaves built their grandiose architecture, instead of the Calradians themselves, and no one felt the need to philosophise or change, for what was change but unrest? The Calradian heartland was at a standstill, content to let the sands of time rush through their freshly scrubbed fingers. In other areas of Calradia, however, unrest was brewing. Indigenous cultures, that had been long thought subdued by the race of the empire, had been flourishing, enforcing the sectionalism scarcely found in the heartland of Calradia. Powerful leaders of secretive rebellious cells were rarely found, and weren't actively sought out by the happily ignorant empire. Some cities, in open rebellion against the empire were crushed, but others were simply thought too insignificant to give way to anything. For years, this secret unrest grew like parasitic moss at the root of a tree. Support was now widely expressed for leaders of the movements, and cities were im need to be subdued at a frightening rate for the emperor. The armies of the empire were far too scarce for the vast areas of land in the empire's possession, and recruitment notices for the miltary were supported, but almost never reacted to by the public. Not much is known about the actual dissolution of the Calradian Empire, but it is known to be a particularly brutal period, with the heartland forming a last bastion of Imperial might, before being squashed like a tiny roach. Quite awhile after this dissolutionment, we find the modern kingdoms of Calradia. Occupying the former heartland of the Calradian Empire is the Kingdom of Swadia. They fly orange colours and possess a massive horde of stately, mounted knights and peasant serf infantry. In the Northern section of the continent is the Kingdom of Nords. These Northmen occupy areas once invaded by their ancestors, who stormed upon Calradia in longships, with fearsome axes and pagan gods. They fly blue colours, and field the fiercest huscarls and stoutest archers of the entire continent. The neighbors to the Nords are the Vaegirs, with their ornamental helmets and vast areas of land, they were once the most powerful force in the north. They fly tan colours, and are known for their versatility and abundance of cossack cavalry, making for a fearsome foe. The Kingdom of Rhodoks was once a Southern, fertile, and calm province of Calradia, until their Kingdom was forged through the fires of rebellion against the Swadians. They are famous or infamous (depending on if you're the Swadians) for their large, elite force of trained crossbowmen, shooting with deadly accuracy onto the hordes of Swadian agressors. To the far East lies the Sarranid Sultanate, which was once the most recently captured prize of the Empire. It fields archers, with deadly, accurate bows and fearsome, scimitar-wielding infantry. They fly the yellow colours, with no particular weak-points in their grand formations of camouflaged soldiers. To Swadia's direct East lies the Khergit Khanate, ruled by the great tyrant, Sajar Khan. Once, the area of the world governed by this massive Khanate was fractured in multiple rebellions. But, the line of the Khans had not yet achieved its true potential. In a matter of years, the Khergits had swarmed all competition in a torrent of fearsome anger. They fly purple colours, and field more troops than any, with hordes upon hordes of bow-wielding horsemen, complemented with skilled archers. So now, it is up to you, tiny and insignificant foreigner in this massive continent, to change its path for the good or worse. Now wouldn't it be nice to be emperor?...
Any mistakes I made are open to correction, I'll be making edits if anyone spots anything inconsistent with the lore. Hope this was helpful, have a nice day :D.

I'll be honest, I'd been avoiding this game even though I'm an avid visual novel and otome reader. I usually like to buy my games with all routes from the beginning because I'm impatient and don't like to wait, lol. So the seperate release dates for the routes and epilogue were really off-putting, but I took a gamble and decided to buy all available routes now instead of waiting for the rest. I'm SO glad I did! While not without flaws, the story was great and immersive. Each route shows you a new and interesting aspect of their world and I found I couldn't get enough.
I do however have a couple of compaints. When you start the prologue, I feel like they just toss you into the story and right into the action of meeting the boys. While this might not bother everyone, I personally like when they give you a bit of an introduction to the MC and give me a chance to connect with her before meeting the love interests. Also, as you go through each route the writting and storytelling begins to improve and I love that the developers skills are growing with the game, but it can also leave some routes feeling like they weren't developed to their full potential.
I'd also like to point out something I don't see often in these games that I absolutely love and that's how the MC develops. I feel like each different route and the different choices she makes develops her personality in different ways. Her experiences influence the type of character she is and I personally love this because there is nothing worse than having an MC with a personality you hate or can't connect with. While this does mean that occasionally I didn't like the MC in certain routes, I absolutely loved her in others and enjoyed watching her show different growth through out the routes.
Overall though, the games pros definitely outway the cons. This game has beautiful art and music, whose style sets it apart from the usual of this genre. I definitely recommend this to otome and visual novel fans or anyone looking for something new and different within these type of games.
Lastly, I've been searching for information about a possible release date for Takumi's epilogue and Hikaru's route and have had no luck. If anyone knows where I can find this information please let me know! It'd be greatly appreciated!

Story and Characters
I have to admit, this is the best character route to date. Takumi has significant character growth and shows a lot of different emotions throughout the playthrough. The main story I believe, is the strongest yet out of all the routes and takes the player in for a rollercoaster ride of emotions. Like previous character routes, I really like how most characters appear in the other story routes and add depth to the development to the world and storytelling.  I also enjoy that unlike most Otome's where the answers are cookie cutter and easy to tell which are the "bad" answers, this game does not insult your intelligence and instead has more complex dialogue between the heroine and romance interests.
Art/Animation
Overall, animation was amazing. I have played a lot of Otome games in the past and this is one of the few that I can always remember for being visually stunning. I get lost just looking at the backgrounds and all the subtle changes in facial expressions each character shows.
Sound
Mystic Destinies: Serendipity of Aeons overall has an AMAZING soundtrack. I was really impressed with the music and sound effects in this game. Takumi's route in my opinion has the best music so far. The music fits the plot, characters and is so darn cool~ Of course that's Takumi approved.
Enjoyment
I am in euphoria at finishing Takumi's route. Takumi's story was intriguing, captivating, and thrilling at the end. It felt bittersweet when I finished and it kept me wanting more. By the end of the game you can really feel the power of the love that is shared between the heroine and Takumi. Takumi is a really well written character and with the strong plot it makes the player wanting to finish the game in one sitting. All this, with a really good soundtrack and one of the best romance routes in the game, I recommend this game because it is one of the best Otome games out right now. 10/10.

Pretty Girls Mahjong Solitaire is an anime-themed solitaire mahjong game from the same developer as the other Pretty Girls games.
Mahjong solitaire is the single-player, tile-matching mahjong game most familiar to western computer mahjong players. The Pretty Girls variant spices it up with timed rounds and the opportunity to see a number of anime girls in 'sexy' costumes as a reward for winning rounds.
The interface is clean and tidy and the tiles are easily distinguishable. Background graphics are nice, but not overly interesting. There's a weird little 'thing' driving round with a lance that's a bit weird, but it maybe an inside joke that I don't get.
Most people playing the game are likely to be most interested in the girls themselves, however, who are nothing special. The anime art is attractive enough, but it's certainly not 'Pretty Girls gone wild' as stated on the Steam store page for the game, and most of the costumes are very tame and not overly sexy.
Music is rather loud and grating, but somehow fits the game. Sound effects are also loud and mostly the sorts of electronic bells and bleeps one might hear walking past a pachinko parlour. There are also various exclamations in spoken Japanese from your chosen girl, but these just seem to increase the sense of depravity from playing the game.
All in all the sound is well produced and appropriate enough, but I found it annoying enough to simply mute my PC most of the time I played.
Pretty Girls Mahjong Solitaire plays like any other solitaire mahjong. Each stage begins with stacks of random mahjong tiles laid out to form a pattern, and the player has to remove the tiles a pair at a time until there are none left, at which point the round is won. If there are tiles left and no remaining visible pairs, then the round is lost.
You start with access to one girl and one stage. As you complete stages (three rounds, or 'hands' of mahjong), you unlock access to further girls and their stages, and each completed three-round stage also reveals a new costume for your current girl. It's essentially solitaire mahjong strip poker, but very tame and without any nudity.
Unfortunately, though, some of the rounds are unwinnable and as you progress through each girl's stages the tile layouts make it increasingly likely that you'll see such a round. This makes the game more about luck than strategy and can be rather frustrating, especially if you're an achievement hunter wanting to get to 100%.
Pros:
+ Easier to get into than the other Pretty Girls games
+ Steam achievements that are simple, but time consuming
+ Trading cards with reasonable value
Cons:
- RNG used for tile layout produces unwinnable rounds often
- Limited costumes and interaction with the 'Pretty Girls' of the title seems likely to disappoint the target audience
- Timer can be tough, although that's probably intentional
Pretty Girls Mahjong Solitaire is a relatively fun solitaire mahjong game, but is rather disappointing as an anime-girl game. Pick it up on special if you're after the trading cards or achievements, or if you want to play a few rounds of solitaire mahjong, but don't bother if you're only interested in it for the pretty girls.

+ Wow, this game is fun!!! You are essentially riding on top of moving Semi Trucks, jumping between each one, while also trying to avoid a large variety of obstacles, while also doing the most insane mid-air maneuvers at high speed while things are exploding all around you. + The level design is great, every level is unique and filled with surprises, new obstacles, and challenges to solve.
+ Good soundtrack

Spore is an amazing story game about a creature. Not only you can customize it, you can lead it how ever you please. At the start of this thrilling adventure, there is two diets to pick. These of which are Herbivorous and Carnivorous. I would say Herbivorous is easiest at this cell stage, as food is reletively everywhere. Carnivorous however is harder, as you have to chase for prey or scavenge for meat bits (Rarer than plant bits). If you manage to kill a cell with a Proboscis part, you may need to balance your diet once you have it on, otherwise you will end out as a Herbivore or Carnivore on land.
Once you head to land, things get a little easier, not for long though. There are two options aiming at other creatures and pack members. Socializing or Attacking. Eiter one if very fun to do.  Once you find the naturally aggressive creatures though, its fun to watch them get attacked. There are also huge versions of any creature (Have a very high attack rate, instant kill per 1 attack) called Epics.
Tribal Stage is quite strange, it changes from being a look sight of a creature, to the overseer of a tribe. You must defend your tribe, or ally with as many as the eye can see! Your animals in your pack (Allying animals at a higher intelligence will allow them to be in a pack, they must be allied though).
Civilization Stage is where things get like those combat games. You learn to get vehichles and weapons of mass destruction. You direct your nation to attack tribes and even other nations! Things get hard on this stage, there may be Warrior Nations, Religious Nations and Trader Nations.
Space Stage is where things spice up, litterally. You can zoom from one corner of the galaxy to another, greeting other aliens as you fly by. Upgrades for your ship are the norm, as each level your 'Captain' goes up, the more upgrafes you can buy. You can also terraform a planet (Adding montains, making it suitable for life). This is the thing i found very exciting.
There is also alot of other options, like making creatures and sharing them online! The community is very vast and nice. You get the often not nice people, but they are very ellusive. There is 'Adventures'. They are like a campain mode in games, but you get to make it. They can be played in at Space Stage or on the adventure menu.
Overall a thrilling game, I've always dreamed of making a creature.

My review of Morrowind.
Pros:
* There are tons of places to explore and visit, and they are all designed pretty well and interesting to look at.
* The architecture and fauna are pretty bizarre, which is a nice touch compared to all the Tolkienisms you find used over and over again in most other RPGs (including later Bethesda games such as Skyrim).
* The lore is well written, and there is a lot of it.
* There are a lot of weapons, armor and other gear to choose from.
* The potion and enchantment systems are pretty interesting. You can mix and match things to create a variety of effects. Note the caveat listed below though.
* There are no especially juvenile or cringeworthy dialogue or characters in this game like there are in your typical BioWare RPG. That said, there are not a lot of unique dialogues, and NPCs have very little to say that (literally) hasn't already been said before by other NPCs.
* I like all the movement modes the game gives you. You can walk, run, jump, fly, levitate, swim, etc.. Traveling the wilderness is pretty fun.
* There is no quest compass. Most of the time you have to figure things out based on written directions. This is a nice touch. Sometimes the directions are a little too vague though, for instance when trying to find an NPC in Vivec without being told which canton to look in.
Cons:
* Combat in this game doesn't have a good tactile feel to it. Compare it to Mount&Blade, for example, which has excellent combat.
* It's an old game, and the game's graphics aren't really that great any more. On the other hand, it doesn't overuse bloom like Oblivion or sepia tone like Fallout 3.
* The UI is bizarre. I expected to use the right mouse button for blocking, and the escape key to exit menus. Instead, you use the right mouse button to bring up the UI, and click a button each time using the mouse to exit menus. Ideally I'd rather open and close menus using the keyboard. (This may have been improved in later Bethesda games.)
* Potion and enchantment systems are fun but overkill. The game starts feeling more like a sim than an RPG. Also, enchanting, while fun, also breaks the game. There is no challenge to combat in the latter half of the game as a result of the enchantment system.
* Quests are just of the usual FedEx and Kill This type. They don't do much to further the story. The game feels like an MMORPG in many ways due to having only very basic interactions with other characters, and overly simple quests. There are no memorable characters.
* The journal is hard to use. For instance, the quest log typically fails to mention the location of quest givers, so you have to rely on the external wiki to look things up.
* Navigating the journal is also a PITA.
* I don't like the wiki-style dialogue system. Every character has a lot to say, but it's the same stuff recycled over and over again, and little of it is important story-wise.
* Building interiors feel recycled, and most space within buildings is dedicated to hallways and stairs/ramps. Rooms are very small. (This is mainly an issue in Balmora I guess.)
* Cliffracers.
* While there's plenty of lore and it is well-written, most of it serves no point, and can be safely ignored. On the otherhand, you gain occasional skill increases from books, so ignoring them completely can be at your own peril.
* The game crashes a lot if it loses focus for too long when you ALT+TAB to another application. This makes using the external wiki or FAQ a PITA! (This may be due to the Morrowind Code Patch.)
* Again, I hate having to rely on the external wiki to figure things out. Sometimes important facts were omitted by the designers, or the journal entries aren't grouped together properly. Also, a lot of times there are no dialogue entries among villagers about people you are looking for that also live in the village.
There is a lot that is appealing about this game, but it's full of too many flaws, and I can't really recommend it to anyone. Note also that I did not play the expansions, so this review does not cover them.

Aozora Meikyuu is a short, branching, kinetic visual novel. It took me under an hour to complete two of the routes. The various choices to be made are a little different fom other VNs I've played, in that they are on a timer bar, so you have click on your choice in a limited time frame. Not doing so is a chooice itself, so there is a bit of a twist from the norm. The story itself is a love story in which the reader plays as a young man who's a shut in who loves playing dating sims as he interacts with a young woman who falls from the sky at the start of the game. There are a couple twists to the story, but nothing earth shatteringly deep. The protagonist is what seems to be the norm in this type of game, a generally clueless individual who you'll feel like shaking on a few occasions as he obliviously wanders through the story. I was personally hesitant to purchase this title, being a little  gun-shy because of a bad translation in another of their published games. This one has a much better translation, and while there are a couple tense specific misses, they are easily overlooked.
Artwork is well done, mainly the cute girlfriend in sprites and CGs. Music ran throughout my gameplay and didn't leave me wishing for tylenol, or a desire to jab sharp objects into my ears, so a definate plus. There is one achievement that is gained when you first start the game, but that's it. The store page says they have trading cards, but at this time I haven't played long enough to have unlocked them, so this is unverified. I think the game is a little bit overpriced normally, it seems to be frequently on sale at a much better value. Other than that, I'd recommend it to anyone looking for a short VN that's enjoyable, but not long on deeper meaning or overly thought provoking. Thanks for taking the time to read this.

Resident Evil Remake- Remastered HD Super Turbo Turkey Puncher 3 edition is what I'd classifiy as a solid remaster where they not only have touched up the games visuals for modern standards, they took steps to make it more than just a fast port.
Optional wide screen support zooms the game in a bit to fit it on screen and the screen srolls as you move about- this actually adds to the smoothness of the now 60fps game. Screens aren't static anymore giving more motion to the game.
The framerate isn't only improved but the blurring motion that was in the gamecube version is not present and it's just super smooth now.
To my surprise you get new outfits for Chris and Jill in the form of their BSAA uniforms which is obviously copy-pasta from RE5's DLC (which is frustrating since we didn't see that PC side) which is fun, but now there's more game modes too including some that are...probably gonna be left to the speed runner pros. True Survival for more realistic gameplay? Fair enough. Invisible Zombie Mode? Atari 2600 game options anyone?
But yes, playing with my Cousin who's a big fan of the series we both noticed the difference and while some may find the scrolling and maybe odd smoothness 60fps gives- they give you the option to change both so there's no reason to hate what's been added.
Hopefully we'll see a Resident Evil 2 remake, I'm hoping they don't push Zero as ..that game was weird with it's items but either way! Solid remaster of a remake of a ol' game.
I didn't run into any performance issues however, that may be because my set up is different though.

Solar 2 is... different. In a good way. It's a very different pace from many games, and is very much a sandbox environment. But it's really fun to use the gravitational mechanics to try all sorts of crazy shenanigans. Since there are no pressing goals (unless you decide to activate one of the quest markers), you can pretty much jump into this game, spend however much time you want monkeying around, and jump back out.
Despite the simplistic graphics, the massive space battles in this game are EPIC -- delivering far more satisfaction than games that were designed to present Epic Space Battles (not that I would name any names). My only complaint is that the game -- at least on Linux -- tends to lose some, but not all, of its sound effects after a little while. Some of the key sound effects in space battles are among those that stop triggering, which really undermines the epicness of the battles. But when the sound effects are working, those battles are just awesome.
All in all, Solar 2 is a relaxing game that lets you decide how, and how much, you want to challenge yourself. I love having it in my library.

It's basically a Match-3 game with Dating Sim elements (similar to how Puzzle Quest is a Match-3 game with RPG elements). If you can't stand this kind of Puzzle game at all, you won't have much fun with Huniepop. If you do like them, even if just a bit, and think that attractive anime-styled girls improve any game, this could be an interesting title for you.
The objective of the game is simply to get all women to sleep with you. If you manage that, you unlock more, tougher, characters to woo. You do that by inviting them to dates, which starts the main part of the game, the match-3 puzzle, which in turn decides on whether you manage to charm your partner or make a fool out of yourself. Successful dates raise the respective character's "relationship value" (shown as hearts). If you have 5 with a girl and do a successful date at night, you get her into bed and basically "won" her.
The most remarkable thing about it is probably the writing. It's, to put it plainly, really stupid. And it's not entirely clear whether that's intentional or not (although it appears to be, considering the description of a "abrasive western writing style"). It's also kinda casually racist at places, although due to being so stupid, it doesn't manage to be actually offensive (kinda like Postal 2). This can be a good thing, as the game doesn't take itself too seriously and one can find it actually pretty funny. On the other hand, it can be very obnoxious.
The game does have quite a bit of depth, though. Through talking with the girls and giving them gifts, you can earn "experience points", with which you can upgrade 8 traits, giving you some advantages in the puzzles. Good memory and empathy (?) is beneficial, as they often ask you to recall a detail about them you asked about beforehand and inquire your opinion about several things (and don't like it, if yours differs from theirs).
Dates also get you money (ironically) and successful ones also new items you can give to girls during dates (but which never actually "run out") to activate various effects. However, to do that, you have to get "sentiment points", by matching up respective tokens. Aside from that, there are also "passion tokens" that raise your "passion level", which raises the amount of affection you gain from matching normal tokens. Of those, there are several different kinds (like "Romance" or "Talent") and the characters don't like them all equally. Affection can also be lowered by broken heart tokens, which can make things tricky at times. All that, combined with the limited number of moves (that can also be raised by certain tokens) give the game a surprising amount of strategic depth.
Amusingly, the sex itself is also represented by a match-3 game, albeit one that's impossible to lose. However, the affection (arousal?) lowers on its own and very fast, which can draw things out and make it quite annoying, if you don't rapidly match tokens. Would be better if there's a way to skip that.
Upgrading your relationship with the girls also nets you some photos of them (up to four, with the fourth one having a few variations), getting progressively lewder, with the last ones being outright pornographic (at least in the uncensored version). Those are very nice, if you like that kind of thing (and if you don't, Huniepop is probably not the right game for you).
Depending on how much you get them to like you (and some randomness, apparently) and where you do successful dates, you can unlock a few hairstyles and clothes for the characters to wear (outside of dates), giving you a bit of customization options).
Overall, the presentation is very good. The music is nothing special, but inoffensive and fits well. The anime-styled characters look very good (as one would expect in such a game), although I think something looks a little bit off about them. The backgrounds are also very well drawn and nice to look at without being distracting.
Overall, it's a pretty (and surprisingly) good game. It doesn't take itself very seriously, knows exactly what it is and what it wants to be and does that very well. If the game sounds appealing to you, then I can recommend it whole-heartedly.

The Fall is an interesting blend of gameplay mechanics and art styles. While it's easy to dismiss this is another "Adventure" point-and-click game, it belies the subtlety and deft execution these elements. Back some new developers, buy the game, and enjoy the journey down the rabbit hole: This is what the new game development market looks like.
I was only turned on to the this game through a Giant Bomb quicklook. I hadn't heard about it from any other sources (and I read game news sites daily). Being too afraid of spoilers, I only allowed myself a few minutes’ viewing of the gameplay footage before I stopped and purchased, The Fall is very heavily steeped in lore and metes out small details while you progress through the plot. It is not an inherently tricky or complex narrative, and for this kind of game (length and genre) it doesn't have to be. Instead Over The Moon takes a decidedly simpler path by establishing, then analyizing, a core theme: Free will.
In terms of its graphical and audio fiedelity, The Fall is not a technical powerhouse, but again, I would argue that it doesn't need to be. The atmosphere is well established as much by what you don't see as anything else. There are genuine moments of uncertainty and heightened awareness as the anxiety of a situation keeps ratcheting up, notch by notch.
In any event it is a short, but very well made game from a group of promising developers. The fact that it is episodic makes me even happier. I can't wait to see where the story goes and what, indeed, happened to my plastic shoe bag, hand, and kitchen knife!

I've been playing Otome type of games for years now, but I rarely get my hands on gems like this (not commercial ones at least)! Each DLC has a unique story, with beautiful art and magical mystery thrown in it, that leaves you breathless and wanting for more. And it gets better with each DLC. I got to play the previous parts thanks to my friend, that recomended it, and I couldn't wait to get my hands on the latest part myself. The characters are realistic, distinctive and the story itself is emotionally engaging. Each story tells you a little bit about other main characters, just enough to pique your interest, and let you to get to know them just a little bit better (plus, I can't wait to finally find out what's up with the elusive 'mother' and her reasoning behind all of this).
Takumi's route is my favourite one, though, tightly followed by Shinji's. I don't usually fall for 'childhood-friends-to-lovers' trope, but this time I fell and fell hard. I just love how gradually and slowly the relationship builds, how they overcome and face the troubles together. I'm a sucker when it comes to tragic endings, but this time, I thanked the creators this is not the case. I couldn't bear to see the character to suffer more than he already has..
5/5 and I just can't wait for the last route to be finally out.

: Recommended, especially if you are just getting into VNs but you can't/are hesitant about dropping 20/30/40 bucks on one of the bigger titles. Great story and character development. Hours of play time for each route. Ability to read some of the story without paying for anything ahead of time.
I count myself as fairly experienced when it comes to VNs these days; I have read quite a few at this point and continue to read them as often as nursing school has allowed me. (Done with that soon, though, so yay! More reading time and more money!)
has been a nice find and add to my VN collection and I'll explain why I think so!
: You play as 20 year old Tsubasa--name changeable!--who has recently come into some powers. How, I shall leave it up to you to discover! Overall, it seems like she is designed to be very proactive, not really needing a lot of rescuing or handholding--once she starts to get a handle on her powers. She isn't a blank slate like the MCs of some VNs, which may be a + or - depending on the person. I do not mind, personally, because I do not find her character annoying in the least. Her responses to the other characters and the world around her seem very believable.
: Don't roll your eyes! This is an otome after all. ;) So far, three complete routes are out and the main story of the fourth--with the epilogue to follow! A fifth route and epilogue--our dear teacher Hikaru!--lies somewhere in the future! Having played all the available routes so far, I feel like I can say with confidence that they each have very distinct backgrounds, personalities, and development to share with the MC. I won't get too specific so as not to spoil anything, but each has some turmoil they are struggling with in their lives. However, this isn't one of those stories where one person changes to suit the other; there are changes seen in both the MC and her chosen partner, but the changes seem healthy for the most part and bilateral. As in any healthy relationship, change occurs together as you both help each other work through problems. (Unless you are going for bad endings, then prepare to see some unhealthy character development, haha!)
: I love all the supporting characters here! Platonic male and female friends plus family with which to interact! The MC's and some of the boys'! Although there are calls for some of them--the friends, not the family! Gross!--to be routes in the future, that is currently not the case and I really like this in VNs. It gets you outside of that bubble that some VNs create where it's just the MC plus 2-5 guys in one space with no one else around. It feels more alive and natural. Special shout out to all the villains. <3 When you make a villain I almost feel bad about hating, I feel like you've done a very good job. You will feel conflicted about some but decidedly against others.
: Depending on the route you take, you may be spending most of your time at the high school, in the main part of town or the shady part, or even on another plane! The backgrounds seem very well done to me--especially on Shinji's route! It's nice to have more than a few locations, such as the MC's home plus the place she meets the all her menfolk--which in some games is often the same location! Not that I am trying to harp on this practice, I merely am appreciating the diversity in this game. I'm an adventurer at heart and I love to see the MC travel.
: Speaking of backgrounds, the other artwork also seems very well done and I think it noticeably improves with each new route! One of the developers responded to a comment of mine in the discussions saying that their poor artist's fingers are being worked to the bone, but I must say that all of her hard work is definitely paying off. I love all of the facial expressions for the MC, the boys, and all of the supporting cast as well. If they have a portrait, they have more than one facial expression. Even during the fully illustrated scenes, character expressions change to the dialogue and moment. It's very satisfying to see the characters display the correct emotions as conversations and scenes play out.
: The music is quite lovely. It's not too harsh but just melodic enough to remind that it's there every now and then, especially during mood or scene changes. Though, I do feel like I have to comment on one sound that made me burst out laughing during a very serious moment. It was during a fight scene in one route--no spoilers, I promise!--and a character was thrown up against a window pain that did not shatter. The noise it made sounded like a small bird hitting it. It just didn't quite match up and made the scene a bit comical to me, haha.
: It's hard to completely comment on the story seeing as how you only learn a bit more with each route and not all of the routes are out yet! However, what I have uncovered thus far has been very intriguing, keeping me on the each of my keyboard waiting for more. I'm interested to see what the ultimate fate of the MC will be as well as that of the one who gave her the powers. While there are few typos and some odd wording here and there, it's nothing that really distracted me too much from the story. Nevertheless, there are threads posted in the forums to help bring attention to these issues so that they may be fixed in the future.
: While I am not here to comment on other reviews, I will point out that the description states that only the prologue and a few chapters for each route are available for free. That being said, when comparing how much each route costs with how many hours of reading you'll get out of them, I think the cost of the main story + epilogue for each is quite well matched. Even had I spent the full amount for each DLC--which I did not--that would have been $26 for 29 hours of gameplay, and I haven't even fully completed every route; there are 3 main endings--mystic, passionate, and dark--for each route plus some bad endings along the way, so the replayability is very good. I count myself someone who reads at an above average speed, so take those numbers for what they are worth. Plus, even if you can't afford all of them, you can buy them one at a time! Each one is standalone, not needing to be bought in any particular order--except you read the epilogues after the main story, of course. I do not think this is deceitful or unclear on the part of the developers/publishers. In fact, I love that you can test out the first few chapters of EACH ROUTE to see if this game is for you BEFORE you even buy anything. Big plus for me.
: I haven't been here for very long, but I see the Devs posting pretty regularly in the forums. They respond usually within a few to several hours of questions and try to resolve issues as quickly as they can. I have been very impressed with them thus far and look forward to seeing what they produce in the future! There is already talk of another Mystic Destinies....
Overall, you can tell that I am very impressed with this game and why. While the typos are an issue, they aren't a big enough issue to put me off of enjoying the game. Whether you're a longtime VN enthusiast or just getting started, I would definitely give this game a try! I don't think that most people will be disappointed.
If you have any issues that I maybe haven't addressed here and would like to ask, feel free to leave your concerns, criticisms, questions, and shouts of rage in the comments section!

Seriously impressive. I love otome games, and this is officially one of my new favorites. I've played the 3 available routes (as of 11/24/16 - more pending), and the work the developers put into this game really shows.
The artwork and music are really well done. The characters have facial expressions, and each route has unique instrumentals. I would buy the soundtrack on Amazon in a heartbeat if it were available.
Most importantly though, the stories are really good and engaging. Each route is unique to the chosen character, and the MC adapts to that. While the MC tries to uncover the mystery of what happened to her, why, and what it all means for her future, the guy you choose also his his own demons to face. You learn something new in each route as well - little details about what happened to the MC, which will probably eventually give you a full picture once you've played all the routes. You also learn more about the story world itself in each route, since the guys are all different types of supernatural beings. Even after the Main Story and Epilogue, there's still plenty of room left for a sequel, which I would also buy in a heartbeat.
It's clear in how detailed this game is that a lot of work was put into it. I know some aren't too crazy about paying for each route individually, but I absolutely think it's worth it. I've played a ton of other otome games where you buy the routes (same price as this game per route), and didn't get even half the quality content that's in this game.
Seriously, I will probably buy whatever these guys put out in the future - new routes, sequels, an entirely different game, or that soundtrack I'm dying for. *nudge, nudge you beautiful developers, you* <3

One of the worst games I have ever played -- not the worst because, surprisingly, it hardly every crashed.  However, there just isn't anything fun about playing this game.  Painkiller games are notorious for being really slow to load saved games.  Since this game constantly has a ton of monsters spawning everywhere in a very small area, you have no place to go.  You don't even have time to turn around so that you can fire.  The result is that you die quickly over and over again.  So the standard pattern is:  play for 5 seconds and die, press F9 to load your last save and wait for 45 seconds, repeat (endlessly).  I finally did make it to the end of the first level (1011 kills) just to see if it was possible.  It was but it sure wasn't fun.
Also note that this a game is a non-stop slaughterhouse/frenzy sort of game.  There is no sense of pacing.  You are fighting for survival 100% of the time.  Obviously no sense of any plot or story either.
I suppose some might get an adrenalin rush from this game -- it definitely does keep you under constant fire.  But I just found the game frustrating while I spent most of the time looking at the "loading" screen over and over again.
The original Black edition is great.  But this version is worse than Resurrection, which was already pretty bad.  I definitely DO NOT recommend this game.

Otherwise, go for something else (most free ones seem to be better than this actually, now that I think about it).

I must admit, I expected more of this remaster.
I was so excited when this was announced that I immediately bought the game at full price (which I almost never do). The fact is, apart from a graphics update, the game offers little more than the original did. I am generally someone who enjoys the feel of the game more than the look, and for anyone who tends towards the same perspective, the Anniversary version is probably not worth it.
However, I can say very little against the game itself; it is still one of my all time favourites. It's witty, intelligent, story-rich with plenty of side quests to sink your teeth into, and it offers a surprising amount of character development considering your controllable 'Hero' doesn't actually speak. You also get to kick chickens. My only niggles with the game itself are that you can only play as a male character, which I find limits my immersion somewhat, and that the camera occasionally refuses to do as you tell it. The quests are also very binary good/evil - no grey areas here. And the guards are totally fine with you wandering around opening fancy chests, but as soon as you try to steal a moustache from a bookshelf, OH NO THAT'S NOT ALLOWED.
I am still glad I bought this version of the game. And as I would confidently say that Fable should be played by everyone, I can hardly not reccommend it.

I haven't played this game for a long amount of time, but I am a strong believer in the idea of gamers deciding on their opinion of a game within the first few minutes of gameplay. So, armed with my little experience wiht this game, I decided to write a review, telling others why
is not that good a game and is not worth a great deal of money.
First of all, one of the most important mechanics in a game to make it fun to play are the controls, the perfectly sensitive mouse controls and their transition to controller in the indie masterpiece
being a prime example of this. However,
game begins with you controlling a meteorite drifting through space. 'An intersting concept,' I hear you utter towards your monitor, 'I would like to see how this game would work.' The game has you control the meteorite with a mouse, which is probably the best way to control something like this, begging the question, 'How did they get it so wrong?'
Your meteorite ends up shooting through space at rediculous speeds (where did its inertia come from? I don't know, but that's only part of my point) and stopping is virtually impossible. Before you decide to buy this game, let me tell you a few reasons why you might want to stick those wonderful dollars back in your piggybank.
1. The game is dead
Ace of Spades used to be a very fun game when it was still crowded with people. When I started the game today after a few years of not playing at all, there were a total of 37 people playing in 4 servers. And as most of the time, Team Deathmatch had a full lobby with 24 people. So either you have to wait an eternity for someone to leave or get kicked, or play in a server with too little players.
2. VOTE TO KICK ‘INNOCENT_PLAYER’ FOR GRIEFING?
I played a full match of Team Deathmatch which takes about 10 minutes, and in those 10 minutes I kept getting these annoying kick polls over and over again. Really, I got like 6 in one match. When I asked the person why they want to kick people so bad, I got a response saying something like “He keeps destroying my house.”
By the way, most of the time these players don’t actually get kicked, that’s why they kept suggesting it again and again.
3. Alternative for Minecraft
As I mentioned before, a lot of kids are just playing this game so they can build a little home, then wanting to kick the people who destroy it. Basically just not playing the game how it’s meant to be played and this really annoys me.
4. The graphics
In my opinion, for a game of 12 dollars, it doesn’t looks so good. Sure, it’s meant to be blocky and all, but it makes me feel like there’s not much work put into it. I’m pretty sure they did, but they could at least make it look a little bit better by maybe using some more and different colors, because right now it’s hard to tell if that guy in the distance is my teammate or not.
So based on my experience and the things I just mentioned, I don’t think this game is actually worth 12 dollars. Though, if you’re hesitating on whether or not you should buy the game, I suggest you wait until it’s on sale. :)

Homesick is a beautiful inde-puzzle game (with a hint of psychological horror)
Rate: 10/10
Pros:
-The graphics are beautiful and visually satisfying. They're very detailed and the first thing you'll think when you start playing is "Wow, this is a beautiful game."
-The controls are standard and simple. Nothing too complicated, which is nice.
-The puzzles have a happy medium of being difficult and easy. (once you finish a difficult puzzle, you are presented with an easier one, so you won't lose your mind)
-If you actually invest time into figuring out the story line, it's very interesting (I feel it's worth the running around).
-The music is very comforting/soothing. It makes the extremly slow walking bearable.
Cons:
- Moving around is very time consuming as the character walks pretty slowly. A sprinting mechanism would be nice. The music makes this bearable, however.
-Be aware that gameplay time is actually quite short (2-4 hours). I left this in my library for a while and forgot how long it was estimated to be, and was disappointed by it's shortness. The story line is interesting but seems incomplete, which could be fixed by a possible sequel.
-Honestly, I think it's a bit pricey. It is visually satisfying and the music is nice, but it seems really short for 15 dollars. It's sale price is totally worth it, though. I got it on sale for 7 or 8 dollars, and I think it was worth it.

The short review: This game lets you date a lot of awesome supernatural guys, including a phoenix, a dragon, and an elf/fae. The MC is awesome. Each route is long, detailed, and has multiple endings - well worth the price. 10/10
The full review:
MDSoA is a wonderfully crafted game with beautiful writing, art, and music. I've played all of the currently available routes (Shou, Tatsuya, Shinji) and have enjoyed all of them entirely. The first route I played was Tatsuya and it took me approx. 7-8 hours. Of course, some of that time was spent simply admiring the art, but it seems 7 hours is the average it takes me to play a route once. I'm very happy with the price - €5 for 7 hours of gameplay in an otome game is an extremely fair price. Each route also has three unique good endings, and some of the routes have 2-3 bad endings as well.
One of the things I love most about this game is that the MC (main character) isn't just a self insert. So many otome games will have a self insert MC and then the story revolves entirely around the character you've chosen to pursue. In MDSoA the MC always has her own life and her own story alongside the guy she's paired up with. What's more, with each route you play you learn more about her, and her past and family. Each route is a bit like unravelling the mystery of the MC. While forming a relationship with each of the guys is really interesting and important, it's difficult to forget that the big questions this game asks are about the MC and her mother. At the moment we know little about her mother, but with two routes still to be released I'm sure we'll find out more.
The worldbuilding in this game is also excellent. All of the developers seem to have given massive consideration to all the supernatural races they introduce and how they fit in, not just with human society, but within their own societies as well. The game is good at presenting different viewpoints from different members of the same race to highlight this. The antagonists are the prime example of this but it can be seen through supporting characters as well.
Overall, I just really enjoyed this game. The guys were obviously what drew me into the game first (who wouldn't want to date a dragon?!) so I was blown away by the love and care that's gone into this, and how it makes me interested in the entire world, instead of just the romance.

To beginn with: Yes, this game isn't entirely for free but what exactly in life is? Get over it! :D
In my opinion the price for each route + epiloge is fair. Especially when you keep in mind that there are often games in this genre, were you need to pay for every single chapter - and don't get nearly this quality. I played Shinijs route and cleared one ending and the epiloge. Took me more than 8h so far, which is in comparison pretty long.
So if you enjoy reading well written Visaul Novels with great artdesign and music as well as a maincharacter with credible personality, give this one a try! You won't regret it. The character development is deep and realistic. The story is easy to follow and there were several times (in Shinjis route) when I actually laughed out loud because of the playfull/snotty dialoges - really loved it so far. ^_^
Edit after 50h gameplay: Still love it. There are places where the story isn't entirely clear (probably to keep the excitement) but I assume  it clears up after playing the whole routes. All in all still fun to play, well written and worth to buy.

Pretty Girls Mahjong Solitaire is an innovative way to bring character to playing the traditionally classic game of Mahjong Solitaire (Match 2 unrestricted tiles). Similar to HuniePop's strategy of playing Match 3 games in order to progress a "date", PGMS utilizes Mahjong to progress a characters story. There are 5 characters with approximately 3 Stages each, containing 4 Rounds in each Stage, that must be completed in order to unlock all outfits for each character. The 4th round in each Stage will progressively undress the character, revealing a new outfit underneath. Every tile clear will make the character elicit some sort of response/noise.
The actual Mahjong gameplay is fairly similar to other games of its kind on Steam. Progressing to a point where no more moves are available will end the round prematurely - there is no shuffle feature. Running out of time will also end the round prematurely; however continuously matching tiles will add more time. You may save the round to return later, and pausing the game will hide the faces of the tiles.
There is only a moderate amount of difficulty faced to clear a round. Veterans of Mahjong will have no problems at all breezing through most of the rounds. The difficulty does increase a little bit further into the later rounds of each character. The game options are pretty basic: fullscreen and music/sfx sliders. There is also a gallery that is essentially a dress room containing all of the viewable outfits unlocked for each character.
Some of the other Mahjong games can get a little boring to play after a while due to the monotony. PGMS at least brings a little bit of color into the gameplay.

Reveal the Deep is a very short, very enjoyable, very atmospheric part platformer, part puzzle, part horror, part walking simulator indie game that was to me the kind of fun I've had from no other game since Eric Chachi's Another World.  Without spoiling too much, it's about a deep sea diver exploring and revealing the mysteries of a sunken explorer ship from the 19th century.  In this 2 hour adventure, you will be doing some light platforming (although there is one frustratingly difficult jump at the very end), some puzzle solving (often involving pushing crates, pulling levers or stepping into an alternate reality), enjoying a wonderful spooky pixel setting that scares without being too oppressive and revealing the rather Lovecraftian fate of the derelict you are in.  The game could definitely benefit from controller support (Please note that controller support for this game has been patched in after this review has been posted) and some tighter platforming, but Reveal the Deep asks for neither much of your time or your money for what it offers, and I think you should play it.

Aozora Meikyuu is a little visual novel, with some suggesting content. Indeed, after being rejected by a girl, Aoi has closed himself from the world, barely trying to go outside and only for groceries or new dating simulations. One of such days, a naked girl fell from the sky: how will Aoi manage Sora? Which secret has she? What fate awaits them?
You might think that the plot isn't really developped and your first thought is that Aoi must be dreaming or that Sora is a product of his imagination or she's alien. However, the twist is really unexpected: I didn't expect that, but I know why I didn't think of such things, as I'm not immersed in Japanese culture. Aozora Meikyuu might be a short game, it has several endings.
Anyway, the graphics are quite colorful and nice, the dialogues are making sense, with Sora being quite naive by moments but staying serious at the same time. I liked also the soundtrack.
I'm quite sad that there is only one achievement, it would have been fun to have more and it's curiosity that guided me to see the bad or neutral endings.
I'm recommending it for those that don't like long visual novels with choices everywhere.
