You control a character moving through a boring black environment, completing some disjointed requests from NPCs and trying to improve your character.
This would be a very lacklustre and boring game, except you're a solar body.
Let me restate that, you are an android aspiring to become a sun (or even more).
This is very clearly the main hook of the game and it is executed well.
You can get asteroids you encounter that are smaller than you to orbit you and have the interesting ability to absorb anything orbiting you. By growing smaller you turn from an asteroid into a planet, into a sun, etc.
Does it make sense from a scientific perspective? Barely.
Is it fun? Yes. Yes it is.
What was especially impressive to me is that you can, should you want to, also become a full solar system, since planets will be able to enter your orbit when you're a star. Combine that with the ability for life to spawn on a planet you can have your own little army of space-faring creatures defending the character (something which you'll need for some of the quests).
The game isn't particularly long, but has nice replayability where you can start a new game as any solar body you've been so far in your previous sessions.
All in all I'd definitely recommend it if you want to be a planet.

I would recommend this game to anyone who enjoys live-action combat, and medieval themes.

Hey achievement hunters: start a new game and you've already completed it! ...achievement-wise anyway.
But the story is over an hour long if you actually read it and check different routes.
("Azure labyrinth" according to various translation softwares) is a visual novel with

theme.
Gosh, who am I kidding. It tells about a shy guy who gets turned down by his crush and he proceeds to embrace the Otaku lifestyle, hardcore fashion. Then a naked girl literally falls from the sky and hits him. Are you seeing what's going on?
It's actually an effing
game, that's what. I didn't know I'd ever play one of those. The things I do for achievements and reviews... Well, I guess technically I still haven't because to activate that content, you have to install a special uncensor patch. In the regular version, those scenes are just several lines of onomatopoetic smooching.
So yeah. Let's get into the dirty details.
The protagonist, a guy called Aoi, is a clueless and frankly all-around irritating person. Being a stereotypical Otaku, he uses such phrases as "3D girls" in a serious fashion. It sounds so awkward that I was actually facepalming and laughing at the same time while reading his lines.
Of course the girl who fell from the sky totally falls for the guy and makes lewd comments throughout the story, being consistently rejected by the oblivious guy. Well, that is obviously until the end. I facepalm-chuckled at her lecherous, suggestive dialogue as well.
Story is seemingly absurd, although some of the blatant bizarreness is explained in the end. The story proceeds through choices and there's a timer on every question, allowing it to run its course meaning silence or indecisiveness, which works well unless you want to save in the middle. There's unfortunately no rewinding. You may show the past dialogue in a list form though.
There are three regular endings and at least four mid-way endings that end the story prematurely. Trying twice I only found the bad ending and ended up using a guide for both "good" and "normal" endings. In my opinion, the good ending was definitely the best of the bunch and my regard for the game rose a bit after seeing that, at least enough for recommendation.
For the purists, a note: there's no Japanese version, nor is there voice acting. The music is alright and cute, and the visuals and facial expressions look good and fit the scenes nicely.
Checking all choices and playing through to the (bad) ending took me 80 minutes. Add 30 minutes for checking out the two other endings with guides, while skipping the already seen dialogue, it was almost two hours of... well, of a surprisingly amusing story. The story is cheesy and mediocre at best but it was surely entertaining. For the users of the uncensor patch it must be more so but perhaps in alternate ways.
Would I recommend it? Well, it amused me for its length but I did get it in a bundle (i.e. almost for free). So in the end, I recommend getting it on sale, especially if you just want it for the single 'cheevo. But the story goes to the "so bad it's good" category so even then you might want to check it out anyway.

At first glance, The Fall looks like just another indie side-scroller. However, with a dark, Limbo-esq atmosphere and unique interface, the title quickly begins to stand out from others of the genre.
Pros: The game is short enough to keep me entertained in a single sitting, and with a few options within the game for a few different achievements. The atmosphere, though not intended, was rather terrifying at times (think Metroid Fusion, only bleaker) with surprising things appearing on screen. The audio left me with the fear that something was breathing down Arid's neck, so I would constantly be checking my back in-game. The world is contained enough that the player shouldn't get lost, and once a piece of a puzzle is found the answer is generally very clear. Many upgrades for Arid are found early on, making them available for the player to use as they desire, but not neccessarily required for success. The motives and theme of the game are also, clear and well established - following protocol. Characters other than Arid were few, but were very entertaining and had very defined structures.
Cons: The game is intended for a sequel, or to kick off a series. Because of that, the game leaves lots of loose ends and a generally confused player, who has only begun to watch Arid adapt. Within such a brief timeframe, the ending comes as more of a shock than a cliffhanger. The shooting (in my opinion) was horrid at best. Using cover and camoflage were both automatically binded to E, which meant that cover might not have been able to be accessed. Interestingly, Arid can only fire straight or upwards when behind floor cover, meaning that it cannot shoot enemies that may be on the other side of the box, crate, etc. The game seems to support contollers, but didn't function properly with my Vakoss GP3321 gamepad - which I know is a sketchy thing to use - but registered the controller before the keyboard, thereby locking the game as the keyboard couldn't be used.
My verdict: I think that The Fall did what most trilogies usually do at this point, set up a story. Unfortunately, I think it may have tried a bit too hard. However, that didn't take away from the experience the game had within it. The pistol is entertaining to fire, even though the cover system has its issues. For the next installment, I would hope to see more use of Arid's abilities. I networked maybe twice in the game, and only needed camoflage to pass a single light for an elevator. It would be interesting to see Arid's abilities become more essential itself than "something else it can do."
7/10 - Worth the time, give it a shot when the next game is available.

I have mixed feelings on this game because of some design issues, but it is a nice pick-up at a discounted price.
The Mahjong aspect of this game is solid.  It is very challenging... to the point where you may rage quit once or twice during the game.  That being said, why would anyone rage quit during a game of Mahjong, which typically should be a very calming/meditative experience?
That brings in the number one complaint you are likely to hear in review of this game:  The timer. In a game of Mahjong, one would do well to make some informed decisions about which matches to "Pick", as choices you make in the game can ultimately become a factor in whether you win or lose.  Mahjong has a strong element of chance in it, but there is quite a bit of well-intentioned thought that it also requires... the timer albeit negates all of your efforts to make such informed decisions.  Ultimately, I think this game would have been adequately challenging from the tile lay-outs themselves and would love if the creators did away with the timer, but it's not necessarily a complete deal-breaker.
Another complaint I would add is perhaps an important one considering that this is a game whose main asset (at least from an advertising perspective) is its ASSETS.  And by assets I totally mean♥♥♥♥♥♥  As with a lot of anime-themed games, the paper-doll work is a little boring.  Well, very boring.  Instead of having different poses for the different character dolls, there is only one pose per girl that gets re-used, the artists just drawing different outfits on the doll (sometimes even borrowing the same lines from other outfits that don't always make sense).  A more important artistic criticism is that two of the dolls have chests that are very clearly misproportioned from an artist's perspective.  Not disproportioned in the sense that real women wouldn't have such large breasts... disproportioned in the sense that the right boob is bigger and at an awkward angle compared to the left.  I think it's unfortunate that anime artists responsible for only 5 characters cannot work in any dynamic aspect to their character art and are rather using these copy & paste method of art that we're seeing in most of these games...  The outfits aren't even that great for most of the girls.  They often seem more fully dressed after stripping, which is disappointing after the already crippling disappointment of there not being actual nudity in this game.
Did I play through this entire game?  Yes.  Did I enjoy playing it?  Mostly :-).  Do I recommend it?  Yes... with the above stipulations added.  When you factor in the fact that there is no nudity--YES, I am disappointed as ♥♥♥♥.

I could truly go into detail about this game, but for now, I'll mostly just say it's a flawed gem or even a masterpiece depending on your opinion.
The game has some very archaic features such as dice rolls determining your ability to hit enemies which means you can miss even if you have a high skill with the weapon, but it's not as bad as some people make it out to be and you just have to learn to cope with it. However, this is a considerably unforgiving game overall.
You have to be careful not to go off the beaten path too much as enemies don't scale in level the way they do in this game's successors. There are also diseases which can give nasty effects to your character such as debuffs potentially lasting until the disease is cured though it can easily be done with potions that you should always have on you.
You also need to be sure you make good choices when it comes to creating your character so you can maximize your chances of survival and killing potential. It's probably best to select a predesigned class or even look online to get an idea of building your character effectively. This does NOT mean you have to follow them exactly and use cookie-cutter builds to succeed. They're just general rules of thumb which you can better understand with. This way you won't go around missing every swing and dying instantly to enemies.
Quests take more attention than they do in successors because there's no compass pointing you to your objectives meaning you must read your journal to see the directions there which aren't always 100% accurate. While this can be confusing and you may just not enjoy it, it serves to better immerse you into the experience and encourage you to explore the surrounding areas of the quests.
The last possibly negative things I'd like to mention are the various exploits and bugs. You should definitely install the fan made patches, that you can find online for free which should fix the majority of the bugs that would otherwise make it a terribly glitchy experience. As far as exploits, these can be avoided if you choose to and play the game normally, but from what I've heard, alchemy can really unbalance the game with things like flying above enemies and shooting them and buffing up to near invisibility. However, you might find this to be a fun aspect of the game.
There are many other things to learn that I didn't cover like this such as disposition and fatigue so I'd encourage anyone to look up some information to guide you a bit where a manual might have if you had a physical copy. This won't take anything from the experience (depending on where you look), unless you're the type who likes to go into a game and figure everything out the hard way, and it will probably prevent a lot of frustration for a beginner.
To talk about the good, I'm sure you could easily look online to find a cult following gushing about this game, but from my own experience, the reason I enjoy this the most in the series is it's complexity, depth, and thematically alien feeling. You can look up what makes this game comparatively deeper and complex than the others with things like each individual weapon type being a skill and how the many factions interact with you and each other, but I just want to mention the world.
Morrowind is a very strange place compared to the other games and real life in general. The environment includes ashlands which are essentially barren shadows of past volcanic eruptions that have caused dry, dusty terrain with calderas mostly providing the only form of pass through the many impassable (without flying) mountains. There's also the 'West Gash Region' which is hard to describe, but definitely unusual. There are other places more familiar like the 'Bitter Coast' being swampland, more that I can't name that are grasslands, beach, shallow waterered areas with stones and land sticking up from it with giant thorn trees where flying wizards reside, a lake area with different plantation grounds where slaves work. Most of the biomes contain giant mushrooms which act as trees. There's even an island in the Northwest, provided in one of the expansions that come with this version where there are traditional forests, ice areas and snowy places. So Morrowind cetainly has the most various environments of the last three Elder Scrolls.
The native npcs themselves where insect armor, ride giant insects to other areas, use large reptiles to serve as mules, have a strange religion featuring many of their own gods not seen in the other games, have cities on water and shun any 'outlanders'. There are also ash dwellers who live in tribes that celebrate the banned god Nerevar who acts as a central plot - point to the story.
The story is compelling enough, but it's the presentation that makes it great. You don't know a lot of what's going on when you first get to Morrowind and you only find out through books, npcs who are reluctant to inform you, and other npcs who help further the plot along. It's a very mysterious game.
Simply put, this game demands a lot from you, but it's extremely satisfying when you succeed and win the main quest, not to mention all the side quests and definitely rewards you for being invested in the story and lore which are truly deserving of the word 'fantasy'.

I recommend this game to those who enjoy visual novels, specifically otome visual novels, and an interesting supernatural storyline and cast.  This is a "set in early university" and "discovering your supernatural abilities" kind of VN.
Pros:
- Interesting characters
- Generally well-written (I like smooth, well-edited writing and MDSA has it)
- You want to find out "what's going on"
-
- Artwork is very nice for the characters (a little basic for the backgrounds)
- Music is nice
- Because each storyline is distinct, you are only skipping text within a particular story arc to get to different endings (other than for the free prologue of course)
- The guys are cute and do "angsty but endearing" quite well; kind of important for this type of game!
Cons:
- No voice acting (a bit of a downside when you consider overall price of game); I'm a big fan of good voice acting, so this is a big one for me, but it's *not* a deal-breaker since this is still a nice game
- Cost: now only about $5 (Canadian) per route
- Little interaction between the various main characters while in a route (but there is some!)
- Maybe a slight feeling of blandness?  Not as emotionally compelling as some other games?  But to be fair, it's still a neat story with an interesting premise and interesting characters.
[NOTE:  Shou's route has had things added to it; later routes have more to them; I did find portions more compelling as the game was tweaked--this is a responsive developer!]
OVERALL RATING: 8/10 although I'm tempted to go to 7.5 because of the lack of voice acting.  It must be said, though that the main character is really interesting and that's a big plus!
FINAL NOTE:  I wish I could take screenshots without the text box at the bottom.  Or even just get to see the beautiful art without the text box more often.

So far I've played both Shou and Tatsuya's routes (but not shou's epilogue) for this game. Overall I'd give the game a 6/10 with Shou's route being better put together than Tatsuya's, imo.
----------------------------------
First off though I'd like to make a note about the marketing for this game. The game is stated as f2p with paid dlc. The free part is really just the prologue and the first chapters for each guy. The dlc is what you need to pay for to get the complete routes for each character. Now, this is really common in mobile dating sims/visual novels, where the aim seems to be to get the user to spend as much money as possible by splitting up the game into sections and then locking them behind price tags. At the same time this allows the game to have some content playable and ready, while working on additional content to be released later. And that's fine for mobile because you usually go in knowing that and it's a well-used strategy. But I don't think steam was the best place to launch this game with that type of business model (it's also not very common on here, hence all the angry/shocked reviewers of this game. First of all steam doesn't seem to have the right type of categories to accurately describe how this game is set up, so you get people clicking on the game (not reading thoroughly - it IS stated clearly in the summary how the game works) expecting the whole thing to be free just to find out that they have to pay to get anything out of it.
I honestly think it would have been better to wait until all of the routes were finished and then release the game on steam with the entire price tag. It's what visual novel romance games that launched on mobile are starting to do: consolidating all the routes under one price tag and porting to steam. But it seems like the devs wanted to get the game out as soon as possible so they went this way, launching each route as it's ready and releasing it as paid dlc. Again, I really don't think steam is the place for that type of model (and really having to pay for the separate epilogue as well makes it an even worse idea) but it's what the devs decided worked best for them and I can respect that.
Anyway to the actual review.
-----------------------------------
The art is 10/10 for Shou, 7/10 for Tatsuya. Everything is really soft with a beautiful painted look. My only problem is that for Tatsuya's CGs his face ends up looking really weird/awkwardly drawn, while Tsubasa's (the main char) was always perfect. Don't know why that ended up like that but it's just something I noticed.
--------------------------------------
The music is okay. I really enjoy the menu song but the other background music is your standard stuff.
--------------------------------------
It's a visual novel. So lots of reading with a few choices sprinkled in that can change what ending you end up with. Shou\'s route has 3 endings that are all happy. Even though one is called the "Dark End" it's not all that dark, you still get the guy it's just not as straight forward lovey-dovey as the other endings. For Tatsuya's route there are 3 happy endings and 2 bad endings.
Shou's route was good. The pacing felt right, nothing was too angsty, the protagonist wasn't a complete moron, and it was just overall a well done story. Tatsuya's route on the otherhand...it was boring. It was longer than Shou's but stuffed with so much bland internal monologue scenes, useless drama or instances where the protoganist over-reacted just to create a situation, that I lost all interest and was glad when it was finally done. And because of the length, Tatsuya's "hot and cold" attitude ping-ponged and dragged on longer than needed which made him come off as a jerk that likes to send off mixed signals. I just really didn't like him by the end of the game, even though I was okay with him at the start. Also I noticed a lot more typos/misplaced words in Tatsuya's route that got to the point where it was breaking immersion. I don't remember Shou's having that many but I could be misremembering.
More of my thoughts on Tatsuya's route here if anyone is interested (shameless blog plug):
If you're interested in this game and don't mind paying for each route, I'd recommend the main chapters for the guys. But I can't really recommend paying for the epilogue as well because that just seems silly to me and feels more money-grabby than anything. Unless you don't care, you do you boo.

********Okay so this is a long review just entirely my opinion. Basically, I rate this game like 9.5/10 definitely give it a try with what's given to you for free and see if it's your thing!************
Okay so the artwork, the story, the music (holy♥♥♥♥♥♥the music though...) and the personalities are all so wonderfully done in this game.
Tbh the artstyle threw me off at first because it was so different from what I'm used to seeing (really anime stuff, you know what I'm talking about) but it is so beautiful, the artwork. It's so well done and the background images look like they took /forever/ to create--it's all beautiful. The facial expressions and subtle differences from when they are blushing and aren't--it's amazing.
The music is probably my favorite thing about the game, though. It fits really nicely and it's just calming to listen to. I could just let it play for hours and never get bored of it. It fits the mood, whatever that may be, and really let's you get a little more immersed in the world.
The story!--it's really interesting! Now I definitely see a few things that they did wrong (completely in my OWN OPINION) but for the most part, the story is nice and original. There were some clichés in the story but nothing is forced and for the most part, it's nicely paced.
All the characters have their own personalities!!! (This one is just amazing) So like even the MC like...ACTUALLY has a personality for once. I CANNOT tell you how many god damn times that I've played a visual novel and then I had to stop because the MC is just so stupid. Honestly, the generic, pushover, girly girl type can only go so far and I am SO glad that they decided against making the MC like that. You can change her name to whatever you'd like and she is--mostly--calm and collected...also she's a nerd who loves anime and that in itself is great.
Overall, this game is really well done. When I'm writing this, there is only 2 routes out (Shou and Tatsuya's) and I've played through Shou's completely, and Tatsuya's halfway. But even so, I can tell that it's only going to get better from here. Please support this company and this game. I can't wait for the other routes to come out (though it may be quite a while before they do) because you can tell that these people actually care about their product.
Also Tatusya is and will be forever my favorite. He's such a dork omg I love him so much ;u;

Bought this game when you got Totally Accurate Battle Simulator with it, because at the time I was only interested in that game. But now that it came out I tried it out and fell in love. Amazing game, I honestly can't think of anything negative to say about it that's not small details.
- Solid level design, some levels are short some levels are a bit longer but all are easily doable under one minute, except the last one.
- Not too hard, but definitely not easy. Some levels were a bit easy admittedly, but overall it was a challenging game.
- It felt fair, not sure how to explain this one.
- There isn't anything to help you with the game except for the small tutorial at the beginning and how to use the ability you get first time you use it. Which I find nice, because I don't like being told what spacebar does when I'm at the last level for example.
- Abilities felt second nature. You know how it's obvious that spacebar is jumping? It felt like that, you use the abilities without giving it much thought.
- Simple idea, but very original. Can't think of any other game that's this fast-paced where you have to jump on - sometimes flying - trucks.
- Going fast FELT fast. And satisfying. Especially reaching the goal at the peak of your speed, using that extra dash ability to get a few extra speed points felt very good.
- Not much to say about the visuals. They were good, the best part about them was probably the particle effects. Simple style, but it works.
EDIT: There was this small bug that sometimes when you enter a level the truck you spawn on flips immediately, making you fall on the ground, making you unable to get the Ace score for completing a level the first time you try it.
EDIT 2: Just realized I didn't say anything about the music, but that's because there wasn't really anything wrong with it, it was decent, but not something very noteworthy. The medieval theme stood out the most for me personally, but other than that nothing to really say about it.
tl;dr: Great game, pick it up when you can. Worth it for the full price, but if it's ever on sale definitely give it a try. Arbitrary rating that doesn't really mean anything: 9/10

A Not So Critical Review of Reveal the Deep:
Reveal the Deep is a super cheap, super short, super fun game that caught me off guard. It is a fantastic exploration horror game that executes the basic concepts of tension beautifully. It only took me about 90 minutes to beat the game, which may be a turn off for some people, but for less than a dollar, I feel I easily got my money worth. I wouldn’t only recommend this game to people tight on time or money, but also to any aspiring environment or sound designer as it shows how vital simple and small effects can elevate a generic exploration game to something pretty special and standout.
Pros:
•	Creepy atmosphere
•	Fantastic execution of horror elements
•	Sound design makes you feel alone, especially if using headphones.
•	Fun thematic puzzle mechanics
Cons:

•	Ending that seemingly comes out of nowhere with little explanation

Reveal the Deep, developed by Lazy Monday Games, is not one of a kind, but wanders outside the box just enough to warrant a playthrough. It’s got the atmosphere, mystery and puzzles to keep you hooked, but it isn’t void of flaws.
The story is interesting in its own respects. You play as a diver, exploring the carcass of a sunken ship at the bottom of the sea. Notes are scattered about each of the 3 levels, explaining how the ship got all the way down there. Basically, explorers discovered an island which once held an entire civilization. Now, only abandoned temples and villages remain. Of course, the explorers take an array of mysterious artifacts home. But, low and behold, the artifacts are cursed, and everyone on board is in for a bad day.
Gameplay is fairly straight forward. You’ll encounter some obstacles and puzzles throughout the game, but nothing too challenging. Reveal the Deep relies on its puzzles the most. Thankfully, the devs have implemented a really cool trick to keep gameplay fresh. At certain times, you’ll be able to jump between alternate realities. Swapping realities changes the map’s layout. Platforms may disappear, certain objects react differently in each reality, and hidden items, such as notes, can only be accessed by utilizing this mechanic. This ability is one of the game’s saving graces and it keeps things interesting.
The graphics are what they are: very simple pixel art accompanied by a small collection of animations. At first, it really is nice on the eyes. Tiny bubbles plume from your helmet, and the light blue tinge of your flashlight illuminates the corridors ahead, but not enough to uncover what horrors dwell beyond. But after an hour or so of gameplay, the charm starts to fade. After Reveal the Deep’s first chapter, you’ve seen almost everything in the graphics department.
Thankfully, sound design is top notch. Each step vibrates throughout the ship’s iron tomb like the beat of a gong, and deep sea ambiance drives home the feeling that you’re all alone. It managed to keep me on edge from start to finish and is done exceptionally well.
Reveal the Deep isn’t a “must buy” experience, and it’ll only take you a little over an hour to complete. But it’s got the atmosphere, intriguing story and thoughtful puzzle solving to warrant a buy. It’s only 99 cents, so there isn’t much of a gamble to be had. Who knows, it just might be worth your time.

*This review DOES NOT contain spoilers*
*The Fall" is part one of a three part game. Part two and three are in the making*
The gameplay consists of exploration, puzzle solving and gunfights. The exploration and puzzle solving go hand in hand. The gunfights are usually a result of successfully solving something. It has a very oldschool feel to it. The game will periodically teach you what you need to survive. After that you're on your own to figure out what to do and where to go.
I did not run into any "game breaking bugs" or glitches that I can recall. I did have an issue with not being able to fire while using an xbox 360 controller. I fixed it by turning off my wireless mouse. Not sure if they have found a fix, but they are aware of it.
The games sound and visuals add nicely to the atmosphere. The voice acting, sound effects and music really speak for themselves. Graphics are not mind blowing but still satisfying.
Overall I really liked the game. I do plan on playing through again. If you call yourself a gamer then you really should play The Fall. It's quite the gem. :)

A classic Resident Evil remade for Gamecube and remastered for PC, just as awesome now as it was back in the early 00's and 90's.
Resident Evil HD has all the jumps and scares with a few extra surprises for those who have only played the original and anyone returning from the Gamcube version will get more or less the same epic game but with improved visuals and effects. A true "Suvival Horror" with Puzzles, a Resident Evil game where ammo and saves are limited and running is sometimes better than fighting, unlike the action games the series has become.
The enviroments are stunningly detailed thanks to the still camera veiws, you're essentially running around a gorgeous portrait. New lighting effects have been added and when combined with the new HD textures of the characters and enemies the game really shines.
Music is perfectly implemented (Saveroom relief) and the sounds of thunder in addition to the groans and moans of the dead (amongst other things) are as jumpy and disturbing as ever.
There is so much I want to mention here, the numerous monsters, weapons and scares but I really don't want to spoil any of the surprises but what I will say is expect the unexpected ..... anyone remember the hounds?
Also the map is incredibly handy, any rooms that still have items in it will be highlighted in red and cleared rooms are blue so this should save you a lot of trouble should you find yourself stuck and wondering where to investigate next.
A choice of new or old style controls (I still prefer the tank method) with 60, varible or 30 FPS locks and runs maxed out easily on my laptop ( I7 4710MQ, GTX 860M, 8 RAM ) so I know my gaming rig will have no troubles what so ever.
Hopefully Resident Evil 0 receives the same treatment (rumoured) and a remake/port of Resident Evil 2 and 3 would be great so heres hoping.
If you've already played the Gamecube version then this Resident Evil is a 9/10 however ... if you're only played the PSX version or never even played Resident Evil ..... 10/10.
If you're after a genuine survival horror that involves more horror and thought rather than trigger action then this is game for you, easily the best Resident Evil within the series.
Pros
• "True" survival horror.
• Beautiful enviroments.
• Tense, atmosphereic.. perfect
Cons
• Too hard for some?
Finally a top tip for everyone .... should you meet the wailing women in chains ..... run .... NO REALLY .... RUN!!!

You play Tsubasa Fujimoto (though you can rename her to anything you want at the start of the game), a 20-year-old female university student who comes to acquire magical powers through unexpected circumstances. Take your pick of 5 good-looking men (one at a time though - don't be greedy!) to accompany you through your mystical journey set in contemporary urban Japan.
So is the music. And there's an "auto" option so you can play through the entire thing mostly hands-free, save for when you need to make choices.
This is the just the first chapter of the game (you have to pay for the rest), so I don't know how things'll unfold later on, but I played through all 5 different prologues (i.e. the 5 different story paths if you choose each different guy) and things seem promising. All the men have very distinctive personalities, which should make for different enough story paths. And the game promises that all men have a "secret" to tell, or some backstory that will be revealed if you play on.
I hate to say it, but this is the #1 factor I won't be buying this game, though I do still recommend it to anyone interested in what they've read about the game thus far. I personally prefer playing through all characters' stories at one go, in one sitting, one after the other, and not having to wait a millennia before each of them becomes available, one by one, in which case my interest in and memory of this game would have largely waned.

But damn isn't it a bugfest - hell, I didn't get further than the first level because the damn game is impossible to play. The audio... Oh GOD the audio! It is loud. TOO loud. You start the game and you're immediately blasted with music so loud it'll make you regret being born with ears. Then, there's no way to tweak the volume in-game. Audio files also have an annoying tendency of bugging out, with audio effects looping over and over, or completely disappearing. It doesn't seem like a lot of work went into that - or any - part of the game.
The controls are too clunky and un-intuitive to use. The mouse sensitivity is set to zero and the camera is inverted by default. I wouldn't mind the inverted camera, but why on Earth is the mouse effectively turned off by default, while NO OTHER WAY to manipulate the camera exists? But I have to say that this was the least annoing part of the absolute fiasco that the control scheme is.
What really makes the game absurdly hard is the parkour system - which isn't functioning. There's not even an effort to explain how it works, unless you count the "Run against the wall to climb it" and doing that doesn't work, which essentially means that what appears to be an essential way of navigating levels is NOT functioning properly. Really, the only way I've found that allowed me to jump high enough to grab ledges, was to use the special attack  for "fists" which, even without any energy (or whatever is that resource) at all, somehow manages to propell the character upwards, as if being yanked upwards by some sort of crane.
Plus, there's a lag when switching weapons. It switches to the fists THEN to the selected weapon. Were you to press "fire" during that time and you automatically switch to fists. It wasn't a problem at the first level, but I can imagine it being pretty lethal if things were a bit more hectic.
Really, nothing seems to work in the hot mess.

Bought this game when you got Totally Accurate Battle Simulator with it, because at the time I was only interested in that game. But now that it came out I tried it out and fell in love. Amazing game, I honestly can't think of anything negative to say about it that's not small details.
- Solid level design, some levels are short some levels are a bit longer but all are easily doable under one minute, except the last one.
- Not too hard, but definitely not easy. Some levels were a bit easy admittedly, but overall it was a challenging game.
- It felt fair, not sure how to explain this one.
- There isn't anything to help you with the game except for the small tutorial at the beginning and how to use the ability you get first time you use it. Which I find nice, because I don't like being told what spacebar does when I'm at the last level for example.
- Abilities felt second nature. You know how it's obvious that spacebar is jumping? It felt like that, you use the abilities without giving it much thought.
- Simple idea, but very original. Can't think of any other game that's this fast-paced where you have to jump on - sometimes flying - trucks.
- Going fast FELT fast. And satisfying. Especially reaching the goal at the peak of your speed, using that extra dash ability to get a few extra speed points felt very good.
- Not much to say about the visuals. They were good, the best part about them was probably the particle effects. Simple style, but it works.
EDIT: There was this small bug that sometimes when you enter a level the truck you spawn on flips immediately, making you fall on the ground, making you unable to get the Ace score for completing a level the first time you try it.
EDIT 2: Just realized I didn't say anything about the music, but that's because there wasn't really anything wrong with it, it was decent, but not something very noteworthy. The medieval theme stood out the most for me personally, but other than that nothing to really say about it.
tl;dr: Great game, pick it up when you can. Worth it for the full price, but if it's ever on sale definitely give it a try. Arbitrary rating that doesn't really mean anything: 9/10

Solar 2 is a universe simulation where you start of as an asteroid growing into a black hole
That's the game in a nutshell
But is it worth your 9.99$?
Well, Solar 2 plays pretty simple. You control an asteroid in a 2D sandbox universe. By bumping into other asteroid, you can grow to planet size. You can even have a life form in your planet if you grow it big enough. Though it serves only as an automatic self defense from celestial forces.
From then on, you can do whatever you want. Slam into other solar system, capture lots of asteroid to orbit your small planet, become a black hole to wreck the universe, anything. You feel that the universe is truly alive and the game mechanics are fluid. The gravity is really the main hook of this game in my experience. It was fun to become a big star and bend planets and asteroids to slam at each other.
The art-style and the music is well merge into the game's atmosphere. The background can immerse you into the world as the music gently soothing your mood in the game. It's overall a relaxing sandbox simulation of a universe.
I highly recommend this for those who search for a non-rage inducing game and in need of relaxing game after a long day. It is worth every penny of your hard earn 9.99$

This game gets a lot of bad recommendations because it's essentially a puzzle game with boobs and it doesn't seem to deliver an 18+ patch by the devs.   Unlike say Huniepop, which can easily be made into 18+ content, this game however has no such patch.
This game easily could have gone that route and made each stage/round a date and use a mahjong puzzle and increase the difficulty and have something else to expand the game.  But it is what it is.  The girls are really just there and they shout random Japanese things at you.  No real use for them at all, outside of collecting outfits to say I beat this level.  But, that's what achievements are for, right?
That said, this game goes on sale for 80-90% off quite often and 3$ vs the price of Huniepop is adequate.  You get what you pay for so to speak.
If you like solitaire style mahjong to relax, and don't mind being called a "hentai" every time you succeed at round 3 of a stage this is pretty good.  As the puzzles actually provide some difficulty and failing puzzles due to poor choices or random chance can happen (which is common in complex layouts in mahjong).
Very good solo game to stress relief.  No innuendo implied, but the music is genuinely upbeat, repetitive, but the focus for my brain at least goes to racing the clock (which isnt really a big deal in honesty) and finding the best move possible.
It's not overly perverse at all, outside of some J-Cup style girls, most of the outfits are cute and at most role play for the imagination.
I would NOT buy this game at full price, and the fact it costs more than huniepop and offers LESS (in adult content, storyline, unique puzzles, more girls, easter eggs, unlockable characters) is quite honestly a big mistake.  Worth it completely on sale, the cards are cute, and if you like crafting badges, consider it.
Overall verdict: Generic boobs to sell mahjong solitaire game.  But the puzzles and layouts are actually difficult. A solid 6 of 10.   If you like the girls add a point, if you expect more content remove a point.  But 6 for me is quite high praise for anime girls used to sell a game.  It could have been made into so much more.
PS: I would love a dating sim mixed with more girls, a bit of plot, and "plot", and mahjong puzzles it would have drastically added some sort of use and meaning for the girls in the game besides a "sex sells" point.  Would have easily made paying more for this game worth it, and would up the recommendation at least 2-3 points.

The music is entertaining and there are a few different tracks while background are diverse and the girls have multiple costumes. But it feels weird in a Solitaire/Patience game, it should be to relax but there is a time limit, the music is upbeat and the girls keep making noises while trying to get your attention.
+Multiple Patterns

Decided to take a punt on this during the festive season sale (I refuse to use the C word until December 2016!) and I'm more than happy I did.
If you want a wee game to pass some time with that doesn't require a great deal of skill, this is a great timefiller.  I don't normally leave reviews but felt it would be irresponsible not to when I enjoyed it so much.
One major commendation I have to make is for the sound design.  I'm studying audio engineering at the moment and am extremely impressed by the quality of the sounds.  That coupled with a few things in game really had me momentarily petrified!
The graphics work in it is absolutely beautiful, and added to the immersion really well.
Atmospheric, simple with no frills, bare bones control system and immersive...took me right back to earlier gaming days where you stopped to think about what you needed to do to progress.  These guys have done a spectacular job with a wee short game.
- Simple
- Curiousity-inducing background story
- Amazing sound design
- Makes you genuinely feel like an explorer in a messed up place with eerie graphics and noises that raise the hairs on the back of your neck
- Great wee headlamp on/off animation with accompanying sound effect
- Clever multiple existence idea
- Doesn't introduce you to the game using kid gloves
(let's face it, every game has it's downsides!)
- Save feature mid chapter would be beneficial
- Possibly some atmospheric background music would be good
- Navigating ladders can be finicky, if you're holding down W/S/up or down when you jump towards a ladder, you occasionally move in the opposite direction...but it's not enough to detract totally from my overall view of the game
I love how I as a gamer wasn't patronised in the introduction to the game.  You're dumped into it and have to figure things out for yourself, something a lot of games fail on for me these days...they over-tutorialise.
Anyways, to finish up, if you like the odd jump scare without it being OTT, buy this game.
If you appreciate having to think for yourself, buy this game.
If you enjoy simple, well thought out games, buy this game.
Big thumbs up to the devs and keep up the good work!  Well worth the small price tag to support their work.

Aozora Meikyuu is a short Romance Visual Novel by YumeCreations. It focuses on a relationship between a boy who dropped out of school after a failed love confession and a girl who falls from the sky.
Just a little note: It will be difficult for me to write a review and explain this game without spoiling the end.
Pros:
Endings at different times- This was a well thought-out move to add in with visual novels (props to Yume).  Unlike other visual novels I have played, not all the endings happened at the end of the visual novel. You could potentially get an ending within 5 minutes of the visual novel. I also noticed that the more the story develops, the less options for endings you will get. It eventually comes down with 1 ending at the very end.
CGs- Nothing I can say about this, CGs always make a visual novel better.
Soundtrack- Love the soundtrack
Con(s)
Saving + Branching paths.- Sometimes, you cannot tell when you get the option to choose, and the fact that you can't save while choosing. Yeah, having a time limit while choosing the path is pretty unique, but at least inform the players that a branching path is coming up so they can save beforehand.
Story-  The story was interesting, for sure. But the way it was written was really "jumpy". It starts on one part of the story, then skipping to a different part of the story within seconds. I'm not saying the story was bad, I just thought that it could use less story skips because the transition of the "good ending" was confusing at first.
Yeah, I'd recommend this short and sweet visual novel if you're interested in romance. (heck, isn't all the visual novels about romance?)
(Also, do people dislike this game just because they failed to pick the right choices to get to the good ending and they end up crying about it?)

Of all the walking simulators I've played this one is probably the silliest.
It's incredibly beautiful and creates a consistent, enchanting atmosphere—which is indeed the baseline that's required of a walking simulator. The cryptography puzzle is a great idea that highlights the decently non-linear level design (for such a short game) with its shortcuts circling back; after deciphering the code, the player is encouraged to double back and explore the previous areas once again, this time being able to read and learn more about what went on. It's a great and inventive use of the game's limited resources.
...But this is also where Homesick fails, I'm afraid. Knowing that in gaming less is often more is a tough wisdom to accept; few developers do. As a result, they try to add more content to their games without realising that it actually leaves their creations emptier than they would have been without it. The texts in Homesick are boring and bland, somehow leaving the player with less story than they had before reading them; at least without those notes (that somehow completely evaded the fire that had destroyed everythng else, must be made of titanium or something) the player could imagine a story to their taste based on audio and visual cues.
And it would probably be a better story than the boring one we ended up with. Not to mention the poorly-executed TWEEST at the end.
I may sound nitpicky, but for such a short game with such a price tag, every aspect must be brilliant for it to be worth it. And I think Homesick would have been a much better game if it just mesmerized us with brilliant lighting and dilapidation—and left it at that.

The best Elder Scrolls title, hands down.
At the start of the game, you are thrown into an alien world, one that you would never expect to see youself in. Everything is different, to the odd fungus flora, to the floating jellyfish that are the Netch. You start as a lowly Outlander, and are constantly told that you, are a worthless outlander. And you don't belong. But as you progress, that will change. You will become an Outlander who barely can swing a sword, to the Nerevarine, legendary Dunmer Saint who can kill gods, and capture their souls.
The satisfaction of this makes the game very rewarding and fun to play. Not to mention the amazing spell-creation system, that allows you to create any spell imaginable.
Now other than that, let's talk Story. Morrowind tells one of the greatest stories you will ever partake in. The 6th House has risen, and a blight pollutes Vvardenfell. Will you be the one to save Vvardenfell from this blight, and destroy the evil Dagoth Ur, who dwells in Red Mountain? Or who knows, you might just become arch-mage of Great House Telvanni. All of this is up to you.
I definitely recommend Morrowind to anyone who enjoys a good story, a great RPG/openworld game, and a piece of art. But don't let graphics put you off! Morrowind is an amazing, must-play game! Alas, some people may be scaared of these "bad" graphics. That's why there's Morrowind Graphics and Sound Overhaul! It makes the game look like any modern game, so haha, there's no excuses now!

I thought Skyrim was a great game.
I saw people talking about how Morrowind was better, how it didn't match up to the game that came out 8 years prior. At first I didn't believe them. How could a game from 2003 compare to a game from 2006 (Oblivion) or 2011? So I saw it on sale at a modest price, and I bought it. Am I glad I made that purchase? Hell yeah.
What a video game Morrowind is. It hasn't aged particularly well, I admit*, but the game underneath the 2003 visuals is something that still worth a look at. A huge look in fact. Yes, while it isn't as packed with content as much as it's newer releases, it still has enough for you to dedicate a sizeable potion of your free time to complete. Some of the mechanics in Morrowind would be seen as "outdated" or "products of its time", I personally felt like these mechanics were more relaxing while wandering around the island of Vvardenfell, but also had the potential to challenge you in combat. Remember, this game came out in 2003, so it's no surprise to find out that it has 2003 video game hard difficulty at times. If you make the same mistake I did and come into Morrowind, hoping to have as simple a time as Skyrim or Oblivion, you're gonna have a bad time.
However, these little difficulty issues or content shortages don't impact too much on the quality of the game here. Morrowind is quickly becoming one of my favourite games on PC and certainly one of my favourite Bethesda games.
*Downloading the Morrowind Overhaul Mod mostly fixes those ugly textures and soft lighting issues though.

There are certain things you have to go through when you're an indie dev. With web comics, making music on youtube, hosting a podcast, making indie games, any online careers that have popped up in this day and age you have to make a few choices related to how you make your money when you start, get an audience keep making money and also keep your audience so that you can still keep doing what you're doing...
This is an example of how not to treat your audience...
I downloaded Mystic Destinies: Serendipity of Aeons for the sake of research (I'm a writer myself and I've been dabbling with visual novel creating softwares because one of my original works may end up working better in that format than in a novel or webcomic format.). Most of my Steam friends and all of my friends IRL will tell you i'm determined to be a web comic artist who doesn't rely on ads on their site in order to make money (because i hate those ads myself). I consider myself a very honest writer. I want to be funded completely by my audience if i can, if i absolutely must do sponsorships i'll only get sponsors that I have experience with or get sponsors related to products and services i have used and approved of, so on and so fourth. In this day and age, if you wanna go indie you need to be upfront and honest with your audience unless you want to end up like the shameful Digital Homicide (using an indie example) or perhaps worse: be accused of being your field's EA equivalent!
So seeing that this game was free to play and i wanted to study how some of my favorite visual novels worked, i downloaded this game under the impression i was getting a whole game... I did not. I got a prolouge and 1 chapter for free with 11 OTHER CHAPTERS behind a paywall...
Now putting some content behind a paywall i can understand... DLC, extra routes that may not appeal to everyone, sountracks, art collections, pre-order bonuses and other stuff like that which may not appeal to everyone i can understand charging for... But if you're gonna put 11 CHAPTERS OF YOUR VISUAL NOVEL BEHIND A PAY WALL, then why not just charge for the game outright?
Speaking for myself in particular my webcomic is still in the process. The story is worked on in a unique way where things are subject to change so no storyboarding gets done until things are final. I have an editor to keep me in line so i don't do anything stupid, but who also makes sure i get stuff done. Currently my web comics have no budget in particular and i do all of the art, 90% of the writing and a good chunk of any research i need for it myself. I don't have a site because I know full well I don't have much material to display currently, and if you have no finished product, you shouldn't post at all... That only makes sense!
That's my main complaint about this game...
They paraded it like a free to play game that you could download and enjoy in it's entirety but once you finish chapter one you realize "Oh... Only the first chapter was free. Now they expect me to pay..." For that, you might as well hold off your project until it's near completion, maybe put it in early access if need be. If you really need the money to work on your product there are plenty of people on Kickstarter who could help fund your game. Being an honest indie dev is hard, i know. You don't make much if any money when you start out, you have to rely on your audience's kindness, you have to build a rather LARGE audience in order to make enough money from donations or through services like Paypal or Patreon alone... These are things I'm willing to face as an indie creator myself. HOWEVER, EVEN I KNOW FULL WELL, IF YOU DON'T HAVE A COMPLETE OR NEAR COMPLETE PRODUCT NO MATTER HOW BIG OR SMALL, YOU SHOULDN'T PUT IT OUT FOR SALE UNDER THE GUISE OF IT BEING 'FREE' ONLY FOR THE REST OF IT TO BE PUT BEHIND A PAYWALL...
According to some of the other reviews I've read, people pointing out what i am saying are facing censorship from this game's developer (how very Digital Homicidal that seems). I'm not sure if this is true or not, but if whether or not it is, this is not how you behave as an indie dev...
I know this review has mostly been ranting about the paywall, but i won't be interested in playing this game further for other reasons as well:
- The writing seems very rushed in the prolouge. I didn't know whether to attribute it to the heroine just giving us little anicdotes of her day and maybe that's why it seems choppy or maybe it's the developer putting more story in the prolouge behind a paywall
- The heroine seems somewhat generic. Maybe it's one of those things where she's supposed to be our in-game avatar but i honestly don't like that approch all that much. It's been so overdone it's almost offensive for your heroine to be so bland (Bella Swan and Anastasia Steel being 2 big examples of this writing sin). There are a lot of dating sims with interesting heroines, I'd rather play those instead!
- The art style is okay. The women look especially nice but for the men it kind of gives them a weird uncanny valley sort of look... but that's probably just me.
- The prolouge is too damn short and rushed... If you wanna release a free prolouge for your upcoming game, that's fine. But at least give us a good chunk of story so we can understand what'll happen in the full game once it's released... All i can gather from the prolouge is that there's magic and alchemy involved but i'm not getting much else...
Overall, this game gets a spank on the butt from me... Unless the devs release it as A: a COMPLETE free to play game (which is unlikely) or B: Get rid of the paywall and just release a finished complete product for 15 or so dollars, I won't bother with this title further...

I tried very hard to like this game, it looked fun and despite the problems others experienced, I thought for 39 pence I couldnt go wrong. Well...
Firstly, the control system is *extremely* finicky, particularly the wall-running mechanic. Sometimes it would work okay, the majority of the time my character randomly jumped and flipped around the screen like a dying flippy thing. I haven't even been able to get past the very beginning of the game as a result. I'm not the worlds best gamer by any means, but I'd rather fail at a game because I'm rubbish, not because it is broken.
Secondly, as has been pointed out before, due to some wierd clipping errors, enemies can shoot at you through 'solid' walls, sometimes, and also wierdly, doors above or below your level open because they think you are near them. Again, being killed because I'm rubbish I can live with. being killed because the game basically cheats, on the other hand...
Graphics-wise, it's okay, nothing amazing, but they serve their purpose. I've seen worse. if I was able to get further into the game I'd probably be able to comment better. However, I haven't experienced frame rate drops, and no crashed to desktopn either and/or freezes, so at least that's something.
On the plus side, the developers are at least trying to engage with the community in fixing the bugs, and acknowledge that it is broken and are trying to fix it, which is better than some AAA companies I could mention. Unfortunately, the buggy, glitchy mess I experienced isn't the sort of thing that can be fixed by patches. Nothing short of a total rebuild from the ground up would resolve this. Which is a shame, as it has potential. Somewhere under there, there is a nice concept, but buried beneath the glitch controls and other issues I have experienced, I really cannot recommend this. if you have 79p burning a hole in your wallet, buy a chocolate bar, it will bring much more joy, and will probably last longer as well.

From what I experienced, this was pretty well written. The fight scenes read a little clunky in some parts but were passible. There was a good variety of descriptions especially for things that repeat, something that other VN's forget to do. You don't see lines like "my heartbeat increased" over and over again (my biggest pet peeve). As others mentioned, there were a few plotholes that didn't get resolved but I'm not too upset about it. The main story arc / romance is most important for me and this one was satisfying.
I'd recommend this to anyone in the mood for a read with a ton of warm and fuzzies.

On the negative side: everything else. It's the ultimate in shooting the same damn enemy over and over and over again in a small featureless square room simulator.

Gameplay: it's a very tough Mahjong Solitaire game. The boards are layed out very good and are pseudo-randomized on each start, but never in such a way that they are unsolveable.
The game loses points because of how the boards are stacked combined with the top-down view: sometimes tiles that are adjacent and appear to be on the same level are actually on different levels and therefore both selectable. If there are no other tiles next to it this can be very easy to overlook.
The gimmick of the game is that you have an anime chick next to the boards who is moaning and saying Japanese things as you progress. After clearing three boards you get to a clothing change level where her moans become sexier and a slider goes down her body which reveals a skimpier outfit. There is no nudity.

At it's current price with a huge discount, I can recommend it for the solitaire as it's done very well and the gimmick is amusing. Don't pay full price for it though.

Summary: A gorgeous unspoken narrative with solid puzzle gameplay undermined by technical flaws, slowness and especially how it asks too much of its player to fully appreciate it.
It looks beautiful and intriguing, it's got decent reviews and those who like it are glowing in their appraisal. So why isn't everyone talking about Homesick? Well it's basically because games like Homesick can't afford to be too slow, technically flawed or in some way inaccessible, and unfortunately Homesick is all of those things.
If you've ever looked at pictures of Pripyat and seen beauty in it, you'll probably dig the aesthetic a lot, and Homesick sticks to small environments so it can render in lush detail the cracked walls and fallout specks, to the tune of a somber, memorable piano theme. It almost completely works, but you can still see rooms load in front of you and the occasional graphical seam, which just shouldn't happen in a game like this.
Regardless it's a joy to simply look at for a while, and then you have to set about finding out how to proceed. Most of the puzzles can be worked out from environmental clues and I wasn't stuck for too long with these, they were satisfying to do and didn't take much guesswork.
The central issue of Homesick concerns the notes scattered everywhere written in a cipher. Most are optional and don't require your engagement, but one puzzle requires you to painstakingly work out the cipher and then apply it to a puzzle. Now, as someone interested in language I found this quite fun and satisfying, but as I was enjoying myself I knew that to many this would be a stopping point. It's not complicated, but it is a slow, slow process exacerbated by your character's subhuman gait.
Once the cipher is cracked it's possible to go around translating all the notes in the game, but this asks FAR too much of the average player, especially since many of those notes are very dense. In fact, that such a wealth of actual written knowledge exists alongside Homesick's minimalist, environment-based narrative undermines the experience for the user.
Homesick could have been a beautiful, self-contained, wordless experience that tells its story with feel and pictures, leaving its world with most of its questions unanswered. But the answers could be there, hidden under all that cipher; the price of translating it all and finding out more is simply too high, so the average gamer will cope with the 'unfinished' feeling the game leaves them with. That's not the feeling the game should be engendering.
I actually enjoyed my time with Homesick and I'm glad I played it, which makes my conclusion complicated. Visually it's a game of rare beauty. It has some solid puzzling that makes you engage with your environment, and you might well enjoy it. But particularly at full price Homesick doesn't deliver on that satisfaction that it promises and simply won't please everyone.

Like a number of Kickstarted games, Homesick suffers from the lukewarm execution of an ok premise. The game is not bad per se, it just does not offer much.
There are some interesting things in the way the game tries to stear the player without using text or cut scenes, but it is a bit hit or miss (there is a whole puzzle that remains a total mystery to me thanks to a lack of clues and feedbacks) and the puzzles themselves are not exactly awe inspiring. There is not much to chew on as far as story go and while the environement and music are commendable in their execution there is a total lack a variety.
A bit of a shame, because I am absolutely in favor of this type of compact format for games. A 2 to 5 hours game requires a quantity of content that is managable for a small team, BUT the format also requires a very high level of quality and/or originality that simply is not there in Homesick.

Hi,
Right of the bat let me just say the latest version is way more improved than what I played some weeks ago. While by no means perfect, this shows the dedication of the person behind it, so kudos for that, this is what warrants a positive review in my book.
Some very noticeable improvements:
- Movement and Control: Way better, now I can control the character and expect it to behave as it should most of the time; also, much easier and natural to replenish ammo now :)
- UI: Looks much cooler, but more importantly now you can easily see what's going on, much easier to read (health, ammo etc.)
- Optimization: Almost no framerate drops now, the game is much more stable than before
- The intro/story screens are something else now, I can't even describe the difference (though this is a minor point for most)
- The new lightning in the levels really bring the whole game to life (although you are mostly surrounded by metal and robots)
In conclusion, the price seems rather fair now comparing to what you get... there is still room for more improvements and tweaks, but if the latest experience shows anything is that work on the game continues and we can expect more updates in the future.
Tip: Mouse can be erratic at first, make sure to adjust sensitivity from the options menu... this is almost a prerequisite here unlike most games, but by no means a deal breaker once you find a setting confortable for you.

The Painkiller: Redemption experience can be more or less summarized like this:
You enter a cramped area filled with a dozen or so enemies. You kill them. A dozen or so more spawn. You kill them. A dozen or so more spawn. You kill them. A dozen or so more spawn. You kill them. You start to notice how obtrusively restrictive the level design is on your movement. You start to feel claustrophobic, but instead of instilling fear it instills disgruntlement. I thought this was supposed to be a Painkiller game, you think to yourself. A dozen or so more spawn with a few tougher enemies. You kill them and stand next to the door to the next shooting cell, because surely that had to be the last wave of enemies.
NOPE ♥♥♥♥ YOU 3 MORE WAVES.
You alt-f4 out of the game, delete it from your library, and stare out your bedroom window, reminiscing about the $5 you just blew on this steaming pile of refuse.

Doing what I do I tend to check the latest Steam releases daily for anything that might be of interest, if I see something interesting I ask for it and I’m always grateful when a developer says yes. This was very much the case with HotLead, there weren’t even reviews on steam when I asked the developer for review code and I didn’t hear anything back. Thats also not unusual as I’m no IGN or Gamespot sized website. You expect it and move on, so when an email hit my inbox late last week with my review code I was a little surprised this long after.
Surprises are a funny things aren’t they, sometimes their nice and sometimes there not. . . Can you see where I’m going with this?
Now my review process is as follows, I normally play the game fully and complete it in games that have a clear ending. Then I like to play again making choices and doing things I didn’t before and see how it impacts the story/gameplay. Lastly I like to let it simmer for a few days and then revisit it if I still have questions.
Thats the normal way I like to do it, HotLead I have done non of this for. I’ve played the tutorial and the first level, so I might seem rather ill equipped to offer any kind of review for this game. But let me assure you I’ve learned everything I need to know about this game and really don’t need to spend anymore time with it. I’m slightly upset I have to revisit it to do the screen shots for this review.
So what is HotLead, well its meant to be a fast paced futuristic third person shooter where your character can use a range of weapons and attacks along with packour to make huge combos devastating your opponents. The reality on the other hand is entirely different. . . Well it is in third person! But as far as the fast paced action goes, well if you hold shift the main character does move a touch faster than the standard snails pace he normally would. But I really shouldn’t get your hopes up as the controls are just bad, from basic movement to jumping thats so vital to a game like this having a complete mind of its own nothing works fluidly or accuracy. It’s a total mess and its only compounded by the fact the level design is atrocious with dead ends and no route made clear to the player.
Even the graphics that from a distance look somewhat interesting loose the polish on closer inspection, there really is little if anything to redeem HotLead and that a shame as the idea behind it has so much potentiol. I’ve always tried to champion Indie games and Indie developers, building some great relationships with some. I love the fact on the PC we have all this raw talent available to us with far less obstacles than other platforms, but I game like this not only damages the indie community as a whole but also goes a long way to show up the issues with steam and this freedom we PC players for the most part enjoy.
That’s not to say this game is the sole cause of all the issues with steam and Indie developers, of course thats not the case. But its a great example of the trash we are seeing more and more in the minefield of Indie titles. HotLead isn’t even fit for a alpha release let alone to be released as a finished title which it is, it resembles a school project rather than a game sold for money.
I understand that no doubt the developer will probably read this and probably be quiet hurt by what I’ve said, but its my job to inform you the consumer not feed any body’s ego. Don't be fooled by the screenshots, while they seem to convey a shallow experience to finish in an hour or two, this game is honestly hard as nails to finish. It's the more, in the west, common match-the-tiles-game, and start off fairly easy, but once the difficulty starts rising, by god is it rising. Beyond the obvious failstate that is "no more tiles to match", you also have a timer ticking down. In addition to this, when the tiles get randomly placed there's a major risk that you'll get a setup that you cannot win, no matter skill, and in my playthrough half my losses was due to this. That said, the game evoke the same feeling where every loss makes you more determined that many find in games like Dark Souls after enough losses. In fact, I for one forgot the whole "Pretty Girls" part of the game until victory was mine. Be warned though, you who are here primarily for the anime images, there's no gallery for the various outifts after you beat the required stages, which is a bit of a let down.
So all in all, it's flawed, but I recomend it. As long as you have up to ten or so hours to spend on finishing it.

If you're into classic games (in particular those of the role playing variety) then it doesn't get much better than the original Fable. Having long possessed Fable: The lost chapters on PC, I was curious to see how the graphics and gameplay had been altered for the anniversary edition; I wasn't disapointed. The graphics are a visible step-up from the vanilla game and the gameplay, which was near perfect at the time of its release, fortunatley remains unchanged.
Some small changes have been made though. The save system of the original game has been altered in this version. The ability to Hero Save has been scrapped, consequently removing game breaking exploits allowing your character to rapidly level up. The reason for this I suspect is to make the new heroic mode, which is essentially normal Fable but markedly more difficult, that little bit more challenging. There are a couple of features that I wish the devlopers had included in the anniversary edition such as an option to switch between the vanilla and anniversary versions of the game but otherwise I'm very happy with the game. Well worth buying and a practical steal when on sale. 8/10.

I honestly don't recommend it.  This game plays exactly like Dear Esther (slow walking speed, no jump, and little in the way of useful interaction), except that it introduces nonsensical mechanics that take a while to understand.   You'll get stuck for minutes at a time, and every time you stumble upon what you're actually supposed to do, in retrospect it makes as little sense as it did before.  Why are there flowers?  Why do flowers allow you to progress forward?  There's no explanation for anything that happens (perhaps at the end, but I didn't get that far), and you don't feel adequately rewarded each time you figure something out.  Games like Amnesia will reward you with loot for figuring out a tough puzzle, but here, you're given nothing.  No story, no items, just "proceed forward and get stuck on the next quirky puzzle".
Personally, if this game suits you, check out INFRA.  Also in the same vein.  Extremely slow plot progression, find keys, open doors, find more keys, open more doors, figure out where a thing is and put it in the slot, move on to the next area.  It can't even be compared to Myst.  At least in Myst you have those "Aha" moments when you finally solve a puzzle.  Here you just think "wait, why did that work?  Why did I need to do that?"
On the plus side, nice stylized graphics.  The screenshots will come out nice for sure.

HuniePop is one of those games you discover after feeling a little...frisky...or after browsing the interwebs a little too long at night. Well regardless of how you discover it, it's either you're sold on the
gameplay or you move on....Oh who am I kidding, it's either you love it, or you love it.
This game is essentially two in one; Bejewelled and a Dating Sim. Your goal is to get laid...multiple times. In fact, you're supposed to get laid with ALL the girls and collect their panties. I've gotta say, I've never been more concentrated in my life. You'd think that a game that appeals to our primal nature would be a walk in the park? Heh. This game tests your memory as well as your bejewelled tactics with a tad bit of luck sprinkled in for good measure. I can't even tell you how many times I was 1 move away from getting the girl; sink or swim. Most of the time I'd fail and go lie down and curl up in my bed trying not to cry. However on those epic moments where I made the right moves, I'd excitedly punch a wall knowing what I was to experience. But no, the struggle wouldn't end there. No no, from start to finish, it would be a fast paced match-3/4/5 minigame as you
calmly watch a woman's chest become exposed and her make some unique sounds.
The game was easy to get into, but was actually challenging in many respects. But let's be real here, who's gonna boast about getting all the achievements in HuniePop amirite?
The cartoony visuals were just fine for this type of game. The most appealing parts were of course....well you know.
The music was fairly good, though at times it could get almost repetitive but at least it was good enough to listen to.
The voice actors for each of the ladies did their parts pretty damn well, though
.
You're either gonna love this game for the girls or you're not going to be interested. The bejewelled style of gameplay and the dating sim aspect are both not unique but done well enough to keep you interested. This will appeal to some people, but not all, and your reasons for playing this will vary.
If you like these types of games then:
8/10 worth a buy

First episode of a nice hybrid adventure-platformer. The concept itself is wonderful (if ultimately a little obvious) and I do hope they finish the series, as the story is pretty interesting. The controls (I played with xbox gamepad) are bad, particularly aiming, and the basic action of the game (interact with something) seems to take twice as many steps as it should. There are a few other things that seem unpolished, like the display of text when you inspect something. On the other hand, the graphic style is hauntingly good, very reminiscent of The Swapper (that game is nearly without flaw so I think you should prioritize it), and the character animations were excellent as well. The voice acting was great, although some conceits meant that the dialog goes pretty slowly, which made me end up skipping some and just reading. Puzzles were good; I finished without any external hints and most of them made sense. The game was more linear and "neat" than I prefer. One downside of this game is that it's essentially a point-and-click adventure game (and a good one), but it has some action sequences that were fairly mediocre and seemingly unnecessary, like they had planned and developed the capability but not really made use of it. I think this might make the game needlessly inaccessible for people who don't really do action. Overall, though, innovative and compelling; recommended.

Do not mistake my low hours on steam for few hours on this game. This game was my entry into the gaming world, never before had I been so lost inside a new universe before.
So I'll tell you the tale.
I was around about 10 or 11 when I was at some local markets in my home city, I was in the 2nd hand stall looking for toys and games as I always did (Along with some churros in hand). The only thing I knew about Morrowind was that it was in the same series as "Oblivion" a game that had still fairly recently come out. I only new this because there was a really cool looing ad for Oblivion in a PC Powerplay magazine I had.
So I begged my dad to buy it for me (It was $5aud if I recall) and the RedAnt published version.
I remember the first time I played it, I only had a brief half an hour when we got back from the markets before we had to go out again so I installed it as fast as I could and got to play about 10 mintues of it before going out.
Until then, the only games I had really played were the battlefield series (nothing later than battlefield 2 at that time) back in the days when we went to LAN cafes filled with fat sweaty dudes playing video games. Yeah those were the ♥♥♥♥IN TIMES YO!
Ahem, back on track. I booted up the game and I remember walking out of the prison ship for that first time and looking around at the world around me, and then discovering that I could go anywhere and do anything. It was eye opening and a stunning experiance, because I had never looked at games like this before.
From the tens of thousands of hours I have invested into this game, I have never even completed the main story line, I always get so lost or offtrack of deside to create a new dark elf or an orc or an imperial.

On top of this, it allows modders to create their own stories without needing to hire voice actors, and as a result of Morrowind being so modder friendly (as well as havig an INCREADBLY easy to learn construction kit to make your own mods) it has perhaps the most incredible modding/community to date.
The last thing I have to say is in the defence of people who conplain how hard it is to hit an NPC.
Don't think of Morrowind as a video game, think of it as a 3D projected table top D&D style game.
