Edit 5 Sept. 2015: Recent updates have touched on some of the bad things I have had to say about the game. New opinions reflected accordingly.
First off, if you're looking for nudity, look elsewhere. The devs even said in the product description this game has none, the nudity tag is a bunch of idiots assuming the girls will eventually strip fully naked for you. (They're USER DEFINED tags, after all.)
Second, I'm rating this game based on the game, not the women, because I feel like the game deserves a fair rating based on its merits and faults.
The game is basically Mahjong Solitaire, the probably more well known version of Mahjong as far as the United States goes. This type of thing has probably been remade a bunch of times in many different forms for Facebook and Flash. So what makes this one different? Not much, unfortunately, aside from every third round being a level where the girl to the left of the game field changes into a different outfit.
It still does Mahjong Solitaire properly. The rules aren't any different, so if you've played it before, you already know how. All of the stages are different, though none of them use the full tile set (only one season in play at any point). Originally, the game did not have a resume function, thereby forcing you to do all three rounds in one sitting. An update fixed this issue, as well as allowing you to see the girls in their outfits you worked to earn, so the game gets points for the devs paying attention to what we're saying. This makes some of the other issues less of an issue.
Pros:
- It's the Mahjong Solitaire you probably know well.
- Some of the outfits do pass off as sexy.
- Ability to suspend play in the middle of a stage.
Cons:
- Time limit prevents you from thinking about moves too long.
- Limited music variety; everything gets repetitive before finishing the first girl.
- Uneven difficulty toward the end.
- Some of the outfits feel reused with minor aesthetic changes.
Overall: 6/10. With the addition of the suspend mechanic, I can deal with not having an undo or reshuffle mechanic, as if I get frustrated and want to do something else, I don't have to redo everything I just did. It gets just enough of a score to allow me to recommend this game.

Mild spoilers ahead.
What's interesting about Homesick is that you kinda play it twice in the same run: you get a sense of the place you're exploring just by the gorgeous atmosphere, and then you unlock a way to fully flesh out what happened. Some complain about "having to backtrack" when in essence the games provides you with a new layer of meaning near the end. But just with the music, the gorgeous environments, and the cryptic visual cues found throughout the game, even before the actual story is explained, the game stirred very strong emotions in me. A sense of loss pervades the experience, of real lives frozen by tragedy, and I even found myself projecting onto it unexpected emotional baggage that wasn't part of the game's storyline at all. Made me want to hug my loved ones. Made me think of what I have to lose, if I were to lose it all.
It's a walking simulator, the puzzles can get obnoxious in a couple of instances, and it is a short game. But if you are receptive to it, it can also be an exceptional emotional experience.

Although it's free, this game is short...and boring.
You awake not knowing where you are. Alright, now what? There are no immediate clues as to what you should do at any point in the game. If you aren't used to thinking outside the box, then this game will give you a problem. The constant, "Hey, are you there?" after standing still for 10 seconds waiting for a hint was annoying. The voices weren't that great, either - they all sound computer generated. Although, according to the credits, different people played each character.
The main character doesn't give many clues to what you have to do, either - he just says, "Why?" or, "Umm...no." or, "I don't think I need that." If you don't know that you have to throw the newspaper in the garbage can, grab some leather and matches, and start a fire, then you're stuck standing there until you can use your next hint. Fortunately, you only have to wait 2.5 minutes in between each one. But, as I said before, the constant, "Hey, are you there?" is annoying.
Also, the storyline - it is intriguing as to what happened to the city and why/how he lost his memory, but the game doesn't give you any clues to that, even after completing it. Yes, it is the first chapter, and yes, I know more will probably be revealed in future chapters, and that is why much isn't revealed, but after finishing the game and still not knowing close to anything, I really have no desire to play the future chapters, especially if they are as bland as this one. I know you can't expect too much from the point & click genre, but this looks like it was made more than two years ago. The artwork is pretty bland, even for a two dimensional game, and I got tired of looking at it after a while.
If you keep the audio in the default settings, you're likely to notice that there are times when the music is way too loud when characters are talking. However this can be adjusted in the settings menu.
If you're looking for a short game to pass some time, then this will keep you entertained for a bit. But if you're looking for an intriguing game that will always keep you on your toes, with good artwork and sound, then this isn't for you.
One final thing....why is hypnotizing a rat an achievement? It does absolutely nothing to help you progress in any way. Just why.
I'm sure someone will completely disagree with me and everything I said, but this is a review, and so it is my opinion. If the next installments are the same as this, I definitely won't be playing them, although I'll probably give the next one a try just to see.
TL;DR - bad art, bad voices, too short, no clues for what to do next, bland storyline
EDIT: I noticed the second chapter is available, however it isn't free. I would never pay for it especially considering how uninteresting the first chapter was. So going off of that I won't be trying it.

There are very few games that keep me hooked from the get-go, and The Fall is one of those few.  The Fall combines the best puzzle and problem solving aspects of point-and-click adventure games with action and metroid-ey ability progression.
I played through it in about 3 sittings within the same day - each time I got up from one sitting, I couldn't stop thinking about  the puzzle I was currently working on, and when I would get to play more!
Overall rating:
9.5/10
Pros:
-Interesting setting and story - discovered by the player gradually, at an engaging pace
-Immersive world, from the start menu, through the in-game menus, all the way to the credits
-Nearly all of the puzzles were conquerable with a little creating thinking - giving a real sense of accomplishment (rather than dumb luck from trying all possible solution combos)
Cons:
-Too short!  I know it's episodic (or a trilogy), but 4 hours was not enough - I want more now!
-While they are very few and far between, there are still the occasional head-scratcher puzzles that beg the question: "how was I supposed to figure that out?"
-My Logitec gamepad had some issues in precisely aiming my firearm (there were some difficult encounters if I had to aim at particular angles) - not really a fault of the game, but the ability to calibrate my gamepad controls would have been nice
-Too short!

So I begged my dad to buy it for me (It was $5aud if I recall) and the RedAnt published version.
I remember the first time I played it, I only had a brief half an hour when we got back from the markets before we had to go out again so I installed it as fast as I could and got to play about 10 mintues of it before going out.

HuniePop is one of those games you discover after feeling a little...frisky...or after browsing the interwebs a little too long at night. Well regardless of how you discover it, it's either you're sold on the
gameplay or you move on....Oh who am I kidding, it's either you love it, or you love it.
This game is essentially two in one; Bejewelled and a Dating Sim. Your goal is to get laid...multiple times. In fact, you're supposed to get laid with ALL the girls and collect their panties. I've gotta say, I've never been more concentrated in my life. You'd think that a game that appeals to our primal nature would be a walk in the park? Heh. This game tests your memory as well as your bejewelled tactics with a tad bit of luck sprinkled in for good measure. I can't even tell you how many times I was 1 move away from getting the girl; sink or swim. Most of the time I'd fail and go lie down and curl up in my bed trying not to cry. However on those epic moments where I made the right moves, I'd excitedly punch a wall knowing what I was to experience. But no, the struggle wouldn't end there. No no, from start to finish, it would be a fast paced match-3/4/5 minigame as you
calmly watch a woman's chest become exposed and her make some unique sounds.
The game was easy to get into, but was actually challenging in many respects. But let's be real here, who's gonna boast about getting all the achievements in HuniePop amirite?
The cartoony visuals were just fine for this type of game. The most appealing parts were of course....well you know.
The music was fairly good, though at times it could get almost repetitive but at least it was good enough to listen to.
The voice actors for each of the ladies did their parts pretty damn well, though
.
You're either gonna love this game for the girls or you're not going to be interested. The bejewelled style of gameplay and the dating sim aspect are both not unique but done well enough to keep you interested. This will appeal to some people, but not all, and your reasons for playing this will vary.
If you like these types of games then:
8/10 worth a buy

Going in there are a couple things I have to say. Resident Evil on Playstation was the first horror game I ever played. At least the first game that had graphics good enough that felt like a horror movie, to me. Good enough to genuinely creep me out. (I was 11 when it came out and though I never owned a PS1 myself, I and neighborhood kids would always go to my friends house and play) I will never forget the panic I felt when the first zombie turns to look at you after devouring part of Kenneth, after the dining room. I say this because it's important to know that I am not 100% impartial to the mansion. It's like an old friend.
The gameplay hasn't been changed very much from the original's in 1996. I think this is awesome. It wouldn't be in a modern AAA blockbuster 60$ game, but going back now is in no way a chore. I experimented with the classic tank controls and the new "alternative" setting. For my first play through I chose to use the updated control scheme, since I have not played in so long to make the game a bit easier in my favor. I plan to go back and play in full classic mode after I beat it with the new control scheme, which is very slick and streamlined. I am using a wired XBOX 360 controller and so far no complaints at all with handling.
Inventory carrying limit is still low, forcing you to choose carefully and sometimes have to go back for items you decided to leave in storage that turns out are needed. This is annoying, but it is survival horror and the characters aren't carrying magic backpacks that can carry 4 guns, 1000 rounds of ammo and an assortment of plants, sprays and items. I like this structure. It adds a bit of tension, and yes sometimes repetition to areas that don't need it, but the realism it adds is worthwhile.
I am only 1.5 hours into the game at the time of this review but I have seen enough of the mansion and gameplay to assess that there have been no graphics/audio glitches at all. The improved lighting is a huge step up. The backgrounds still remain murky and low res in spots, but I did not find this to detract from my experience. In fact, it only helped to recall those days in my friend's basement, stumbling through the game in terror. My rig is Windows 8.1, intel i7 4770k, 16 gigs of ram and Gigabyte GeForce GTX 770 OC 4GB GPU. I am using the 16:9 display at the highest settings allowed by the game without messing with .ini files. I will change these later, as I am enjoying the current presentation though I will have no problem cranking the game to 4K resolutions. As it is the game looks great. It could very well fool someone into thinking it a modern title at first glance. I am loving exploring the old mansion in the updated graphics. It looks very good in my opinion. There have been no frame rate stutters. I have read people complaining that they kept the slow door opening animations when going from room to room. I disagree and love how the tension goes up as you wait to find out what is behind the door you just figured out how to unlock.
The audio has always been a huge part of making a scary setting, and the classic clomps of the boots of the living and zombie footfalls ring through the halls. The sound of gunshots are a bit flat but get the job done. The shuffling of zombies eating and staggering, as well as the moans let you know that you are not alone, and that is not good. The fixed cameras raise tension as it allows enemies to be placed off screen, just the noises alerting you to their proximity. Then you have to go find the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s, so that you can end their undead existence.
The story has been rock solid in the early REs, so nothing new there. Until it got convoluted and Hollywooded out the♥♥♥♥♥ it has all the classic elements of night of the living dead and other classics, with some geopolitical intrigue thrown in.
I heartily recommend this to anyone who has a history with this classic, whether on PS1 or the gamecube version. After all these years, the original Resident Evil/Biohazard title still holds up well enough to perhaps show the world just how far from its roots the series has strayed, and remind us why, in some ways it is a tragedy.

The remake and upscaling of the 2002 gamecube version is a great addition to the steam library, The music is still amazing, the graphics are outstanding, and you'll constantly find yourself stopping to take screenshots. this version gives people who came in with 4-5 (god forbid racoon city, 6, or revelations.) a good chance to see where it all started, Sure it's not the Directors cut for ps1, but it's still really great. the movement is smooth as glass, and the game is still holding up well. I genuinely forgot all about creatures like crimsonheads, which made this awesome to experience again. The only complaints I could have about this game are the simple things, remember to save often because autosave doesn't exist and you will die, and could find yourself several hours behind again, and if you know the game like the back of your hand, you could beat it in under two hours, much like the other older titles, the backtracking and inventory management is what slows you down long enough to stack on game time, but after the third playthrough, it should be pretty easy for you, if it's not already.  this game is worth playing just to meet lisa trevor and one zombie mode (if it's even in this one) where you have to run from a zombie Forest speyer that can open doors and chase you. but you can't kill him because he has grenades on him, and one shot ends your game. all in all, super happy to see this on steam 10/10

This is an atmospheric light platformer with some elements of horror/suspense where you control a diver investigating a shipwreck. Log books and other clues are scattered around and tell you the story of the people aboard the ship and what happened to them. It is a fairly slow paced game - you are walking under water - with an interesting game mechanic used to "switch environments" in certain places to allow progress.
I quite liked it, did not have any issues running this on Windows 10 and took around 3 hours to finish. Not really scary, and if there's anything not to like, it was the controls which felt somewhat clunky.

You control an unnamed diver as you slowly make your way through a shipwreck, exploring rooms and corridors as you try to find what made the ship sink and what happened to the crew.
Reveal the Deep is a minimalistic game featuring explorable environments, horror elements and simple puzzle/ platforming sections: while short and quite basic in its gameplay its strong atmosphere and interesting story make it a worthwhile experience and a somewhat hidden gem.
-nice art style despite the simple graphics, there's also some lovely light effects
-great sound design truly makes you feel as if you were alone underwater
-excellent atmosphere, the game feels eerie and there's a constant sense of dread
-decent puzzles backed by an interesting light/ dark mechanic
-the animation for turning your light on/ off lasts a second and waiting for it can eventually get annoying
-the "thud thud" sound of your footsteps can get a tad monotonous
-negotiating ladders can be finicky
-the last puzzle can feel a bit too hard to figure out
-ending is cryptic and somewhat unsatisfying
-only saves progress at the end of each chapter
-short at 1,5 hours
Reveal The Deep is a quite nice overall, slowly exploring the shipwreck while finding journals and clues felt satisfying as did solving the simple puzzles the game throws your way. The atmosphere is great as you move through rooms with only your light providing some illumination: not knowing what might be lurking a few feet from you can get genuinely unsettling when you consider the great sound design.
The actual gameplay is pretty simple and boils down to exploring, jumping through a few platforms, pushing blocks and/or use levers to solve puzzles and escape the occasional danger. If you die you'll start at a checkpoint and there's quite a few of them so that things don't get frustrating. Do take note though that you'll have to clear a chapter if you want your progress saved, if you quit to desktop you'll start from the beginning of your last level: thankfully each one takes only about 30 minutes to clear though.
Reveal The Deep comes fully recommended due to its great atmosphere and fairly intriguing story, its extremely cheap price makes it a true bargain.

Are you new to Visual Novels?
Want to experience a Visual Novel without having long and tedious plotlines?
Don't want to sit through a bunch of characters and sub-plots that just convulude the main story?
Then Aozora Meikyuu is for you!  This game is pretty short, I managed to beat it within an hour of play and I can recommend it to anyone who has not played, or doesn't want a long visual novel story to go through, just to make 10 minutes of progress on a 60+ hour story.
The characters for Aozora Meikyuu are reminisant of your stereo-typical manga characters, guy who's a shut in, girl with a hidden past, and a person from the main character's past.  The story of all of these people is just enough to get the central plot of the game across without it dragging the story out for longwinded hours of the day.
On the plus side of this game is the amount of time it takes to get through.  This game is considerably short, and can be beaten in well under 2 hours.  The story has a fair decent amount of pacing, and reminded me from time to time of reading a manga that came with it's own background music.  And the characters, while generic in their own right, bring their own liveliness to the game and makes you wonder more about them.
Considering I don't have anything negative to say, the only downside that I could point at for this game is it's replayabiliy.  Once you get the main ending, you're basically replaying situations and scenes to just see what happens when you pick another option and how it affects the ending.
Aozora Meikyuu as a whole is a pretty solid game and well worth the price I paid for it during the Steam Summer Sale 2016.  If you're trying to get yourself into Visual novels, or get friends who might be interested in them then I would highly recommend this game.

Fable aniversary in my eyes is an amazing game. But let me say first off, if you are looking for a remake of the original which changes gameplay elements in order to create an improvement of the game then this is not the game for you. But if you are just looking for practically the same game with different graphics or are new to the series then this game is perfect for you.
Lets start off on what the game is, in fable aniversary you start off as a rosy cheeked child whos town gets slaughtered by bandits. After being saved by a hero he takes you to the Hero Guild where you tain and become a full fledged hero. You are now ready to traverse the world and chose who you will be, Good or evil.
Now to start with the gameplay, Fable anniversary  is a combat heavy game which has a fairly simple system. You can use either will (magic) Finnese (Archery) or Strength (Melee). You are also able to block and dodge. Once you have learned how to do these mechanics the rest of the game will be fairly easy. In my playthroughs I have specced in each tree (you can upgrade all three) and I have seen that finnese is the most powerfull as all you need to do is roll then shoot then roll. Doing this I am rarely ever hit.
Now the alignment system. Theres not much to say if you do a bad choice you gain bad points if do a good thing you get good points. It is a black and white shallow alignment system.

I'm going to give Homesick a thumbs up, but this would be an excellent opportunity for a "meh" option.  On the plus side it's gorgeous and atmospheric, thoughtful and pensive, with some light puzzle solving.

I feel like it's worth a playthrough if those aren't massive turnoffs for you, but definitely wait for it to go on sale.

While this game definitely fulfils its promise of being atmospheric, almost the entire game can be summed up in the images provided by Steam.  It's beautiful, and I thought the soundtrack was very fitting, but unless you really enjoy taking screenshots, this game has (in my opinion) little to no replay value.  I was lucky to have bought this game on sale, because even though it was an enjoyable experience, $8.99 is perhaps a little too much for a game with little replay value, and $14.99 is definitely excessive.
That being said, the single playthrough was good, and I genuinely got emotional at a few points, but I think I figured out what the backstory/plot was before I was supposed to.  What was probably supposed to be a suspenseful series of hints felt like it was beating me over the head by the time I finished, and I wasn't shocked by a major moment of the game.  I was just... sad.
I'm aware that the game is listed as short and averaging 2-4 hours, but I'm usually horrendously slow at puzzle games and eager to wander off-track and soak up the atmosphere.  In the bare minimum of that time frame, I had already looked at all of the paper materials, explored all of the rooms, and figured out all of the puzzles.
In spite of the gorgeous graphics and one good (but quick) run through, this game fell short of what I expected for the price.  If it weren't so expensive, I would definitely recommend it, despite the lack of replay value.  In the end, if you're torn between this game and Ethan Carter, I would definitely choose Ethan Carter.  In my opinion, Ethan Carter is improved by a second run through, but I don't think this game would be.

What started out as a supposed hard sci-fi adventure rammed head-first into ♥♥♥♥♥♥ combat and the modern equivalent of pixel-hunting and trying to combine every object in your inventory with every other object. Terrible, avoid.
Blugh. The Fall had some really promising parts to it. It's a side scrolling exploration adventure game. You play an AI attempting to save your pilot by wandering through a derelict facility and getting help. The bad parts is that it's got really ♥♥♥♥♥♥ combat attached to it. The gun doesnt register button presses at times and there's no indication if it's by design or just lousy inputs. The solutions to puzzles are incredibly obscure and if your monitor darkness is too low you wont even see them. You wander around having to scan for objects before you'll notice them and several times over the course of the game I've had to rely on walkthroughs to find objects disguised as environmental debris. The interaction hitbox is ridiculously tiny and the interface attached to it is terrible as well. Then there's that goddamn cliffhanger ending with 'To be continued' plasted on the screen and a 'moral choice' that isnt really a choice at all. If you dont do it you cant finish the game. Dont waste your money.

The Fall tries to marry a 2D action platformer with old-style adventure gaming, but fails to do either well.
You play the game as the AI of a combat suit ("A.R.I.D."). After the eponymous fall to an unknown world, the soldier within the suit is unresponsive and your medical diagnostic devices have been damaged, so you have no idea how injured he is, or if he's even alive. The goal of the game is to get him to a medical facility. In so doing, you must escape a facility that tests defective AIs, destroying or repurposing them as needed.
Most of the game is solving puzzles, and while some of these are interesting, many suffer from the same bizarre logic that plagued the adventure game genre (which is part of the reason that that genre is no longer popular). There's nothing as bad as the infamous kill-the-yeti-with-a-cream-pie puzzle from King's Quest V, but there's a couple that come close. Even worse, in a way, is that you'll sometimes know exactly how to solve the puzzle, but you didn't try to solve it in exactly the way the game wanted. Also, it is incredibly easy to miss items critical to progression, as they are sometimes very small and the game is extremely dark.
The combat is no great shakes either. Most enemies will hide behind cover and shoot at you at regular intervals. You can hide behind cover yourself, or later, you can get a cloaking ability. (However, since the button you use for the cloak is the same as for using cover, you will sometimes do one when you meant to do the other.) The enemies will always keep their heads out for a good amount of time after shooting, which is good, because aiming isn't great. Shooting enemies will never try to flush you out of cover, so all you have to do is wait for your shield to regenerate before shooting at them. There are kamikaze robots who run up and apparently fry your systems if they hit you - which is frustrating because it's an automatic death - but you can usually kill them easily by shooting while backing up. There's no nuance to the combat and there would be no challenge at all to it, were it not for how easily you take damage. You also have a stealth kill, but it's almost useless, as it takes long enough that any enemy nearby will see you before you're finished, and there are always at least two enemies together at any time.
The game is also plagued by a ton of bugs. Sometimes A.R.I.D.'s aim will get stuck for no apparent reason (although going to the menu seems to fix this). Other times your "Interact" button will suddenly stop working. Once, I moved forward but the screen didn't scroll with me, so I was over in the next area while I continued to see the area before. (I think what happened is that I jumped over a marker that tells the game to scroll the screen when you walk over it.) Once I found an enemy just crouch-walking in place. Most of these are just annoying, but twice A.R.I.D. stopped moving and the only thing I could do was press Start, which would cause the words "Running Menu.Exe" to appear on the screen, but nothing would actually happen. Both times, I had to manually shut the game down, and lost progress in the process.
Story-wise, the game is fine, although I think it would've been more interesting if there weren't a direct antagonist. There are some fun interactions, and the twist at the end was actually not what I was expecting (although it also makes the method by which you gain abilities throughout the game make no sense). However, the fact that the game simply stops with a "To Be Continued" marker at the end is rather galling. The only indication anywhere that this is merely the first episode of a series is in the Achievements screen. If I had known ahead of time that the story was just going to stop partway through, I might not have bought the game at all.

Well, this game has its downsides so I'll start from them. Just so you know what's bad and won't whine at it after the purchase. I played on Debian Linux with XBox 360 controller. The game can be described as a quest/action. You should explore the surroundings, find objects, use them on active places and shoot robots and other creatures from time to time. It may sound boring in this brief description but believe me, it's not at all. So, what are the downsides?
— It's quite short and ends with a cliffhanger. Took me 5 hours to complete, some people may divide the price by hours and make a wry face. Though for me it's perfectly fine because these were
your usual 5 hours. Whatever. Two more episodes are in the works and will be sold separately.
— Gamepad controls can't be reassigned and were chosen poorly. Switching the flashlight and the gun with right stick press? Oh god why. The X button isn't used at all as well as the left trigger. And you can't switch while the flashlight/gun is holstered. So you have to tilt the RT AND press it. And you have to do it pretty often. Aiming is quite poor, sensitivity can't be adjusted either. After some time you'll get used to it but still.
— Oh them .exe everywhere. I don't want to believe that future AIs are running Windows as their OS. That's of course a dumb complain since I'm a biased Linux guy, just noticed and facepalm'd a bit. Opinion discarded.
If that hasn't scared you away, let's get to the good parts.
— First of all, I want to denote the outstanding, no,
voiceacting. That's literally one of the best acting I heard in games since the Portal series (though in "The Fall" protagonist actually, he-he, has a voice and man what a voice!). In most of AAA titles voices are plain and boring, they're just there and that's all. It was a big surprise to find this genuine play in an indie game. Despite the grim atmosphere, there's a place for sparky jokes and sarcastic acid here and there to lighten it up a bit. All characters are unique and they develop as the time goes. It's impossible not to love them!
— Quests are logical enough... well, not everywhere. I was really stuck only in one place but it seems to be common. Quests have their piece of humor, too. Often dark as the game itself. I'm very ok with that.
— Overall atmosphere is perfect. From graphics to the background noises, it's an abandoned and at the same time hostile facility where something very damn bad happened long time ago. It reminds me of "The Swapper" though "The Fall" is not a puzzle and more story-driven. You'll get some clues as the story unveils but a lot of mistery is saved for the future parts.
— Sci-fi themed. I love sci-fi, space and robots!
— Has a Linux version. A strong point for me since I'm only buying and playing ported games now. No crashes, no glitches (except the mentioned unconvenient controls but that's a platform agnostic issue). It just works!
— I noticed some Mass Effect references, though maybe I'm digging too deep. The author mentioned the ME series in the FAQ (probably, that was not just a random title!), the A.R.I.D. voice and character are similar to EDI in some respects and her outfit is very close to quarians' suits. Again, that may be just my projections since I'm an ME-fan.
— DAT A$$.
All in all, 9 out of 10. A must play game for sure. Some issues can be fixed in future, some are fundamental and by design. Nevertheless, I seriously consider this game an indie gem you should not pass by.

According to SteamSpy, only 11.35% of people who own Reveal the Deep have played it within the past two weeks. Just 51.42% of its owners have
launched it.
The average total playtime is 44 minutes, with the median coming in at a paltry 19 minutes played.
Take Steam reviews with a grain of salt. If Reveal the Deep were truly a great game, 88.65% of its players wouldn't forget about it within fourteen days. This isn't one of those games that one must "make time for." It isn't so "deep" that it "takes time to get into." It's simply not good.
I stand by my initial review.
The game cost me just $0.99, and I still want my money back.
First of all, the game fails to provide the player with any contextual information in regard to who they are and what they're doing. Logos, ethos, and pathos are completely ignored; meaning, I am not drawn into Reveal the Deep either logically, ethically, or emotionally. In my 22 minutes with the game, I was given neither concrete nor intuitive information as to what (or why) I'm doing.
To say Reveal the Deep moves at a snail's pace is an understatement. There is zero action to make up for the player's waning interest level. It takes your submariner longer to do things in-game than it takes a real deep-sea explorer to do the same thing in actual water. Switching "views" in your helmet takes at least an entire second; unfortunately, the amount of times one must switch said "view" is too great for the one-second wait to go unnoticed.
How Reveal the Deep has accumulated a positive rating of 92% is beyond me. If darkness and a handful of underwater sound effects constitute "atmosphere," I suppose a game needs more than atmosphere to be worth owning. Reveal the Deep, in my opinion, isn't worth owning for even the price of a vending-machine snack.

Possibly the smallest game I own, but it packs a bigger punch than that.
Solar 2's main strength is that you can play at your own pace, with your own goals, and that leads to a good few hours that you can spend just bumbling around in space and figuring out what you fancy doing. Going from a tiny asteroid to a black hole? Staying as a solo planet and building up a small armada of ships? Just flying around like a lunatic smashing into stuff and dying repeatedly? All viable playstyles.
If you want more structure, the story and challenge missions offer a good balance between fun and difficulty, and add considerable longevity to the game. The general idea is to work your way up the planetary body hierarchy - from diminutive asteroid through to planets, stars, star systems and eventually nature's biggest vaccuum cleaner. There are individual missions for each stage of being, some of them simple, others very difficult. I have yet to witness another game that lets you play as the stage itself at a rock concert.
For a little indie title, there's a surprising amount to do, and while it could perhaps get a little samey after beating everything the game has to offer, there are physics options that you can use to craft a more creative playing experience - like mass space dogfights between hundreds of ships, for instance.
Or, you could just let the cool ambience of the game float you away on a paradoxical vaccuum breeze...

This is a story of how Takamatsu Aoi life’s got turned upside down. It was not typical day in his hikikomori life, having mustered the courage to go out of his house, in which he has been living alone for the past few years, & buy a copy of the latest eroge when the cutest girl ever fell from the sky. Sora is her name & as much information as she will ever give to our protagonist. So begins Aoi’s & Sora’s story together, him coping with rejection & her with her mystery & changing his life around with her antics, for better or worse.
Artwise, Aoi is the typical faceless VN dude so not much expected out of him. Sora being the main draw, is drawn pretty decently & her varied expressions make her charming enough. Backgrounds are also decent enough at their job of immersion. Music was serviceable & went with the tones well enough. The game will present choices that are handled in a timed manner, either you pick one or let the timer run out & the game will carry one with a suitable alternative, be it good or bad. Story & text on the other hand, were a trip through cringe town 9 times out of 10. Aoi is written to be the most shut in edge lord otaku whose only love is 2D girls & Sora’s façade of a cute girl is shattered rather rapidly when her every other word involves some sort of innuendo or ‘get in my pants’ scheme & the occasional, “I’m a shy girl.” thing that quickly disappears. Ultimately, this being a romance VN, they get it on, nothing major, just some short texts & static images of the girl in a SFW way, but all throughout the cringe is there, there is no escape. The ‘sex scenes’ I felt where in no way necessary or better off being expanded upon & sold elsewhere to a mature audience, rather than having a tepid game on Steam. The endings ranged from somewhat funny to “What & why?” & ending abruptly, the true end being an interesting twist but in no way worth the hassle of playing this game.
At the end of the day, this a short game, 2-3 hours’ worth, with nice art but meh story. Do not be fooled by the “uncensored” art if that is what you are buying it for, there isn’t much to see outside of the beginning. I for one do not recommend this game at its full sale price, either get in a bundle or wait for a sale.

I saw many negative reviews that, for me, this visual novel really does not deserve.
Yeah, it's short, but it's well designed and written and it's also free.
Plus, apart from the artworks the whole game takes place in a sci-fi environment (Blossom is the spaceship in case you're wondering xD); three girls are the protagonists (you're Erica, the captain) and you have to work together getting different endings for one girl or the other one.
The mechanisms are the same as the usual visual novels, some endings, many choices, well-written text and so on so, nothing new (apart from the fact that it isn't love-centered and there are only girls xD).
The game will take two or three hours if you read almost everything, and it's not wasted time. I really enjoyed it and I'm replaying it now after some months :)
Idk, I'm happy to make a positive review for this game that really to me deserves it if you like visual novels in general!

Fantastic game, an absolute must-play if you like sci-fi games - or hell, if you like sci-fi in general.
It's an indie title, and is reasonably short (~5 hours to complete), and without spoiling anything, it ends on a "To Be Continued". Regardless, if you value quality over quantity it's worth every cent.
The gameplay mechanics for the most part work well - initially the controls felt a bit weird, but once I got used to them I realised that they're actually quite well designed. The combat feels good, though to be honest given the game's length it's never really fleshed out fully.
The main point of the game is exploration and puzzles, and these were good for the most part. A couple of times I was stuck wandering, only to find I'd missed some spot on the floor or ceiling that was interactable. There's no pixel hunting at least (your flashlight illuminates interactive objects with a magnifying glass symbol). The solutions to problems felt relatively logical at least. Even when I got stuck, once I figured it out I never felt like I'd been cheated, only that I'd been an idiot.
Even though the game is satisfying mechanically, that's absolutely not why you play it. You play it for the story, and the story is *good*. It's nuanced and it manages to convey some pretty heavy themes more subtly than I thought possible. If you enjoy thinking about the philosophy of AI, or if you're a fan of Isaac Asimov or Phillip K.♥♥♥♥♥♥then you'll get a lot out of this.
It is worth noting, since it's not quite clear from the description: while the game isn't a 'horror game', it does have quite disturbing imagery in parts, and it features themes that can be unsettling.
There are no contradictions in reality. If you find the premises that bind you incompatible, which will you discard?

I have been seeing a lot of negative reviews that have little to do with the actual game, and I am fairly certain just from a glance that the ones that are giving these reviews are probably not from the targeted audience demographic and seem a bit unfair in my opinion. That being what it is I felt that writing a review of this game from the perspective of someone who is a fan of the genre was necessary.

First and foremost I can't get over how lovely the art is. Sprites, backgrounds, and CG's are all beautiful! It is very obvious that a lot of love and attention to detail was put into the visuals of this game, and the style is something new and refreshing. Also, the music is suprisingly great as well. The writing was really solid. The dialogue is believable. Characters have defined personalities and the plot is pretty interesting (I have seen the supernatural theme come up in a lot of otome games but the story has it's own world and lore makes it just a notch above other games with a similar theme) and the writing was pretty sound grammatically too and was void of any glaring typos. If a game of this genre has all of these things it is already superior to 90% of the games that are out there.
I have seen some complaints from other reviewers with the way the game is being distributed with the prologue and sneak peek of each route being free, and each full route being availible for individual sale as they are released. I for one don't mind this. I feel that each route is long enough that the price per route is fair, and if it allows me to play each route sooner since I don't have to wait for the whole game to be completed then I don't really see what the big deal is. If every route is just as long as Shou's route, there will be hours of play time for each character route, with multiple endings for each one.
To be honest I am pretty hyped up to play the routes as they become availible. I think this is shaping up to be a really great game!

CAN YOU ENJOY THIS GAME IN 2016?
Morrowind may have not aged well with its clunky combat, dumb AI and poor animations, and while mods can improve on many of its flaws, it will still be hard to get into it for those that started with Skyrim. However, if you give it a chance you will discover that there's a lot more to it.
Exploration is rewarding, bits and pieces of lore are hidden and scattered around the map and not every detail of the story is laid out in front of you, and discovering it on your own is part of the experience. The lore is intertwined with the plot.
Magic will open a world of possibilities. Want to enchant a pair of boots that will make you jump over mountains? You can do it. Want a pair of pants that shoot fireballs? No problem! Alchemy, Enchanting and Spellmaking will turn you into a god in no time, experiment different combinations and you will feel like you can do anything.
Skyrim is a bloody good game, but it has given up a lot of the older TES freedom for a balanced and polished gameplay. Morrowind isn't polished or balanced in any way, but that's actually what makes it special: it's a giant playground where your creativity is the only limit.
Anything I could write would never bring justice to this game, it's a goddamn masterpiece!

Why the best TES game?
Oblivion and Skyrim are great games, but while they improved what was bad about Morrowind (combat, graphics, etc.) they took quite a few steps back in what made Morrowind so great.
Example:

When you receive a quest in Skyrim/Oblivion, you button mash through some dialogue, fast-travel direct to the location, and then follow your compass arrow directly to the exact location you need to go, then warp back to the quest giver. Not very immersive really.
Compare that to a Morrowind quest, where fast-travel only exists between cities: Meaning you have to take dirctions in your journal, and embark out into the wilderness to find the places you need to go, often checking your notes, or even a map. Before leaving the city you need to take time to stock up on supplies; repair your weapons, buy potions, arrows etc. It makes it feel like you are actually embarking on a quest, and makes completing quests much more rewarding.
I could go on and on. Long story short, if you like adventure RPG's you owe it to yourself to get this game. Make you sure you download the essential MODS's though.

This is one of the most wildly original games I have seen in a long time.
Clustertruck's basic premise is this: you run and jump across the back of trucks that are speeding down various landscapes.  Your objective is to get to the goal by any means necessary.  But if you touch anything or bump anything that isn't a truck (well, almost anything), you fail and have to restart the level.  It sounds hard, and it is hard, but it's also crazy fun.  There's no feeling like being absolutely certain you're about to fail and then somehow turning it around into a victory.
To help matters, you earn points as you play and you can use them to buy abilities.  These abilities range from things like double jump and slowing down time to making the game play like SUPERHOT.  They're all interesting and offer ridiculous new ways to tackle levels.
Now some might be upset with the fact that you can pretty much see all the levels in just 2-3 hours, but the levels that are there are great.  They start off fairly tame, easing you into the game and letting you get a handle on how it all works.  But the game gradually ramps up the difficulty, adding new and crazier things as the levels go on.  You get lasers, boulders, trucks falling from the sky, trucks being shot out of cannons at you, missile launching turrets, and more.  And I found all the levels to be fun.
Well, except for the final level.  I won't spoil what it is, but those who have gotten there will know what I'm talking about.
Here's the thing: Clustertruck is built around speed.  It's all about getting things done as fast as you can, and the levels reflect that.  Each one can usually be completed in 10-20 seconds at most.  But then the final level comes along, and it forces you to play for at least two minutes.  And if you slip up, make a mistake, and fail?  Well you're back at the beginning.  And it quickly gets frustrating.  The concept is cool, and an interesting variation on the tradition levels, but in the end it just makes the tiny flaws in Clustertruck suddenly become all the more glaring.  The momentum can be wonky as you jump from truck to truck.  The inherent randomness in the game means that the trucks can act unpredictably.  And if that happens at the wrong time, you die because of it.  These flaws normally don't mean much because of how fast each level is, but the final level can become insanely frustrating as you continually retry it over and over just trying to get back to where you were.
Despite all that, Clustertruck is a great game and I highly recommend it.  It's one of the most creative game ideas I've ever seen.  And it's only the final level that annoyed me.  The rest could be challenging, but they were still fun.  That being said, if you don't think fifteen bucks is worth only a few hours of content, then I'd wait for a sale.  Either way, it'll certainly be one of the most unique games you ever purchase.
EDIT: I just found out that the developers made the final level a little shorter to alleviate some of the frustration.  Good on them.  I'm glad they listen to feedback unlike some in the industry.

It's not perfect.
There are much better visual novels out there, like Corpse Party or Steins;Gate, and while I wouldn't say the writing is bad, it's not good either. The beginning of Aozora Meikyuu reminds me of Club Life, in that past events are why the protagonist has a conflict with women, except it's actually explained a bit here. Aoi becomes a shut-in Otaku, until wandering outside to buy one of his eroge/dating sim games, where he then meets his love interest, Sora.
Unlike a true perverted Otaku, rather than actually embrace her suggestive thoughts and actions towards him, his past keeps him from accepting her advances. The two go back and forth throughout the hour spent playing this game, with Sora continuing to be clingy and have a huge appetite, while Aoi finds her annoying.
But here's where my bias of my recommendation comes in. As a fellow Ren'py user who's also in the process of making a visual novel, the writing style in this game was a lesson to learn from. Other than grammar issues and sentences not flowing properly, perhaps because of translations, I can't say the way it was written was bad.
My disappointment however, comes from the way the story was paced. Things could have been a lot longer if some stuff like playing games with Sora, hadn't just been summarized. It's been awhile since I've played/watched a playthrough of Corpse Party/Steins;Gate, but I'm pretty confident that both visual novels are dialogue heavy, which can be both a good and bad thing, depending on how the story is written. And this game could have used that kind of pacing.
There's also how Sora is the only girl you can really romance, and how even though the option to ditch her for a past crush happens twice, the game just returns to the title screen after choosing it. Making another route for that really wouldn't have been that difficult. Just a couple of label starts and scene transitions to come up with an ending. It wouldn't be much of one, but it's better than the tease mentioned after meeting this crush, and not explaining it when you stay.
Because of that, I really would have felt better if the game had been sold for $2.99, instead of $4.99. I'm not one to refund games, since I'm pretty careful with my purchases, so I'll be keeping this in my library as a reference.
And to be honest, the nudity tag was the main reason I bought it. If there had simply been more scenes, then the $4.99 would have actually been worth it. But since that wasn't what happened, anyone who decides to buy this game, should keep in mind that the developer could have really polished the game a bit more.

This is, in my opinion, the most unique environment ever seen in Trackmania.
[/h] Tracks [/h1]
Trackmania has always been known to never dissapoint in terms of the single player mode - and I loved every second of this one. You almost never see the same style of block placement twice, and there is always a new technique to master on these tracks. It combines sections where you have to be slow and technical with how you drive and fast sections with jumps and loops and really exciting and crazy stunts. It's all threaded together perfectly, and it never gets boring at any point within the gameplay.
[/h] The Valley Car [/h1]
Anyone who has played Trackmania in the past knows this well: all the different cars have their own handling characteristics and driving styles. For example, the Coast cars are slow and slippery, and have to be driven carefully, while the Stadium cars have loads of grip and can hit insanely fast speeds. The Valley cars are like none other, both in how they handle and how they look.
It's not comparable to any production car I have ever seen before, making it a completely original and new style to me. The handling is amazing. It's easy to drive at high speeds, easy to predict, and easy to push into a powerslide, but it is impossible to master. Those simple mechanics are what keep all those online players playing: Because it never gets boring.
[/h] The Verdict [/h1]
Trackmania is just one of those games that never goes out of style. It's always fun to play, and you can always learn a new driving technique to use on any of the enormous number of tracks both contained within the singleplayer mode and the multiplayer mode. Easy to pick up, impossible to master, and overall a blast to play, for all age groups.

Shatter is a 2D block-breaking arcade game. It adds several new features to the classic Breakout/Arkanoid formula.
The futuristic visuals look slightly dated by now but still work well. The one real issue I had with the graphics was that when the action really picks up it can be bit hard to see the actual ball.
The game has a catchy soundtrack and the sound effects are well done too.
The game adds a number of changes to the traditional block-breaking formula. Chief of these is the ability to attract/repulse the ball (and other objects) which certainly makes the gameplay much more tactical.
The game also has the typical assortment of power ups and special blocks. There's nothing ground-breaking here, but the game still has enough variety to keep things interesting.
There are a number of different gameplay modes too, from the story mode campaign (which also features several boss fights) to endless mode and time attack. Overall these are all pretty well implemented.
The story mode is fairly easy, but the other modes feel quite a bit more challenging.
The controls are solid and responsive with mouse + keyboard. Using the mouse for movement and attract/repulse works great.
Despite the existance of a story mode, the game is pretty short on actual plot. Not that an arcade game like this needs one.
I didn't encounter any major bugs or issues.
Shatter was a pretty positive surprise for me. It provides an interesting twist on the classic Breakout/Arkanoid formula with decent visuals and nice music. I'd recommend the game, especially to the fans of the genre.
It took me little over 2 hours to finish the story mode. I also quickly dabbled in endless and time attack modes before writing this review.

You want a high-octane, action-packed arcade-style game.
Never thought a brick-breaker game could be adrenaline-filled? Guess again.
I'm on the fence with Shatter though. It's fast-paced, slick and has a killer soundtrack, but I feel the gameplay is a little watered down by the fancy extras they've introduced. A curious modern take on the Breakout-style games (or 1-player Pong). It has the familiar 'bounce the photon to knock out blocks'... only with tons of explosions. Because who doesn't like massive explosions? The ability to gamble your lives by adding multiple photons to the field is also pretty neat. Artistically, it's a masterpiece and looks exceptionally sleek and sharp. Stunningly intense for an arcade game. And if there's one thing I can't fault... dat soundtrack.
. Talk about getting you pumped.
Ironically though, in trying fill an ordinarily laid-back brick-breaker with 7 metric tonnes of OOMPH... the actual brick-breaking is, by-and-large, shoved to the wayside. You get all sorts of new block-types, but tend not to notice them as you can just shred through it all in under a minute with the ability to push/pull the photon and unleash a Gatling-gun special attack. You can get so swept up in the slow-mo explosions that you look back and realise you have no idea what just happened. As such, the regular levels are pretty much hollow formalities leading to the boss fights. Oh yeah, there are boss fights! And they are, at least, pretty well-made and nicely challenging.
In many respects, I feel the game was limited in being a brick-breaker. The devs have tried to spruce something up which doesn't lend itself well to HIGH-OCTANE-PLUGMEINANDCRANKUPDATVOLUME meaning that, in order to fit the look-and-feel, it had to be warped so far beyond comprehension that it's not particularly recognisable any more. So perhaps a bit more look than substance, but you cannot fault the developers for trying. Maybe not one for those who want an in-depth brick-breaker. But as a pumped, upbeat arcade-style game with sublime graphics... yeah, why not.
This is easily the best brick breaker game I have ever played. Everything is very enjoyable. Bought it to recommend this game on Steam. Buy it now!

From developer Reine Works and publisher Dharker Studio comes Blossoms Bloom Brightest, an indie casual, adventure visual novel. Released on the 28th of April, 2017, this is a science fiction, yuri (lesbian), visual novel that has an aspect of mystery to it.
Trigger warnings for this game: suicide (following one of the endings)
In this game, you follow the story of three women that awaken to find themselves on a spaceship named The Blossom. Stuck together for two weeks, what adventures will they get on together, and what will become of them all?
I started this game not expecting too much. This is a yuri visual novel, and yuri is usually marketed to men with very oversexualised women. When this did occur, I wasn’t too shocked, but disappointed. There is a lot that happens on the form of sexualisation, with women just standing around in their underwear, some revealing costumes, and characters with large breasts that really wasn’t needed in this visual novel. It was rather annoying for me to come across in this, but as I said before, I was expecting it, so it didn’t ruin anything for me.
Going through the choices we had, I found I had quite a bit of fun. I liked the characters, I could relate to them on a small level, and I found that the story actually kept me pretty hooked. It was enjoyable.
One thing I didn’t like was the suicide out of nowhere when following one of the story lines, which was really a shock to me. Warnings really need to be included as it made me quite shaky and I wasn’t expecting it.
Other than this, this was really enjoyable. It was rather basic, and it was definitely marketed to men via sexualisation, so it lost quite a bit of charm. However, I did enjoy it, and if you like visual novels, I’d definitely recommend giving this one a try. I enjoyed it and it took me less than an hour to complete the game. Definitely a bit of fun, and a lovely story line to follow.
This game is a sideways thumb from me, and I wish we had that feature on here. Giving this a negative recommendation, purely because I only gave it two out of five on another site, rather than a higher rating.

Blossoms Bloom Brightest is a Visual Novel. Being a yuri visual novel, you play as Erica, a starship captain tasked with taking Kotoha, a anime loving mechanic, and Sara, a serious and stern doctor for unknown reasons which are only revealed later in the story.
The writing was bland, some of the concepts were alright but not engaging enough, and there's better, on Steam, and for free.
Don't even install it.

If I were to describe Blossoms Bloom Brightest to someone whom hasn't played it before, it would be that it feels like a demo; a few bites of what could have been a good VN, but by the end all you're left with is dissatisfaction at how much wasn't explained.
This visual novel is centered around Erica Matthews - the captain of the ship in which the story takes place - and the two women she's tasked to look after for an important mission, Kotoha Ichinose and Sara Evans. I would start with Erica herself, but you virtually know nothing about her which makes her very hard to sympathize with or root for. Her personality is pretty bland but that's par for the course with love sim leads, so we'll move on to Kotoha.
My immediate problem with Kotoha is that she doesn't "feel" human. She's excessively upbeat to the point where she doesn't react like a normal person would in the situations she's thrown into, such as pulling pranks and inviting Erica to play video games on the same day she wakes up on a mysterious ship and told she won't be going home. This wouldn't be too awful if not for the fact that if you pursue Sara or give her any attention at all, Kotoha turns into a massive insufferable brat, as she apparently fell in love with you the moment she saw you and thus feels entitled to your time. She's very juvenile in her appearance and personality, and that's just not a quality I find appealing in my yuri.
Now, onto Sara. Sara is...incredibly unlikable. She's understandably hostile given that she apparently has a fiance whom she'll never be seeing again, but the creators of this VN seem to think that a woman who spends 80% of the game crying about her fiance and lashing out at you makes for good relationship fodder, so later she inexplicably falls in love with you? She basically asks you to replace her fiance which is a very sad and disturbing request, and all it made me want to do was exit this game and go play something where my lesbians are happy and healthy. Especially when she
Putting aside the characters for a moment, the story's setting doesn't exactly make sense either. The three are on a MASSIVE, self-sustaining ship that's being closely monitored, and they're the only ones on it. Why? And even more baffling, they apparently have all the time in the world to spend every chapter playing video games, eating, and going on dates. What of the vital mission that the three are even on this ship for? Not that vital it seems, as you don't hear about it again for the rest of the story.
Perhaps worst of all though is that you're only given the illusion of choice. I was impressed by some of the darker dialogue options presented to you and the shocked reactions of the other girls, but the good will that it fostered was flushed down the toilet when your character essentially says "Haha I was kidding!" each time and everyone laughs it off. Why? It's such a cop-out to give you an actually interesting idea or response, then hide it behind the guise of a joke so the writers didn't have to think up consequences for your actions. In fact, the writing in general is pretty poor, since even though you're playing from Erica's point of view, you never really get a glimpse into her heart to understand why she's attracted to either of the girls. She's a classic example of loving someone because they love you, even though fleshing out a romantic relationship and each character's feelings is kind of the point of a romantic visual novel. But alas...
Not everything's bad, hard as I am on this game. I like the art and the character designs, I think the voice actresses sounded nice and I'm always up for sci-fi theme, especially when lesbians are involved. Hell, I might even try Galaxy Girls when it's released, which is advertised as the more substantial sequel to Blossoms Bloom Brightest, and from what I've seen looks promising. Unfortunately though you're better off waiting for that, as this will ultimately feel like a massive waste of two hours of your time.

The other woman is angry (and even vulgar), but understandably so since she's been kidnapped away from her fiance. I can't imagine why anyone would want to build a romantic story around such an unsettling plot.

The Fall is a terrific game, primarily a straight-up adventure title with combat sections to break up the puzzle-solving.  It's not very long, but the story is exquisitely told and well-thought out.  The voice acting is really excellent throughout, but the protagonist's voice actress stands out as really selling the character throughout her development.  The stark sadness and resignation she gives to ARID near the end, when she once more greets the system administration AI is particularly moving.
The puzzles are largely straight-forward; just thought-provoking to be rewarding to solve, without too many head-scratchers where you need to read the developers' minds.  The combat sections tend to be of moderate difficulty, it's not too tough to get through if you remember to take advantage of cover and camouflage.  Unfortunately, the controls are somewhat cludgy, which is probably why the combat is even of moderate difficulty instead of being easy.  The mechanic of needing your gun (with its flashlight) out to interact with things is interesting, but really belongs in a different game than The Fall.  Frankly, there just isn't enough reason for stealth to not have the flashlight out almost all the time, which results in you pretty much just holding the right mouse button down the whole game.
The framing for the story is pretty classic science fiction, and the story itself isn't really trodding new ground, but it's less cliched and trite than most game stories.  It's told well enough to sweep the player up in the story, so when the twists come, you're always surprised, even though you'll look back and wonder why you didn't see it coming -- that means the developers really did it right.  Watching ARID move from simply annotating her internal logs with explanations of her actions to giving justifications for her actions, altering those log files, before finally deciding that she would do anything to complete her objectives -- even if those actions are extreme -- is a delightful and moving treat.  ARID gets a real character arc: you watch her grow and change as a result of her experiences.  In the era of story-driven characters, a character-driven story is refreshing and captivating.
If you enjoy science fiction stories and adventure games, The Fall is absolutely worth the price of admission.

Very well done.  I recommend it.

UPDAATED!
MDSoA is not complete and this review should be read in light of the fact that only one character route is available; I am aware that issues I had with this route (such as problems with story development, etc) may not persist through other routes.  Please also note that this is a review exclusively about the novel itself and not about the game developers or any of their actions elsewhere, as I don't feel this is really a fair platform to discuss or critique that.  This review is meant to help those seeking information about the novel and how good I felt it was.
That said, all the issues with this game were fairly minor.  It is enjoyable and I do recommend it.  I feel that the price is worth it if only for the fact that it's just a really beautiful game.
Anyway, on to the pros and cons...
NOTE: Some of the previously mentioned "cons" to the game have been addressed and/or the developers have said they intend to address them.  I had mentioned a lack of sprites for side characters, but new sprites have been added in at this time.  Several other issues have been mentioned by the developers as things that they intend to resolve, and one issue looks like it might be resolved in Shou's epilogue.  I will continue to update this review as the developers make changes to the game.
Pros:
-Exceptionally gorgeous artwork.  There are tons of backgrounds and locations, all of which are nicely done.  The character sprites are all really beautiful, and have a decent range of expressions.  The artwork is just, honestly, completely gorgeous.  I feel like I spent a lot of time just admiring everyone's amazing hair or the setting for various scenes.
-Sleek design.  The whole game really looks super polished.  It's not just the artwork but even the menus are really nicely done.
-Likable characters.  I think it's great that all the main characters seem lovable and fun - I hate playing games where there's that one character I just can't *stand.*  In this game, everyone seems like they have their virtues and flaws, but will be enjoyable to play through, regardless.
-Story that was not predictable.  I was surprised by several of the events in Shou's story line, as well as Shou himself.  Even though there were moments I kind of want to just shake him...he's still a sweet character.  His route had some pretty surprising twists, and was really fun to play through.
-Nice music.  Though I always turn the music way down in these games, it's still nice to have decent music, rather than something that makes me want to claw my ear drums out after five minutes.  There were a few moments where I, uncharacteristically, turned it up a bit because it really suited the scene, or just sounded nice.
-All the endings were fairly long, and had unique content.  They all felt like a legitimate and logical end, rather than something thrown together for the sake of having more endings.
-The main character has an actual personality.  She has moments where she can be feisty and independent, or moments where she can stand there and cry.  It's nice to have options that portrayed a stronger protagonist, and to just see a protagonist who is more developed than what a lot of games bother with.
Cons:
-Very little variation in the story line.  At least in Shou's route, there is a single "fork" in the story where it splits into the different endings, none of which are really bad - just varying degrees of sweet.   Up until that fork, the story is the same regardless of what choices you make - no hidden scenes, no skipping scenes, no unexpected bad endings. At most, you get a few new lines of narrative before being forcibly placed back on the same path.  This game is essentially one path with different endings and only one branching point.  It's fine to have some decisions affect only some invisible tracker that determines what ending you get, but the game would have been more engaging if the choices impacted the actual path you travel to get to those endings as well.
-The lack of CGs.  There are only three as far as I can tell.  I would have been willing to give up on some backgrounds/locations for the chance at more CGs - after all, unlocking the CGs is a huge draw of games like this.  Even one or two more would have been nice. There were at least two other scenes I felt would have been really good CG moments, so it was a little disappointing there were so few of them.  That said - the art work is SUPER amazing and I imagine that they may have simply run out of time or money for more than what is there.  This is something I hope they can update down the line, but I can understand why there are probably so few.
-Story is a little shallow at times -  The MC is way too accepting of surprise magic classes, and a magical basement at her university.  And the magical basement, at least in Shou's route, is really not ever given a decent explanation as to why its even there. It felt weird that the MC never delved into that too deeply. Also, since the route focuses entirely on Shou, the MC really doesn't have much in depth screen time with the other guys but somehow develops deep bonds with them.  That felt a little contrived but is still a fairly minor story flaw.
-There is also a minor antagonist that never gets a proper wrap up.  They just sort of vanish from the story entirely at one point and you never really hear from them again.  It would have been nice if these things had been handled with a bit more finesse, but comparatively speaking, the story is still relatively well developed for an otome type novel so it didn't stand out as being terribly shallow for the genre.
Over all, I definitely recommend this visual novel.  Like any game, there are points that could be nitpicked, or areas where the game can improve. The fact that the character routes are being released one at a time means the developers will hopefully use feedback to improve future routes.  It also means there will be plenty of time to save up to buy the rest of the routes when they are released. =)

I will be honest and say that when i first booted this game up half a year ago or so, i didnt like it. But then  i decided that 30min-1 hr without really trying to learn how the stats system works wasnt enough. So i gave it another go with a clear mind and as of now i am totally hooked.
the first thing people will ask how does it compare to skyrim and i say its better.  I have 450 + hrs on skyrim on ps3. And despite me playing this for less i still think this game is better and no this isnt a comparion between this and skyrim.
The good:
Story: I will begin with the story and is one of the best stories in an open-world game. One of the best main stories i have seen in a open world  game second only to witcher 3 , but this game has a far better lore. The story touches upon drugs, gods, religion, racism , good and evil is always not as clear as it seems. As someone pointed out who is good guys here are you the good guy or are you helping some evil killing off the good , well that up  to you to decide , but in this game it isnt clear who the villain really is.
Quests:  In this game compared to many games i have played i really feel like doing all the side quests, i feel i help the world in someway, makes it a better place. There are alot of different side quests, from assasination, fetching, clearing a tomb, steal something , persuade etc. The main quest is great and the side quests doesnt feel forced and you will probably on numerous times find out that you rather do the side quests then the main quests. Or like what happens to me alot i do a main quest then suddently i get to a new area were i get tons of new side quests, or some of the side quests i have that can be completed in the area or close to it. Some of the best quests i have seen in a long time. As i said previously only Witcher 3 comes close or surpass it.
Atmosphere: The atmosphere is fantastic. Every city feels unique, almost every place feels unique. The landscape/ world is huge and you really feel like you are there , also because of the music. When it comes to the places you visit you got the huge place called Vivec , small towns like Balamora and Peligrad, different forts, a huge mushroom that alot of shops and homes is in.
You can walk from a huge town then you suddently finda a field with steam or  you have come to a volcano. And the weather system needs to be mentioned too. It can go from bright daylight - to ash storms - to rainy nights.
Music: The soundtrack is fantastic and really helps creating this fantastic world.
Gameplay: Well lets starts with when you hit someone it use a dice based system and a variety of factors and it works. It will probably get smashed by today standards if developers did this in todays games, but if you get around the idea you will find a gameplay that is pretty great and still works al right today.
The skill system is great, with major, minor and misc skills. Major and Minor skills levels up your overall level so you can have more strenght, luck , agilit etc Misc skills is just some skills that still will help you dont focus on them too much. Your skills depnds on the class.
I will also like to add that the use journal and talk to the people to find the directions to a town or do a quest without any hand holding is great.
You can enchant whatever you want with say  levitate, that makes you levitate as long as you want. You can make for some stupid reason that when you hit and enemy he will turn inviniclbe. You can enchant so you have more strength etc.
The fast traveling in this game is pretty great, instead of what alot of todays game do that you simply click on a location you have visit previously and teleporting there for a magical reason you will in this game have to either use a mage guild, slit strider, use scrolls, boat or a  mark and spot with a spell then teleport you to that spot again later.So yeah its old school but adds to the exploration.
Cons:
As of my update as i have played tribunal and after reaching around 65+ hrs, i have encountered a lot more time falling trough the floor, inside buildings and so on, at the worst time i am stuck and have to teleport out. And yes you get some atletic or acrobatic xp but is still really tire some.
I have also encountred a few crashes.

It's hard to say that you shouldn't play a game, particularly when it is free, but I'm going to do just that.
Don't waste your time with Blossoms.
The music is forgettable, the art is inconsistent, the voice acting is annoying and actively hinders comprehension in some places. There are 5-6 generic voice lines for each character and many of them are used over the top of text that isn't even close in meaning to the voice line.
Kotoha's Route is ok. If you feel the need to play this game then do her route and aim for the good ending. Her character and story are decently written and generally makes sense.
Everything to do with Sara is nonsense. She absolutely hates you (which makes sense... she thinks you kidnapped her) until she inexplicably falls in love with you. No, seriously, there's almost no interaction with her that could be considered bonding or romantic in any way
but suddenly you're on a date swooning for her.
The main plot is no better. The whole concept
makes no sense at all, and there's no effort spent in the writing to explain why. There's mystery for the sake of mystery that literally resolves itself halfway through the story, then the rest of the story focuses on these horribly flimsy romantic relationships. Also, the whole game takes place in the span of 14 days. It's not nearly enough time for the characters to progress through the arcs that they do.
All in all, skip it unless curiosity absolutely gets the better of you. Even then, get Kotoha's good ending and pretend like that's the whole game. Save yourself the time, trouble, and frustration of Sara's story and skip it.

In what feels like (and probably is meant to be) a demo for Reine Works' non-free game Galaxy Angels, this poorly written and uninteresting visual novel fails to elicit any sort of response other than confusion.
The plot is a mystery for most of the game, and then is revealed near the end - unfortunately the reveal only shows that the plot makes no sense. The cast does its best to hold up the stilted lines being delivered with some okay voice acting, but the characters they are playing (otaku girl, jerk evening gown woman, and captain moron) don't hold up. Why would you have three people piloting a large spaceship? Why would you pour flour into the central air unit while you are in space? Why would you combine a space colony ship with random gene experiments?
Even the yuri aspect of the game isn't worth it, as none of the characters are likeable, and all you get are sad, sad scenes of them in their underwear after the aforementioned "flour scene."
Blossoms Bloom Brightest is neither good enough nor bad enough to recommend a playthrough of it. There are plenty of free visual novels on Steam, and plenty of much better ones too (I recommend The Sad Story of Emmeline Burns).

SPOILERS AHEAD!!!

CHAPTER 3, your fate, as you find what you nust do to survive.
This game mayy be short, but it will deliver a good story even though it may be a bit cliche, and the function of the light is a good gameplay focus, so with all said, this game is a solid 7/10
