The Fall has a distinct graphical style that, although a bit dark, fits the story and mood quite well. Having the protagonist be an A.I. bound by a preprogrammed ruleset is unique and has some interesting potential. Unfortunately the potential isn't well explored, having the game lack depth. Furthermore, the story is ill explained and does not give you the opportunity to develop attachment to any of the characters you encounter.
The major gameplay element is taken from the old point-and-click adventure game format: collect objects and use them with other objects in the game world to proceed. Unfortunately this mechanic is implemented poorly, as there are too few areas and items held at once to make for challenging puzzles.
The Fall also has combat, although it is implemented just as poorly as the adventure mechanics. There are a grand total of 3 enemy types, out of which 1 type is barely responsive. It resembles the style used in the old game 'Flashback', but lacks depth. As a result, the combat encounters are cumbersome rather than enjoyable, furthermore lacking alternative solutions to a straight up firefight.
The control scheme is again similar to Flashback, and again lacking in refinement. Jumping looks and feels odd and the control scheme is bad. For instance, the default control scheme on an X-Box controller uses the right analog stick for aiming, while pressing it changes between flashlight and laser sight (searching and shooting, respectively), which you may want to switch between without resetting your aim. The control scheme doesn't use enough buttons to warrant this odd setup.
The game is riddled with bugs to the point where it warrants its own section. Throughout the game it has crashed or locked me in 4 times (e.g., by falling through the floor and going out of bounds after using an item or leaving cover). The Fall lacks polish, as occasionally you can glimpse the outer bounds of the level, as well as target objects through walls. Thus, the bugs not only break immersion, but also your progression throughout the game.
Another flaw warranting its own section is that the game is incredibly short. It takes roughly 1.5 to 2 hours to complete the game without the use of a walkthrough. With the combat and puzzles being dull gameplay elements you're left with no replay value what so ever.
According to the developer (via discussion boards) the game will be a trilogy and won't be split into episodic content. I'm not sure what constitutes as episodic content nowadays, but I disagree with the developer for the following reasons: (1) the story abruptly ends on an unsatisfactory cliffhanger leaving many questions unanswered, (2) the game is ridiculously short, and (3) the menu displays several slots for more suit unlocks that are not obtainable in this game.
I strongly recommend not buying this game at all. If you feel compelled by its story and theme, I advise you to at least wait until the trilogy is complete and buy it as a packaged deal. This title, at least, is not worth the 10 euro price tag it currently has. As it stands, the gameplay is boring, short, bland, and offers no replayability. The game is structured in an episodic way and its first episode is bad. It lacks polish and contains several annoying and potentially game-breaking bugs.
At 50% off it is an excellent, yet short Platform/Adventure/Action game. I absolutely love the AI conversations in this game.

Morrowind is a timeless classic of the open world RPG genre and is quite possibly the best Elder Scrolls game.
Morrowind dosen't hold your hand or give you much of an idea of what to do quests dont feel forced and rushed but rather require you too actually think however there is atleast a minimap even if there are no quest markers.
I would recommend this great game to anyone that is a fan of open world rpg's or has enjoyed the Elder Scrolls or Fallout series in general.
The combat system is rather dated and most things in this game atleast combat wise are RNG based however once you get the hang of it fighting becomes very rewarding and fun.
This is definetly a game that has replayability value and can only be enjoyed to the fullest extent by making multiple characters.
Also I highly recommend getting the "Morrowind Overhaul Mod by Ornitocopter" It is essentially a mod pack that contains mods that fix bugs left in the game after the last update by bethesda as well as phenomenal graphical improvements I would honestly say that Morrowind with the overhaul looks better than Oblivion at max settings or even compared to Skyrim without the high res texture pack.
Overall a 10/10 game that is a must play for everyone that enjoys open world Role Playing Games.

I am loving this game so far! At this time only Shou’s route is available (The prologue and 1st chapter of each route is free. Full routes can be purchased) so my review will be for his route.
Pros:
-really beautiful and varied music. It changes to match the mood of the scenes quite well.
-lovely and consistent art style.
-the main character is wonderful! She is compassionate, but willing to stand up for herself. She also struggles with some fear and insecurities. She is not a blank slate and has believable responses to the situations she is placed in. I suppose it could be a downside if you are wanting a character you can mold to match your own personality, but I really enjoyed reading the MC’s thoughts and opinions.
-the story starts out seeming like a typical school setting where this group of guys is thrown in with you but it has a wonderful twist in the prologue that I won’t spoil here. The fantasy setting seems very well thought out and has lots of backstory that is relayed to you in a way that is not overwhelming, but intriguing. Love it!
-the writing style is very lovely and descriptive. It really pulls you in.
-the relationship between the MC and Shou grows slowly and believably. It also strikes a great balance between some really cute, sweet moments and some darker, intense scenes.
Cons:
-that title. Come on, “Mystic Destinies: Serendipity of Aeons” is a mouthful. And upon first hearing it, you’re not really sure what it’s supposed to convey. Um, it’s a fantasy type game? A mystical fantasy? I might be nitpicking, but even shortening it to “Serendipity of Aeons” would be better, IMO.
-while the artwork is lovely, there are only 3 CG images for Shou’s route (one contained in one of the endings). Would have been nice to have a few more…but again, this is a minor thing.
-my biggest downside may not even be considered a downside. Let me explain. There are certain moments in the game where your character (default name, Tsubasa) must make a choice. These choices will decide which of the three endings you get (Passionate, Mystic, or Dark). But other than the ending, your choices only seem to affect a few lines of dialogue before you go right back to the main story. For example, at one point Tsubasa is asked by another character to meet them somewhere. You can choose to say yes, say no, or hesitate. No matter what you choose, Tsubasa will still end up going to the same place. The next few lines after your choice will be different, but then everything will be the same as if you chose the other options. Again, this may not be considered bad, as long as you view this more as a story being played out by characters that you can nudge one way or the other, instead of a “choose-your-own-adventure” type story with a self-insert MC. Once I accepted that, I did enjoy it as it allowed Tsubasa to stay true to her character and let the story unfold how it was intended. However, I didn't feel like my choices made that much of an impact (especially since even the "Dark" ending isn't really a "bad" ending. In fact, I liked it better than the "Passionate" ending.)
I honestly didn’t think I’d enjoy Shou’s route that much…out of all the characters to choose from I probably would have picked him last. Since his route was the only one available so far, I went ahead and took a chance. I’m so glad I did! Now I’m wondering if any of the other routes will be able to live up to Shou’s story. :) It was sweet, funny, heartbreaking, and exciting. I will definitely be coming back for more.

After getting the complete version of TM2 during the Steam Winter Fail 2016 (Most of the discounts weren't my cup of tea), I have one thing to say about this game compared to the only other TM game I have played, TM Sunrise.
This game will TEST YOU. It will test you to no end on your precision and how well you can powerslide without sending your car careening into a lampost. One you get it down, you can get that adrenaline rush that the whole of Sonic The Hedgehog wishes it could give you. Getting medals is also a challenge, even with the lower difficulty tracks. I just go for silver medals in single player, because the golds are basically MLG pro (At least they don't quickscope you the moment you get in the lead). The only problem I see with single player is currently, I don't think you can have multiple opponents to race against. Solo is 1v1 the whole way through (As far as I can tell). The physics are still what you'd expect from trackmania: go fast and you'll win, but you might wind up launching yourself off the track at that bump in the road or fly off at the next dip in the road and put yourself into a roll that costs you your silver medal.
Complimenting the challenge is the great aesthetics and performance. My computer runs this game at near perfect frames, and the vibrant color palette (DAT SKYBOX BE DOUBLE-D SEXY) makes the game pop.
This review is just based on my completion of all the white-flag challenges, so my experience can't say the same other players.
In the end, I say that this is a good installment in the Trackmania franchise, and worth my 20 bucks. I recommend you do what I did, and grab it before the Steam Winter Fail ends, or wait for the next discount on the franchise. Fans won't be disappointed (Maybe).

I can honestly see no reason to want to play this game when there are much better visual novels on Steam and on the internet in general. This game is painfully short, which isn't a good thing when the writing isn't particularly noteworthy in any way.
There
actually choices and multiple endings in this game, to which I can give it some points. However, since everything is so bunched up together due to the game's length, there's no time to feel any impact to your decisions besides "oh hey, I got a good ending," or "oh hey, I screwed up."
The characters are incredibly one-note, to the point where I can't even call them stereotypes because that would imply they have some substance. Any of the "romantic" scenes are downright cringe-worthy (Seriously, there's kissing onomatopoeia for multiple text boxes in a row. Nothing but kissing onomatopoeia.), and it really doesn't even make sense for the protagonist to care about the lead girl by the end of the game, especially since he's an unlikable jerk to her for no real reason at all for the entire game. He has a sudden change of heart for basically no conceivable reason, and I honestly don't think I missed some vital part of the story or anything. It just happened.
The art and music are both passable, but forgettable. Nothing to particularly note here. I can't really complain, but I also can't really compliment anything.
On the subject of the art, you can see all the CGs in the game the first time you boot it up, without even playing the game. Maybe that's why there's an achievement for actually bothering to hit "new game."
That's not to say this game is all bad though. As I said, the art is genuinely passable, and I didn't dislike it. The choices you make in this game are on a timer, which I think is an interesting mechanic, and not choosing a choice in the time limit actually counts as its own choice. That's a legitimately neat feature. But one neat feature isn't enough to float this game, especially in the short time you have to experience it. If this game was longer, and the protagonist was actually a decent person, I'd totally say that this could be a good game.
As it stands, I can't recommend it.

Have you always wanted to be a celestial object? In this interesting take on the "grow bigger" genre you finally can. You begin as a smallest of asteroids and have to hit other asteroids to grow in mass and avoid marauding space ships and anything too much larger in the process. You move with arrows or ASDW (I used keyboard) in a 2D universe, while everything else is dictated by gravity.
At some point you will grow into a planet. This changes mechanics: no longer will you try to hit stuff but instead try to make asteroids orbit your piece of rock, after which you can absorb them. Mechanics are different for each phase: asteroid, planet, star and black hole. Planet phase is separated into regular and life planets (all with shields, planetary cannons and spaceships).
Orbiting is pseudophysical: that is, not real physics at all. The objects will actually be attached to the orbiting system. You should know that this is not a real physics simulator, so this is totally fine. This makes for some truly bizarre possibilities: you can form multi-star ring systems with ridiculous numbers of stars and yet have aggressively orientated fully evolved killer planets orbiting the system.
Story and achievements provide some 10-20 hours of playtime within three missions and 2-3 challenge mini games for each phase and finally a boss fight. They often make clever use of the game's physics and mechanics. You can also stop anytime you want and the cloud will make sure you can continue from where you left, or if you'd like to, from somewhere entirely different. Playing is very enjoyable and the only time I remember it getting tedious was when I grinded my way to 40 stars supersystem. Fortunately, you can save your favourite configurations (like that one with super-multistar megasystem) to be loaded any number of times again (handy for achievements) and play with physics options if regular pseudophysics gets boring.
Once you're done with the universe simply grow your planet-eating super-heavy neutron star into an all-devouring black hole and consume the world in a Big Crunch. A fitting end to a crazy little game.

Fantastic breakout-like game - with the one caveat that you can't remap the controls, which is
irritating.
Loads of little and big innovations to the genre - the ability to affect the ball while it's in the air, the spike showing where the ball's going to hit next (which in turn helps you learn how the Suck/Blow controls work best), mobile bricks you have to dodge or they'll knock you out of doing anything for a few seconds, the ability to throw multiple balls at once for faster wins / target plays (but 1 ball == 1 life, so make sure you can handle it), different level shapes, boss fights (which I'm usually not a fan of in games - they too often turn flow into grind - but here, they're mostly not too difficult, just a nice change of pace) - and more.
Oh, and a bunch of them - the guidance spike, some ability to maneuver the ball mid-air, the ability to launch additional balls, and more - let you almost entirely avoid that irritating end-of-level "just 1-3 stray bricks that you keep missing by a hair" phase most breakout-like games have.

Any more in-depth introduction would defeat its purpose since most of you probably spent your time with the original the same way I did: in a darkened room, nose glued to the screen, on the brink of wetting yourself. That was almost 20 years ago and the series changed quite a bit since then - depending on who you ask, not necessarily for the better. Resident Evil left behind its survival horror roots a long time ago in favor of a more dynamic, action-oriented approach. Ever since you had fans yearning for survival horror to make a return while others embraced the new ways, stating that tank controls and fixed camera angles simply wouldn't hold up anymore. But do they hold up? Short answer: Yup, sure do.
It's funny to see developers jumping through hoops to make their game feel "cinematic" when Resident Evil achieved that feat almost 20 years ago without sacrificing the actual game: Fixed camera angles offer the perfect balance between tension and field of view while the pre-rendered backgrounds provide the eye candy as you creep through the mansion and perforate the undead. And due to the control scheme, forward always remains forward when you move out of the picture. The scarce resources along with your limited inventory keep you on your toes and make sure each encounter stays tense. Resident Evil is a slow-paced game that is supposed to be played with foresight and the controls only emphasize that. All of this can be applied to the REmaster.
As a result, the REmaster also inherits many of the original's problems: Some camera angles don't offer as much visibility as they should and at times you find yourself awkwardly jerking around between pictures. And due to the drastically limited inventory the backtracking is strong in this one. You end up visiting the same locations at least twice since you often enter a new area only to realize that the item you need to solve the next puzzle is resting in your locker at the other end of the mansion. You only get six item slots (or eight respectively) where a piece of paper takes up as much space as a mother♥♥♥♥ing shotgun. A more elegant item management system could have prevented many unnecessary trips to Mount Doom and back.
Essentially, REmaster is a tarted up version of REmake for Nintendo's Gamecube. If you're like me and never owned one, the REmaster will make the game feel fresh all over again. But if you already own it for Gamecube, the effect will probably not be as strong. Especially considering that the quality of the remade backgrounds is all over the place. There are times when REmaster will flex its muscles and show off its amazing new lighting, but there are other times when you drag your character through low-res, grainy areas that look like they have been chased through a lanczos filter in Photoshop.
In a way, playing REmaster is like spending time with an old friend you haven't seen in ages. It's been so long that you're not sure whether or not he's still cool or if he ever was cool in the first place. When you finally meet again for a drink, you can tell that he tries to give the impression that nothing has changed, yet you can't help but notice some wrinkles along with the receding hairline. Still, you spend some quality time together and you can confirm that he is cool, even now.
Some people would question whether or not it's worth paying for an HD remake that isn't that HD to begin with. Everyone else is already playing it. Like they should.

I hate that I have to give this game a negative review. The foundations of a good game are there, but it just falls so flat. Given the nature of these problems, I might pick this game up again if it gets updated to fix these problems.
The biggest issue is that it's a buggy mess. There's this bizaare glitch where your gun fires when your NOT holding down the fire button. This would be fine, just let go when you want to fire, but it fires at random. There have been huge gaps where the lil' guy wouldn't fire his gun when being swarmed by bats. There is also a bug where if you try to jump while a ladder is underneath you, you will instead hop off the ladder. Given how many ladders there are and how much you need to jump, this is a huge problem.
By far the worst bug is not being able to pick up the space ship part. You're supposed to press F, but it did nothing. I thought it might be an error with key mapping, so I pressed every single button on the keyboard; I got nothing. (This is how I found out that 9 can be used to jump. Wierd)
As long as I'm listing bugs, I found an exploit that involves you turning around when facing a wall. Because you move backwards slightly when you do this, you can clip into the wall and shimmy down to the lower level. I thought it was fun.
Aside from the bugs, I don't like the text. The maker literally used the logo text for everything. It's unnecessarily hard to read for things like menu text and descriptions. The creator should have toned it down a lot or used a normal font.
As for *positives,* it's fun to move around and shoot, and it's satisfying to kill enemies. Music's alright, fits well. I like the *prospect* of unlocking new characters, but that's unfortunately not possible with the aforementioned ship part bug not letting me progress.
I would love to play this game as a finished product, but the bugs REALLY need to be ironed out. I hope Charlie Evans reads this, because I'm hoping for a big patch,

Interesting idea, but I am sad to say that the execution is lacking. There are some serious quality of life improvements required to make this less frustrating for regular terminal users.
The game (and terminal) doesn't properly resize to fit the resolution (2560x1600), so you are stuck with a lot of scrolling to read stuff that would have comfortably fit on the monitor otherwise. The mouse wheel doesn't work and the scroll handle is tiny and therefore very fiddly. There doesn't even seem to be any keyboard shortcuts for scrolling, which would have been fine, too.
I got through Episode 1 easily enough, but stopped playing during some puzzles in Episode 2 that require typing a lot of rather wordy commands in a very specific order. Failing one of these apparently requires re-typing all of it. The solution was easy, but extremely tedious to enter. This, combined with the lack of context (due to the small window and lack of halfway decent scrolling) made it frustrating enough for me to just quit right there.
My experience with the puzzles is limited by the fact that I stopped playing, but most puzzles so far seem to consist out of rather repetitively digging through emails, finding a clue and entering the result. Sometimes it also requires you to Google for some piece of text that the clue references to find the answer. Also, this is nowhere near a "full-featured hacker" experience. There is only a handful of limited commands, and you could probably just brute-force your way through all of it.
I would have liked to know how the story ends, but in its current state, I am not willing to put more time into it to find out.

###############################ORIGINAL POST ####################################
Why I can't recommend this game.
I am a streamer, I have had experienced players coming into my twitch and hanging out.
I participated in the official faction TeamSpeak.
I devoted over 60 hours to this game and had 2 lvl 5 soldiers, including a tanker, and 1 lvl 6 soldier.
It was fun if not frustrating at times as this game is grind heavy and the starting weapons in this game are in my opinion drastically underpowered.
One critical flaw of this game was that it dropped you in with all levels of player once you reached lvl 5 making the player skill and gear you were facing jump heavily, this experience alone would be enough to deter many players.
That being said I still enjoyed it and pushed through and got better gear.
Why am I quitting and leaving a negative review?
Cheating/exploits. This company is either not large enough or does not take this aspect of the game seriously enough.
Througout my experience I constantly came across enemies who seemed to outlandishly snap around and shoot me when approached from odd angles, often instantly finishing me with a headshot.
I reported these players.
Also folks seemed to strangely know where you were, making me suspect that radar bot use was rampant. I would also report these players.
The thing that made me quit was a gentleman standing in a pillar in a church, immune, shooting enemies, and more or less putting his team in a winning position.
This represents shear laziness and selfishness on the part of the developers. It is extremely hard to control, and resource intensive, to counter aimbots/radarbots, so that I understand.
However, developers have complete control over maps and clipping and should easily counter folks who do things like pass into objects for immunity. The game engine can be built with coding which doesn't allow this or warps players back into playable parts of the map. This game doesn't have this.
It is this sort of laziness which makes it so that I can not recommend this game.
I also mentioned the developers are selfish.
I paid these guys $20 which I regret.
This game has been out for over 2 years and they have been accepting money the whole time.
If this was a new game and a new map I would understand, but it isn't.
The developers are clearly communicating their lack of care and their misplaced priorities.
It is for this reason that I can't recommend it, that I am leaving a negative review on my twitch page, a negative forum post and avoiding this game until I have reason to believe these problems are fixed.

Mystic Destinies: Serendipity of Aeons is a beautifully compelling story about a young woman called Tsubasa whose life is suddenly turned upside down when her mother drops the big reveal. The world she has always known has been a lie and now she must face the truth.  Aided by some new wonderful supportive friends, Tsubasa begins her journey into the Unseen World, the magical realms where supernatural beings lie hidden from the human realm. MDSoA introduces a rather interesting moral dilemma; what does it mean to be human?
StarMaidenGames has done a fantastic job with this game. They have listened to feedback from fans and have implemented changes that have really made this game shine. While it’s not the traditional ‘anime’ art style that comes with many otome games, the artist should be congratulated highly for such a beautiful style that highlights and captures the story in amazing ways. The characters are very well rounded and complement each other wonderfully. Character stereotypes have been broken apart and it’s such a nice sight to see. The story is complex but well-structured; there are moments of confusion, which I believe is well intended because like Tsubasa, we are experiencing this world for the first time. While it does leave some rather big questions open, this is the first route of the game and I do expect that they will be addressed in future routes.
Playing Mystic Destinies: Serendipity of Aeons will give you warm fuzzy feelings but it will also make you feel some angst as not everything is sunshine and roses. So if you’re ready to embark on a beautiful journey of self-acceptance, love and magic then press that purchase button and play until you cry. <3

Just finished my first playthrough  and I am already looking forward to so much more from Star Maiden Games. I love the richness of the characters, and especially the villain. I really find it a victory in a story when you can empathize with a villain as well as the protagonists. And I love love love sassy main characters.
Also, I highly appreciate that it’s available on Mac via Steam. So go support this new company, with stunning artwork, lovely music, and fabulous writing.

This is a remaster of a 12 year old game whose core gameplay is good enough to stand against the giants available for purchase today in the genre - the definitive version of Fable/Fable: TLC. I spent countless hours playing Fable for the Xbox growing up, and when I saw Anniversary up on the winter sale this past December I jumped at the opportunity to experience the version of the game I never had when I was younger (I never played through TLC).
What a great experience! I've loved every single minute of my playthrough thus far, and will probably do a second one shortly after!
Controller support is great (I use a Steam Controller when playing), but I'm sure the KB+M controls work fine as well. The old hero save glitches are gone which could be a boon or a negative depending on who you speak to. The graphical updates are noticable but still retain the charm that the original Fable had.
If you played this game when it was originally released and you were a fan - GET THIS! Get it on sale, get it full price, whatever you may do - just buy it. If you have the patience to wait, pick it up on sale (it goes on sale frequently) and get the best value for your dollar. You will not regret it.

If only there was a more middle of the road button. D:
Anyway, I'll say this much-- I haven't run into all the same glitches everyone else has reported yet, and some of them are quite the same as what Fable had prior to remodeling. It's an overrated version of the original, which is why I only bought it when on sale. I give credit where credit is due; it does look somewhat nicer than it was (Read: They cut corners), but I guess I'm a bit harsh when it comes to game aesthetics.
Also let's be realistic here; the game itself is still good content-wise. If the glitches happen to hinder your ability to play it, then go back to the original copy if you've got one floating around. The only bad bug I encountered so far is that the voices tend to cut out randomly. With subtitles, I can live with that.
Bottom line is, its still Fable. Its still buggy-yet-easy as ever, it's still basically the game so many know and love. Could it have been redone better? Absolutely. But evidently, this is what we're getting. Here's to hoping they decide to clean it up a bit more.
Meanwhile, I'll continue playing it on and off until more glitches annoy the living hell out of me. :3

Homesick is extremely reliant on its atmosphere to conduct the story, as for much of the game it it's all you have to go on. They've done plenty of things right, but could have perhaps done some things better. The initial game gives almost no tutorial or introduction, which even I found somewhat daunting at first. After a few trial-and-errors, you begin to figure it out if you have the patience for it, which I'm afraid a lot of people might not have.
If you can get over this hurdle, the game opens up rapidly. It does get bogged down in some areas with puzzles that, while the solutions usually make sense, can take a lot of patience to figure out. I have to admit, I needed to use some user hints on the forums because a game mechanic wasn't explained to me. The mechanic in particular was the block puzzle. I was not aware I could press a keyboard letter to change the symbol to that letter, despite looking at a dozen blocks, it never occured to me that you were able to do that. It's a great idea, but if you don't provide some context, people won't know what you want from them.
The beautiful environment is a healthy balance between grey and green, and it sounds good to boot. The story even starts to come together at the end with a little twist. The walk speed during the day is a bit slow though and the ending scene was rather abstract and didn't fit.
Great game, though it demands a lot of patience, but I felt it gave a just reward.

Spore is...unique, to say the least.
Spore is basically five games and an art tool all bundled together into one coherent piece of software.
The art tool is the primary focus of the game. With it, you can design several different elements that you'll use in the five games, but the one everyone knows about Spore for is the creature creator. You're given a spinal column with skin on it, and you can increase or decrease the number of joints in the spine, resize each joint (and the surrounding skin), and change its overall default shape. This alone is something you don't see in any other game, but Spore isn't anywhere near done yet. You also have access to an enormous amount of "parts"; this includes limbs, eyes, ears, mouths, noses, and many other details. Every part can be rotated, resized, tweaked, and painted. The only limit is your imagination (And a sanity limit so your computer's memory doesn't overload, but I've never hit that). You can easily make quadrupeds, bipeds, lizard things, dinosaur things, human-shaped things, things shaped like any animal you know,
. Heck, I wouldn't be surprised if some overly-dedicated person has created a Spore rendition of every single Pokemon. It's definitely possible.
At any rate, lets get on with the game. Spore is a retelling of the history of life, from the very beginning, to the future we humans hope to reach. You'll progress through five stages, which act like completely separate, yet linked, games.
First is the cell stage. You begin as a single-celled organism in the ocean of a planet just seeded with life by a meteor. You have one goal: Eat! You can choose to be either a carnivore or an herbivore. If you pick the former, you eat by attacking and devouring other cells while not getting devoured yourself. If you pick the latter, you eat plant matter lying around, while also not getting devoured by the carnivores. At any time, you can call for a mate to create a new cell with more and better parts. This stage ends once you have eaten enough food. (I like to call this the Agario stage, because you eat other things and get bigger. At least, if you're a carnivore.)
From there, you enter the creature stage. Your organism, now fairly large and complex, swims out of the ocean, grows legs, and settles on land. Now, you must evolve further in order to fully develop a brain. Doing this involves attaining a sufficient number of DNA points (which also enable you to evolve more and better parts for your creature). To do that, you need to interact with other species of creature. You can choose to ally with them, or (typically if you're a carnivore) continue to brutally murder them as you (maybe) did with the cells. Either way, you still have to eat; being a carnivore lets you kill two birds with one stone. (I like to call this the Diablo stage, because it's a little bit like the Diablo games, but mostly because it fits the naming pattern for the rest of the later stages.)
After that, you enter the tribal stage. This is the last chance you have to modify your creature. The tribal stage has the same goal(s) as the creature stage; either make friends or mincemeat out of all the other tribes. However, this stage has RTS mechanics, as opposed to the creature stage, which used basic 3rd-person action mechanics. You still have to eat; herbivores gather plants to each, while carnivores can hunt wild animals or fish. (I like to call this the Warcraft stage. It's an RTS with a pretty low unit cap, and a "hero" unit.)
Next is the civilization stage. It functions quite similarly to the tribal stage, except that you now have better control over how your settlements function. Your goal is to take control of every city. This time, you have three options; murder them, convert them to your religion, or just buy them out. (I like to call this the Starcraft stage. It's an RTS with a considerably higher unit cap and no "hero" unit.)
Last is the space stage. Now that you've taken control of the entire planet, you have only one more place to go: another planet. This is the most complex stage with goals of all sorts. (I like to call this the World of Warcraft stage. It's got tons of interface buttons and an MMO-sized universe to explore.)

The game has too many ideas to bring together under one title. The first two levels are a 'feeding frenzy' style with the second adding the ability befriend other animals. The three remaining levels are 'civilization' style. You start as a tribe, attacking or singing to other tribes. Then you are a city with the goal of controlling all other cities. Then you get to the point that seems to make the game loose focus, space age. You explore the galaxy interacting with other planets. Colonizing, abductions, space wars, etc. I've learned from research that the goal for this stage is to get to the center of the galaxy and obtain an artifact of sorts.
The biggest problem I have is that the space stage feels like it should be the one with the fewest restrictions, but you always have to do missions for your home planet and other planets. Every item and upgrade to your ship is so expensive. Your purpose in this stage, the one you have been working towards ever since your microbial self fell from space, is to be the galaxy's babysitter.
I had fun with it while the novelty of the game was fresh. But it looses its luster fast due to weird body mechanics and other short falls.
If micromanaging the interworkings of the cosmos sounds fun, buy this game. Otherwise go buy Galactic Civilization and/or Kerbal Space Program

I bought this game because of my love for Isaac Asimov's robot novels. I am positive that the game designers are also huge fans of that series. The plot hinges on the fact that AIs are bound by three primary functions, which are different depending on the robot's purpose. The scenerio deals with the potential repurcussions of logical paradoxes that arise in an AI when trying to acheive those primary functions.  For instance, it may be necessary to put a human's life in jeopardy for the purpose of trying to save his life.  Or it may be necessary to break one of the functions in order to satisfy another.
Regarding actual gameplay, the game achieves exactly what it intends. The puzzles are intuitive but not obvious. They are also difficult enough that you feel very satisfied once you figure them out.  The action aspects of the game are pretty easy, but it really isn't intended to be an action game. The shooting sequences are really just inserted to bring added drama to the story, and in that they succeed.
Some people have complained about the length of the game. This didn't bother me at all. I for one don't want to be solving puzzles for 15 hours. The game took me 4 hours and I found that to be the perfect time.  Also some people have complained about the ending. These people are stupid. The ending opens up the story in a fantastic way.
Bottom line, I loved the story. It was moody and dramatic, with moments of great humor. Even though the story could never happen in Asimov's universe (the laws of robotics would prohibit this entire scenerio), it still honors his contribution to robotics theory and science fiction in general. If you are an Asimov fan you should definitely give this game a try. I can't wait till the 2nd part, which I am sure will deal with the dilemma of an AI achieving free will.

This short free to play visual novel from Reine Works and Dharker Studio feature three female characters aboard a spaceship Blossom - Erica Matthews the captain, Kotoha Ichinose the mechanic and Sara Evans the doctor. After being sent into space with no viable option to return to Earth, the trio decide to work together to overcome their differences over 14 days in which Erica can develop a relationship with Kotoha or Sara and have a good or bad ending with.
Each route will take approximately 30-60 minutes. Soundtracks, CGs and overall game presentation are good after factoring in appropriate background music for the futuristic space and romance themes in the story and animated sprites for each of the main characters. It would be nice to have an extras section featuring CGs and music gallery in the game. Recommended as a free to play visual novel for those who like a short yuri visual novel with light-hearted moments in-between or for those who like a short game to finish and get all achievements in less than 10 hours. Would be interested to see Galaxy Angels and further sequels with nice artwork and easy/reasonable achievements being released in future.
Blossoms Bloom Brightest, decent, short, free. I recommend any Visual Novel fan check it out, especially if you like sci-fi VNs.

Solar 2 is a wonderful little game that can be played however the player wants.
One can simply gather enough mass to eventually engulf the universe, or take on one of the many challenges presented to them at varying stages of the game. While some of these challenges can prove to be quite difficult, most of them are quite fun and enjoyable, even the hard ones can be extremely fun once you get the hang of it. They are challenges after all, not simple, "Move here, destroy stuff, achievement!" In the end, the missions are entirely optional, the player has no obligation to complete them what-so-ever, they are there for players who enjoy something a little more than simply getting bigger.
There are portions of the game that could use improvement. A warning for upcoming hazards other than black holes would be wonderful! I can't say how many times I've died due to zipping across space and then running straight into a star. The collecting of mass latter on also becomes somewhat of a chore due to the player needing to get asteroids or planets into an orbit first before absorbing rather than just smashing into them like similar games. It does somewhat prevent the player from going straight to the last stage with minimum effort, but it can still prove to be a pain when you are trying to mass up only to constantly crash into stuff instead.
However, these are minor issues, some of which are gameplay mechanics others just personal preference.
Solar 2 is visually stunning, seeing all the universe has to offer and all the things you can mess around with is truly magnificent. The controls for the asteroids, planets, and stars, all respond and feel like you are controlling them, asteroids just zip around effortlessly, while stars and solar systems are sluggish and take time to get going, giving that sense of just how truly massive you are.
Overall, I find Solar 2 a joy to play for brief periods of time, longer play sessions I would not recommend unless you are going soley for achievements or high scores, otherwise you might quickly burn yourself out. The gameplay, soundtrack, and visuals all make Solar 2 an out of this world experience for people who love messing around in cosmos.

RE1 Remaster is basically the GameCube port to the PC, but it does come with a few extra bells and whistles. The most obvious is the up res'ed textures, backgrouds, and overall resolution. There's also a new control scheme and a even new character skins.
If you're an old timer looking for an excuse to replay one of your childhood favorites, RE1 Remaster won't disappoint. All of the classic tank control, hallway rerunning, and key collecting goodness remain intact. I do recommend turning the difficulty to hard on your first go if you are looking for that "true" classic RE experience. (Normal would definitely be considered easy to series vets)
If you are new to classic RE, this would be a great time to see what all the hoohaa is all about. Playing the old PSX version for the younger generation might be difficult due to the dated look, but now that we have a much superior visual product that still has the classic mechanics, it can potentially show case that these older mechanics still has merit in today's gaming world. But be aware, if you are new it won't play like modern games. There will be a large degree of backtracking, and confusion at first. But if you can get over that hump, I think most can get a lot of enjoyment out of RE1 Remaster

Stunningly rendered, the waking world has a thick atmosphere of brooding and lingering dust.  Books, pages and photographic slides litter the defunct and decaying apartment building - hinting of history, of the people who once dwelled within these corridors of plaster and peeling wallpaper.   Somber music punctuates the melancholy as you explore the modern ruin seeking answers: what happened, where did everyone go, why am I still here, and why is the sunlight so painfully bright?   Some of the writings and pictures I found rummaging through the kippleized environment spoke of answers to come.
Asleep, the world is transformed into a shadowy nightmare version of itself.  The unconscious world is a place of frantic, terrorized sprinting as the darkness aggressively moves in to gobble you up in its hellish maw.

The puzzles are well-thought-out, logical, and fluid; meshing perfectly with the environment.   It’s feels less like coming to a “puzzle section” like in some games, and more like creatively seeking out ways to move around the environment.
This is what I liked about Homesick, the atmosphere, the mystery, the logical puzzles, the tip-of-the-iceberg world building that promised something more; a reward for pushing further into the game’s brooding depths.  The game didn’t deliver.   I’ve clocked about three hours in the game and I can tell you without exaggeration that 80% of that time was spent staring at books trying to decipher their script.   (I managed to work out most of the alphabet, the key I scribbled down in a notebook lacking only the ciphers for Q and X).   After about 30 minutes of actual gameplay and head-scratching, Homesick abruptly ends with no answers, no story, and what amounts to a cheap jump-scare and a vague sense of “paternal-ness”, for lack of a better word.   Homesick feels like a project that someone did a lot of work on, felt strongly about, and obsessed over for a while, but got tired of producing 10% of the way through, polished it up, and slapped a half-hearted ending on it.   I bought the game on sale, so I’m not upset that I spent money on it.  But the game is in no way worth the $15 USD price tag.
My recommendation is mixed.  But since I have to pick yes or no, at this price the answer is no, I would not recommend this title.

It's essentially a game where you control a pin, and move it to prevent a bouncing ball from falling off the screen.
The visual effects are good, and the physics work as expected, but I felt the player doesnt have much control over where the ball goes despite the push/pull controls.
The game doesn't present much of a challenge, beyond occasionally failing one time and getting it the next go.
The bonus rounds are enjoyable, and the bosses provide more of a challenge, but ultimately the game is let down by it's lack of risk/reward.
The gameplay also becomes repetitive fairly quickly, it is the sort of game you would play for 10 minutes once a day rather than in a long playstreak.
3/5

A very enjoyable Arkanoid clone with some interesting variations in stage format and ball behavior, including circular levels, with interesting boss fights. An excellent soundtrack by a group called Module that can be found on bandcamp. Both coop and competitive multiplayer modes are available.

Don’t honestly have too much to say about Shatter. It’s a breakout clone with a twist, the ability to manipulate the balls trajectory mid-flight, by blowing or suctioning. This is a great concept, as it helps to eliminate that ‘last block’ moment, and the way it affects other elements of the game is satisfying. However, controlling this ability can be a bit tricky, the circular levels almost always end up having that ‘last block’ struggle anyways and a couple of the boss fights are frustrating because of it. Overall if you’re looking for a new experience with a breakout-style game, this is for you.

But.... the dark times have come. The developer becomes sick on mind - the bad and the ugly ones tell he becomes greedy. His sickness drowned him into darkness, and he was no longer the same. He forgot about his creation, leaving it on a cold stone deep in the mountain cave. The game, lying on the stone, cried for a first time, and all people who put their hopes in it cried with it.
The time have passed, world has changed, mordor faded away long time ago and everybody forgot about the game. The developer grew old, probably died or hidden somewhere in the great forest, in fact nobody knows. The game itself is now lost, noone cared about it for a long time, and it lays in ruin, being slowly consumed by the sickness of its creator. The legend says that some day someone will find that cave, take out the game to the daylight, fix it from the bugs that are poisoning it and flooding its veins, and the people will give their hearts to Heroes & Generals once again.

Best TM2 Environment (IMO)

Stadium is better IMO because it has more population, more community generated content, and more persistent playerbase than this game.
Racing gameplay here is largely based on rally racing. Note that the car steers very well, and can handle sharp turns.  But, it doesn't do so well at high speeds and will spin out at any attempt at braking.  As such, racing tends to be more technical than drifting related or fullspeed.
This was the third of the TM2 series, and its the most graphically polished, however TM2 still excells in content.
Note that environments are canyons, concrete roads, and stadium-like structures.  There is a fair balance of natural environment blocks and manmade blocks, but they cannot be mix and matched.  Road blocks are for road, and aesthetic blocks are for aesthetics.  It can also be very hard to create beautiful maps here, since good maps require smart placement of foliage, buildings, landscaping, and roads.
However, this game is beautiful and its fun to play. It comes 2nd in my recommendations of the Trackmania 2 franchise.  Note this is the most graphically taxing of the TM2 franchise to this date.

Quasi-hacking game that leans on the 4th wall, requires online searching to solve puzzles
Graphics are minimal. most of the interaction is with a Linux-like terminal. There are no sound puzzles. any spoken text is shown on the screen. Some instances have items that are very low contrast, so you may need to adjust your monitor's brightness. That being said, the screen seems locked on 1920x1080 resolution, so if you have a QHD monitor the text will look *tiny*. I used the Windows magnifier to deal with this, although it seemed to make some of the videos crash as they were being played.
Calling this a "hacking" game is a stretch. There are maybe 5 Linux commands that you use in the entire game. Without giving away anything, you'll be using 'cat' and 'ls' alot. There is one place that you absolutely need to understand the Linux commands that you are given to you in order to solve a  timed puzzle. But most of the time you are either solving puzzles by snooping for clues to passwords in the computer system or opening up a search engine outside the game and Google-ing for clues.
Overall, I enjoyed playing it. Much of the time playing was looking up things online. Maybe there's 4-5 hours of gameplay here. I got it on discount so I had a good value for my money, but I wished the game were longer.

Headshots:
+ Fresh coat of paint on a seminal horror game, HD backgounds and improved character models look amazing.
+ It's actually scary. Even if you memorize the path to completion, BOOM! zombie just bust through a door. Wha... that didn't happen last time!
+ Replay value, after a hard earned completion there's new game modes and unlockables.
+ Puzzles, yes a game that rewards you for using your brain and not just your trigger button.
+ Consequences for dying: Oopsy-doodles!  That fast zombie gutted me before I got to the safe room now I have to fight that giant ***** again.
Zombie Barf:
- Cut scenes are blurry Standard Definition.
- It's still a convoluted story. Personally, I just ignore it.
- Was so hopeful Capcom would have created a brand new Mercenaries/Raid mode bonus for this remaster, even if it is a DLC that costs more money.
Some will argue it's an outdated game with bizarre controls. I would like to see new games return to this level of challenge and mood. The fact that this 12 year old game has been on Steam's Top Seller list for this long is a clear indication of it's success.
I've got another $20 ready for a Resident Evil ZERO HD Remaster.

First I'd like to get this off my chest. Resident Evil remake is not only my personal favorite game of the series by far, but it's also in my top 5 most favorite games of all time. That being said, I couldn't describe how excited I was to hear that this was coming to steam. So how does this stack up to the original remake on Gamecube?
In my opinion, 60 fps on this game is very much a welcome addition to this hd remake. Character and enemy designs are better and some areas in this remake are even more goregous compared to the original. The sound quality is better too. Also, there's a new control scheme for newcomers to the classic Resident Evil formula, which is yet another positive added to this version. I prefer the old tank controls however, but then again, I've played and beaten all of the numbered Resident Evils from 1 to 6.
As far as my gripes with this version, there are a few that do get on my nerves. First, while there are areas that look better than the original version of the game, there aren't really that many. A good amount of them look rather pixelated, and the quality of the video cutscenes don"t seem to be that great either. The pixelated areas kind of detract from the atmosphere in this game,  which is kind of irritating.It also seems that a lot of laptops who have more than enough power to run this game are still having difficulties getting 60 fps. Last, they should really do something about the mouse in game. I don't want to have to keep hiding my mouse in a corner so that the arrow doesn't get in the experience.
Is this game better than the gamecube version? In my opinion, the gamecube version is still better than this one, but even so, this is still a game that everyone should have the chance to experience at least once. If there is anything for me to wish for, I can only hope that a patch can come for this game soon for laptop owners.

Mu Complex is a game about hacking into an old research complex, going through people's files, and trying to help a mysterious AI called Lya. You do this by typing various available commands from a list to open files, unlock computers and make your way to even more computers to do the same.
So, the consensus on this game seems to be that if you are a program/or a fan of Linux, you will be disappointed. However, I as a non-programmer, loved this code-lite "hacking" game. It's far from real hacking, obvious to even one who is not a hacker, because all these bozos keep their passwords on their computers in text files or hid with ciphers and codes that they reveal to others in emails. You are also required to use google for various other puzzles, like looking up ciphers or codes or gps coordinates. The list of available commands is small but not consistent, so that when the "camera" function shows up on a computer, for instance, you know that you must have to use it for this puzzle, removing a lot of the mystery. I know they do that to keep you from being overwhelmed, but it's a dead giveaway. There was one puzzle that was timed and required a LOT of typing. I type about 60 wpm and comparable on a number pad, but the typing for that puzzle required switching between the two and using a keystroke (the vertical bar i.e. | ) I have rarely used and so had trouble finding it quick enough to solve the puzzle. I can't imagine anyone who can't 10 finger type solving that one. (Plus no copy/paste function! The horror!)

So, is this real hacking? Almost certainly not even close. Is it fun? Maybe not for programmers, but as a neophyte I definitely enjoyed it. It took me about 4 hours, but there was a LOT of idle time when I was looking stuff online or trying to figure out some programming puzzles on my own.  The story is not super involved and some of the commands get tedious, but if you find it on sale, this game is worth a buy.
7/10. Fun, but probably wouldn't replay it.

I'll keep this as spoiler-free as possible.
Homesick is a visually impressive walking simulator that isn't entirely sure what it wants to be. Unfortunately, there are multiple reasons why I must give this game a negative review.
While I was loving the graphics (and can easily see the VR potential), it needs some polishing. Some aspects seemed like they didn't fit in an otherwise stunning game, and some rooms felt overwhelmingly cluttered. Less is more.
The controls worked alright, but were not entirely fluid. I found myself getting slightly dizzy or sick while moving, even though I haven't experienced it in other games (Firewatch, anyone?). Not to beat a dead horse here, but as many other players have said, your character moves painfully slow. The only explanation I can find for this is to add to the already short play time (currently two hours for a $15 game).
The biggest grievance, however, is the irony that this game grapples with. While it is entirely a walking simulator with puzzle aspects (which are discouragingly difficult at times and counter-intuitive), it tries its hardest to hide the story from you. In fact, you can very easily go through the motions of this game without any explanation as to why things are the way they are! The reason being that you must decode symbols in the game before going all the way back to the beginning to read all sorts of burnt pages and books streen throughout the game. Then, you must try to piece together some sort of explanation for your adventure. Upon completion, it became painfully clear that the lack of story is because there isn't enough gravitasse in the one they've conceived, but rather they found a potentially sad idea and wanted to present it in an obscure way.
It's important for your games to make you think.
However, they probably shouldn't make you feel like you're working to haphazardly slap together why you just spent two hours walking around an abandoned building.
TL;DR
Unfortunately, the way the story is orchestrated suggests that the creators had a moderately dark story that they couldn't piece together themselves or couldn't afford to voice-cast.
This game gets a 3/10.

I must start by saying I really enjoyed this game. For those who saw the trailer, do note that this is not a horror game. While there is some creepy visuals, there are no scares. In a way, this is less of a game and more of a narrative, which you have to piece together via the clues that are given.
This game is about atmosphere and about making the player feel what the character they are playing feels. And yes, you may feel a sense of loss, loneliness, and sadness. The title is "Homesick," after all. It is a compelling story that is quite relevant today. I do not want to give anything away. Suffice it to say, there are no twists and turns. It will not take you long to work out what is going on. The idea is simply to take it all in and spend a few hours in the shoes of this particular protagonist (for lack of a better term).
The puzzles are fairly straight forward and when you get to the kids building block puzzle, that is when the full story will come into focus. I thought that puzzle was fantastic. I created a systematic way to solve that puzzle and then revisited the areas I had already been to soak up anything I may have missed. Yes, I'm trying to stay vague because it is, in my opinion (of course), the most compelling puzzle in the game.
The graphics are beautiful. Unreal's HDR lighting capabilities and high-res multi-textures are put to great use here. The atmosphere is not quite forboding but definitely forlorn. Everything feels as if it has been decimated, it feels old, run down. The stark, worn environments have so much detail in them that you will want to walk up to each wall to closely inspect the nooks and crannies.
Some people have complained that your character walks too slowly in the game. I think the character walks at the right pace. The area of the building that the game covers is not very large and the designers have done a very good job of setting up openable paths that you can take to fairly quickly move back to a location you have visited previously.
I do agree that the game is too short. I would have liked more back stories on some of the tenants of the building. There were lots of storylines hinted at but not fully explored. Of course, once you get to the ending, you will understand why some of the stories you read about in various previous tenants' journals do not have a resolution or more story to them.
For those looking for a game rich in atmosphere with a compelling narrative told completely without any voice over, then I recommend giving this a try. It is quite short, so if you are one that compares the length of the game to the cost, you may want to buy it when it is on a Steam sale.

I've been wanting waiting to play when the demo came out but since I'm impatient after playing demos, I wanted to wait until it came out.
As you already have seen, the artwork in this game is gorgeous from the sprites to the backgrounds.  The GUI felt a little weird at first, but in the end, I got used to it since it's nice and dark and easy on the eyes.
The intro music was beautiful, and I normally don't like to listen and go through those but it's one of those that I don't mind it.  The BGM while playing the game is really relaxing and exactly how background music should be.
The first meeting with a guy is a typical cliche but the heroine makes it different, which is a good breath of fresh air in this sort of genre. It has a familiar atmosphere with guys to choose from but it soon becomes something different from the usual path in the visual novels.
I personally did not find the prologue rushed at all.  It was at a good pace and it opened up the beginnings of the plotline very well.  Perhaps I'm one who likes it quick to the point and not need so many details.
It does, however, gives an insight of all the guy's personalities as well as the MC (aka you), which is a huge thing for me.  While the guy's may be attractive, seeing their personalities in the prologue is a huge selling point.  Without it, I wouldn't even bother to play onward to Shou's route, or other routes of the guys.
I know that or some, the MC in this genre can be annoying, but the MC here is far from that.  She thinks of situtations with logic rather than shrug it off or let others walk over her.  What I really loved too is the MC actually has a purpose to meeting these guys plus the school she is attending.  That alone is fantastic.  While I do love other games have no reason at all, to see one have it is very refreshing and enjoyable.
I'm taking it slow playing Shou's route so that I won't rush it, but so far, I really love how the choices I've been presented.  The player can be serious, funny, sassy, and mean back to a bit of texting on the cellphone and I really enjoyed that.  I don't know if it will affect the outcome, but it's still great that they included personality related choices to respond to the guys.
Definitely going to be looking out for the other routes to release.  I don't mind paying at all like the ones on mobile since the amount of time and work Star Maiden Games has done can be shown just like the professionals in this industry.  It's not perfect, but it's way better than good.  It's great and lovely and I cannot wait for more!

Mystic Destinies: Serendipity of Aeons is another free to play visual novel on Steam. Compared to many of the other free VN games that get released here with increasing regularity this one seems to have a higher standard of art and music quality. That however is just my opinion on the matter. Currently the game is set to receive some amount of regular updates. I hear more story paths are coming and we are supposed to get achievements and trading cards for it. While the game seems to have a lot coming for it, its playable now so if you want to jump in ahead its not bad. So far I feel there are quite a few mysteries in the story. If any of this sounds like something you would like, you should try it. Especially if you are already a fan of visual novels.

Even though I supported this game's fundraising and was bound to play the other routes, I decided to jump in early and actually purchase the first route to see what I'll be expecting. :D
(If the prologue was disappointing in any way, I still suggest you try Shou's route, at least while his route is still price-reduced! I can say that it takes at least a good 5 hours to run through his route and get one of the 3 endings.)
Writing: Watching anime on TatamiRoll? Instant 10/10!
On a serious note, the writing in Shou's route is one the best I've seen from this genre of gaming. (Well, with the competition being larger companies and translations, the bar doesn't seem that high, but the humor is pretty decent.) Some options play out differently from what they would seem like, so it's not always clear which option is the best/worst--- I think that's a good thing.
Characters: 8/10
Well, with only Shou out, it's kinda hard to judge. Personally I'm waiting on other routes, but from what I saw Show isn't half bad of a character, though his development seems slow at times (then condensed at other times). Still, he gets plenty of interaction with the main character.
I'll also throw in the protagonist into this category. She seems somewhat relatable, but one thing I noticed is that
<spoiler alert?> she cries a ton, like...at least enough for me to feel dettached from her sometimes. <end spoiler alert?>
Still, this is being picky. The side characters, particularly the ones that don't have sprites, were probably the reason why I had to deduct some points here. I'm glad the father has a sprite, though.
Actual Plot: 8/10
I think the plot is unconventional in a way? The antagonist took me by surprise (I'm glad you gave the antagonist development though, even though it was treated like an afterthought in my opinion.)
For Shou, it was a straightfoward plot, and it kinda had a feel of many tropes that you've probably seen before in dramas and anime. I didn't notice huge changes in text from the choices made...perhaps the result of a very minor problem changes, but for the most part the plot is intact.
The foreshadowing and some elements of the plot were clear enough to predict, which does subtract from this rating, but just a little. Regardless, the writing does compensate for this greatly. I wish there were more moments involving fluff/comedy (there's plenty of angst and tension in the mix, though!), but having 3 endings was a nice touch.
Art: 9.99/10 (realistically, 9/10)
Oh bless the art staff. This game had some real love put into it. I particularly love how the characters actually have multiple outfits (some being absolutely gorgeous--- one particular sprite of Shou being in mind ;)  The background art was standard and polished. I wished that less time was spent in the same settings in the middle of the plot, though.
The only reason why I would not give this a perfect score was because of the number of CGs obtained in the route and the lack of sprites for the minor characters, which interrupted the flow of the story in my opinion. (Though I'm pretty sure they are in the works? I find it hard to believe that Tatsuya's parent didn't have a sprite yet, hopefully it isn't because this parent is not actually that involved in his story.)
Consider throwing some concept art or sketches/doodles into the gallery too. It feels a little empty there. >.>
Music: 6/10
This is probably the last thing I paid attention to, so don't take my word for it. I honestly did not find the music memorable (maybe except for the menu theme, even so, it's not memorable in a positive way-- I would describe it as "meh.") and I really wish the soundtrack was stronger. Maybe use a piano for the sad theme and something more lively for the street/town music? The battle music was acceptable, but again, none of the music stuck out to me.
The toute ending song did not resonate as much as I hoped. Hopefully this will change with the other routes.
Sound effects were fine-- it's funny that you used the iPhone jingle and apparatus.
GUI/Controls: 8/10
Average, to be honest. I actually wished that the design would change with the character or maybe even with the plot (the spell circle in the text box! I wished it would change with the situation but it's static...). Do note that the protagonist's sprite changes quite a bit, and that is very much appreciated.
I'm a litte surprised there is no section for instructions on controls? (Maybe I missed it?) Anyways, the skipping and saving function works, so no problem there. It would help to have an indication of sorts about how the route is going, but I suppose it's natural if that doesn't exist.
Overall, give this project your time especially if you're into the genre. I'll be looking foward to the other routes!

I noticed that Mystic Destinies doesn't have any particularly helpful reviews from anyone who had finished the route currently released, so I figured I might as well try my hand.
I'll start with this positives because ultimately I do recommend this game and I did enjoy it.  Beautiful art, amazing sound track, intriguing story and characters and all of the dialogue has a nice flow to it. My absolute favorite thing about this game is the protagonist. She's a good balance of vulnerablity and strength, helping to make her believable. She gets stressed in stressful situation, but she doesn't behave unreasonably, in fact in many of those situations you even have the choice to give extremely pragmatic responses.
I'm actually not bothered by the release method the developers chose to take with this game, in fact I actually see it as another plus. It means we get to experience more of the game sooner rather than waiting months for every single route to be completed. I'm among those who have been passively watching the game development and progress, and frankly I was surprised they managed to even finish Shou's route as quickly as they had.
Now moving on to some of the negatives to consider. There were a few aspects that left me wanting. Every part of the story that was there was good and strong, but there were a lot of plot points, story elements, and character aspects that could have been explored more deeply. In particular I had been hoping for something to the effect of a side plot involing Shou's acting rather than a single event in the story.
There were also fewer CGs than I was hoping for. I'm not sure the exact number in the route, and because of how the Gallery is set up it's hard for me to tell how many I'm missing, but after finishing with the "Passionate End" I only came across two.  I know I'm probably missing at least one from what is likely the best ending, and possibly one or two more that require particular response connditions to be met.
It's not the best otome I've ever played, but it is good. It made me laugh and grin like an idiot and I look forward to the next route. Now I think I've touched on all my thougths, more or less. I hope my review was helpful :3

Either a game is for free or I have a finished product I want to sell.
I'm not a big fan of the whole system most mobile phone games use as well
in which you get a free prologue, but after that you have to pay for each story/ each character to continue.
And for whatever extras are still coming up.
Don't misunderstand me though, I can understand that people want to get paid for the work they did, but using this kind of system is just horrible, like mentioned, not a big fan of it.
I played through the prologue of the game until I reached the first chapter and spotted the 'Buy Button',
which quickly explained to me why the whole story, build-up, prologue seemed so terribly rushed.
The art style is beautiful, the characters seem interesting just like the story itself, but--
I really don't know what the parts look like that you have to pay for,
but if the story branches are as bad as the prologue I recommend to not buy it.
All in all, if this had been a finished product offered to me to buy, I would have considered it,
but like this I'm not going to get any deeper into this.
(Or maybe just buying one of the stories sooner or later to give a different review about that, but for now..)
I'm already upset seeing this kind of thing in app stores, I'm really not glad at all to see this kind of paying-system also reached the steam store. Just my personal opinion though.
All in all I think this could be a great game if the branches you pay for are more detailed and as long as the description says, with beautiful CGs and all that stuff. They just lost me on the paying-system and after such a hurried prologue and introduction into the story that kind of was like "Here are the details. Now please give us your money so we can actually let you continue." So yeah- as much as I like to support good Visual Novels, this really isn't the kind of thing I like to see.
EDIT:
After some time to think about it and having received a reply from the developers, I realized that I might have been a bit harsh on them and their game by saying "I recommend not to buy it." just based on their poor choice of paying-system and a prologue that was so rushed it made me feel like there was no effort put into it because they weren't gonna get paid for that part. I forgot that this wasn't a big company, but a group of girls who tried to do what they enjoy doing or maybe playing themselves, I suppose.
So here I go again, after reading the first Chapter "Firestarter" and some of the 'sneak-peaks' offered in the game as well. I'm not going to change my mind about what I said before: "This game feels incredibly rushed." The art is amazing, the music is beautiful, the characters are each interesting in their own way and the ideas for the story itself are awesome as well. However, in my opinion, they're jumping from one huge plot point to the next, one big happening to the next. For me it was hard to connect to the Main Character that is more or less supposed to giving me the feeling of 'me' I suppose, before I was already thrown into the cold water of the story itself. I suppose the introduction of the guys was nicely made, typical Otome, to get to know them all on your first day at the university. That part I liked, I admit. But after that it's back to the jumping back and forth between places and plot happenings, which (also in my opinion) don't give me enough details on how or why my character is feeling like she does or why she sees things a certain way. I can tell that she's not the most emotional of all people out there, probably thanks to her 'mother' and all that, but it's kinda sad that so many amazing ideas for a visual novel get lost on me and probably others as well simply because we're not given the chance to actually get into the situation the character is in. It kinda feels like your favorite book got caught in half, cutting out all the 'unnecessary' details so it ends up rather being a history book than a beautiful fantasy novel. Or something like that. Same with the guys. The character barely knows them and as much as we as the player hope to get close to the boys as soon as possible, it was a tiny bit too quick for my liking. Like, with a character like her that feels so distanced at first (to me at least), to suddenly get all flustered over the company of a male person, doesn't seem right. And me trying to get into her kind of mindset, the boys suddenly being all up in my face felt like they were invading my private space. Strangely. Except for Takumi, of course, who had been a flirty character from the start.
That's probably the reason why I'm so butthurt over this as well, because there's so much potential in this visual novel, so many good ideas and so many beautiful things like the art and music. It kind of frustrates me that this whole thing that could probably easily be one of the best visual novels out there not from Japan, feels so rushed. With amazing ideas for a story like that, I would have loved to be allowed to get into it as well, maybe experience the kind of things the developers experienced when they first thought of those things. Sadly, I'm not really given the chance and that upsets me a little.
Rather than seeming like a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ who only complaints, I really hope that this review can be a tiny bit helpful to the developers at least. I'm not meaning to discourage them, quite the opposite, I'm already looking forward to their next project, in hopes the whole thing gets a better start than this one. I might edit this review again once a DLC comes out with one of the characters I'm interested in to see how that goes, since it really does seem promising and hopefully I'm given the chance to actually feel like a part of the story then.

Who needs real life 3D women who will hurt and betray you when you can find comfort in the smile of a gentle 2D virtual love? That was Aoi’s point of view until Sora came into his life.
is a visual novel that
. This unlikely pair have to figure out how to co-exist as Sora tries to bring out the kinder side of Aoi. A tale of human emotions, sexual desires and personal growth,
will take readers on an interesting journey with lovely artwork to bring everything to life.
Aoi is a normal high school student until his love confession to a classmate goes wrong and he drops out after the rejection. Years later he is now a, hikikomori, shut-in who spends most of his time watching anime and playing video games, especially visual novels. One day on his way home from the store a beautiful young woman with cotton candy-hued hair literally falls from the sky on top of him, naked. The lovely Sora then proceeds to force herself onto Aoi’s life, moving into his home and becoming his housemate. Despite Aoi not wanting to deal with her
, the game following their relationship until the shocking end.
I can’t really go much more into detail about the story without spoiling anything, however it did take a bit of an unexpected turn. During most of the game Sora doesn’t talk about herself at all nor does she give much reason for being so attracted to Aoi. He treats her pretty badly for the first half of the game, you can even kick her out of the house and not let her stay but that will end the game prematurely. There is also another girl after his affection, Misaki, however she seems very shoehorned in and it’s also odd that she wants anything to do with the protagonist.
, he’s rude and rather depressing. He only becomes more likeable after falling in love with Sora. The second half of the game is mainly about their relationship, sex life and him coming to terms with where his life is at the moment. Misaki, despite being another romantic option, only shows up twice and only has two ending; a good and a bad one. She also has no CG pictures which is a shame.
All of the CG is of Sora, and it’s well done. She is drawn to be very busty and sexy and the artwork ranges from cute to downright sexual. There is no nudity in the game, save for one picture so everything is pretty tame.
but they mainly consist of kissing and then fade to black moments. I don’t mind this but for the amount of times sex does happen it makes the lack of CG for the scenes very apparently. The music is nice, there isn’t a huge amount of variety however. There were a few times where the music seemed to be a bit creepy but nothing of the sort was actually happening which created unnecessary suspense.
is a simple game, it won’t take that long to finish one play-through and the other endings are easy to get after that. The story itself has a few dull moments, unfortunately having to do with a lot of the day-to-day interactions between Sora and Aoi. When the plot takes twists and turns, they’re very interesting and well written but overall the game hoovers in neutral territory with not much happening. However, it’s a good read with lots of choices to make and the choices are a timed which is a nice feature for this genre of game.
, especially at the irony of it being a visual novel about a shut-in who plays visual novels. The price is very reasonable for the game’s length and there are also trading cards to collect, if you don’t mind a bit of naughty humor I would recommend this game wholeheartedly.
