I expected this to be about aiming, but no matter what angle you hit the ball at, it will pretty much fly straight, and then you can redirect it freely in the air. The challenge in this game is dodging the various stuff thrown at you.
The ball is often hidden behind fancy useless particle effects.
If you're fine with those criticisms, I guess it's a fine game.

From a pure mechanics standpoint, this is quite possibly the best brick breaker game of all time. The push and pull mechanics allow the player to feel like they are always in control of the ball and it greatly reduces the 'takes forever to hit the last few bricks' issue that plagues this genre. The constantly changing level design, interesting physics based blocks and boss battles keep it fresh and entertaining throughout.
Shatter has incredible presentation. The audio and visuals are top notch with impactful and satisfying VFX and sounds.
My one major gripe and the reason I will probably never play this game again: Controls. Its always surprising when a high quality game has no keybinding options. The main keyboard buttons are (Right Shift(, (/) and (Ctrl)... really? I have never played a game with a worse button layout. Im assuming all the developers use left handed mice or they just like trolling their players. If you can get past a few poorly placed, unchangable buttons, this is an amazing game.

This game was the reason I became a PC gamer. Before being introduced to this game I was a console fanboy and played minecraft on occassion. It was not until I was introduced to this game that I fully understood what was all possible. I started off by joining a regiment in Napoleonic Wars called 34e. This regiment stayed active for I think around 6 months or some where near that. It was some of my best experiences to date. I met friends in that unit and through this game that I have played with ever since.
After NW was overplayed for myself, I switched to Persistent World. That brought a whole new world of possiblities. Learning about medieval times in history and actually participating in it was a whole new experience. It allowed me to act out what had always interested me, along with allowing me to join some factions to ultimately meet some pretty amazing people.
I have spent maybe 400 hours playing NW, 500 hours playing PW if not more, and around 100 hours for native. While this game lacks some graphic capabilities, the game play makes up for it all. If you are even remotely interested in history or fantasy games/movies I would recommend this game and the thousands of mods out there ready for consumption.
All and all, amazing game and cannot wait till bannerlord.

As much as i like "staged battles", they can be misleading to the general image and gameplay experience of the whole game.
Staged battles offten last from 10 to 15 minutes, though i have played ones that lasted up to 30 minutes, but the thing that is missing is the general feel of a greater goal oposing to the feel "If we lose this battle we lose the war", "If we win this map we capture the city". Not talking about Americans ruling Europe, or germans or russians but for the perks that this grands your character which could be up to +50% warfunds to spend them as you please.

You can buy a Veteran membership(bonus Exp, warfunds and the other gold thingies i forget at the moment), you can buy guns and mods for the guns, you can generally buy everything that you can unlock at your current rank and if you are bored out of your brainjuices from the grinding you can always buy a new soldier with the specialty that you like. If you still want to spend money on the game you should know that the +100% exp you get from being a "Veteran" does not affect much of the "grinding" as you still have to spend a good amound of time leveling up your character to join the war.

A great WWII shooter than can be frustrating if you're new- less frustrating if you're a veteran. This game starts you off with basic weapons for any of the three factions you want to join- US, Soviets, and Germans. Each faction has its upsides and downsides, such as 4 bombs in a soviet plane, versus one bomb in a German plane, or the German MG42 with its 1200rpm versus all other machine guns. This game is viewed as pay to win by many, but it really is pay to progress faster. The Fall is a story-driven side scrolling adventure with intermingled action sequences. I picked it up in a daily sale and would highly recommend it - it's really strong on building its story and mood through exploration and the plot rapidly drew me in. The game is strongest on the artistic side: level backgrounds are simple but beautiful and effectively convey the desolation of its setting, the voice acting is enjoyable and supports the story themes well, and the story itself kept me interested for the duration of play (about 4 hours). I would say that if the game is one thing, it is coherent: Main menu and GUI, the world it builds and the story all mesh together nicely.
The game's mechanics are a bit more variable in quality. The shooter mechanics are bland 2D-cover based shooting, and I personally found them to be a bit pointless. The puzzles worked reasonably well, and meshed nicely with the exploration aspect of the game which is highly linear but significantly contributes to the game's creepy mood. Unfortunately, the game fails to signpost adequately how far you have to travel to acquire the items you need to solve the puzzles, notably in the game's middle section you have to travel through large areas that are "shut down" and point out to you that you should not go there yet, but to progress you must travel through them. In fact, at several points characters specifically tell you that you are in the wrong place and not completing your tasks in the right order... which may be very clever meta-game commentary given the nature of the story, but if so, I missed it.
I won't comment on the story itself, mostly because I am an idiot and will inevitably spoil something, and I think the game is best approached blindly.

is an Indie first-person 3D puzzle-adventure title driven by exploratory gameplay, environmental interaction, and an emotionally sensible narrative. The game has a focus on atmospheric surrealism, and is the first game developed by Lucky Pause on the Unreal Engine after a
It is a relatively short game, spanning about four hours.
You wake up, and your first and most important clue is half a drawing of a child next to some blue flowers.
lacks anything close to a dialogue, what it doesn’t lack is information sprawled throughout the game’s world (a building), all there for you to decipher so that you can deduce what happened that left the inside of a building in such decay. Any text that you might come across -be it a book or a loose piece of paper- is in something that appears to be code or a foreign language; in the last puzzle you are able to decipher these and turn them all into proper letters. That progression encourages the player to turn back and revisit the previously explored places, and in doing so, revealing the lives of the people that resided in the building along with what catastrophic event left the building in its current shape.
The gameplay consists of exploring a decaying building and interacting with various aspects of its environment. During the day you can go nearly everywhere you want, but cannot stand too close to the windows because you are hypersensitive to sunlight. When you go to sleep you have nightmares, these consist of darkness seeping and dripping upwards from the floor; you have to try to keep moving so that it doesn’t swallow you and wake you up, which prevents you from further progress. Parts of each puzzle are done during the day and other parts during the night.
but I will mention that they are satisfyingly challenging without being frustratingly difficult. To solve each puzzle you will have to explore and search, as well as interact with as many things as you can.
As I mentioned above, a big part of the gameplay is picking up and reading texts laying around the building. There are books, letters, and newspapers from which to acquire information.
Okay, this is where the game shines brightest (figuratively AND literally).
This is one of the most photorealistic games I’ve had the pleasure to play. What little animations the game has are done well. All the environments and every object in them are modeled
well, but most of all it’s the textures that make this game a truly and strikingly impressive feat, and an absolute joy to look at.

Something I’d like to add about the visuals, the game is relatively customizable for its genre. It has console commands, where you can change your FOV and how fast you move, to name a couple of its features. Another thing that is
worth mentioning is the built-in camera; if you press ‘F4’ while playing it will save a screenshot that is double the resolution you’re playing at (this is the reason my screenshots are at 4K resolution).
has a soundtrack that goes very well with the atmosphere and ambience that Lucky Pause is trying to achieve, courtesy of Heather Schmidt. The music has a little bit of a relaxed acoustic style to it, with a hint of classical. Other than the amazing soundtrack the environmental sounds -such as doors opening and closing, keys jingling, or file cabinets opening and closing (and falling over)- are also done very well. The true MVP in sound for this game though, is the soundtrack, hands down.

I would venture to say that this game's only downfall is that the story mode is rather short and easy. I plowed through in one sitting - but I must say it was some 2 hours of good fun!!!
It takes an age-old classic and refines it to perfection. Thanks to physics manipulation - push and pull - it fixes one the original's biggest flaws and makes it nearly perfect - full interactivity. At no point in the game did it ever feel dull - I was constantly in full control and never had to wait for the ball to get unstuck, nor struggle endlessly for that last annoying block. There's even a powerup that makes the ball even easier to manipulate! (though its hard to get used to at first)
As I mentioned, the game is pretty easy - it felt like whenever I was lacking lives, blocks would drop lives more often. During boss fights especially they are very generous and lives pop out for almost each fail, garanteeing I would not get game over. In fact, I never had a single game over - plowed right through story mode in 2 hours, but it was a bit difficult at times, esp. when blocks are really close to your paddle.
You have 2 special abilities on top of all that - a shield and a super bullet attack, which need your energy bar to be filled to use. The super attack is so powerful that it can sometimes instantly clear a level, which is very satisfying. It may be cheap, but it require a decent amount of time to actually fill, so you can't overuse it. It also *looks* amazing.
SO BASICALLY
The game looks AWESOME
Plays AWESOME
Easily handles on most machines
BUT ITS VERY SHORT AND NOT WORTH THE 11$ pricetag for what your get*******
HOWEVER - it has a very decent co-op mode. IF you have a friend (or kid/girlfriend/wife) to play this with, then go for full price. Its worth it then.
If on SALE, its a MUST BUY!
I HOPE THIS HELPS MAKE YOUR DECISION!

Trackmania has always been a unique racing series and really fun to play in my opinion. However, it has always been overshadowed by more mainstream racing games (Need for Speed, Forza, Gran Tursimo, etc.). Trackmania² Valley specifically though is the most realistic of the Trackmania² line, but this doesn't mean it's bad. It still has your insane tricks and high-speed action, but it feels much more sensible from Trackmania² Canyon and Stadium, and in my opinion, more fun. It's much more grippy then Canyon, but still has enough power to easily drift unlike Stadium. It's an arcade game in a nutshell, so if you (for some reason) hate arcades, then you might want to sway from this, but if you want to try something unique, I highly reccomend this. The main attraction I'd say in Valley (and basically all Trackmanias) is its track creator, which makes the game have huge replay value, as well as the community tracks.

TrackMania 2 Valley is a rally car racing refeshment of TranMania United Valley pack.
Does Valley hold up to the original and is it worth your money?
Graphics:
I'm just going to be short and sweet. At max settings, this game is georgous. Everything from the lighting to the amount of detail on the courses is excellent. I sometimes found myself slamming into a tree or careening off the track simply because I was distracted by the enviornment. My only two gripes with the game's visual presentations is that water doesn't animate when your car moves through it and it can sometimes be difficult to tell where to go on dirt roads or courses that have fragmented roads due to the heavy amount of detail.
Soundtrack:
Trackmania 2 Valley has my favorite soundtrack out of the three packs available. It's rather groovy, consisting of electronic music that's easy on the ears. But thankfully, you are able to add your own music to the game if you grow tired of the limited soundtrack.
Gameplay:
Of the three packs available, Valley has the steepest learning curve and because of it, I don't think it's the most ideal selection for newcomers to the TrackMania series. Throughout your playthrough you will have to adapt to the stiff yet fluid control of the asphalt to the incredibly sensitive to the touch controls of the dirt. Thankfully the staff created tracks provide a great amount of variety with progressively challenging courses to test your driving skills without seeming unfair. The keyboard controls work, but a gamepad or wheel are much more favorable. When your done with singleplayer, you can dive right into the online multiplayer to test how your times compare to players from around the world on courses that are either staff created or custom.
Where TrackMania shines is the Editors mode, where players can create tracks with an incredibly deep track creator or play the creations of another person.
So in the end Valley is a phenominal improvement over its TM United counterpart and is worth every penny.
But as stated before, if your new to the Trackmania series, I would reccommend either raising all flags in Stadium or Soaking up some sun in the Canyon. But besides that, this is a must buy for racing and Trackmania fans.
